title: Messi came, mayhem followed
text:
Kolkata’s Messi moment imploded. On Saturday, Lionel Messi’s much-hyped appearance at Kolkata’s Salt Lake Stadium ended in chaos.

What went wrong: Fans paid up to ₹25,000 ($276), waited for hours, and got under 10 minutes of Messi, which was mostly visible to VIPs. The rest got blocked views and broken promises.

Crowd turns: Pissed off fans turned to vandalism. Bottles flew, seats were torn out, barricades broke. Police stepped in.

Damage control: To calm the angry public, Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee apologised to fans and Messi, called the scenes unacceptable, and ordered an inquiry.

- Lead organiser Satadru Dutta was detained at the airport and arrested on charges tied to mismanagement and attempted flight.
- Over the weekend, police announced that organisers must refund ticket holders and said authorities will monitor compliance.

Bigger picture: This event exposed thin planning, weak crowd control, and poor coordination, all red flags for India’s global event ambitions.
sound_smarter: Refunds issuance and how the remaining tour stops run will decide whether Kolkata was a one-off failure or proof India still isn’t event-ready.

title: Emergency brake, dirty air
text:
Delhi slammed the brakes on Saturday. With AQI breaching 450, authorities invoked GRAP Stage IV, the toughest pollution curbs on the books.

What tipped it: Air quality slid into the ‘Severe+’ band. By Sunday, several pockets were flirting with 500, pushing a 30-million-plus region into an air emergency.

What Stage IV means:

- All construction and demolition across Delhi-NCR stops, including public works. Daily-wage labour takes the first hit.
- Non-essential trucks and many diesel goods vehicles are barred from Delhi, snarling supply chains and raising logistics costs.
Schools move younger classes online or hybrid. Offices push roughly 50% staff to work from home, reshaping commuting and spending overnight.

Why it hurts: Informal workers, small builders, truckers, and street businesses absorb the shock. White-collar residents retreat behind air purifiers.

What’s next?: The Commission for Air Quality Management has warned more steps may follow if ‘Severe+’ sticks — wider closures, tighter vehicle curbs, even odd–even schemes.
sound_smarter: GRAP IV is an emergency brake, not a fix. It’s usually rolled back once AQI stablises. Tough – but necessary – governance changes are needed to sustainably tackle Delhi’s pollution challenges.

title: BJP goes younger at the top
text:
The BJP has named Bihar minister Nitin Nabin its new working president — a clear signal of where the party is headed. On Sunday, the ruling party picked the 45-year-old cabinet minister, with a formal election to the top job expected in January. The move will be endorsed at the BJP National Council meeting in April 2026.

Who is Nabin? A five-term member of Bihar’s legislative assembly from Bankipur, Nabin is an organisation man. He cut his teeth in the ABVP, the BJP’s student wing, and entered the Bihar assembly in 2006 after his father’s death. He’s stayed put ever since.

Why now? The BJP is leaning toward leaders who rose internally, not parachuted in. Current party chief J.P. Nadda took charge before the 2019 election and steered the party through 2024. The baton is slowly passing.

What’s ahead? Nabin will oversee the BJP’s push into key state polls next year: West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Assam.
sound_smarter: This is less about Bihar and more about 2026. The BJP is betting fresh faces can crack states it has never ruled – except Assam, where it’s defending turf.
anchor: The BJP has named Bihar minister Nitin Nabin

title: License to burn
text:
Goa Police are circling the Arpora panchayat (aka village government). On Saturday, they recorded statements from five members over how a north Goa nightclub kept operating – illegally – before a deadly fire.

The toll: Twenty-five people were killed and six injured when a blaze tore through Birch by Romeo Lane in Arpora around 11:45 pm on December 6.

How was it open? The nightclub was operating without a valid construction licence or occupancy certificate. Its trade licence had also expired.

- “Under Section 72-A of the Goa Panchayat Raj Act, the local body is empowered to seal such premises. However, they failed to do so,” investigators said.

Paper trail problem: The 2023 trade licence unlocked approvals from the pollution control board, food and drugs administration, and excise department. Even after the licence expired in March 2024, the panchayat didn’t seal the premises. A demolition order was later stayed on appeal.

Who signed off? Investigators say the village head issued approvals for power, water, repairs, and business operations.

Don’t blame me: Panchayat head Roshan Redkar insists all permissions followed resolutions passed collectively, not his personal call.

Enforcement update: Police custody for four managers has been extended. The two owners are being deported from Thailand. Two other clubs and spas have been sealed.
sound_smarter: Crackdowns follow tragedy, not inspections. Until local bodies face real penalties, illegal businesses will keep running – fires or no fires.

title: A 22-year pitch
text:
Chhattisgarh Chief Minister Vishnu Deo Sai has set his sights on 2047. On Sunday, he unveiled a long-term development roadmap on day one of the Assembly’s winter session.

The pitch: Dubbed Anjor Vision 2047, the plan promises phased growth, governance reforms, and a push on infrastructure, investment, jobs, and social development. Sai says work began soon after the BJP took office, drawing on public consultations. The document flags 13 priority sectors and 10 missions.

Political subtext: Sai contrasted the BJP’s “2047 vision” with what he called Congress’s corruption-tainted five-year stint.

Quick rewind: Chhattisgarh was carved out of Madhya Pradesh in 2000. Power has swung between BJP and Congress since, with the BJP ruling roughly 17 of the past 24 years before losing in 2018 – and returning in 2023.

Opposition pushback: Congress boycotted the session’s opening day, calling the plan “heavy on claims but weak on substance,” and accused the government of ducking everyday governance issues.
sound_smarter: Vision documents aren’t new. What’s different is the time horizon – and the bet that talking 2047 helps the BJP argue it deserves multiple terms to get there.

title: India upgrades its “regular trains”
text:
India just widened its new “everyday travel” rail push. On Sunday, PM Narendra Modi flagged off five Amrit Bharat Express services across Assam and West Bengal.

What this is: These are non-air conditioned, long-distance trains built for the bulk of Indian rail travellers. The pitch is simple: better basics like CCTV, charging points, improved berths, and modular toilets, without turning the ticket into a premium product.

Where they run: Two services start from Assam (Northeast India)—Guwahati–Rohtak and Dibrugarh–Lucknow, while three launch from West Bengal (East India): Howrah–Delhi, Sealdah–Varanasi, and Santragachi–Chennai.

The big deal: Indian Railways is trying to make long-haul travel more predictable, with fixed fares and higher reliability on crowded corridors. Official notes say thirty Amrit Bharat trains have been running since December 2023, and this marks the next expansion wave.
sound_smarter: Upgrading third-class travel is how you reach India at scale. The current government has now got something to show for its infrastructure capability.

title: Tap water, now with sewage notes
text:
India’s latest “governance scandal” isn’t a leaked memo. It’s what’s coming out of the tap.

The trigger: On January 2, 2026, Reuters reported that contaminated drinking water in Indore (Madhya Pradesh) sparked a diarrhoea outbreak, killing at least nine and hospitalising 200+.

Spreading panic: By mid-January, residents in Greater Noida (near Delhi) reported stomach illness after allegedly receiving foul, sewage-mixed water for days; local officials said pipelines would be replaced.

Regulators step in: The National Green Tribunal has taken action over reports of sewage contamination in drinking water across parts of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, and Uttar Pradesh as of last Thursday. Separately, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) issued a notice over a typhoid surge in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, tied to contaminated supply on January 8.
sound_smarter: Alongside resuming water supplies for the affected area, it is more crucial to take accountability for the issue, and a government-appointed bench was appointed to do just that. The hope is that the issue can be fixed in time and lessons learnt can prevent any similar cases in the future.
anchor: India’s latest “governance scandal” isn’t a leaked memo.

title: BRICS goes nautical. India goes missing
text:
India refused BRICS shift towards security.

The timeline: South Africa’s “Will for Peace 2026” naval exercise ran from January 10–16, 2026 off Cape Town, after warships began arriving around January 9. The guest list included China, Russia, Iran, UAE and South Africa, and it drew loud US-side criticism, so loud that Pretoria launched an inquiry into Iran’s participation on January 16.

Official readout (MEA): On January 17, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said the exercise was “entirely a South African initiative,” not a “regular or institutionalised” BRICS activity, and not all BRICS members joined. It added India hasn’t participated in previous such activities, and pointed to IBSAMAR (India–Brazil–South Africa) as its standing maritime format (last held October 2024).

Why the absence: Analysts and regional reporting frame this as optics management. India avoids being viewed as a joined force in a China/Russia/Iran-led tableau, and it doesn’t want BRICS to slide, by habit, into a security bloc.

Been here before: South Africa’s Russia–China drills have run in prior years (as of February 2023 and before), and India wasn’t in the water then either.
sound_smarter: India isn’t boycotting South Africa, it’s rejecting keeping its participation in BRICS solely economic in nature, lest it earn the ire of key partners, especially the US.

title: No pause button
text:
Modi has West Bengal in his sights, and he’s moving early. On Friday, the Prime Minister tweeted that West Bengal’s voters were “fed up” with the Mamata Banerjee–led Trinamool Congress (TMC) and ready to reject the state government.

Why now: Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is riding momentum after a strong showing in the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), Mumbai’s powerful municipal body, where it won 89 of 227 seats. With assembly elections due in Assam, West Bengal, Puducherry, Tamil Nadu, and Kerala in a few months, Modi is quickly converting local victories into national messaging.

Target locked: West Bengal matters symbolically as much as electorally. Mamata Banerjee has run the state since 2011, winning three straight mandates and positioning herself as one of the BJP’s most vocal national critics.
sound_smarter: Bengal once hosted the world’s longest democratically elected communist government (34 years) before Mamata ended it in 2011. The BJP now wants to recast her rule as another exhausted regime, using a municipal win to sell inevitability.

title: India’s RSVP to Trump’s Board of Peace
text:
US President Donald Trump has invited Prime Minister Narendra Modi to join the newly created “Board of Peace,” an international body aimed at resolving conflicts globally, starting with Gaza. Washington calls it a “critically historic” initiative.

The story so far: The UN Security Council approved the board’s mandate in 2025, but it’s limited to Gaza and only until 2027. The Board will oversee a “technocratic apolitical Palestinian committee” governing Gaza, with Trump at the helm. The executive board includes Marco Rubio, Jared Kushner, Tony Blair, and Ajay Banga of the World Bank.

Who’s on it: The board includes a global mix of nations, such as Pakistan, Turkey, Canada, France, and the European Commission. Trump has invited around 60 countries so far.

India’s response: India has yet to respond. While maintaining its stance on a two-state solution and ceasefire, it must balance relations with Israel and its ties to the US.
sound_smarter: India’s acceptance can give Trump an easy diplomatic win on a non-core forum to build goodwill where it actually matters – in trade negotiation where the US has failed to ease high tariffs on Indian exports. The board is bloated, the executive circle is tight, and participation is mostly symbolic, which is precisely why Delhi can say yes.

issue_title: From Gulf ties to guided rockets
title: A flying visit, heavyweight agenda
text:
The President of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) made a pit stop in New Delhi and still made it count. On January 19, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ) met PM Narendra Modi during a visit the MEA said was scheduled to last less than two hours.

Quick context: MBZ is the UAE’s head of state. For India, the UAE is a top-tier Gulf partner in trade, energy, and investment, with a significant Indian diaspora also playing a role in this relationship.

What happened in Delhi: Modi received MBZ at the airport, a signal of how closely Delhi tracks this partnership. It was reported that the two sides planned to cover bilateral ties, plus regional and global issues.

What moved the needle: The MEA joint statement is packed with deliverables, including pushing trade to USD 200bn by 2032, investment promotion (including Gujarat’s Dholera project), cooperation on AI and supercomputing, payments connectivity, and a 10-year LNG supply agreement.
sound_smarter: This was MBZ’s fifth visit to India in a decade – a clear signal that India–UAE ties now operate on routine access at the top.

title: BJP’s “election” with one name on it
text:
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is set to change its top organisational boss, with Nitin Nabin left as the only candidate for national president after nominations closed on January 19.

Quick context: The BJP president runs the party organisation and oversees key appointments within the party.

The making: Returning officer K Laxman said 37 valid sets of nomination papers were filed for Nabin. With withdrawals over, the race for Nabin is effectively unopposed.

How support looks: NDTV reports that 36 nomination sets came from states, each with 20 signatories. A 37th set was proposed by Parliamentary Board members, including PM Modi, along with 37 MPs. Senior leaders, including JP Nadda, Amit Shah, Rajnath Singh, and Nitin Gadkari were among those listed as proposers.

What’s next: Nabin is expected to be formally declared and take charge on January 20, succeeding JP Nadda, who has been in office since January 2020.
sound_smarter: An unopposed result doesn’t prove popularity. It reflects a party that prefers managed succession and tight organisational control at the top.

title: Pinaka goes abroad
text:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh flagged off the first tranche of guided Pinaka rockets bound for Armenia. The system, developed by Defence Research and Development Organisation’s (DRDO) Armament Research and Development Establishment (ARDE), was first deployed during the 1999 Kargil War between India and Pakistan, and has since been upgraded to extend range and precision beyond its original 37.5 km.

Some trivia: Named after Lord Shiva’s celestial bow, Pinaka anchors India’s planned Integrated Rocket Force alongside the Pralay, Nirbhay, and BrahMos missile systems.

Private sector push: The current batch was produced at Solar Defence and Aerospace’s Nagpur facility, underscoring the growing role of private firms in India’s defence supply chain. Singh said defence exports have now climbed to ₹24,000 crore (USD 2.9 billion), driven largely by increased private sector participation.

Who’s watching: Armenia signed its Pinaka deal in September 2022. France is running evaluation trials, while Indonesia and Nigeria have expressed interest.
sound_smarter: This is more than just a defence sale. India is pushing indigenously built systems into foreign arsenals, testing whether decades of domestic R&D can finally translate into sustained exports.

title: Environment Protection Fund established
text:
Who doesn’t like more structure? India’s environment ministry has notified rules creating a statutory Environmental Protection Fund, pooling penalties from environmental violations and recycling them into cleanup and compliance.

What feeds it: The fund will collect penalties imposed under the Environment Protection Act (1986), Air Act (1981), and Water Act (1974).

Who gets what: Of every rupee collected, 75% will be remitted to the state where the violation occurred. The Centre keeps 25%. States and UTs must set up Project Management Units, with periodic audits mandated.

What it pays for: Eligible spending spans 11 categories, from installing and maintaining air and water monitoring equipment, to lab upgrades, capacity-building, and remediation of environmental damage.
sound_smarter: Until now, penalty proceeds often sat idle or were spent unevenly, with no common rules on sharing, reporting, or oversight. A single, audited fund turns environmental penalties promises to make implementation more standardised and targeted.

title: Rupee, meet the digital rails
text:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has proposed linking BRICS members’ central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) to ease cross-border trade and tourism payments. It has recommended that the government place the proposal on the agenda for the 2026 BRICS Summit, which India will host later this year.

What this builds on: The idea flows from the 2025 BRICS declaration in Rio de Janeiro, which called for greater interoperability between member countries’ payment systems.

Why India’s pushing this: New Delhi has long tried to internationalise the rupee. A recent attempt to settle trade with Russia in local currencies stalled after Moscow piled up rupee balances it struggled to deploy. Digital rails are being pitched as a workaround.

CBDCs over stablecoins: The RBI prefers central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) to private stablecoins, citing risks of de-facto dollarisation and weakened capital controls. RBI Deputy Governor T Rabi Sankar warned last month that stablecoins pose “significant concerns” for monetary stability and financial resilience.

The geopolitical backdrop: The proposal lands amid sharper rhetoric and tariff threats emerging from The White House. President Trump has labelled BRICS “anti-American,” and Washington is likely to view any such move through a de-dollarisation lens.
sound_smarter: India’s messaging has been consistent: BRICS is a payments and trade platform, not a geopolitical or security alliance. This push firmly stays in that lane.

title: Compute ambitions, power constraints
text:
Uttar Pradesh (UP) is scaling its AI ambitions. On the Davos sidelines, the UP government signed an Memorandum of Understanding with AM Group to build a massive AI compute hub in Greater Noida.

Who’s behind it: AM Group is backed by the founders of Greenko Group, India’s largest clean energy player – a clue to how this project plans to stay switched on.

The scale: The proposal involves roughly USD 25 billion in staged investment. Phase One is slated for 2028. By 2030, the facility aims to hit 1 gigawatt of compute capacity, positioning it among India’s largest digital infrastructure bets.

Why this compute matters: India has AI talent and demand, but lacks large, reliable domestic compute. A hub of this size would reduce dependence on offshore capacity and anchor AI workloads closer to Indian data, regulation, and users.

Why energy matters: The hub is designed to run on 24/7 carbon-free power, blending solar, wind, and pumped storage.

- UP’s grid is thermal-heavy, with renewables at about 27% of installed capacity, and is already strained during summer. Compute at this scale forces a rethink of how power is sourced.
sound_smarter: India’s AI bottleneck is reliable compute, not talent or capital. Projects like this work only if digital ambition is paired with dedicated, clean power, not an already stretched grid.
anchor: Uttar Pradesh (UP) is scaling its AI ambitions.

title: Delhi’s air eases, rules don’t
text:
Delhi-NCR lifted GRAP Stage IV on Tuesday after AQI improved to 378 (“Very Poor”), from 410 on Monday and 440 on Sunday. Wind did the heavy lifting, and forecasts still point to “Very Poor” air in the coming days.

Break-glass policy: The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) – a federal panel that triggers pollution restrictions across Delhi and neighbouring cities – turned Stage IV on January 17, then switched it off three days later.

What’s different now: Since November 2025, CAQM has tightened GRAP by pushing several measures into earlier stages. Translation: even when Stage IV disappears, Stages I–III feel heavier than they used to.

What changes today: Easing focuses on Stage IV add-ons like truck-entry curbs and the Stage IV-linked hybrid schooling provision for senior students.

What doesn’t: Stage III limits still apply, including restrictions on older vehicles, so the commute and logistics pinch doesn’t vanish, it just downgrades.
sound_smarter: Delhi is now learning to govern pollution in shorter, sharper bursts, with stricter curbs becoming the new winter norm.

title: Night shift, coal shift
text:
India’s renewables boom is running into the same wall everywhere: peak hour surges. On Monday, an adviser cited a government projection that the state may need 4.4 GW of additional coal capacity by 2036 (up from 1.9 GW earlier), even as it retires 1.35 GW of ageing coal in Rajasthan.

- Planners argue wind and solar can’t yet guarantee round-the-clock supply at scale, and storage remains limited.

Storage arrives: A day later, GoodEnough Energy announced that it had commissioned a 7 GWh battery storage system in Uttar Pradesh, claiming it to be India’s largest. The message is clear: batteries are shifting from niche add-on to grid backbone.

Policy context: New Delhi is still targeting 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and says non-fossil sources crossed 50% of installed capacity in June 2025. Coal stays central in the interim as demand rises and grids strain.

Looking out: Rajasthan’s regulator may revisit a previously denied 3.2 GW coal permit. Storage momentum will depend on Viability Gap Funding (VGF) support (up to 40% of capex) and faster transmission and grid connectivity.
sound_smarter: Until storage scales, coal fills the gap. That just delays coal’s exit.

title: The biggest handshake yet
text:
Europe and India are finally (almost) ready to sign. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told Davos audiences on Tuesday the EU-India free trade agreement is close. Spain’s foreign minister teased in New Delhi that it’s just days away.

Long courtship: Talks began in 2007, collapsed, then restarted in June 2022. Von der Leyen and Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed to fast-track negotiations to land a deal in 2025.

Why it matters: The agreement would link a market of nearly 2 billion people, covering roughly a quarter of global GDP.

- The EU is India’s largest trading partner (USD 130 billion in goods in 2024). India ranks ninth for the EU.

Sticking points: Brussels wants sharper tariff cuts on cars, wine, and spirits. New Delhi wants easier mobility for skilled professionals. Carbon border taxes remain India’s worry, especially for steel exports.

What’s next: Von der Leyen lands in India Sunday, aiming to close gaps before the January 27 EU-India summit, where signatures are expected. She and European Council President Antonio Costa will also attend India’s Republic Day (January 26) parade as chief guests.
sound_smarter: As with all trade agreements, it’s about market access: Europe wants to sell more into India, India wants the same in Europe. The bigger play is diversification: both are hedging against US policy whiplash and too much reliance on China.

title: No plus ones in Dhaka
text:
India has decided to withdraw the families and dependents of its officials in Bangladesh ahead of Dhaka’s general elections, designating it a “non-family posting.” The polls will be the first since the July 2024 ouster of Sheikh Hasina’s government, and New Delhi is presenting the step as a precautionary security measure.

Why now: Bangladesh is entering a sensitive political period, with elections approaching amid heightened tensions and sporadic violence. Indian officials say the decision reflects updated security assessments rather than an immediate diplomatic rift.

Political backdrop: India-Bangladesh relations have been strained since the fall of Sheikh Hasina’s government in 2024 after widespread protests. Many Bangladeshis were angered by New Delhi’s support for Hasina – who was later convicted in absentia of crimes against humanity by the interim government – and by India’s decision to shelter her after her resignation and flight. India has also expressed ongoing concern over attacks on minorities, particularly Hindus.

What this means: The “non-family posting” status is rare in the Indian Foreign Service and is typically applied in locations where security concerns make it unsafe for dependents to stay. The list of such postings is based on internal security reviews and is updated periodically.

Beyond diplomacy: Security worries have emerged in other areas as well. The ICC rejected Bangladesh’s request to move its 2026 Men’s T20 World Cup matches away from India, citing risks to teams and staff.
sound_smarter: Redesignating Bangladesh as a non-family posting is a bureaucratic but symbolic move, signaling unease while leaving room for de-escalation if security conditions improve after the elections. Still, tensions are likely to persist as long as Hasina remains under Indian protection.

title: When a hill stops being a hill
text:
Stop mining in the Aravalli range. The Supreme Court directed states to stop unauthorised activity in the region and said it will constitute a high-powered panel of independent experts to formally define the Aravalli range and lay down what activities are permitted.

Why this matters: The move follows the court’s own November 20 ruling that defined an Aravalli hill as any landform rising more than 100 metres above surrounding terrain. Environmental groups warned the definition was so narrow it could exclude large parts of the range from protection.

The reversal: After protests from conservationists, the court stayed its own judgment on December 29. The expert panel is now tasked with fixing the boundary problem and the regulatory confusion it created.

What’s at stake: The Aravallis, running south of Delhi into Gujarat, are often described as the “green lungs” of northwestern India. They slow desertification, support groundwater recharge, and sit atop mineral-rich land – making them both ecologically vital and commercially contested.
sound_smarter: In a region choking on pollution and water stress, the Aravallis are a buffer India cannot afford to incorrectly define.

title: Deed or disturb?
text:
Rajasthan wants the right to say “not so fast” to property deals in sensitive neighbourhoods, citing “demographic imbalance”, a shorthand for fears of communal change.

What happened: On Wednesday, the BJP-led Rajasthan cabinet approved a draft Disturbed Areas Bill. It’s expected in the Assembly’s Budget Session starting 28 January (next Wednesday).

In plain English please: The state can label a locality “disturbed” if it claims tensions, intimidation, or forced sales. In those pockets, selling or buying property may require prior clearance from the district administration. Deals done without approval could be cancelled, and the draft contemplates 3–5 years’ jail plus fines.

The government’s justification: Ministers argue it prevents distress sales triggered by pressure tactics and keeps communal flashpoints from turning into land-grabs.

Pushback already: The Indian National Congress is calling the draft unconstitutional and politically motivated, arguing existing law-and-order tools are enough and warning it could sharpen social divisions and spook investors.
sound_smarter: Even if used sparingly, the Bill will inject permission-risk into real estate, which can mean slower transactions, tighter lending, and a premium on “safe” neighbourhoods.

title: Govt names IndiGo fall guy
text:
IndiGo’s December meltdown just got a face. The Centre told the Delhi High Court that it had asked the airline to dismiss a senior VP from its operations control nerve centre.

Regulatory bill: DGCA has already levied a record INR 22.2 crore (~USD 2.4 million) penalty and demanded a INR 50 crore (~USD 5.5 million) bank guarantee. The court is sending a clear message that the penalty will be serious.

Why this went national: IndiGo isn’t a monopoly, but it’s close enough to be systemically important, dominating roughly 60-65% of domestic traffic. When it stumbles, rivals can’t soak up the spill. Stranded passengers become a headline factory.

Antitrust aftertaste: With alternatives scarce, fares can jump fast. That’s why the episode has dragged the competition regulator into the story: dominance plus disruption is a politically sensitive mix.
sound_smarter: IndiGo’s dominance went largely unchecked, until it failed loudly. In India, scrutiny follows breakdowns, not balance sheets.

title: Brasilia checks in
text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spoke by phone on Tuesday, setting the stage for Lula’s upcoming state visit to India.

What’s locked in: Lula will travel to New Delhi from February 19-21, where he will be in attendance at the Brazil-India Business Forum. The visit will also see the inauguration of Brazil’s APEX (Brazilian Trade and Investment Promotion Agency) office in New Delhi.

Why now: The call leaned heavily on momentum. Modi described the India-Brazil strategic partnership as ready to “scale new heights,” while both leaders underscored cooperation among Global South economies.

Beyond trade: Lula said the conversation also covered global issues, with both leaders reiterating support for multilateralism, democracy, and peace.

The timing matters: India and Brazil are aligning more closely inside groupings like BRICS and the G20, while both hedge against a more fragmented global order.
sound_smarter: India–Brazil ties are about building weight inside multilateral forums where Western consensus is thinning and Global South coordination increasingly matters.
anchor: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Brazilian President Luiz

title: Hard power joins the agenda
text:
India and EU are upgrading defence ties. Brussels announced a new Security and Defense Partnership (SDP) with New Delhi, covering maritime security, cybersecurity, and counterterrorism.

The timing: The pact will be signed next week during the Delhi visit of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa, who will co-chair the 16th India-EU Summit with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and attend Republic Day celebrations.

What’s new: Details are thin, but the SDP is expected to open the door to defence industrial cooperation, including Indian firms accessing the EU’s Security Action For Europe (SAFE) programme, a EUR 150 billion financing tool to accelerate European defence readiness.

Why SAFE matters: This is an opportunity for India to plug into Europe’s defence supply chains as the EU scrambles to rearm.

Packed agenda: The SDP sits alongside a broader bundle: a long-delayed free trade agreement (see our January 22 issue), a Security of Information pact, a mobility framework for students and workers, and a joint strategic vision for 2026-2030.
sound_smarter: Europe is hedging against US unpredictability and India is monetising that anxiety.

title: GAAR-dians of the Past
text:
India’s startup lobby is asking Delhi for a retro-tax truce. On Tuesday, the Startup Policy Forum, representing 60 startups, urged the finance ministry to publicly confirm that pre-1 April 2017 investments routed via Mauritius won’t be re-scrutinised or taxed.

Why they’re spooked: On 15 January 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that Mauritius-based entities used by Tiger Global in its 2018 Flipkart stake sale to Walmart were “conduits,” denying them treaty protection and allowing India to tax the gains.

Quick rewind: For two decades, Mauritius was the standard “holding company” stop for investing in India, thanks to the India-Mauritius tax treaty (1982). Reuters cites government data showing Mauritius accounted for USD 171 billion inflows over 23 years to 2023.

What changed now: The Court said India’s general anti-avoidance rules (GAAR) can override treaty benefits if a structure looks designed mainly to dodge tax, raising fears that old startup cap tables get reopened.

What to watch: A clarifying note from the finance ministry/CBDT drawing a clean line around pre-2017 deals could not come sooner.
sound_smarter: Investors can price taxes, but they can’t price rule ambiguity. What’s worse for the startups is that the limbo area like this can freeze up funding for them.

title: Back in the saddle?
text:
India’s energy pragmatism is back on display, with caveats. India’s biggest refiner, Reliance Industries is set to resume purchases of sanctions-compliant Russian crude oil in February and March after a one-month pause, as refiners recalibrate sourcing strategies under rising Western pressure.

Backstory: Reliance was one of the top Indian buyers of discounted Russian crude after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. It last received Russian shipments in December under a short US concession allowing it to wind down dealings with sanctioned producers.

Why this shifted: Indian refiners have been boosting purchases of Middle Eastern crude as they adjust strategies in response to increased American tariffs and India’s broader economic engagements, including ongoing talks on a bilateral trade deal with the US.

Unclear horizon: It remains uncertain whether Reliance will continue Russian crude imports beyond March. Overall Russian oil purchases into India are expected to remain subdued through the period.

India’s position: New Delhi has consistently maintained that its energy sourcing decisions are guided by national interest and market conditions. Securing predictable, affordable energy supplies for the Indian consumer rather than geopolitical signalling, and the Ministry of External Affairs has emphasised this rationale in response to criticism.
sound_smarter: India isn’t choosing sides on Russian oil. It is timing its exposure, tightening the tap when US pressure peaks, and resuming when it eases.

title: Nipah flares, panic doesn’t
text:
India is moving rapidly to contain a Nipah virus outbreak in West Bengal. Five cases have been confirmed, including infected doctors and nurses, with one patient critical.

Containment mode: Nearly 100 contacts are under home quarantine. Infected patients are being treated in hospitals in and around Kolkata.

Pathogen reality check: Nipah has no vaccine or cure and sits on the WHO’s high-risk list. Human transmission is rare, and the virus is typically linked to bat spillovers via contaminated fruit. Fatality rates can range from 40-75%, depending on strain and response speed.

Not India’s first rodeo: Nipah has surfaced before in West Bengal in 2001 and 2007, and repeatedly in Kerala since 2018. India’s health system now treats Nipah as a known threat, with protocols for tracing, isolation, and hospital control already in place.
sound_smarter: Nipah looks scary, but it’s familiar. This is not the start of another COVID-style global crisis.
anchor: India is moving rapidly to contain a Nipah

title: Rolling everywhere
text:
India’s election watchdog is pressing ahead with its voter roll clean-up. Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar said the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls will be extended to remaining states soon, after already covering key poll-bound regions.

Where it stands: The SIR has been conducted in 13 of India’s 36 states and union territories so far. The Commission says the exercise is now firmly part of its nationwide approach to roll maintenance.

What Kumar said: Speaking ahead of the Election Commission’s foundation day – observed as National Voters’ Day – Kumar argued that the exercise has helped restore the “sanctity and credibility” of the voter list and has renewed trust in the democratic process.

Political echo: Prime Minister Narendra Modi reinforced the message in his first Mann Ki Baat address of 2026, urging first-time voters to participate actively in elections.

The friction: The exercise has not been controversy-free. Opposition parties and civil society groups have flagged concerns over deletions, administrative burden on election staff, and the risk of eligible voters being left out, especially in migrant-heavy constituencies.
sound_smarter: The Election Commission is betting that tightening rolls early is worth the political pushback. The harder test is in proving that clean-up doesn’t quietly turn into exclusion.

title: Strike for weekends
text:
India’s public-sector banks could effectively go dark for three straight days because one strike day lands on a holiday pile-up.

What’s happening: The United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU), a coalition of nine staff unions, has given notice of a nationwide strike on January 27 to demand a five-day work week. With January 25-26 being holidays, routine branch services could be disrupted across a long weekend. Most state-run banks have already warned customers.

Why now: UFBU says the Indian Banks’ Association (IBA), which negotiates for banks, agreed in a March 2024 wage settlement to make all Saturdays a holiday, but the government sign-off and implementation are still pending.

A short history: In 2015, banks shifted to 2nd and 4th Saturdays off. UFBU has periodically revived the “all Saturdays off” demand. Proposed strike actions in 2023 and 2025 were deferred after talks.

The justification: “There would be no loss of man-hours as we have agreed to work an extra 40 minutes daily from Monday to Friday,” UFBU had said earlier this month. “It is unfortunate that the government is not responding to our genuine demand.”
sound_smarter: While framed as a labor dispute, the strike exposes a paradox: India leads the world in real-time payment transactions, yet its physical banking system remains tethered to a legacy view of the branch, rather than the smartphone, as the primary avenue of banking.
anchor: India’s public-sector banks could effectively go dark for

title: Desi Ozempic arrives
text:
India’s drugmakers are gearing up for a GLP-1 shake-up. Sun Pharma, Dr. Reddy’s, and Alkem Laboratories have received clearance from the Drugs Controller General of India (DGCI) to manufacture generic semaglutide. Semaglutide is the active ingredient in Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic and Wegovy.

What changed: Novo Nordisk’s Indian patent on Ozempic expires in March, and Indian firms are moving early to be ready on day one. So far, Sun Pharma has approval to manufacture and market generic versions of both Ozempic and Wegovy, while Dr. Reddy’s has manufacturing clearance and is awaiting marketing approval for Wegovy. The companies have already started exporting the drug to non-patent markets.

Same drug, different use: Both Ozempic and Wegovy contain semaglutide, but they differ in dosage, delivery, and approved indications (diabetes versus weight management).

Why India matters: India is often dubbed the world’s diabetes capital, accounting for roughly one in five diabetics globally. Lifestyle changes, diet shifts, and low physical activity have accelerated the burden, prompting government pushes like the Fit India Movement and yoga-based wellness programmes.

The price effect: Japan’s Nomura expects generic semaglutide to be priced around INR 3,600 (USD 40), less than half the current cost of Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic in India.
sound_smarter: This is India’s pharma industry doing what it does best: scaling a global blockbuster into a mass-market drug and pushing access beyond first-world pricing.
anchor: India’s drugmakers are gearing up for a GLP-1

title: India’s invisible tax
text:
Pollution, not protectionism, is India’s biggest economic drag. That was Gita Gopinath’s blunt message at Davos as India eyes third-largest-economy status.

The provocation: Speaking at a panel on India’s growth trajectory, the former IMF chief economist said pollution’s economic damage already outweighs the impact of tariffs.

The human cost: Gopinath cited a 2022 World Bank study showing nearly 1.7 million pollution-linked deaths annually – about 18% of all deaths in India.

The growth hit: “The real costs of pollution are not merely environmental… They are deeply intertwined with economic growth, productivity, and the health of citizens,” said Gopinath. Lower labour productivity, higher healthcare spending, and slower activity all compound into a long-term drag. A 2021 study found that air pollution costs Indian businesses about USD 95 billion annually or around 3% of India’s total GDP.

Policy prescription: Gopinath called for treating pollution control as a national mission, on par with deregulation. She warned that while India could become the world’s third-largest economy by 2028, pollution would erode per-capita gains and deepen inequality.

Execution problem: Air and water pollution routinely cross district and state boundaries, outpacing local regulators and exposing weak monitoring and enforcement.
sound_smarter: Pollutants don’t respect administrative lines. India needs regional environmental governance that matches how pollution actually spreads.
anchor: Pollution, not protectionism, is India’s biggest economic drag.

title: Brussels gets the best seat
text:
India’s Republic Day parade is a military show and a diplomatic seating plan. This year, Delhi put Brussels in the VIP booth.

Dias diplomacy: The “chief guest” sits beside the president – closer than India’s own top ministers. It’s the state’s loudest non-verbal signal about who matters right now.

Who got the seat: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa attended as guests of honour yesterday. Not one leader, but the EU’s two top power centres.

Quick rewind: In 2024, Emmanuel Macron was the chief guest. In 2025, Indonesia’s Prabowo Subianto. 2026 shifts from big bilaterals to a bloc.

Before-and-after: The EU duo is attending the EU-India Summit today in New Delhi. Von der Leyen has hinted that a trade deal is near last week at Davos. Reporting suggests that FTA talks have concluded, and an announcement will likely be made later today.
sound_smarter: Republic Day seating sends the signal, and the summit confirms it. India and the EU are building a “third lane” between China’s scale and US tariff chaos.
anchor: India’s Republic Day parade is a military show

title: Business first, baggage parked
text:
India-Canada ties are shifting back into deal-making mode. On Tuesday, Indian High Commissioner to Canada Dinesh Patnaik said Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is expected in India in March, with multiple agreements lined up spanning energy, critical minerals, AI, education, and culture.

The rupture: Ties froze in 2023 after then-PM Justin Trudeau alleged Indian involvement in the killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar, a charge India denies.

Normalisation: Since taking office in March 2025, Carney has focused on normalisation, not closure. That worked as Narendra Modi attended the 2025 G7 in Canada. Since then, Canadian ministers have been frequent flyers to New Delhi.

Advance party: Energy Minister Tim Hodgson is in India this week. Between his visit and Carney’s, both sides are expected to announce deals on energy and critical minerals, including a proposed 10-year, USD 2 billion uranium supply agreement. Hodgson’s logic is blunt: Canada needs “large and growing” economies. That’s India.

Trade talks resume: Patnaik said India and Canada will restart formal negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) in March after a two-year pause. Both governments say the pact could help more than double bilateral trade to USD 30 billion by 2030.
sound_smarter: This isn’t reconciliation, it’s risk management. Canada wants insulation from US trade pressure; India wants energy resource access and diversified trade relationships. The thaw holds if the deals do.
anchor: India-Canada ties are shifting back into deal-making mode.

title: Hot mic, heavy tariffs
text:
Ted Cruz’s private candour just went public. On Sunday, Axios reported that it obtained an audio recording of the Texas senator criticising Vice President JD Vance and mocking President Trump’s tariff strategy in donor meetings last year.

What leaked: In nearly 10 minutes of audio, Cruz casts himself as a free-trade, pro-intervention Republican. Cruz appeared to be positioning himself for a 2028 primary against the more hawkish Vance.

India angle: Cruz told donors he has been “battling” the White House to accept a trade deal with India. When questioned as to who was blocking it, he named Senior Counsellor for Trade and Manufacturing Peter Navarro, Vance, and “sometimes” Trump.

Public cleanup? On Monday, Trump congratulated India on its 77th Republic Day, calling the relationship a bond between “the world’s oldest and largest democracies.” Last year, he skipped a personal message, delegating the task to his secretary of state, as Joe Biden had before him.

Why this matters: Trade ties are already strained. In August 2025, Trump doubled tariffs on Indian goods to 50%, adding a 25% tariff over India’s Russian crude imports.
sound_smarter: The leak shows an India-US trade deal is blocked at the very top of the White House, making a deal structurally unlikely, not just delayed. With India close to signing an EU trade deal – something Trump will likely see as a slight – New Delhi’s odds with Washington fall further.
anchor: Ted Cruz’s private candour just went public. On

title: Handshakes and holdbacks
text:
India and the EU just declared the “mother of all deals” done. New Delhi and Brussels reached political consensus on a long-stalled Free Trade Agreement (FTA) at yesterday’s summit. Talks dragged for years, then restarted in 2022. Next comes the unsexy bit: legal scrubbing and ratification.

Market-access swap:

- India will eliminate or reduce tariffs on 96.6% of EU goods exports (by value) – the EU pegs that at €4bn/year in duty savings for European firms.
- The EU will cut tariffs on 99.5% of imports from India over 7 years, a clear boost for textiles, leather, chemicals, gems/jewellery, and other labour-heavy items.

Farmer-proofing: This is a geopolitical win for Ursula von der Leyen and a tidy contrast to last week’s EU stumble, when the European Parliament stalled the Mercosur pact amid farmer backlash (notably France and Poland). The India deal tries to dodge that by carving out agricultural products and food, while trade liberalisation leans harder into autos and industrial goods.

Why now: Call it mutual de-risking. Both sides want less exposure to US demand as trade tensions rise. Momentum picked up after the US slapped 50% tariffs on some Indian goods, amid broader tariff threats.

Climate sting in the tail: India didn’t win any leeway from the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) levy but only a promise to keep talking about technicalities. The EU agreed to provide India with EUR 500 million in support tied to emissions cuts and 1.6 million metric tons of duty-free steel exports to the EU.

Next steps: The final agreement will undergo a technical and legal review before being signed, likely happening in six months. After signing, the FTA needs to be ratified by both sides. If all goes smoothly, the FTA is likely to be implemented in early 2027.
sound_smarter: This is less about immediate trade volume and more about positioning India as the EU’s pragmatic supply-chain alternative to the US and China. By navigating the world’s most complex regulatory environment, India signals to global capital that it can play by the EU-grade rules, earning a massive credibility boost.

title: India pops the bonnet
text:
India is prying open its auto market, albeit carefully. The India–EU FTA delivers the sharpest tariff reset the long-protected sector has seen.

What Europe gets: Preferential access, with guardrails. Up to 250,000 European-made cars will enter India at lower duties. Around 160,000 internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles will see tariffs fall to 10% within five years. 90,000 EVs get delayed relief; tariffs only drop by year ten, shielding India’s young electric vehicle (EV) market.

Pathways to integration: European carmakers can ship 75,000 completely knocked down (CKD) kits a year, priced above USD 18,000, with tariffs cut to 8.25% from the existing 16.5%. Duties on auto components fall to zero, encouraging European manufacturers to plug into India’s parts ecosystem. Europe is already a major destination for Indian auto component exports and the deal is expected to deepen integration.

Hidden leverage: Quota reviews are tied to steel, a core Indian priority. That linkage gives New Delhi a built-in pressure point in future negotiations.

Value market, premium trap: India buys cheap, reliable, stable cars. Suzuki dominates by adapting kei car economics to Indian price points. Europe’s mass-market offerings, notably from Volkswagen Group and Stellantis, are widely seen as overpriced and poor value. Where Europe does win is in the premium segment, and tariff cuts risk squeezing India’s Tata Motors and Mahindra & Mahindra just as both try to move up the price ladder.
sound_smarter: The quota reviews are what matter, letting India open the door without surrendering control.

title: High-stakes handshake
text:
Brussels and Delhi are closer than ever. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and EU leadership endorsed the Joint India-EU Comprehensive Strategic Agenda, a massive policy framework designed to deepen ties.

The agenda: The framework covers everything from green energy and defense to the "holy trinity" of tech: AI, quantum computing, and semiconductors.

Economic muscle: India and the EU seek to deepen economic resilience with a Free Trade Agreement and expanding green cooperation, and securing strategic value chains, particularly in semiconductors and critical minerals.

Tech collab: The partnership focuses on collaborating on AI, quantum, semiconductors, clean tech, and biotech while fostering a secure, interoperable digital ecosystem and shared research through programs.

Security ties: Both sides are elevating their strategic ties by implementing the India-EU Security and Defense Partnership, including exploring possibilities for India to participate in EU defence initiatives, possibly including the EU’s Security Action For Europe, which we covered here.

Improving connectivity: The agenda prioritizes strengthening connectivity through the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor corridor and coordinated leadership in multilateral forums to drive global reforms in climate, health, and trade governance.

Keep things moving: To sustain these efforts, the partners will streamline skills mobility and visa procedures while strengthening institutional cooperation through annual summits and dedicated business and academic exchange platforms.
sound_smarter: The deepening relations between India and the EU center on realigning relations to diversify economic dependencies, secure technologies, and thrive in a multipolar order. This framework signals a move toward a "de-risking" alliance that values geopolitical stability as much as market access.
anchor: Brussels and Delhi are closer than ever. On

title: From airports to aircraft
text:
Adani wants to build the planes flying from its airports. On Tuesday, India’s Adani Group and Brazil’s Embraer signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to explore a regional aircraft manufacturing venture in India, pushing Adani into commercial aviation production.

Why Adani fits: The group runs seven operational airports across India and is building Navi Mumbai International, India’s largest greenfield airport. Adani also has a fast-expanding defence and aerospace arm.

Why these planes: Embraer’s 70–140 seat jets are built for thin routes. That aligns with India’s regional connectivity scheme (UDAN), which subsidises regional connectivity to smaller cities where wide-bodies make no sense and turboprops are hitting capacity limits.

Not the same game: Indian airlines have spent the last two years scaling. IndiGo and Air India placed record Airbus and Boeing orders to fuel global expansion and dominate high-density trunk routes. That strategy is about reach, frequency, and international ambition. Adani is playing a different game, aiming to capitalise on regional connectivity, where 180 seater aircraft are seldom justified.

Diplomatic tailwind: The announcement lands just as President Lula is set to travel to India for the Brazil-India Business Forum, which we covered here.
sound_smarter: Regional jets won’t steal the spotlight, but they will decide whether India’s aviation growth actually spreads from metropolitan cities to Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities.

title: Budget season, decoded
text:
India’s Parliament opened its Budget Session yesterday. This is the run-up to the government’s most consequential annual decisions.

What this session is: A two-act fiscal play, with a pause in between.

- Phase 1 (late January to mid-February): President Droupadi Murmu addresses a joint sitting. The Economic Survey drops January 29. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman presents the Union Budget on February 1. Parliament debates fiscal policy, economic priorities, and the government's overall approach.
- Recess (mid-February to mid-March): Parliamentary Standing Committees explain the budget in detail, ministry by ministry. This is where technical scrutiny happens.
- Phase 2 (mid-March to early April): Parliament returns to vote. They debate and pass the Finance Bill and the Appropriation Bill. Without these, the government cannot legally tax or spend beyond bare essentials.

Why February 1: An early budget gives ministries and states time to plan before the fiscal year starts on April 1. That April date is a colonial hangover, tied to old revenue and harvest cycles.

These two documents are critically important.

- The Economic Survey looks backward and explains what worked, what did not, and where the problems are.
- The Union Budget looks forward and tells us what the government will prioritise through its spending allocations.

Why this year’s budget is worth watching: India’s growth has leaned heavily on public capital expenditure. Welfare has expanded too. Both were funded by higher borrowing, but New Delhi wants to shrink the fiscal deficit. This Budget will show whether the government stays the course or pivots harder toward crowding in private investment.

If you’re convinced it’s worth watching (we’re convinced), here’s how to read the Economic Survey and Union Budget to know what’s on the agenda for 2026:

- Survey mentions it + Budget funds it: problem acknowledged, action underway.
- Survey mentions it + no money: problem admitted, issue deprioritised because of other priorities.
- No mention, no money: ignored.

Don’t worry if it sounds too complicated.
The Bharat Briefing will unpack both as they land.

title: A crash that reshapes the state
text:
A plane crash has blown a hole through Maharashtra’s politics. On Wednesday, Deputy Chief Minister (CM) Ajit Pawar and four others died when their chartered aircraft crashed while landing in Baramati, Maharashtra. The crash happened in Pawar’s home turf, where he was headed to campaign ahead of February local polls.

The man: Ajit Pawar was a political heavyweight. A six-time deputy CM, he most recently governed with the BJP after splitting from his uncle Sharad Pawar’s Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) in 2023. He didn’t just defect, he took the party name and symbol, crowning himself NCP president and effectively creating two NCP factions.

What we know so far: The Civil Aviation Ministry has released aircraft details and a timeline, but no cause. Sharad Pawar has publicly ruled out conspiracy and urged supporters not to politicise the tragedy.

Condolences: Prime Minister Narendra Modi called Pawar a “leader of the people.” Tributes poured in across party lines, framing his death as an “irreparable” loss.
sound_smarter: Ajit Pawar’s death creates a leadership vacuum inside the NCP, not the ruling alliance. With both factions of the NCP signalling reconciliation, a post-Ajit merger looks likely.

title: Survey before the Survey
text:
Congress is trying to seize the economic story before the Economic Survey does. On Tuesday, the party released its annual “Real State of the Economy” report for the year, arguing that inequality is increasing while welfare is decreasing.

The party’s brain trust: Congress Research Department, headed by MP Rajeev Gowda, together with Congress leader Amitabh Dubey released the heavy hitter.

The attack line: The report takes aim at glossy macro numbers, arguing they mask everyday distress. Growth, it says, is being captured by a narrow elite while most Indians are left treading water. It also flags the rupee as Asia’s worst (or among the worst) performer in 2025 amid outflows and trade/tariff uncertainty, and says net Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) was negative for multiple months through November 2025.

The fine print: This is a political brief built from selective indicators, not a definitive macro audit. The Economic Survey (due today) is the government’s official data-heavy framing for the Budget as a baseline for fiscal choices.
sound_smarter: Congress is trying to raise the political cost of ignoring wealth distribution and forcing the government to explain who benefits, not just how fast GDP grows. Should the Economic Survey lean hard on “India is resilient” while jobs or inequality questions stay fuzzy, the challenging voices will already have a concerned audience.
anchor: Congress is trying to seize the economic story

title: When performance isn’t enough
text:
The Economic Survey 2025-26 is a mixed bag. It is upbeat on India’s macroeconomic resilience, yet candid about a distrustful world where geopolitical frictions punish even strong performers. For the first time, the Survey cites Australia-based Lowy Institute’s Power Gap Index, noting that India operates below its strategic potential with a score of -4.0 – the lowest in Asia (excluding Russia and North Korea). In short, India is punching well below its weight.

### 1. Strong Delivery, Punished by the System

India’s fundamentals are screaming “buy,” but the markets are saying “sell.” Real GDP growth cleared 7% in 2025, with FY26 estimates hitting 7.4%. Fiscal consolidation outperformed (4.8% deficit vs 4.9% budgeted), and three sovereign rating upgrades followed. Yet, the rupee took a beating anyway. This is the Survey’s central paradox: stellar domestic management is no longer a shield against external currency pressures and fickle capital flows.

### 2. Geopolitical Tailwinds Turned Headwinds

The hope that India would be the "exception to the rule" in the new U.S. tariff regime has evaporated. Instead of securing quick exemption, India was slapped with an additional 25% tariff in August – piling onto the 25% reciprocal duty from April. Later negotiations did not result in a reduction. These shocks, combined with Asia’s widest strategic power gap, has left India’s macroeconomic strength feeling surprisingly fragile.

### 3. Global Fragility: The New Normal

The Survey outlines three scenarios for 2026.

- Best case (managed disorder) (40-45%)
Volatility and interventions, but no systemic collapse.
- Middle case (disorderly multipolar breakdown) (40-45%)
Intensifying rivalry, coercive trade, and financial stress transmitted across weaker buffers.
- Worst case (systemic shock cascade) (10-20%)
Leveraged AI bets correcting alongside geopolitical escalation, potentially worse than 2008.

We’ve explored these in detail below.

### 4. Toward Strategic Resilience and Indispensability

India needs to graduate from blunt, across-the-board swadeshi (import substitution) to "strategic indispensability." The goal isn't to make everything at home, but to make the world need what India makes. The Survey proposes a tiered playbook:

- In high-risk, critical areas
Move fast and build deep domestic capacity.
- In medium- or lower-priority sectors
Stay pragmatic. Source globally where it’s efficient, and localize only where it makes economic sense.
- Across the board
Aggressively slash input costs. Indian manufacturing cannot win if it isn’t price competitive.

This “blending” in less-critical areas avoids the pitfalls of forcing everything domestically, allowing India to stay integrated into global value chains while selectively building resilience.

### 5. State Capacity: The Binding Constraint

India doesn't have a "good ideas" problem; it has an execution problem. This ultimately boils down to the people inside it: their culture, skills, execution discipline, and capacity to design smart, enabling regulations. Breakthrough growth requires a three-way alignment:

- The State acting as an entrepreneurial enabler, not a micromanager.
- The Private Sector treating nation-building as a core KPI, not an afterthought.
- Citizens upholding the social trust that makes collective effort possible.

When strong institutions back this alignment, deregulation stops being mere rule-cutting and becomes a true growth multiplier.
sound_smarter: Though relatively better positioned than most, India can no longer count on easy insulation. Navigating 2026 will require the endurance of a marathon runner and the reflexes of a sprinter.
anchor: The Economic Survey 2025-26 is a mixed bag.

title: Welcome to the age of economic statecraft
text:
India’s Economic Survey sees a harsher world ahead: less trust, more shocks, thinner margins. Efficiency is out. Power politics is in.

The worldview: The global economy is shifting from efficiency-driven multilateralism to economic statecraft, economic means are used to achieve political ends.

India sees three possible futures:

- Managed disorder (40–45%)
Today’s mess, but governed. Trade frictions persist, and states step in to calm markets.
- Disorderly multipolar breakdown (40–45%)
Sanctions, coercive trade, and forced supply-chain rewiring. Growth, autonomy, and stability collide.
- Systemic shock cascade (10–20%)
A financial rupture. Think AI-infrastructure excess meets geopolitical shock; worse than 2008.

India’s edge: Big domestic demand, lower financialisation, hefty FX reserves, and strategic autonomy give India more shock absorbers than most.

The catch: No immunity. All paths risk capital flow volatility and rupee pressure. This won’t be a one-year problem.

Delhi’s prescription: Earn hard currency, diversify trade and payments, move from import substitution to indispensability, act before certainty, and tolerate competition to boost industrial muscle.
sound_smarter: This is a bet on state capacity. Every solution needs an active government. The budget will show whether Delhi is serious – or just philosophically prepared.
anchor: India’s Economic Survey sees a harsher world ahead:

title: Smaller models, bigger impact
text:
The Economic Survey makes a blunt case: copying the US or China’s capital- and energy-heavy AI stack is straight-up inefficient.

The pivot: The Survey rejects US- and China-style mega-models. Bigger models aren’t better – they create fragile dependencies on foreign compute, capital, and supply chains. Instead, it backs sector-specific, small, open-weight models built for real use, not leaderboard glory.

Coordination first, rules later: The Survey backs sequenced regulation: build ecosystems and regulatory capacity first, then impose binding rules once risks are clear and enforceable.

Resources in place: The Survey argues that India has the structural advantages to succeed.

- With over 1 billion broadband users, India offers the world’s largest behavioural and transactional data base.
- It hints at data governance that avoids rigid localisation while keeping value anchored domestically.
- Creating an “AI-augmented” workforce that prioritises judgment and adaptability over tools that quickly go obsolete.
- An “AI-OS” layered onto India Stack, giving startups access to public data and shared compute without billion-dollar burn rates.

Why this matters: The focus shifts from flashy chatbots to hard problems that actually scale in India. Less spectacle; more administrative and economic payoff.

Late, by design: The Survey treats global AI hype as a cooling bubble. India’s late entry, it argues, could help it avoid the energy intensity and financial instability now troubling early movers in the West.
sound_smarter: This is a sovereignty play. Minimise dependence on mega-models, keep bargaining power domestic, and make foreign compute a choice rather than a choke point. Expect the Budget to favour targeted tools like compute access credits over splashy AI subsidies.
anchor: The Economic Survey makes a blunt case: copying

title: Density Over Demos
text:
The Economic Survey ditches the “Smart Cities” aesthetic. Urban reform is recast as a hard-nosed productivity play: unlock dead capital by fixing how cities are built, priced, and run.

The core problem: India’s top 10 cities generate nearly 28% of GDP with barely 9% of the population – yet none function as true global nodes like Singapore or London.

The hidden tax: The Survey pins underperformance on fragmented governance and poor planning that force long commutes, calling it a direct tax on worker output and mental bandwidth. Indian cities have the talent but the physical environment is capping growth.

Land, the real bottleneck: Restrictive land use is the single biggest urban bottleneck. Existing rules keep cities short and wide, forcing horizontal sprawl that makes infrastructure costlier and housing scarcer.

The Survey pushes a “holistic rethink” of vertical development: Build up, not out.

The plan: All million-plus cities should adopt a 20-year statutory spatial-economic plan, refreshed every five years, with three non-negotiables: transport-first design, annual housing targets, and land-value capture so public infrastructure projects don't create private windfalls while city budgets stay stressed.
sound_smarter: India will spend on urban infrastructure anyway. Fixing land use rules, increasing density, and improving transit ensures each rupee buys productivity, not sprawl.
anchor: The Economic Survey ditches the “Smart Cities” aesthetic.

title: From Access to Control
text:
The Economic Survey treated lifestyle habits as a macroeconomic risk for the first time. The state is clearly preparing to police the quality of private consumption.

The new frame: Phones, food, and freedom were the last decade’s pitch. This chapter reflects a government now worried about what people do with their phones – and what ultra-processed food does to people.

Cognitive capital alarm: The Survey calls out “compulsive digital use” as a productivity threat. It flags “compulsive scrolling” and “short-form video loops” as a direct hit to focus.

Policy breadcrumbs: It floats age-based access limits for social media and gambling apps, proposes a “digital wellness curriculum” in schools, and even suggests basic phones for children to curb early addiction.

The fiscal angle: Mental health is framed as a productivity tax. The Survey links digital over-consumption to anxiety and sleep deprivation, warning that this could blunt India’s demographic dividend.

The health trap: On obesity and ultra-processed foods (UPFs), the tone hardens. The Survey notes that obesity has doubled alongside a 150% jump in UPF consumption over 15 years and significantly increasing healthcare costs and decreasing productivity.

The toolkit:

- GST as a weapon
Moving UPFs to the highest GST slab plus a surcharge.
- Ad blackout
Banning UPF marketing during daytime and evening hours across media.
- Label shock
Replacing vague ratings with clear front-of-pack warning labels.
sound_smarter: This marks a shift from the “nudge state” to the “penalty state.” Once habits are framed as GDP leakage, bans and taxes become easier to sell. For upcoming sessions, ministries can now justify new compliance burdens as growth policy rather than purely public health issues.

title: Boring is the new bold
text:
Fiscal discipline trumped market expectations. In her ninth budget, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman traded populist sops for a lean ledger, prioritising selective spending over broad tax breaks. Markets responded with a cold shoulder, as the Sensex and Nifty both slid 2% on the news.

The fiscal diet: New Delhi is cooling the post-pandemic spending spree to anchor long-term stability.

- Fiscal deficit: Target trimmed to 4.3% (down from 4.4%).
- Debt-to-GDP: Pruned to 55.6% (from 56.1%).
- Capital Expenditure: Increased to USD 133.1 billion, a disciplined 9% bump. This marks a significant pivot from the 30%+ surges seen during the 2021-2024 post-pandemic recovery years.

Upgrading manufacturing: The focus has shifted from simple assembly to higher-value manufacturing.

- Electronics Outlay: The components manufacturing scheme nearly doubled to USD 436 million. It targets high-value goods like display modules, camera sub-assemblies, and circuit boards for everything from iPhones to EVs.
- Critical Minerals: New dedicated rare earth corridors in Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu.
- Semiconductors: India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 moves beyond fabs into the specialised equipment, chemicals, and gases required for chip-making.

Hardware, not hype: A tax holiday until 2047 was announced for foreign firms providing global cloud services. To qualify, these firms must route services to Indian customers through a domestic reseller. The budget also introduced a 15% safe harbour on costs for related-party data centre services to reduce transfer pricing litigation.

The war chest: The total military outlay rose to USD 85.6 billion, a 15% increase.

- Modernisation: Capital funds for new hardware jumped 22% to USD 23.9 billion.
- Aviation focus: A dedicated USD 6.95 billion was earmarked for aircraft and aero engines, supporting the push for 114 multi-role fighter jets and indigenous engines.
- Operations: Revenue expenditure for day-to-day maintenance and fuel rose 17.2% to USD 39.8 billion.
sound_smarter: By prioritising a “boring” budget, the government is signalling that a move from post-pandemic recovery to long-term creditworthiness, characterised by measured government spending and (hopefully) greater private investment.

title: Minerals for trade relief
text:
A nice chat before the trip. On Thursday, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar met US Ambassador Sergio Gor, a prelude to Jaishankar’s February 4-5 trip to Washington.

The backdrop: Gor, a Trump confidant, arrived in January to a chilly bilateral climate. Last year, Trump slapped a 25% reciprocal tariff on Indian goods and a 25% punitive levy over New Delhi’s purchase for Russian oil.

The convo: While there was no official readout, Gor described the meeting as a “highly substantive discussion.” The dialogue touched on the usual suspects – defence, trade, and critical minerals – aiming to find common ground in a relationship currently defined by friction.

On Jaishankar’s agenda: Jaishankar will attend the US’ inaugural Critical Minerals Ministerial. The goal is simple: secure mineral supply chains essential for national security and the energy transition, specifically to break China’s stranglehold on the market. He is also expected to negotiate Pax Silica, a US-led effort to wall off semiconductor and AI supply chains from Beijing. India is widely expected to sign on.
sound_smarter: By leaning into Pax Silica and critical minerals, India is offering the Trump administration a strategic win in the tech cold war with China to bargain for relief on the tariff front.

title: New Pawar in power
text:
The deputy CM is still a Pawar. On Saturday, Sunetra Pawar became Maharashtra’s first female deputy chief minister, stepping into the role following the death of her husband, Ajit Pawar, in a recent plane crash, which we covered here.

The profile: Daughter of former Maharashtra minister Padamsinh Patil, Sunetra is no political novice; she is a seasoned veteran of the state’s influential cooperative sector. To accept the appointment, she resigned from the Rajya Sabha seat she secured only last year.

Political tightrope: Sunetra’s resignation leaves a hole in the Rajya Sabha for the BJP-led alliance. The coalition now faces the delicate task of filling that vacancy without upsetting the precarious balance between local grassroots power and central representation.

The NCP rift: Any lingering hopes for a family reconciliation are evaporating. Patriarch Sharad Pawar confirmed that merger talks with Ajit’s faction were effectively “interrupted” by the crash. Despite rumours of a February 12 reunification announcement, the elder Pawar is now pointedly distancing himself from both the merger and Sunetra’s promotion. We covered the merger here.
sound_smarter: By elevating Sunetra immediately, the BJP is moving to secure the Ajit Pawar loyalist base before it can fracture. While headlines may suggest chaos, fears of instability in Maharashtra are likely exaggerated; the BJP maintains a firm grip on state governance through its alliance with the NCP and Shiv Sena.

title: Caste away
text:
The Supreme Court has hit the brakes on university equity rules. Last Thursday, the Supreme Court ordered a pause on the University Grants Commission (UGC) Equity Regulations 2026.

The backstory: Released on January 13, the UG’s equity rules were a response to an unprecedented rise in the number of caste-discrimination-related complaints in recent years. The commission proposed that every higher education institution must now mandatorily establish an Equal Opportunity Centre (EOC) with an Equity Committee. The 2026 rules replace the 2012 guidelines, which were widely ignored because they lacked enforcement power and whose implementation was optional.

Judicial scepticism: The Court slammed the definition of discrimination as too narrow, noting it excluded General Category students from protections against gender or regional bias. It also worried that separate hostels mentioned in the text would trigger US-style segregation.

The “weaponisation” fear: Critics and the Court flagged the removal of penalties for fake complaints. Without safeguards, the bench warned the system could be "exploited" for personal vendettas.

What’s next: A new expert committee will rewrite the rules. Until then, the status quo remains.
sound_smarter: This halt will create a massive readiness gap. Universities prepared for the new rules must now scramble back to 2012 standards, leaving administrators in a compliance limbo. The Court is signalling that social engineering fails when it alienates the majority. To survive judicial scrutiny, equity rules must be framed as a shield for all students, not a sword for specific groups.

title: Heavy crude, heavy lifting
text:
Indian refiners are eyeing a return to Venezuelan crude. On Sunday, President Trump claimed that India would start buying, but the actual "pivot" depends on US Treasury rules rather than rhetoric.

The prequel: Last Friday, Acting President Delcy Rodríguez phoned PM Modi to “deepen ties.” Two days later, news emerged that Indian refiners would consider buying Venezuelan crude. This follows a familiar pattern, much the Adani-Embraer deal surfaced almost immediately after Modi’s chat with Lula (we covered it here and here).

Compliance first: Reliance Industries is interested, with a massive caveat. It will buy only if American regulations explicitly permit sales to non-US buyers.

Operational friction: State-run HPCL is staying on the sidelines. While its 301,000 bpd Vizag refinery is technically upgraded for heavy Venezuelan grades, it is sticking to Iraqi Basrah crude to maintain stability during its current ramp-up phase.

The bottleneck: Supply is tight. Most Venezuelan barrels are currently earmarked for the US market, leaving little for Indian buyers regardless of their appetite.
sound_smarter: This is economic statecraft in commodity form. Washington is using its sanctions rulebook as a carrot to pull India away from Russian and Iranian barrels. For refiners, the commercial discount isn't worth the compliance risk until the legal pathway is watertight.
