title: From 50% to 18%
text:
Indian goods just got a whole lot cheaper. On Monday, US President Trump announced that tariffs on Indian goods would be cut from a staggering 50% to 18% after Prime Minister Modi reportedly agreed to buy a lot of stuff from the US and stop buying Russian crude.

The deal: Following a phone call on Monday, Trump announced that India will phase out Russian oil in favor of U.S. and “potentially” Venezuelan crude. Trump claims Modi committed to “BUY AMERICAN” to the tune of USD 500 billion, spanning energy, tech, and coal. India will also move toward zero tariffs and non-tariff barriers on US goods. In exchange, Washington is rescinding a 25% punitive duty and lowering its “reciprocal” tariff from 25% to 18%.

Refinery reality check: While Modi cheered the 18% rate, New Delhi hasn't explicitly confirmed the Russian exit timeline. Indian refiners warn that “winding down” existing contracts will take months.

Devil in the details: Trump’s announcement was low on specifics. We’re still missing a start date for the new rates, a firm deadline for the Russian exit, and a list of exactly which U.S. products India is buying. Crucially, the White House hasn’t yet issued the presidential proclamation or Federal Register notice needed to make any of this binding.
sound_smarter: Implementation is the invisible hurdle. Look at South Korea: they signed a deal in July, but legislative gridlock stalled the rollout. By last week, an impatient Trump was already threatening to snap their tariffs back from 15% to 25%. If India wants to keep its new 18% rate, it needs to move faster than Trump can change his mind.
anchor: Indian goods just got a whole lot cheaper.

title: The fast lane out
text:
India is quietly testing a UPI export, albeit with a different strategy. Reuters reports that the government and the central bank are in talks with Ant International to allow Alipay+ to link with India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) for overseas use. Two government sources confirmed the discussions, which are not yet public.

How it works today: UPI has already been taken abroad through bilateral corridors with countries like Singapore and the United Arab Emirates. These deals are negotiated market by market, with the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) tying up with local payment networks and regulators on settlement, compliance, and access. It works, but it’s slow and bespoke.

What’s different now: Linking UPI to Alipay+ shifts the model from corridors to platforms. One integration could unlock acceptance across multiple countries where Alipay+ already has merchants, giving Indian travellers instant reach without fresh bilateral negotiations.

Why it’s sensitive: Ant International is legally offshore but strategically tied to China’s Alibaba, whose consumer apps – including its payments arm Alipay – have remained banned in India since 2020. Any UPI linkage would therefore be scrutinised by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). The studied silence from regulators reflects political as much as technical caution.
sound_smarter: India wants UPI to travel. Partnering with whoever already owns the pipes may be the fastest way there.

title: The rulebook arrives
text:
India’s labour reform is finally getting its instruction manual. On Monday, the Centre told the Delhi High Court it will finalise the remaining rules to operationalise parts of the Industrial Relations Code by end-February, after petitioners warned the system was running without an instruction book.

Why the court cared: Petitioners argued the Code was “in force”, but key nuts-and-bolts were missing, especially how labour courts or industrial tribunals operate under the new framework, and how members are appointed. The Centre said draft rules have already gone through public consultation, and final rules are imminent.

Reform backstory: Since 2019, India has folded 29 labour laws into four “labour codes.” But the rules are where the real compliance lives: forms, timelines, procedures, and who exercises power.

Federal wrinkle: Labour sits on the Concurrent List. The Centre writes the code; states write their own rules. Expect uneven rollout, especially early on.
sound_smarter: Finalising rules lets New Delhi claim reform without owning enforcement. The hard politics now move to state capitals.
anchor: India’s labour reform is finally getting its instruction

title: Clearer, but not clear
text:
India will buy more, with caveats. On Tuesday, Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal confirmed that a landmark trade deal with the US is coming “shortly” and a joint statement will be released when the final details have been ironed out.

The backdrop: On Monday, Trump announced a massive shift: India will swap Russian oil for US (and “potentially” Venezuelan) crude, commit to buying USD 500 billion in American goods, and dismantle various trade barriers. In return, the US will slash tariffs on Indian goods from a staggering 50% down to 18% (we covered it here).

More deets: On Tuesday, US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer and news outlets reported additional details, including:

- India will drop tariffs on US industrial goods from roughly 13.5% to zero.
- The US gains “limited access” to the Indian agricultural market, though New Delhi is maintaining key protections.
- India will eliminate duties on US tree nuts, fruits, vegetables, wine, and spirits.
- Both nations have reached an agreement on recognising US technical standards
- India plans a gradual ramp-up of purchases in petroleum, aircraft, defence, telecom, and pharmaceuticals to meet that USD 500 billion commitment over five years.
- The deal includes an immediate tariff reduction on American cars.
- India will officially halt Russian oil imports to secure those lower US tariffs.

What’s missing? Greer stayed silent on rice, beef, soybeans, sugar, and dairy. These remain the crown jewels of Indian protectionism – commodities so guarded they were even excluded from India's recent deal with the EU (which we covered here).

Timeline: We still don’t have a start date. Greer mentioned officials are currently “putting terms on paper,” while other US sources hope to wrap up the paperwork this week or the next.
sound_smarter: The devil is in the (missing) details. Until the fine print is public, it’s impossible to tell if this is a genuine structural shift in India-US trade relations or just an expensive temporary truce.

title: The helicopter bet
text:
India’s helicopter ambitions are moving from orders to infrastructure. On Tuesday, Adani Defence & Aerospace and Italy’s Leonardo signed a Memorandum of Understanding to establish an integrated helicopter manufacturing ecosystem in India. The partnership centres on Leonardo’s AW169M and AW109 TrekkerM platforms.

What’s in scope: The plan goes beyond assembly. It includes phased indigenisation, local manufacturing, maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO), and pilot training. The initial focus is military demand, with potential spillover into civil aviation later.

Why it matters: India’s helicopter fleet is tiny for its size, with fewer than 250 helicopters for a population of 1.4 billion. Industry estimates suggest demand of roughly 100 helicopters a year for the next decade, driven largely by the armed forces. Adani Defence CEO Ashish Rajvanshi said the Indian Armed Forces project more than 1,000 helicopters over the next 10 years, a scale that makes local production commercially viable rather than symbolic.

Context: The announcement follows last week’s Adani-Embraer tie-up on regional aircraft manufacturing, which we covered here. Together, the deals signal a broader push to anchor global aerospace OEMs inside India’s supply chains.
sound_smarter: Earlier contracts focused on local content percentages and offsets, often delivered through assembly after the deal was signed. Adani and Leonardo are betting that future demand will favour firms that arrive with full ecosystems already in place.

title: Claude casts a long shadow
text:
Indian IT stocks had their worst day in nearly three years. The trigger: a sharper-than-expected AI leap from Anthropic.

What happened: Shares of Indian IT exporters fell about 6% on Wednesday, tracking a global selloff in software and professional services after Anthropic rolled out new automation tools. NIFTY IT was set for its worst session since May 2022, with all 10 constituents in the red. Persistent Systems dropped 7%, while heavyweights Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys slid over 5%.

The trigger: Anthropic launched 11 plug-ins for its Claude Cowork agent, including a Legal Plugin that automates document review, contract analysis, compliance tracking and basic briefs. Investors fear that similar AI agents could replace the thousands of human employees currently handling routine professional services.

Why it matters: The Indian IT model depends on large workforces and thin margins, and has long absorbed a significant share of India’s engineering graduates each year. Agentic AI does more than just cut client costs. It replaces junior teams, shrinks project sizes, weakens pricing power, and challenges the industry’s function as a large-scale jobs engine. This moment is pivotal not just for strategy, but for how India’s tech workforce is trained, deployed, and valued.
sound_smarter: Indian IT was built on offshore labour arbitrage that doubled as a mass jobs engine. Agentic AI breaks that bargain, forcing firms and engineers to move up the value chain or be priced out.

title: Three’s a crowd
text:
Manipur is back under local control after a year of President’s Rule. Yesterday, Yumnam Khemchand Singh was sworn in as Chief Minister, ending direct administration from New Delhi.

Previously in Manipur: Since May 2023, the state has been torn by ethnic violence, mainly between the Meitei (valley majority) and Kuki-Zo (hill minority). Former Chief Minister N. Biren Singh resigned after becoming a face of the divide, prompting the Centre to step in to prevent deeper institutional collapse.

The new episode: This government is designed to look less like “one-man rule” and more like a negotiated truce.

- Chief Minister: Yumnam Khemchand Singh (Meitei) – A veteran politician pitched as a bridge-builder; he has visited rival relief camps.
- Deputy Chief Minister 1: Nemcha Kipgen (Kuki-Zo) – First Kuki woman in the role, a signal to pull the aggrieved minority back into the system.
- Deputy Chief Minister 2: Losii Dikho (Naga) – Gives the third major bloc a stake so they don’t become collateral damage.

Why now: Direct administration stabilised the state but could not rebuild political legitimacy. Restoring an elected government shifts responsibility back to local actors, spreads political risk across communities, and gives New Delhi distance from day-to-day fallout as Manipur enters a slower, more fragile phase of recovery. A prolonged security vacuum also weakens India’s eastern flank, making indefinite central rule strategically costly.

The man and his plan: Singh is branding this a “mission for reconciliation and restoration.” His 100-day roadmap includes the resettlement of displaced persons, active power-sharing, and reviving the citizen grievance platform, CM da Haisi (“Let’s tell the CM”).
sound_smarter: This is a controlled experiment. For the first time in three years, leaders from warring sides are sitting at the same table. The new leadership inherits a fractured police force, 60,000 displaced people, and deep-seated trauma. Symbolic inclusion in a cabinet is the easy part; the real test is whether this political “reset” can actually manufacture trust on the ground.

title: Didi takes the stand
text:
A Chief Minister is accusing India’s election watchdog of selective scrutiny. West Bengal Chief Minister (CM) Mamata Banerjee personally argued in the Supreme Court on Wednesday to halt the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls, claiming the SIR targets her state ahead of the 2026 elections.

What is SIR: Unlike annual reviews, an intensive revision requires every single voter to be re-verified, often demanding fresh documentation. It’s a massive bureaucratic lift that inevitably triggers “logical discrepancy” flags – often interpreted by parties as a tool for targeted deletion.

The grievance: Banerjee alleged the ECI is rushing “to do something in 2 months which takes 2 years” using trivial errors – minor spelling mismatches or post-marriage surname changes – to disenfranchise legitimate voters. She also questioned why West Bengal is being targeted.

Selective scrutiny: The SIR was initially slated for five states heading to the polls in 2026. However, eyebrows were raised when the ECI postponed the exercise in BJP-ruled Assam while going forward in opposition-held West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, and Kerala (plus Puducherry where the BJP is in an alliance with the government). While Phase 2 now includes BJP strongholds like UP and Gujarat, the timing remains a political lightning rod (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: The Centre’s willingness to weather this pushback suggests a high stakes bet: that the long-term benefit of a revised voter list in these states outweighs the immediate political cost of being accused of electoral rigging.

title: Handshakes now, paperwork later
text:
Details of the India-US trade deal are imminent. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal announced Thursday that the first “tranche” is almost ready, with a joint statement expected within five days (we covered the available details here).

The timeline: While the statement drops next week, the formal legal text will take up to a month and a half. Goyal expects a signature by mid-March.

The implementation gap: The US can cut tariffs via executive order immediately. India, however, must wait for the formal signing to lower its Most-Favoured Nation (MFN) rates, which are standard rates applied to countries that India doesn’t have a preferential trade agreement with. New Delhi requires Cabinet approval and potential legislative tweaks to implement preferential rates and other terms.
sound_smarter: While the administration doesn’t strictly need a green light from Parliament, it must ensure the deal satisfies key domestic interests – specifically the sensitive agriculture sector – without alienating other global trading partners. Fortunately for the BJP, their comfortable majority means they can push forward regardless of the opposition’s noise, provided the deal's merits hold up under scrutiny.
anchor: Details of the India-US trade deal are imminent.

title: When the big boy gets it wrong
text:
IndiGo’s December meltdown is no longer just an aviation mess – it’s now an antitrust problem. On Thursday, India’s antitrust regulator, the Competition Commission of India (CCI), ordered a formal investigation into IndiGo after the airline cancelled over 4,500 flights in early December 2025, stranding tens of thousands of passengers.

The allegation: The CCI suspects IndiGo used its 60% market share to “withhold capacity,” creating artificial scarcity and fare spikes during peak travel season.

Double jeopardy: While the aviation regulator (DGCA) already slapped IndiGo with a USD 2.45 million fine for roster failures (we covered it here), the CCI is hunting for predatory market behaviour. It’s no longer just about stranded passengers, but also a potential monopoly play.

Jurisdictional joust: IndiGo argued the CCI should back off because the DGCA is already on the case. The CCI dismissed this, asserting that sector-specific rules do not grant immunity from competition law.
sound_smarter: Should IndiGo be found guilty by the CCI, competitive dynamics in the market will be shaken up. That’s potentially good news for consumers that benefit from genuine market competition.

title: Not your next Uber
text:
India now has a state-blessed, cooperative answer to Uber. On Thursday, Union Home and Cooperation Minister Amit Shah launched Bharat Taxi, pitching it as a driver-owned, zero-commission ride-hailing platform.

Early traction: After a two-month pilot in Delhi-NCR and Gujarat, Bharat Taxi says it has signed up 300,000 drivers, 100,000 users, and is clocking 10,000 rides a day.

How it works: A zero-commission, surge-free platform where drivers receive the full fare and any surplus is routed back to members. The app supports cars, autorickshaws, and two-wheelers. Since the pilot, just over USD 1 million has been paid directly to drivers, alongside bundled health insurance, accident cover, retirement savings, and physical support centres.

The ecosystem contrast:

- Corporate aggregators like Uber and Ola are investor-owned platforms. Even where they shift to subscriptions, control over pricing, data, and rules stays corporate.

- Software as a Service (SaaS) marketplaces like Rapido monetise access, not ownership. Drivers pay to participate, but don’t share in the profits.

- Cooperative models like Bharat Taxi make drivers members, not users. Fees fund operations and welfare; surplus flows back to those who generate it.
sound_smarter: The gig economy favours platforms over workers. This is an attempt to shift ownership to the people that make the business possible, with protections to boot.

title: A framework, not a finish line
text:
After days of claims, counters, and clarifications, Washington and New Delhi have finally put text on paper. The US-India joint statement confirms this is a framework for an Interim Trade Agreement, not the full trade deal. The document explicitly positions the framework as a bridge to the broader Bilateral Trade Agreement talks launched in February 2025. Politically billed as “historic,” it is, in legal terms, an opening move.

What’s locked in: India commits to eliminating or reducing tariffs on all US industrial goods, alongside cuts on a broad basket of American agricultural and food exports. This formalises what earlier briefings suggested, which we had covered here.

What Washington actually gives: The United States applies a reciprocal 18% tariff on Indian goods for now, with removal explicitly conditional on the interim pact being concluded. It agrees to lift steel, aluminium, and copper tariffs on Indian aircraft and parts, grant India a preferential tariff-rate quota for auto parts, and defer pharmaceutical relief until a Section 232 national security investigation concludes.

Rules, standards, escape hatches: India formally agrees to address long-standing barriers affecting US medical devices, Information and Communication Technology (ICT) goods, food, and agriculture. Rules of origin will be designed to keep third countries out. If either side changes tariffs unilaterally, the other may modify its commitments.

The headline promise: India signals intent, not obligation, to purchase USD 500 billion of US goods over five years, spanning energy, aircraft, graphics processing units (GPU), and coking coal.
sound_smarter: The press release strips away the hype. This was never meant to be a clean, final deal. An interim framework keeps leverage intact as politics and geopolitics remain volatile while negotiations continue.

title: Ringgits, rupees, chips, and more
text:
Prime Minister Modi wrapped his two-day visit to Malaysia on Sunday, his first trip there since upgrading bilateral ties to a "Comprehensive Strategic Partnership" last August.

The joint statement revealed what was discussed during the visit.

The trade play: Both nations are pushing local-currency settlement (INR-MYR) to bypass the dollar. While bilateral trade hit USD 18.6 billion in 2025, the goal is to cut hedging costs for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and grease the wheels for larger importers.

Chip diplomacy: Semiconductors featured extensively in the joint statement, with both sides looking to deepen trade and cooperation as they combine India’s strengths in chip design with Malaysia’s extensive experience in assembly, testing, and packaging.

Digital exports: The push to link India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) with Malaysia’s PayNet serves two goals: boosting tourism spending and exporting India’s digital public infrastructure as a soft-power service.

The tech alignment is official: The joint statement confirmed the launch of the Malaysia-India Digital Council, a body tasked with accelerating cooperation across semiconductors, digital infrastructure, cybersecurity, Artificial Intelligence, and fintech.
sound_smarter: India is trying to build a domestic chip ecosystem. Partnering with Malaysia for its know-how rather than building a siloed ecosystem from scratch is a shortcut to resilience.

title: Qubits being built
text:
India just laid the first brick for its quantum future. On Sunday, Union Minister Jitendra Singh kicked off construction on the 50-acre Amaravati Quantum Valley in Andhra Pradesh, the nation’s first integrated campus for quantum research and manufacturing.

The blueprint: Backed by the USD 662 million National Quantum Mission, the site aims to house the entire value chain, from skill development to hardware. The goal is ambitious: 1,000 physical qubits within eight years and a 2,000-km quantum communication network.

Strategic necessity: Singh framed the tech as a “necessity, not an option,” essential for defence and secure communications. The mission spans 43 institutions across 19 regions, divided into four thematic hubs.

The big picture: The US and China are the global leaders in quantum technology.
sound_smarter: Commercial return on investment is currently a mirage; practical, scalable quantum computers don't exist yet. However, because quantum can theoretically shred modern cryptography, India is investing in defensive research and development.

title: Trade deal, farm veto
text:
India’s interim trade deal with Washington has turned combustible. Farm unions and the opposition are calling for nationwide protests, warning the pact opens the door to US imports that could undercut already fragile farm incomes.

Flashback: The backlash echoes 2020-21, when months-long farmer blockades around Delhi forced the repeal of three farm laws aimed at market deregulation. That episode showed how rapidly farm protests can escalate and box the government in.

Market safeguards: Officials say the current deal excludes imports of staples such as rice, wheat, corn and dairy, while offering duty-free access to the US market for Indian exporters of basmati rice, fruits, spices, coffee and tea.

Not buying it: Farm leaders say the row isn’t just about market access but about uneven competition and quiet openings. Farm rights activist Rakesh Tikait argues Indian growers cannot compete with larger, heavily subsidised US producers. Unions warn that lower tariffs on crude soybean oil, apples and animal feed products could hurt domestic producers, with distillers dried grain imports in particular seen as a threat to maize and oilseed prices. Farmer anxieties have sharpened after US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins publicly celebrated higher US exports and gains for rural America.

Farmers’ demands: The Samyukt Kisan Morcha coalition of unions – which was heavily involved in the 2020-2021 protest – has called nationwide protests for February 12, branding the framework a surrender to US agribusiness. It has also demanded the resignation of Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal and urged the government to walk away from the deal.
sound_smarter: Indian agriculture is both politically powerful and deeply resistant to liberalisation by surprise. Without releasing the fine print and taking farmers into confidence, this deal risks political rejection before it’s even signed.
anchor: India’s interim trade deal with Washington has turned

title: A week’s grace but no exit
text:
West Bengal’s SIR got a little relief. On Monday, the Supreme Court extended West Bengal’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) deadline by one week beyond February 14, while warning that the Court will not create any impediments to the SIR.

The backstory: West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee personally argued in front of the Supreme Court last week to halt the Election Commission’s (ECI) exercise, alleging the state is being unfairly targeted ahead of the 2026 assembly elections (we covered it here). Unlike routine reviews, an SIR requires every single voter to be re-verified, a massive bureaucratic lift ripe for "logical discrepancy" flags.

The Court’s decision: The Court struck a balancing act. It ordered the State to cooperate and maintain order while instructing the ECI to ensure that actual decision-making power remains strictly in the hands of authorised officials.

Logistics over politics: The ECI needs manpower; Bengal offered 8,550 Group B officers. The extra week allows for the screening and training of these new recruits to ensure the job is done.

The limit: In a win for the state, the court clipped the wings of micro-observers — Central Government employees who monitor and report on the SIR process. They may assist, but cannot adjudicate. Final decisions on voter deletions stay with Electoral Registration Officers (EROs), addressing Banerjee’s fear of shadow decision-making by outside observers.
sound_smarter: The extension serves as a pressure valve. While it hands Banerjee and the opposition a minor victory, it ensures the SIR process remains in motion. Since the Centre cannot realistically avoid charges of political manoeuvring, its primary goal now is simply to minimise the blowback.
anchor: West Bengal’s SIR got a little relief. On

title: Liberté, égalité, strategic autonomy
text:
France and India are coming together to plan the future. On Tuesday, the Ministry of External Affairs announced French President Emmanuel Macron will land in India on February 17 for a three-day tour to India.

The backstory: India and France have a uniquely deep strategic partnership that dates back to 1998. Unlike other Western powers, France remained a consistent partner even when India faced international sanctions, building a relationship based on strategic autonomy. To put it plainly, neither country wants to be a junior partner to a superpower.

The itinerary: Macron will arrive in Mumbai to launch the India-France Year of Innovation before heading to New Delhi for the AI Impact Summit on February 19 that’s expected to focus on practical applications of AI (a direction Delhi is pursuing, we covered it here).

The strategy: The visit leans on "Horizon 2047", a 25-year roadmap designed to align Paris and New Delhi on defence co-production, AI governance, and maritime security in the Indo-Pacific.

Beyond the banquet: The trip will likely deliver updates on defence co-development and a heavy emphasis on critical technology research.
sound_smarter: Macron and Modi are signalling where the partnership is headed. India–France ties are shifting from buyer–seller defence deals to jointly shaping rules, standards, and R&D ecosystems that will define both technology and security policy.
anchor: France and India are coming together to plan

title: Mediterranean moves
text:
Athens and New Delhi are flanking rivals. On Monday, India’s Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and Greek counterpart Nikolaos-Georgios Dendias met in New Delhi to cement the India-Greece Strategic Partnership.

The alignment: Both nations signed a Joint Declaration of Intent to partner India’s Aatmanirbhar Bharat (self-reliance) goals with Greece’s Agenda 2030 military reforms.

The goal: Joint production of advanced military tech.

The roadmap: A five-year plan for industrial cooperation is now in play, alongside a 2026 Military Cooperation Plan for joint exercises. The Greek delegation has also scouted for talent at defence startups and state-run firms in Bengaluru.

The trend: This follows recent Indian defence pushes with France (see entry above) and the EU (we covered it here), signalling New Delhi's growth as a defence provider (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: This is a counter-alignment. As Turkey eyes a defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia (signed September 2025), India is flanking Islamabad by deepening ties with Turkey’s primary rival, Greece

title: Spreading the minerals risk
text:
India is shopping for insurance against mineral shocks. New Delhi is in talks with Brazil, Canada, France, and Netherlands to jointly explore, extract, process, and recycle lithium and rare-earths.

Why now: India’s energy transition means moving from fossil-heavy power and transport to renewables, electric vehicles, grid-scale storage, and defence electronics, all of which are magnet and mineral-intensive. Today, that supply chain runs largely through China, which dominates rare-earth processing and supplies nearly 90% of India’s magnets.

Partner logic: Brazil and Canada offer depth in mining and resource development. France and the Netherlands add strengths in processing technologies, advanced manufacturing, and long-term capital. India is pairing geology with technical expertise.

Constraints, acknowledged: Building mines and processing capacity is slow and uncertain. Exploration takes years, permits are hard to come by, and viable deposits are never guaranteed. That’s why India is spreading bets early.

Policy push: In 2023, India classified 20+ minerals as “critical” to its aim of being self-reliant. In November 2025, it approved an USD 800mn incentive scheme targeting 6,000 tonnes of permanent magnets annually within seven years. The Dedicated Rare-Earth Corridors announced in this year’s Budget aim to cluster mining, processing, R&D, and manufacturing, shortening timelines, easing approvals, and giving investors predictable infrastructure.
sound_smarter: It’s nearly impossible to beat China at scale, which is why this is about building 10-15% global capacity to gain leverage, assuming India can keep policy steady, clear projects fast, and convert defence and renewables demand into anchor contracts.
anchor: India is shopping for insurance against mineral shocks.

title: Takedowns in a jiffy
text:
Deepfakes must be removed ASAP. On Tuesday, India’s IT Ministry hit the "fast forward" button on internet regulation, mandating that social media platforms remove flagged deepfakes within just three hours.

The context: India is currently a global hotspot for deepfakes, with AI-generated videos of politicians and celebrities frequently going viral. The 2021 IT Rules originally gave platforms a 36-hour window to comply with government takedown orders; as of February 20, that window shrinks by 90%.

The “synthetic” definition: For the first time, the law formally defines “synthetically generated information.” It covers any AI-altered audio or video that looks real, though it carves out “good-faith” edits like colour correction or accessibility tweaks.

Operational squeeze: Large platforms (like Meta and X) must now force users to declare AI content at upload and use automated tools to verify those claims. They must also embed permanent, unremovable metadata to trace the content's origin.

The catch: A three-hour deadline is a logistical nightmare for human review. In practice, this forces platforms to rely on aggressive AI filters that often struggle with satire or nuance, leading to a “delete first, apologise later” culture.
sound_smarter: By making the timeline physically impossible for human legal teams to meet, the government is forcing platforms to hand over moderation to automated algorithms. The pressure to meet this deadline while ensuring it doesn’t worsen the user experience will force innovation in automated content moderation.

title: Pencil still out on the historic deal
text:
The US–India trade deal is being rewritten in real-time. On Wednesday, within 24 hours of its grand unveiling, Washington quietly revised its official factsheet, replacing firm promises for intentions and deleting entire categories of goods.

The quiet walk-back: Several headline-grabbing claims vanished. “Certain pulses” (lentils and chickpeas) were deleted from the tariff-cut list, and the claim that India “will remove” its digital services taxes was downgraded to a mere "commitment to negotiate."

Why pulses matter: In India, pulses are a political third rail. They are the primary protein for hundreds of millions and the livelihood for 26 million farmers. Any hint of cutting protections for local growers can spark the kind of massive rural protests that forced the Modi government into embarrassing legislative U-turns in 2021. Farmers have already called for a strike against the deal (we covered it here).

The USD 500 billion math: The eye-popping USD 500 billion purchase figure was softened from a “commitment” to “intends.” While the joint statement suggests a five-year window, the White House version now lacks any timeline at all. Currently, India runs a USD 41 billion goods surplus with the US. Importing USD 100 billion a year in American energy and tech would flip India’s trade balance – a move the Indian private sector, not the government, would ultimately have to bankroll.

The Russia wrinkle: The White House factsheet explicitly linked tariff relief to India halting purchases of Russian oil, yet the official joint statement is silent on the matter. The real test will be whether Indian refiners quietly rebalance sourcing.

The status check: Both sides are calling this an “interim agreement,” which is diplomatic code for “we agreed on the easy stuff and are still fighting over the rest.”
sound_smarter: This isn’t a trade deal (yet), it’s a framework for one. Until legal text is signed and tabled, every headline number and tariff promise remains negotiable, especially promises that touch on sensitive sectors like agriculture.
anchor: The US–India trade deal is being rewritten in

title: Importing trouble
text:
Indian corn and soy prices dropped 10% and 4% this week as traders priced in a flood of cheaper American imports ahead of a finalized US-India trade deal.

The price of anticipation: Traders are betting that future supply – specifically for animal feed and cooking oil – will be cheaper and more plentiful. Instead of buying now, they are sitting on their hands, waiting for the discount and making prices drop.

A political tinderbox: Indian agriculture is a world of smallholders, not industrial giants. Farm incomes are the most explosive variable in Indian politics. When prices dip, farmer groups don't just complain; they protest, and those protests frequently force the government into humiliating policy reversals. Farmers have already called for a strike against the deal for today (we covered it here).

Connecting the dots: This market reaction explains why the White House recently scrubbed “pulses” (lentils) from its official trade factsheet. If the mere hint of a deal can sink corn and soy, a formal commitment to import pulses – a daily staple and protein source for millions – would be a political disaster for the ruling party.
sound_smarter: Market stability remains the real constraint on any trade deal. If New Delhi’s trade openings cause domestic prices to crash, the resulting political backlash from the powerful agricultural sector will likely force a reversal of those policies, or a softening as the edits have shown.

title: Harvest of discontent
text:
Indian farmers burned copies of the interim India-US trade deal in protests nationwide on Thursday, alleging New Delhi surrendered rural interests. Opposition parties amplified the protests outside the parliament.

The terms: Under the interim deal, India will eliminate or reduce tariffs on a wide range of US food and agricultural products, including dried distillers’ grains (DDGs), red sorghum for animal feed, tree nuts, fresh and processed fruit, soybean oil, and wine and spirits.

Political scarring: The backlash echoes 2020-21, when months-long farmer blockades around Delhi forced the repeal of three farm laws aimed at market deregulation.

Pushing back: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal claims that 90-95% of domestic produce is shielded. Farmers argue that the entry of US agricultural products could depress local prices.
sound_smarter: Modi is in a tough spot. He must choose between pacifying high-voltage farm interests at home or keeping Indian industry competitive against neighbours who would leap at any gap left by a collapsed US deal.

title: Neighbour reset
text:
The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) secured a landslide victory Friday in the first elections since the 2024 uprising, crushing an 11-party Islamist alliance. Leader Tarique Rahman – son of the late former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia – now inherits a fractured nation after 17 years in self-exile.

The diplomatic reset: Prime Minister Modi congratulated Rahman, emphasizing support for a “democratic, progressive, and inclusive Bangladesh.” This follows a December meeting between Minister of External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Rahman, another sign New Delhi is moving past its long reliance on Hasina.

Lingering friction: The relationship is on a knife-edge. Dhaka wants Hasina extradited for crimes against humanity; New Delhi is still sheltering her. Add to this the BNP’s interest in the China-backed Teesta River project near the sensitive Siliguri Corridor, and the reset looks increasingly uphill.

Old ghosts: India remains wary of the BNP’s history with border security and the safety of the Hindu minority, while many in Dhaka remain embittered by India’s unwavering support for the previous regime.
sound_smarter: A successful reset would be purely transactional and fragile. As long as India shelters Hasina while the BNP demands her extradition, New Delhi is merely managing a cold peace as a holding action to keep Dhaka from pivoting fully into China’s orbit.

title: The hit that missed
text:
Delhi's denial just hit a courtroom wall. On Friday, Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to assassinate Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York City.

The target: Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice, has campaigned globally for Khalistan, a proposed sovereign Sikh state carved from India's Punjab. India designated him a terrorist in 2020. He has organised rallies, offered rewards for anti-India graffiti, and warned Indo-Canadian Hindus to leave Canada.

The plot: Prosecutors say Indian intelligence official Vikash Yadav, employed by India's Cabinet Secretariat, which houses the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), recruited Gupta in May 2023. He arranged USD100,000 for a hitman who turned out to be a DEA undercover officer. A USD15,000 advance was delivered. Delhi has dissociated itself from any plot, calling it against government policy.

Two allies, two playbooks: In September 2023, then Canadian Prime Minister Trudeau accused Delhi in parliament of involvement in the assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar. The fallout was swift: India expelled Canadian diplomats, suspended visa services, and dismissed the allegations as politically motivated. Ottawa responded in kind, expelling Indian diplomats and launching a criminal investigation. Washington chose a different path entirely. Rather than go public, it ran a sting, built a federal case, and let the courtroom do the talking.

💡 Sound smarter: The guilty plea hands Washington courtroom-backed leverage, which is something Ottawa never had and makes the situation invariably harder for Delhi to dismiss. Given ongoing efforts to finalise the India-US trade deal, the likelihood that Washington employs this leverage is low… but not zero.
anchor: Delhi's denial just hit a courtroom wall. On

title: Seoul searching for critical minerals
text:
India and South Korea wrapped up the 6th Foreign Policy and Security Dialogue (FPSD) in Seoul last Friday, shifting the focus from pandemic recovery to economic security.

The agenda: Discussions covered the whole gamut of ties, but the real weight was on shipbuilding, economic security cooperation, critical minerals, and AI.

Evolution of a dialogue: The FPSD is a barometer for Indian and South Korean priorities. In 2014, it was about defence; by 2023, it was post-COVID resilience. In 2026, the focus is economic security.
sound_smarter: New Delhi’s aggressive push for critical mineral partnerships is a direct response to China’s export controls. By courting Seoul (and many others as we’ve covered here), India is seeking investment to boost domestic production and partners for overseas projects.

title: Day 1 stumble
text:
India's AI Impact Summit opened Monday with long queues, overcrowding, and organizational chaos at the New Delhi venue, undercutting the very tech competence it was meant to project.

Day 1 meltdown: Attendees reported poor signage, limited seating, and unclear entry procedures. Some were ejected from exhibition halls mid-visit for security sweeps ahead of VIP arrivals. Journalists juggled conflicting QR codes and physical passes that weren't ready. Several Day 2 panelists were still awaiting confirmation of their sessions.

The stakes: This is the first time the global AI summit has been held in the developing world. Modi's government is using it to position India as a voice for the Global South on AI policy. Roughly 250,000 attendees, including many heads of state and industry titans, are expected through February 20.

Course correction: IT Minister Vaishnaw acknowledged the mess on Tuesday, announcing a "war room" to handle complaints. "About 70,000 people have attended the summit and we can say the organisation is very slow," he said. Day 2 ran noticeably smoother.
sound_smarter: India pitched this summit as proof it can lead on AI governance, then couldn't manage a queue. Day 1 gave critics an easy headline, and first impressions at marquee events tend to stick.

title: AI’s utility bill
text:
IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw projected USD 200 billion in AI and data infrastructure investment over the next two years (USD 70B already committed) on Tuesday at the India AI Impact Summit. The goal is a full-stack domestic cycle spanning hardware, software, and the energy-hungry plumbing in between, alongside a long-term tax holiday for companies that set up data centres.

The background: This aligns with the 2025-2026 Economic Survey, which explicitly rejects the prestige race of frontier models (ee covered it here). India wants to be the world’s AI utility provider. By designating data centres as “Strategic National Infrastructure” and offering tax holidays until 2047, New Delhi is building an AI ecosystem with a focus on frugal, sector-specific applications rather than resource-heavy chatbots.

The diplomatic pivot: India is pushing a “Global AI Commons,” a shared repository of use-cases. It is a strategic move to shape global norms around affordability rather than just raw model power.
sound_smarter: Data centres are power and water hogs. Whether India’s AI push succeeds depends on creating physical infrastructure to fix grid stability or cooling water shortages in a warming subcontinent.

title: HAMMER time
text:
Prime Minister Modi and President Macron upgraded bilateral ties to a "Special Global Strategic Partnership" on Tuesday, moving beyond just trade to co-manufacturing everything from Everest-bound helicopters to AI health tech.

The hardware: The duo inaugurated an Airbus H125 helicopter – the Everest-capable helicopter that both sides are targeting for export – assembly line in Karnataka and greenlit a BEL-Safran joint venture to manufacture HAMMER precision-guided missiles in India. This follows the defense ministry’s recent approval to buy 114 more Rafale jets.

The soft power play: Beyond the bombs and birds, the "India-France Year of Innovation 2026" was launched, focusing on AI in health and digital science. A new Swami Vivekananda Cultural Centre will also open in France.

Strategic signaling: By labeling this "Special Global," India puts France on par with its top-tier Japan and US relationships.
sound_smarter: India is leveraging France as a high-tech corridor, securing sovereign capabilities in renewable energy and defense that don't come with the geopolitical strings often attached to US or Chinese tech exports.

title: Nicobar of time
text:
The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has cleared the INR 900 billion (USD 11 billion) Great Nicobar mega-project, ruling that strategic necessity outweighs the "half-baked" procedural objections of critics.

The ruling: On Monday, the NGT dismissed challenges to the 2022 environmental clearance, relying on a High-Powered Committee to declare that adequate safeguards are already in place. The project – a transhipment hub, airport, and township – can now proceed, provided it meets "full and strict compliance" with approval conditions.

Strategic pull: Located near the Malacca Strait, the hub aims to break India's dependence on foreign transhipment ports (like Colombo or Singapore) and counter China's network of military and commercial facilities by firming up India's presence in the eastern Indian Ocean. The bench highlighted the strategic benefits of a presence in the area to counter pressure from foreign countries and the benefits of creating an economic hub.

Ecological brawl: The plan is to construct the project near Galathea Bay, which is a biodiversity hotspot and a disaster-prone zone. Critics warn that habitat fragmentation and light pollution for nesting leatherback turtles cannot be “mitigated” away by conditional paperwork.
sound_smarter: By inserting strategic considerations into an ecological issue, the judiciary has handed the government a master key. Expect future infrastructure and critical mineral projects to lead with national security to bypass green concerns.

title: The common man’s compute
text:
India is using its first AI summit on Global South soil to argue that the world's next AI layer should be built for everyone.

The pitch: An AI Commons, a shared pool of multilingual models, open datasets, and compute resources designed for economies that can't afford Big Tech's price tag.

Why now: Frontier AI is an English-language, US-China duopoly. Models are trained on English-heavy datasets, priced for markets that can afford expensive compute, and built as closed black boxes whose code nobody can fully examine. The problem isn't technical; It's about who controls AI and whose biases get baked in invisibly.

India's credential: This isn't a new push. Aadhaar, UPI, and India Stack showed that open, interoperable digital infrastructure can scale to billions. This year’s Economic Survey made a similar argument for AI specifically: skip the mega-models, build small open-weight systems for real use cases, and layer an "AI-OS" onto India Stack so startups aren't burning billions on compute (we covered it here). New Delhi wants to run the same play globally and host the proof of concept.

What India is proposing: A funding facility where nations contribute data, compute, or use-case development rather than building everything independently. The goal is to create affordable, locally relevant AI deployable in public services, education, and rural economies across the Global South.

The catch: Open infrastructure has a complicated track record. GNU/Linux democratised computing, then powered the corporate giants who built walled gardens on top of it. Wikipedia is the rare exception that held the line.
sound_smarter: The real test isn't whether India can build an AI Commons – that part is easy. It's whether it can remain a digital public good rather than an engine for walled gardens.

title: Voltage over vendettas
text:
India is swallowing its pride to keep the power coming. Yesterday, New Delhi began easing post-2020 restrictions that effectively froze Chinese suppliers out of public procurement, finally unblocking a backlog of stalled energy projects.

Background: Following a deadly border clash in 2020, India mandated that any Chinese bidder on public contracts register with a government committee and secure political and security clearances. This effectively locked Chinese firms out of a government contract market estimated at over USD 700 billion.

The pivot: State-run firms can now import critical power-transmission components from China without the standard government “Mother May I.” A similar temporary waiver for coal-sector equipment is reportedly under review.

Desperate measures: The move is a nod to reality. India faces a 40% shortfall in transformers and reactors over the next three years. Without the Chinese hardware, the 2030 goal of 500 GW non-fossil capacity is little more than a pipe dream.

The national interest: By framing this as a targeted waiver, the government is signalling that infrastructure bottlenecks now outweigh border anxieties that have cooled. Earlier reporting suggests that the government was considering scrapping the restrictions following a landmark meeting between top leaders where both nations agreed to foster deeper commercial ties as shifting global trade pressures (aka Trump’s tariffs) make regional cooperation a necessity.
sound_smarter: While cheaper parts and faster timelines offer a quick win, the long-term risk is twofold: local manufacturers may never catch up, and plugging a rival’s tech into the national grid invites obvious security headaches. The real question is whether this is a temporary bridge or a quiet admission that Chinese dominance is simply irreplaceable.

title: Pulling power
text:
India wants to stop mining for others and start manufacturing for itself. Mining minister Kishan Reddy said the country aims to have production of rare earth permanent magnets by year-end, in partnership with the private sector.

Why this matters: Neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) magnets are inside every electric vehicle, wind turbine, and modern weapons system. India's consumption is expected to double by 2030. China controls 90% of global processing, and when it restricted shipments last year, governments and industries worldwide found themselves with no alternative. For India, the exposure was acute: defence supply chains and green energy ambitions both run on these magnets.

The plan: In November 2025, New Delhi approved an USD 800 million programme to build an end-to-end rare earth permanent magnet manufacturing ecosystem. This year’s Budget (which we covered here) complemented this with dedicated rare earth corridors focused on mining, processing, research, and manufacturing.

The hard part: India has the ore but not the industrial stack. Converting raw rare earths into finished magnets requires the kind of chemical and manufacturing expertise China spent decades building as a strategic choice. New Delhi is betting on up to five private sector partners, selected through global competitive bidding and supported by capital subsidies and production-linked incentives, to close that gap. That is an approach untested at scale.
sound_smarter: India's rare earth play isn't really about mining. It's about processing, the step China weaponised last year. If India can crack that, it stops being a raw material exporter and starts being a supply chain alternative with a credibility advantage China no longer has: a partner that won't use market dominance as political leverage.

title: Silicon subcontinent
text:
India’s AI Impact Summit turned into a deals extravaganza. Domestic titans and global players are racing to build the country into an AI services powerhouse, backed by aggressive tax breaks.

The heavy hitters: Reliance and Jio are leading the charge with a massive USD 109.8 billion seven-year commitment to build AI and data infrastructure. Not to be outdone, the Adani Group pledged USD 100 billion by 2035 for green-energy data centers, claiming this will trigger a USD 250 billion wider ecosystem.

Global and local plays: Microsoft is on track to invest USD 50 billion by 2030 to expand AI to Global South countries, while Yotta Data Services is dropping USD 2 billion to build one of Asia's largest AI computing hubs using Nvidia's latest Blackwell Ultra chips. Meanwhile, Tata Consultancy secured OpenAI as its data centre customer, and infrastructure giant Larsen & Toubro is partnering with Nvidia to build AI-ready infrastructure.

The sweetener: To keep the momentum, the government announced a 21-year tax holiday for cloud service providers setting up shop in India earlier during the summit (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: While the capital is flowing, the resources might not. Data centers are power-hungry and water-intensive. India has a roadmap for boosting non-fossil energy but none for water management, which risks parching already water-stressed cities.

title: Friends with blueprints
text:
India and Israel signed a defence Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in Tel Aviv on Thursday, a move designed to institutionalise cooperation between their private companies in weapons development.

- The agreement arrives just ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s expected visit to Israel on February 25.

The backdrop: Since establishing full ties in 1992, defence has been the bedrock of the relationship. India originally turned to Israel to diversify away from its heavy dependence on Russian arms, while Israel found a massive, reliable customer for its high-tech sensors and drones.

The shift: The buyer-seller era is ending. Under its “Make in India” policy, New Delhi now demands that foreign partners manufacture equipment locally. This week's seminar, involving 30 Indian and 26 Israeli firms, signals a pivot toward joint ventures and co-development, highlighted by the signing of the defence MOU.

Strategic timing: Following the October 7 attacks, Israel has sought to surge its defence exports, while India is racing to modernise its military amid regional tensions. Strengthening these ties now ensures a steady pipeline of technology regardless of global supply chain shocks.
sound_smarter: The Indian defence market is moving from buyer-seller transactions to institutionalised industrial partnerships but India’s complex procurement rules remain a hurdle. Success depends on whether Israeli firms are truly willing to share intellectual property to meet India’s domestic manufacturing mandates.

title: Day 151
text:
India's Washington-bound trade delegation never boarded its flight. New Delhi pulled back Sunday after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's “Liberation Day” tariffs, the legal scaffolding the entire India-US interim deal was built on.

What the court did: In a 6-3 ruling on February 20, the court held that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), a 1977 emergency law, does not authorise the president to impose tariffs. The word “tariff” does not appear in the statute.

What India had on the table: An interim deal nearly a year in the making, and one that both governments had celebrated publicly as a diplomatic win. Washington would cut tariffs on select Indian exports to 18%; India would signal intent to purchase USD 500 billion in American purchases over five years, covering energy, aircraft, precious metals, and technology, which we covered here. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal had pencilled in an April launch. No new date for the visit has been decided.

India's problem now: Trump didn't stand down; he pivoted. Within hours of the ruling, he invoked Section 122 of the 1974 Trade Act, a temporary balance-of-payments provision that allows the president to impose a flat tariff of up to 15% on all countries for 150 days. Trump immediately hit the ceiling. India's negotiated rate was 18%, so it is paying less right now. But this is a placeholder: Section 301 investigations already underway could restore country-specific rates within months, with no statutory ceiling. India's concessions remain on the table; the tariff relief may not.

Silver lining, maybe: India could slow-play its USD 500 billion purchasing pledges while Washington scrambles to stabilise deals with dozens of countries simultaneously. New Delhi has leverage it didn't have last week.
sound_smarter: The real risk isn't 15% for 150 days. Section 301 investigations already underway could replace it with tariffs that have no ceiling and no expiry. No one knows what Day 151 looks like.
anchor: India's Washington-bound trade delegation never boarded its flight.

title: Chipping at the Great Wall
text:
India has officially joined Pax Silica, a US-led initiative designed to ringfence semiconductor and AI supply chains from Chinese dominance, on Friday. The initiative spans cooperation on critical minerals to semiconductor fabrication to AI infrastructure.

The roster: New Delhi joins a heavy-hitting signatory list including Japan, South Korea, Singapore, and the UAE. Noticeably, the EU and Taiwan are participating as non-signatories.

- Notably, India was not part of the founding group when Pax Silica launched in December 2025. Its absence was linked to trade tensions with Washington, which improved just this month (we covered the interim trade deal here).

The Voldemort approach: While official statements avoided naming China, US Under Secretary Jacob Helberg slammed “weaponized dependency” and “blackmail,” clear shorthand for Beijing’s grip on critical minerals.

India’s multi-track mind: Joining the club is only part of the play. New Delhi is simultaneously hunting bilateral deals with Brazil, South Korea, and Canada to jointly explore, extract, process, and recycle lithium and rare-earths (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Pax Silica is a non-binding declaration with a crowded table. Operationalizing it will be a nightmare compared to the nimble, bilateral mineral deals India is signing on the side. Instead, see this as a low-cost diplomatic nod to Washington (with potential upside) while India leans on direct partnerships that are more likely to bear fruit.

title: Mining for Friends
text:
India rolled out the red carpet for Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva at Rashtrapati Bhavan this weekend, a full state welcome that signalled New Delhi's intent to treat Brazil as more than a distant partner.

Resource play: Central to this visit was a landmark mining and minerals pact focused on iron ore and critical minerals. It provides a mutual win, securing India's supply chain for its massive steel and manufacturing push while offering Brazil the scale of long-term, reliable demand.

Trade ambition: Bilateral trade stood at USD 15.2 billion in 2025. Building on this momentum, Prime Minister Modi set an ambitious USD 20 billion trade target to be met within five years, signalling that while tech and digital collaboration are on the horizon, raw commodities will anchor the relationship for now.
sound_smarter: As major powers compete over supply chains and critical minerals, India is looking to reduce dependency on any single partner, which is why it’s aggressively pursuing bilateral deals like this one that are easier to operationalize than multilateral ones, like the Pax SIlica (which we covered above).

title: AI for the global family
text:
The AI Impact Summit wrapped Saturday with the New Delhi Declaration, a high-level pitch to ensure AI adoption helps everyone, especially those in the Global South.

Democratic diffusion: The centerpiece is a voluntary Charter for the Democratic Diffusion of AI. It aims to lower the barrier to entry by promoting access to foundational models and supporting locally relevant innovation.

Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam: Invoking the “world is one family” philosophy, the Declaration frames “meaningful and affordable connectivity” as a necessity for deploying AI rather than a luxury. It specifically champions open-source AI and wide-scale diffusion of AI use cases as the engines driving economic and social development.

The AI Commons: To move beyond prose, the Declaration proposes the voluntary “Global AI Impact Commons,” a practical repository intended to help countries replicate successful AI use cases across borders (we covered the details here).
sound_smarter: Declarations following multilateral summits often talk a big game, but the real signal is in the money. We’ll know this isn't just fluff if and when the government allocates hard cash to operationalize the AI Commons.

title: One doctrine to fight them all
text:
India has unveiled PRAHAAR (Policy for Response Against Hostile Activities and Radicalism), its first comprehensive national counter-terrorism policy.

What’s new: The framework brings intelligence agencies, police, and prosecutors under one coordinated system. The goal is to stop attacks early, investigate faster, and secure convictions more reliably.

Threat map: PRAHAAR focuses on cross-border militancy, encrypted messaging, crypto funding, drones, and CBRNED (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, explosive, digital) risks. Delhi is preparing for future threats that are digital, remote, and harder to trace.

Legal reset: Prosecutors are involved from the start. Terror cases are meant to survive court scrutiny, not just dominate headlines.

Political positioning: The document stresses zero tolerance while rejecting religious profiling.

Centre-state wiring: Real-time intelligence sharing between federal agencies and state police is now formal policy, not a system that relies on interpersonal ties.

The bigger shift: For decades, India relied on agency-by-agency responses. PRAHAAR replaces that with a single national playbook.
sound_smarter: The Government of India is making it clear that security policy will now run from the centre. The "zero tolerance, no profiling" framing gives PRAHAAR credibility both in domestic courts and in international counterterrorism conversations. For telecoms, fintech, and data-heavy firms, security gains will come with paperwork.

title: Goodbye, Lutyens
text:
India's presidential palace has a new face. President Droupadi Murmu on Monday unveiled a bust of Chakravarti Rajagopalachari at Rashtrapati Bhavan. The bust replaces that of Edwin Lutyens, the British architect who designed the building and much of the capital around it, an area still colloquially known as Lutyens' Delhi.

The symbolism is layered: Rajagopalachari, better known as Rajaji, was the only Indian to serve as Governor-General. He occupied the same building from 1948 until 1950, when India became a republic and the role was abolished. He placed a portrait of Gandhi in his rooms when he moved in. Prime Minister Modi called the replacement an act of “mental decolonisation.”

The pattern: In 2022, the ceremonial boulevard outside Rashtrapati Bhavan, Rajpath (King's Way), also designed by Lutyens, was renamed to Kartavya Path (Path of Duty). The same year, the Indian Navy replaced the St. George's Cross on its ensign with the seal of Maratha emperor Shivaji, who built one of India's first indigenous naval forces to resist European colonial powers in the 17th century. Monday's bust replacement is part of a systematic effort to strip colonial symbols from India's most visible institutions.
sound_smarter: This is more than domestic politics. Each colonial symbol Modi retires sends a signal to the Global South that India has arrived as a civilisational power, not just an emerging market. Washington and Brussels may shrug, but for countries that lived under the same empires, it resonates.

title: A little less turbulent
text:
Canada launched legal proceedings to revoke Tahawwur Hussain Rana’s citizenship on Tuesday, a calculated move arriving just days before Prime Minister Mark Carney’s scheduled visit to India.

Who is Rana: A Pakistan-born businessman who obtained Canadian citizenship in 2001, Rana is accused by Indian authorities of helping orchestrate the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks. Following his 2025 extradition from the US, he is currently in Indian custody awaiting trial.

What’s the basis: Canada is not acting on terror charges. Immigration authorities (IRCC) allege Rana committed “serious and deliberate deception” by lying about his residency details on his citizenship application.

Long-running tension: India has long complained that Canada gives space to activists and groups it sees as anti-India or extremist. Canada responds that its laws protect speech and require strong evidence for criminal action.
sound_smarter: This is an effort to ensure Carney’s landing in India is a little less turbulent. By targeting Rana’s legal status now, the Carney administration is signaling a willingness to cooperate on high-profile security cases without explicitly folding on its broader judicial principles.

title: What’s in a name?
text:
Kerala has a new name. The BJP-led Union Cabinet approved renaming the state “Keralam” on Tuesday, nearly two years after the state's own CPI(M) – the Communist Party of India (Marxist) – government passed a resolution demanding it, just in time for assembly elections in 2026.

Why Keralam, and what happens next: India's states were drawn on linguistic lines in 1956. In Malayalam, the state has always been “Keralam.” The Constitution's First Schedule, which lists all states by name, never reflected that. Tuesday's Cabinet approval kicks off a constitutional formality: the President refers the bill to Kerala's legislature for their views, then Parliament votes. With both the state and centre aligned, the rename is as good as done.

The politics: The CPI(M) government passed the original resolution in 2024 on linguistic grounds, arguing the Constitution should reflect the state's Malayalam name. The BJP-led Centre approved it, with PM Modi calling it part of “efforts to strengthen the connection with our glorious culture.” BJP Kerala president Rajeev Chandrasekhar called it a “privilege” his party could “initiate” the renaming, curious framing for a bill the CPI(M) moved first.
sound_smarter: The CPI(M) wanted a linguistic correction; the BJP wants a civilisational statement. Modi's “our glorious culture” does exactly that, quietly reframing a regional identity question into a national cultural project. No policy changes, no money moves, no lives altered. But in an election year, a rename can do more work than a budget line.

title: Hi, Modi—Bibi
text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s two-day visit to Israel has turned a decade of "friendship" into a formal, top-tier alliance. By upgrading ties to a Special Strategic Partnership, India now holds an elite status Israel usually reserves for its allies, such as the US and Germany.

The iron backbone: India is folding Israeli tech, including the Iron Dome and Arrow interceptor, into Sudarshan Chakra, its planned indigenous missile shield. A USD 10 billion "Make in India" defence pact is the target.

Laser focused: Talks are underway for the co-production of the Iron Beam, Israel’s 100kW laser-based defence system.

The Hexagon play: Netanyahu unveiled a "Hexagon of Alliances" linking India, Israel, Greece, and Cyprus with moderate Arab and African states, as a counterweight to what he called the "radical Shia axis" (Iran and its proxies) and an "emerging radical Sunni axis." It also gives a boost to the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC).

The balancing act: Modi remains the master of de-hyphenation. He received a standing ovation at the Knesset for standing by Israel against terror, yet in the same breath, backed the Gaza Peace Initiative and called for a "just and durable peace" for Palestinians.
sound_smarter: The Hexagon may look like Netanyahu's grand vision, but India is already laying the groundwork. A defence pact with Greece signed just two weeks ago, which we covered here, means New Delhi is threading the same alliance quietly, on its own terms, without formally joining anyone's "axis."

title: The growth deflation
text:
India is launching a revised national account series this Friday, to better reflect economic reality.

The methodology shift: The Ministry of Statistics (MoSPI) is ditching single deflation for double deflation, which separately adjusts input and output prices to capture real value added.The price basket expands from 180 items to 600, drawing from both the consumer price index (CPI) and wholesale price index (WPI) series. The base year moves from 2011-12 to 2022-23.

The reputational hit: The IMF graded India's national accounts a "C" in late 2025. For a country marketing itself as a top investment destination, that is a liability.

The ‘real’ problem: Critics argued that the WPI-only approach artificially inflated growth figures when global commodity prices dropped but domestic consumer prices held.
sound_smarter: The revised numbers may actually show slower growth, but for investors and policymakers who have long suspected the gap, credible data is worth more than flattering data.
anchor: India is launching a revised national account series

title: Modi-Bibi’s 27-deal finale
text:
After a first day defined by defense hardware (we covered it here), Prime Minister Modi spent Day 2 institutionalising ties through 27 new agreements spanning labor, payments, and tech.

Manpower: India will send 50,000 workers to Israel over five years. This deal solves a critical labour drought in Israel’s construction and nursing sectors.

Digital rails: India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI), the world's largest real-time payment system, is launching in Israel. This allows Indian tourists and businesses to pay via QR code, bypassing Western credit card networks.

Agri-diplomacy: The Centres of Excellence network that facilitate the transfer of Israeli agri-technologies will expand to 100 hubs, along with the launch of a Villages of Excellence that will bring technologies to the grassroots level.

Cyber security: An India-Israel Centre of Excellence in Cybersecurity will be established in India to facilitate cooperation on cybersecurity, an area where Israel has established itself as a global leader.
sound_smarter: India’s non-alignment streak continues. New Delhi runs the same playbook with every volatile partner: separate the economic from the political, bank the gains, and let others argue about the contradictions.

title: Draft ‘mother of all deals’ released
text:
On Friday, the Ministry of Commerce released the draft India-EU Free Trade Agreement, revealing a ‘Most Favoured Nation’ (MFN) pact that prevents either side from offering better tariff deals to third parties for five years.

MFN lock-in: Both sides plan to grant each other Most Favoured Nation status that prevents either side from offering better terms to third parties for five years. That means if India cuts a better deal with the UK or UAE, the EU gets those same perks automatically.

By the numbers: India will slash tariffs on 96.6% of EU exports by value, while the EU reciprocates on 99.5% of Indian goods (we covered it here).

Operational alignment: The draft goes beyond duties, targeting ‘non-tariff barriers’ by aligning food safety and plant health measures with WTO standards. It also introduces a structured mediation process, though it requires mutual consent to trigger.

Transparency and appeals: Both sides will exchange annual import data starting one year after the pact kicks in to monitor implementation and the use of tariff preferences. They’ve also committed to appeal procedures for customs decisions, ensuring businesses aren't caught in a bureaucratic black hole.
sound_smarter: Raising the quality floor for exports creates a lift for the rest of Indian industry. As producers align with Brussels' benchmarks to stay competitive, the resulting improvement in manufacturing standards makes India a far more credible alternative for global supply chains looking to diversify.

title: Friend to all, ally to none
text:
On Saturday, New Delhi urged all stakeholders in West Asia to exercise restraint after US and Israeli strikes on Iran triggered regional retaliation, stressing dialogue, diplomacy, and respect for sovereignty.

What happened: Over the weekend, the US and Israel struck targets in Tehran and other cities. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded with missiles and drones aimed at Israel and US-linked military facilities across Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.

India–Israel reset: In recent weeks, India and Israel expanded cooperation in defence tech, arms procurement, counter-terrorism, intelligence sharing and cybersecurity. Modi visited Netanyahu in Israel last week (we covered it here).

India–Iran ballast: New Delhi’s ties with Tehran date to 1950. Iran was once a key oil supplier before sanctions squeezed flows. India still backs the Chabahar Port corridor linking India, Iran and Afghanistan. The relationship has swung with geopolitics, especially India's closeness to Washington.

The tightrope: India buys Israeli weapons, invests heavily in Chabahar Port, and calls no one an enemy, a deliberate policy of keeping leverage with every side.
sound_smarter: India has defence deals with Israel and billions tied up in Iran, with Chabahar Port and its energy supply directly in the line of fire. New Delhi won't escalate beyond diplomatic statements, as decades of Middle East entanglement remains a trap it has consistently avoided.

title: Case dismissed, tears included
text:
A Delhi trial court just tossed the case that put Kejriwal in jail. On Friday, the court refused to frame charges against former Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal and 22 co-accused, including ex-deputy Manish Sisodia, in a corruption case tied to Delhi’s 2022 liquor licensing policy. The judge was unusually scathing, saying the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)'s chargesheet rested on “surmises, conjectures, and inferential leaps.”

The case: Kejriwal, a former bureaucrat turned anti-corruption activist, built his Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) into a political force on a promise of clean governance. He was arrested by the CBI in March 2024 over allegations that his government gave unfair advantages to private liquor retailers. The irony was pointed: India's most prominent clean-governance campaigner, jailed on corruption charges. The AAP lost Delhi's February 2025 election, handing the BJP the capital for the first time in 27 years.

Not so fast: A discharge is not an acquittal. The CBI appealed to the Delhi High Court the same day, and the Enforcement Directorate (ED)'s parallel money laundering case stays alive. A BJP spokesperson called the ruling a “technical matter”, pointing out that voters delivered their own verdict in February.

The political play: Kejriwal used the discharge to go on offence, challenging Modi to call fresh Delhi elections and vowing to quit politics if the BJP won more than 10 seats. The verdict also handed opposition parties fresh ammunition for a long-running argument: that the Modi administration has weaponised central agencies like the CBI and ED against political rivals. Nationally, AAP holds power only in Punjab, which goes to polls in early 2027.
sound_smarter: The discharge hands Kejriwal a narrative, not a comeback. The more important question is whether Indian voters distinguish between legal exoneration and political accountability, and in 2025, Delhi suggested that they don't.

title: Atomic Bond
text:
The deep freeze is over. Canadian PM Mark Carney met PM Modi yesterday, closing out his first official visit to India with a multi-billion-dollar economic reset.

The roadmap: Both nations signed Terms of Reference for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA). The goal is to raise bilateral trade to USD 50bn by 2030, with negotiations to conclude by the end of this year.

Atomic alignment: Canada's Cameco signed a USD 1.9bn deal to supply 22 million pounds of uranium through 2035. The fuel feeds India's 24 operating reactors as it races toward a target of 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047. Beyond fuel, both sides committed to joint ventures in AI, supercomputing, and semiconductors.

The olive branch: Ottawa cleared the path by moving to revoke the citizenship of Tahawwur Rana, a Pakistan-born businessman accused of helping plan the 2008 Mumbai attacks. The move was a high-value security concession after years of friction over Khalistani separatism. We covered it here.
sound_smarter: Canada’s heavy reliance on US trade is a liability under Trump, making diversification a necessity. As a rapidly growing global economy and a growing global supply chain hub, India offers the scale and long-term potential Canada needs.

title: Burning through the buffer
text:
India is staring down its worst energy crisis in years. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's oil flows, has been effectively shut since the weekend. Not by a naval blockade, but by the market itself: insurers have cancelled war risk coverage for vessels in the Gulf, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has threatened to fire on any ship that tries to pass, and major shipping lines including Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have suspended transits. Around 150 vessels, including oil and LNG tankers, are sitting at anchor in and around the strait. Transit plummeted 81% in a single week.

For India, the timing is disastrous.
anchor: India is staring down its worst energy crisis

title: Crude calculation
text:
On Wednesday, Russia offered to divert 9.5 million barrels of crude to India to offset massive disruptions in the Middle East, potentially covering 40% of India's crude imports as regional conflict disrupts the Strait of Hormuz.

The predicament: India's reserves cover only 25 days of demand. With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed since the start of the conflict, 40% of India's oil imports are stranded. Moscow is also offering LNG supplies after Qatar, India's top supplier, halted production on Monday.

The Washington factor: This puts New Delhi in a bind. Under a recent interim trade framework with Washington, India agreed to curb Russian oil purchases in exchange for lower tariffs (we covered it here). Resuming Russian imports could provoke retaliation, but the Supreme Court's ruling on February 20 gutted Trump's main tariff weapon. His fallback, a blanket 15% levy under Section 122, expires in July. Washington's leverage is weaker than it was two weeks ago.

Alternative routes: Policymakers are scrambling to prepare should the conflict last beyond a few weeks. Trump himself has projected the military operation at four to five weeks. Indian refiners are asking Saudi Aramco to reroute supplies via the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Shipments would still pass through the Bab el-Mandeb strait, within range of Iran-backed Houthi forces. Other options include expediting supplies from Venezuela and squeezing more from domestic fields that cover less than 15% of India's crude needs. Meanwhile, Trump has floated US Navy escorts and political risk insurance for Gulf shipping.
sound_smarter: If the Strait stays shut for weeks, survival beats trade compliance. India will likely resume Russian imports, perhaps seeking safety in numbers by coordinating with other energy-starved nations to blunt any US retaliatory tariffs. With Trump's toolkit already clipped by the Supreme Court, the political cost of defiance is lower than it looks.
