title: Torpedoed trust
text:
A US Navy submarine torpedoed and sank the Iranian frigate IRIS Dena on March 4, 40 nautical miles off Galle, Sri Lanka. The ship departed India on February 25 after participating in the International Fleet Review and MILAN 2026, the Indian Navy's flagship exercises in Visakhapatnam. According to Iran's ambassador to India, the Dena was unarmed, as it was still operating under the exercise's peace protocol. Washington confirmed the strike as part of Operation Epic Fury, the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran. Sri Lankan authorities recovered at least 87 bodies, with dozens of crew reported missing.

Though the strike took place in international waters, the Dena was in those waters because India invited it to Visakhapatnam. A ship the Indian Navy had hosted, destroyed by Washington without advance notice to New Delhi, within range of the Indian coastline. For a country that positions itself as the Indian Ocean's premier security provider, the lack of warning from Washington undermines that claim.

### The limits of diplomacy

India's maritime strategy rests on a simple proposition: that the Indian Ocean can be a cooperative space rather than a contested one. MILAN, Hindi for “coming together,” is the centrepiece of that vision, bringing together navies from over 70 countries, including nations on opposite sides of geopolitical fault lines. The Dena strike challenges that proposition directly. Washington treated India's neighbourhood as an extension of its own theatre of operations, with no apparent regard for the diplomatic setting the ship had just left. The immediate fallout is practical: strikes in these waters drive up insurance premiums, disrupt tanker routes, and invite further intervention from outside powers. The question for New Delhi is whether it can enforce the norms it promotes, or whether those norms only hold when major powers choose to respect them.

### A dangerous double bind

New Delhi now finds itself squeezed between two relationships it cannot afford to lose. (We dived into this yesterday.) The US is a key security partner, with deepening cooperation on intelligence sharing, defence technology, and a shared interest in countering Chinese expansion. But India's ties with Iran predate both the Islamic Republic and India's partnership with Washington. Tehran was one of New Delhi's largest oil suppliers before US sanctions and hosts the Chabahar Port, India's only direct trade route to Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan.

Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri's visit to the Iranian embassy on March 5 to sign the condolence book for former Supreme Leader Khamenei was a quiet but pointed signal: India intends to maintain ties with Tehran regardless of the regime change Washington is pursuing. But quiet signals are all New Delhi has offered so far. Strategic autonomy has, for now, become strategic silence.

### The response

New Delhi has issued no formal condemnation and no direct criticism of Washington. India's defence establishment has actively distanced itself from the strike, noting that the Dena departed Visakhapatnam on February 25 and that India had no control over the vessel after that. The Indian Navy deployed two ships from Kochi and a P-8I maritime patrol aircraft for search and rescue, framing its involvement as a humanitarian obligation rather than a political response. Opposition politicians have demanded a stronger stance, but the government has held the line.

### The Verdict

The strategic cost for India goes beyond this crisis. If a ship that participated in an Indian-hosted exercise can be struck in international waters on the way home, future participants will weigh that risk. Iran's foreign minister has already framed the Dena as a guest of India struck without warning. Analysts have pointed to an unwritten code of naval hospitality: while India has no legal obligation to guarantee safe passage, attacking a ship shortly after it leaves a host's waters breaks an informal norm, and the reputational cost falls on the host. The fact that this question is now being asked is itself the damage.

title: From mayor to mantri
text:
PM Modi congratulated the people of Nepal for its successful elections on Friday. The vote is Nepal's first since last year's Gen Z-led protests. Balendra ‘Balen’ Shah, a rapper turned politician who became the face of the movement, is on track for an outright majority, a rarity in Nepali politics.

Gen Z earthquake: In September 2025, what started as a digital rights protest quickly snowballed into a nationwide uprising against corruption, nepotism, and youth unemployment. The protests culminated in the ousting of PM KP Sharma Oli and his administration. For decades, New Delhi managed Nepal through established relationships with the traditional parties. That playbook will now need to be amended - Shah's RSP is barely three years old.

Why India cares: Anti-India sentiment in Nepal runs deep. In 2015, Nepal fast-tracked a new constitution over India's objections that it failed to accommodate the Madhesi community, an ethnic group with ties on both sides of the border. An unofficial blockade followed, choking off fuel and medicine to a country still reeling from a devastating earthquake. The episode pushed Kathmandu toward Beijing and radicalised a generation against Indian influence.

The India file: Shah is Madhesi, the same community whose rights India cited when it choked Nepal's economy in 2015. India has a long history of shaping Nepali politics through economic leverage, back-channel relationships with established parties, and its near-monopoly on trade routes to the landlocked country. As Kathmandu mayor, he displayed a Greater Nepal map in his office claiming parts of India. India and Nepal have an unresolved territorial dispute in the western Himalayas, and Shah has been consistently hawkish on the issue.

Beijing in the background: Nepal signed onto China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in 2017. Chinese-built projects like the Pokhara International Airport and the proposed Kathmandu-Tibet railway are already on the ground. For decades, India could count on Kathmandu's old guard to keep Beijing at arm's length. Shah has no such loyalties, and sees both countries as overbearing neighbours that need to be managed on Nepal's terms.
sound_smarter: Shah's near-supermajority gives him something no recent Nepali leader has had: the mandate to actually make decisions. Previous governments were too fragile to settle border disputes or commit to long-term partnerships. For New Delhi, a strong leader in Kathmandu can resolve decades-old disputes, but he can also pick fights that weaker governments never dared to.

title: Crude awakening
text:
Washington made a pragmatic call. Last Friday, the US Treasury granted India a 30-day waiver to buy Russian crude already loaded on tankers, as the Middle East conflict disrupts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and jolts global oil markets.

The disruption: Insurance firms have pulled war-risk coverage, shipping companies have suspended Gulf transits, and dozens of vessels are idling near the strait. Hormuz normally carries about 1/5 of the world’s oil trade, so even partial disruption sends prices higher.

Vulnerability exacerbated: New Delhi sits near the epicentre of that risk. Around 40% of India’s crude imports pass through Hormuz, while strategic reserves cover only 20-25 days of crude supply, ranking high on the energy vulnerability chart amongst global economies (we covered it here). Meanwhile, the dilemma was that India had recently reduced Russian oil purchases under US pressure as part of a broader trade framework.

The uncomfortable reality: When Middle Eastern supply faltered, the most accessible replacement turned out to be the same barrels India had been asked to avoid. Moscow quickly offered to redirect 9.5 million barrels of crude to India and provide LNG to replace disrupted Gulf shipments.

Washington’s calculus: Enforcing sanctions in the middle of an oil shock risks pushing prices even higher and worsening global shortages. This short-term waiver reflects that constraint more than any shift in US policy.
sound_smarter: The waiver is a temporary response to supply disruptions. Even if the waivers are extended due to a prolonged conflict, US pressure on India to cease Russian oil imports will remain constant.

title: Humanitarian harbor
text:
On Saturday, Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar defended India’s decision to allow the Iranian naval vessel IRIS Lavan to dock in Kochi, framing the move as a humanitarian necessity rather than a political statement.

The situation: The IRIS Lavan reported engine failure and docked on March 4. It remains in Kochi under Indian supervision. Jaishankar argued that legal issues aside, providing refuge to a ship in distress was simply the right thing.

Maritime principles: Nations often allow foreign naval vessels to dock for repairs or to escape adverse weather, adhering to maritime safety and humanitarian principles, even in tense geopolitical situations.

The backdrop: The move follows a chaotic week in the Indian Ocean. On Wednesday, a US submarine sank the Iranian frigate IRIS Dena 40 miles off the Sri Lankan coast as part of ‘Operation Epic Fury.’ The IRIS Dena had just departed India after participating in New Delhi’s flagship MILAN 2026 exercises (we covered it here).

Collateral damage: Sri Lankan authorities have recovered 87 bodies from the Dena strike. Meanwhile, Colombo is currently holding 200 sailors from another Iranian vessel, the IRIS Bushehr, which had reported ship issues.
sound_smarter: After a ship was torpedoed shortly after leaving an Indian naval exercise, New Delhi’s silence drew fire. By coming out now with news of granting the Lavan safe harbor, India is trying to save its reputation by using maritime tradition while avoiding risking the ire of Washington.

title: Missiles with a passport
text:
BrahMos goes global. Indonesia's defence ministry confirmed on Monday that Jakarta has entered an agreement to procure the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile. This marks New Delhi's second major arms export, after a USD 375 million deal with Manila in 2022.

What is BrahMos: A joint India-Russia venture, BrahMos is the world's fastest operational cruise missile, travelling at Mach 3. Competing Western and Chinese systems are subsonic. It can be launched from land, sea, and air, and needs no guidance after firing. Its reported use during Operation Sindoor, India's May 2025 strikes on Pakistan, gave it real combat credibility and turbocharged export demand.

Why Indonesia: Jakarta has a maritime dispute with China over the South China Sea and Natuna Islands, making BrahMos a pointed procurement. President Prabowo Subianto flagged the deal during his state visit to India in January 2025. The deal covers the maritime variant and is valued at roughly USD 200-450 million. BrahMos is 49.5% Russian, meaning every export requires Moscow's approval. Beijing has previously lobbied Russia to block deals it dislikes, though no formal objection to the Indonesia deal has been voiced yet.

The queue: Vietnam, Malaysia, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and several Latin American nations are in various stages of discussion. India's defence exports hit a record USD 2.76 billion last year, and BrahMos is carrying most of the ambition to push that further toward its 2029 target of USD 5.9 billion.
sound_smarter: BrahMos is India's best argument that it is becoming a defence exporter, not just a defence buyer. But one flagship product does not make an industry, as India remains the world's second-largest arms importer. The real test is whether BrahMos opens the door to a broader export ecosystem or stays a one-missile show.

title: Clearing the clearance
text:
India wants a backup when environmental regulators stall. On Monday, New Delhi proposed to create the Standing Authority on Environment Impact Assessment (SAEIA) to prevent development projects from getting stuck in the approval process.

The proposal: The new body would consist of ex-officio members appointed by the central government. When state-level environmental appraisal authorities become inactive, the standing authority would temporarily take over their responsibilities.

Regulatory background: Environmental approvals in India operate under the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) framework introduced in 2006. Large national projects are reviewed by the central government under the EIA framework, while most regional projects are handled by the State Environment Impact Assessment Authorities locally.

Reality check: In practice, these state authorities often stop functioning. Terms expire, and new members are not appointed quickly. When that happens, environmental clearances simply stop moving, and projects accumulate in a backlog.
sound_smarter: India’s next investment cycle depends on ports, industrial parks, power grids, transport corridors, and urban expansion. Every one of these projects requires environmental clearance first. Slow approvals can quickly become a growth bottleneck.
anchor: India wants a backup when environmental regulators stall.

title: Running on fumes
text:
One week into the West Asia conflict, India is rationing gas, burning more coal, and watching its steel mills, restaurants, and cooking oil supply all buckle at once. We covered the full energy and trade picture in our deep dive here. Today, the focus is on the ground reality.

The triage order: New Delhi invoked force majeure late Monday and ranked who gets gas first. Households and vehicles are fully protected. Fertiliser plants, factories, and commercial users get a fraction of their usual supply. Everyone else waits. Petronet LNG, India's top gas importer, followed with its own force majeure notice to customers including GAIL, Indian Oil Corp, and Bharat Petroleum, after Qatar and Abu Dhabi National Oil Company halted supplies. To stop hoarding, the government also extended the minimum time between LPG cylinder bookings from 21 to 25 days, after some households that previously booked every 55 days started booking every 15. Algeria, Australia, Canada, and Norway have all approached India offering alternative LPG supplies.

The restaurant problem: The National Restaurant Association of India, representing over 500,000 restaurants, warned the food processing ministry that disruptions would cause ‘catastrophic closure.’ LPG stock in some kitchens is down to two days. Indian companies have raised LPG prices for the first time in about a year, as the war drives up the cost of imports that fill two-thirds of annual LPG consumption.

The steel problem: Small steelmakers are warning of 50% production cuts and complete halts within a week if supplies don't improve. About 6% of India's steel output uses gas-based production. The other 50%, which runs on coal, is also under pressure: South African thermal coal prices at Indian ports jumped 10-13% last week to a three-year high. Small and secondary steelmakers supply a large share of construction-grade material, and any output contraction feeds directly into the cost and availability of steel for India's infrastructure rollout, the engine of economic growth for the past three years.

The power pivot: Gas-fired power plants, which typically run at 6-10% capacity, were expected to ramp to roughly 30% this summer. Every year, the government invites private power companies to supply gas-based electricity to the grid during peak demand, subsidising the cost to make the economics work. This year, a tender for 12,000 MWh received zero bids as no private player is willing to commit with LNG either unavailable or too expensive. The workaround is to bring coal plants back online.
sound_smarter: What makes this week different from past energy scares is the simultaneity. Gas, coal, and steel are all being squeezed through the same chokepoint at the same time, while India sits on 25 days of crude reserves with peak summer power demand still ahead. The government's instinct will be to absorb costs through state oil companies and keep retail prices stable. That buys political time but it does not buy supply.

title: A very particular kind of hall pass
text:
On Monday, the US signalled to European allies that any further easing of Russian oil sanctions will likely be just for India.

Cooling prices: President Trump suggested removing ‘certain oil-related sanctions’ to cool global prices following a phone call with Vladimir Putin on Monday. While details are sparse, the administration is framing this as a one-off rather than a policy shift.

An exception: The US granted India a 30-day waiver to purchase stranded Russian oil last Friday at sea, which we covered here. Nomura analysts note the estimated 20-30 million barrels available cover just four days of Indian demand.

Reassurances: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent assured G7 ministers that these cargoes won't pad the Kremlin’s pockets, as the oil was already loaded. Bessent added that India will eventually buy more American crude instead.
sound_smarter: Unlike other major powers, India lacks the strategic reserves to weather a supply shock. By granting these hyper-specific waivers, Trump delays an Indian supply collapse while keeping New Delhi on a short leash until the conflict ends “very soon” according to Trump.

title: Borderline investments
text:
India has scrapped blanket approval requirements for investments from land-bordering countries with minority beneficial ownership, part of a broader policy covering all such neighbours but squarely aimed at rebuilding commercial ties with Beijing after six years of friction.

The change: Under the previous policy, any firm with a Chinese beneficial owner required government approval to invest in India, regardless of the ownership stake. That caught global PE and VC funds with Chinese limited partners in its net. Now, investments where Chinese beneficial ownership stays below 10% enter through the automatic route. Proposals in electronics, batteries, rare-earth magnets, capital goods, and solar cells will receive a government decision within 60 days, provided Indian residents retain majority control.

Getting here: Since the 2020 Galwan clash froze ties, New Delhi has been methodically walking requirements back: Modi visited Beijing in August 2025 for the first time in seven years, business visas for Chinese technicians were cleared in December, state-run power and coal companies were allowed to resume equipment imports in February, which we covered here.

The freeze in numbers: The six-year chill went well beyond FDI inflows. Visas for Chinese technicians were frozen, stalling projects like Bengaluru's Yellow Line metro for years despite stations and tracks being ready. Across PLI manufacturing projects, the freeze cost an estimated USD 15 billion in losses. Chinese FDI into India stood at just USD 2.67 million last year.
sound_smarter: India's production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes were supposed to build domestic capacity, but they haven't filled the critical technology and components gap fast enough. This FDI easing is an acknowledgment of that reality, while the 10% threshold and residency-control requirement keep security guardrails in place.
anchor: India has scrapped blanket approval requirements for investments

title: Art of the deal
text:
On Tuesday, President Donald Trump announced that Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries will fund the first new US oil refinery in 50 years, a USD 300 billion project in Brownsville, Texas.

The deal: Developed by America First Refining, the facility is designed to exclusively process American shale oil. Trump labeled the massive investment "historic," though the USD 300 billion figure reflects 20 years of projected output, not construction costs.

Cool your jets: Reliance has not confirmed any of this. The company has stayed silent since the announcement, and neither the investment size nor Reliance's precise role – equity stake, offtake agreement, or strategic partnership – has been disclosed.

Reliance’s background: Reliance operates the world’s largest refining complex in Jamnagar, Gujarat, capable of processing 1.4 million barrels of crude daily. Reliance currently holds no overseas refining assets.

Quid pro quo: This engagement likely helped secure India’s 30-day Russian oil waiver, which we covered here. Since the waiver, Indian refiners have snapped up 30 million barrels of Russian crude.
sound_smarter: In the Trump era, high-profile capital commitment is the most effective form of diplomacy. Whether the deal materialises, Reliance’s investment has secured vital breathing room for India’s energy supplies and goodwill for future India-US negotiations.

Poor planning around new pilot duty rules forced the cancellation of roughly 4,500 flights in December, the fallout from which cost IndiGo its senior VP in January, which we covered here. title: Z+ for effort
text:
Farooq Abdullah, 88, narrowly survived an assassination attempt at a wedding in Jammu on Wednesday night. He is president of the Jammu and Kashmir National Conference (JKNC) and the patriarch of the region's dominant political family. His son, Omar Abdullah, is the union territory's current chief minister.

Who is he: Farooq's father Sheikh Abdullah founded the National Conference in 1932 and steered Kashmir, a Muslim-majority state, into joining India. Farooq served as chief minister three times between 1982 and 2002. The family has governed Jammu and Kashmir for most of the post-independence period. In 2019, the Indian parliament revoked Article 370, which had granted the region its own constitution and special autonomy. Jammu and Kashmir was split into two union territories, placing it under direct central administration with a lieutenant governor appointed by New Delhi.

What happened: A gunman approached Farooq from behind as he left a wedding in Jammu and fired at point-blank range. A security officer deflected the shot. No serious injuries were reported.

The attacker: Kamal Singh Jamwal, 63, was arrested at the scene. He was carrying a licensed pistol and appeared to be drunk. Jamwal told police he had wanted to kill Abdullah for twenty years and found his chance when he was invited to the same wedding. He identified himself as chairman of a little-known group called Jagran Manch. Police have ruled out a terror angle.

The uncomfortable question: Farooq holds Z+ security, the highest tier in India, with National Security Guard cover. His son Omar asked publicly how an armed and intoxicated man managed to get within arm's reach of a Z+ NSG-protected former chief minister
sound_smarter: A drunk man with a licensed pistol got past NSG cover and fired at a former chief minister from arm's length. Jammu and Kashmir's elected government is barely a year old, operating in a region where the militant threat never went away. If India's highest security tier can be beaten this easily at a public event, that's a problem that extends well beyond the Abdullah family.
anchor: Farooq Abdullah, 88, narrowly survived an assassination attempt

title: Tariffs that stick
text:
On Wednesday, the US launched a sweeping Section 301 investigation into major trading partners, including India, the EU and China, targeting what Washington calls structural excess capacity in manufacturing.

The backstory: This new development comes weeks after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s emergency tariffs under IEEPA, which we covered here. The White House pivoted to Section 122 of the Trade Act, imposing a temporary 15% global tariff. That expires in late July. Section 301 is the replacement strategy.

Why it matters: Emergency tariffs were fast but legally fragile. Section 301 is slower but harder to challenge. It builds on formal investigations and findings of unfair trade practices rather than presidential discretion, giving any resulting levies a stronger legal foundation.

What changes: Section 301 allows Washington to impose targeted import taxes on countries deemed to engage in unfair trade practices. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he hoped to conclude the investigations before the current temporary tariffs expire in July and new levies could arrive as soon as this summer.

India's exposure: New Delhi and Washington reached a framework for an interim trade deal in February (which we covered here), setting an 18% baseline tariff on Indian goods. Section 301 could override that with higher, sector-specific duties targeting industries where the US finds excess capacity. The deal was meant to stabilise the relationship but this investigation reopens it.
sound_smarter: Section 301 lets Washington go industry by industry, picking apart where India is most vulnerable, making it a bigger threat and less predictable than a flat rate. New Delhi built the interim deal around a single number it could plan for. Now it faces a process that could produce different rates for different goods, with timelines it cannot control, while both sides are still at the negotiating table.

title: A tall order in the Strait
text:
On Thursday, reports emerged that New Delhi is negotiating with Tehran to secure safe passage for 28 Indian vessels through the volatile Strait of Hormuz.

The energy crunch: India is vulnerable. It relies on the Middle East for 40% of its crude and nearly all its LPG. With limited strategic reserves and existing fuel disruptions, any bottleneck in the Persian Gulf is an immediate economic threat (we covered the impact of ongoing disruptions here).

Diplomatic channels: External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar confirmed multiple high-level talks with his Iranian counterpart this week, focusing on ‘the safety of shipping and India’s energy security.’

Mixed signals: While some sources suggest a transit deal for Indian-flagged vessels is imminent, others in Tehran deny any such agreement. The confusion comes as three ships were attacked near the Strait on Wednesday alone.

The Israel factor: Prime Minister Modi recently deepened ties with Israel (we covered it here), a move that likely depleted India's diplomatic capital in Tehran.
sound_smarter: Iran’s current strategy is to spike the global cost of conflict to pressure the US and Israel. Granting India a hall pass undermines that leverage. Expect New Delhi to receive polite diplomatic nods but no functional immunity on the water.

text: India has warned drugmakers against directly or indirectly advertising prescription weight-loss drugs, as global and domestic firms ramp up marketing in the country’s fast-growing obesity market. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) said even “awareness campaigns,” influencer promotions or claims exaggerating drug effectiveness could trigger action. Prescription medicines cannot be marketed to the public under Indian law. The move comes as local companies prepare to launch cheaper generic versions of Novo Nordisk’s semaglutide once its Indian patent expires later this month.

title: Better off waiting?
text:
India is in no hurry to sign a trade deal with the United States. The interim framework agreed in February (we covered it here) would lock in an 18% tariff on Indian exports. A shifting tariff landscape and a new American investigation give New Delhi every reason to wait.

What changed: The US Supreme Court struck down Trump's reciprocal tariffs on February 20. Washington replaced them with a flat 10% duty on all imports under Section 122, valid through July 24. Trump intends to raise it to 15%, but no formal order has been issued. Either way, Indian exports face a lower rate than the 18% the deal would lock in.

New friction: On March 11, Washington launched Section 301 investigations into 16 economies, including India, targeting excess manufacturing capacity in sectors like steel, solar, and petrochemicals, which we covered here. Unlike Section 122's 15% cap, Section 301 tariffs carry no ceiling and no expiry. Indian officials view the probe as a pressure tactic.

The oil reversal: The interim framework required India to halt Russian crude imports, which India only slowed. The US has, since the breakout of the war, issued two temporary waivers allowing India to receive Russian crude already at sea. Though the volumes only cover a few days of demand, the reversal matters for what it reveals: six weeks after demanding India quit Russian oil, the US is issuing Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) licenses to purchase more of it.
sound_smarter: Waiting is the only logical play. With Section 301 investigations pending and the current flat duty set to expire in July, the situation is too fluid for a long-term commitment. Locking in 18% now is foolish when the rate is currently 10%.

title: Cushion before the crash
text:
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman proposed a USD 6.20 billion ‘Economic Stabilisation Fund’ last Friday, a war chest designed to insulate New Delhi from global volatility.

The objective: The fund allows the government to deploy cash fast when supply chains snap or energy prices spike by creating a pre-authorised pool of cash that can be spent.

The big caveat: Despite this new spend, the government is sticking to its FY26 fiscal deficit target of INR 15.58 trillion (USD 168 billion), roughly 4.5% of GDP under the revamped accounting system.

Domestic firewalls: Spending will be targeted. Expect the cash to flow toward fertilizer subsidies and rural income support, which currently are hammered by the conflict in Iran.
sound_smarter: Fertilizer subsidies aren't exactly ‘headline-grabbing’ policy, but in an economy where consumer spending is tied directly to how farmers feel, they’re a lifeline. By using these subsidies, the government can stabilize domestic demand quickly and quietly. It also keeps the economy moving without the kind of spending that rattles bond markets or eats up the budget for long-term infrastructure.

title: A gap in the blockade
text:
On Friday, Indian reported that Iran allowed two Indian-flagged LPG carriers to transit the Strait of Hormuz, providing a brief reprieve from the Iranian blockade strangling global energy flows.

The transit: Escorted by the Indian Navy, the vessels Shivalik and Nanda Devi – chartered by Indian Oil Corp – are passed the bottleneck and will reach western Indian ports by March 16 and 17.

The stranded: New Delhi isn't exhaling yet. It is currently negotiating the transit of 22 more vessels trapped west of the Strait, including four crude tankers and an LNG carrier.

Fuel jitters: India draws 40% of its crude and nearly all its LPG from the Middle East. With thin strategic reserves, any prolonged Persian Gulf closure triggers an immediate economic cardiac arrest (we covered the impact here).

Geopolitical gymnastics: India is in an awkward position. While Modi recently bolstered ties with Israel (we covered it here), New Delhi allowed an Iranian naval vessel to dock in Kochi after the US sank another Iranian ship (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: By selectively opening the valve, Iran is incentivizing India – the current BRICS chair – to use its diplomatic weight to push for de-escalation.

text: India's Election Commission announced assembly elections in Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Puducherry on Sunday. Assam, Kerala, and Puducherry vote on April 9; Tamil Nadu on April 23; West Bengal in two phases on April 23 and 29. Counting for all five is on May 4. The Model Code of Conduct is now in effect, freezing new policy announcements in all five states until results are declared.

title: Three ships for a strait
text:
India is negotiating safe passage for its vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, but Tehran has a price list. Iran's ambassador met Indian foreign ministry officials on Monday to discuss the release of three tankers seized in February, along with supplies of medicines and medical equipment.

The tankers: India's Coast Guard intercepted the Asphalt Star, Al Jafzia and Stellar Ruby about 100 nautical miles off Mumbai in early February, alleging they had falsified their identities and conducted illegal ship-to-ship fuel transfers. Stellar Ruby flies an Iranian flag; the other two are registered in Nicaragua and Mali. All three sit docked off Mumbai, linked to a shipping network Washington accuses of transporting Iranian oil.

What India got: India's crude imports have largely bypassed the strait, rerouted via Russian supplies and alternative Gulf ports. Cooking gas is the bottleneck. Almost all of India's LPG imports come from Qatar and the UAE, and there is no bypass for it. Tehran recently let two Indian LPG carriers, Shivalik and Nanda Devi, through the strait. Six more LPG-laden vessels remain stuck in the Gulf.

The diplomatic pitch: MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said Monday that nothing was being exchanged. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar went further, stating there was no blanket arrangement with Tehran and that every transit is negotiated individually. He pointed to the two LPG carriers as proof that "talking has yielded some results." Jaishankar is in Brussels on Monday for a meeting with EU foreign ministers, where he offered to share India's approach. Trump, meanwhile, called on nations to send warships to force the strait open, a path India has conspicuously avoided.
sound_smarter: If India hands the tankers back to smooth negotiations, it risks being seen as helping Iran circumvent American sanctions at the exact moment Washington is asking allies to help force the strait open. That's the tightrope: 22 Indian ships and 611 seafarers need to come home, but the price Tehran is quoting could cost New Delhi far more in Washington.
anchor: India is negotiating safe passage for its vessels

title: Blowing in the wind
text:
On Monday, Reuters reported that New Delhi may soften proposed penalties for wind and solar projects that were supposed to come into effect in April 2026. The move follows warnings that aggressive grid-discipline rules could vaporise developer profits and stall the energy transition.

The friction: Draft rules released by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) in September 2025 aimed to force renewable players to match their promised supply to the grid. Currently, developers have a wide tolerance (+/-15% for wind; +/-10% for solar) where they can miss their promised supply targets without heavy costs. Under the new proposal, tolerance bands would shrink to +/-10% for wind and +/-5% for solar by 2026 then gradually reduce until finally having the same tolerance bands as conventional generators by 2031.

The pushback: Industry groups claim wind projects are being set up to fail. Because of the intermittent nature of renewables, developers estimate revenue losses of up to 48%. In a January sit-down with ministers, developers warned that the approach would simply kill investment.

The retreat: The government has asked the CERC to re-examine the penalties. Implementation had already been pushed back to April 2026, but further dilution now looks likely to keep the renewable investments flowing.
sound_smarter: While the grid needs discipline, penalties on intermittent sources often backfire by making projects unbankable. Expect the government to pivot from penalties toward mandating storage or flexible power generation to meet gaps.

title: Dressed as a massacre
text:
Pakistan launched airstrikes at a drug rehabilitation hospital in Kabul on Monday, killing over 400 people. India's response was its sharpest rebuke of Islamabad in years.

The target: The Omid Addiction Treatment Hospital, a 2,000-bed facility near Camp Phoenix, a former NATO base that Pakistan says the Taliban converted into an ammunition depot. Pakistan claims it struck the base, not the hospital, and that the two are kilometres apart. The Norwegian Refugee Council visited the site and said the toll was almost certainly in the hundreds.

India's response: MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said Pakistan was ‘trying to dress up a massacre as a military operation.’ This is New Delhi's third statement in a month on Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan, and by far the most severe. India has been the only country to condemn Pakistan's actions outright. Notably, India anchored its condemnation entirely on sovereignty and civilian harm, avoiding the harder question of whether the Taliban harbours militants, a question the UN Security Council raised hours earlier. Meanwhile, China has had a special envoy shuttling between the two sides for a week. India is issuing statements, not brokering solutions.
sound_smarter: For decades, a Pakistan-aligned Afghanistan was New Delhi's worst nightmare, but that alliance is now in freefall. Delhi is currently walking a fine line: voicing support for Kabul just loudly enough to widen the rift between Kabul and Islamabad, without becoming the Taliban's unofficial PR firm.

title: MEA denies tanker-for-passage
text: India's foreign ministry called reports of a tanker-for-passage deal with Iran ‘baseless,’ insisting there have been no such discussions with Tehran. Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal added that the three vessels seized in February are not Iranian-owned. Discussions to secure safe transit for the remaining Indian ships in the Strait of Hormuz are ongoing, which we covered here.

title: Park and ride
text:
India tries to remove the executive delays in its manufacturing story. On Wednesday, the Cabinet approved the Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojna (BHAVYA), allocating USD 3.6 billion to develop 100 plug-and-play industrial parks nationwide.

What gets built: Parks ranging from 100 to 1,000 acres will receive financial assistance of up to USD 100,000 per acre. The idea is to deliver fully serviced industrial sites, including internal roads, underground utilities, drainage systems, common treatment facilities, ICT networks and administrative support, through partnerships between the central government, states, and private developers. The aim is to cut logistics costs, support greener production standards, and create jobs at scale by concentrating firms in ready-to-operate zones.

Growth by groundwork: The scheme builds on the National Industrial Corridor Development Programme, which already has 20 projects across 13 states, and fits squarely into New Delhi's strategy of large infrastructure spending to accelerate private investment and lift industrial growth, which we covered here. Project selection will require states to compete with reform-oriented, investment-ready proposals to win funding.
sound_smarter: India has launched industrial cluster schemes before, often with patchy execution. What makes BHAVYA notable is its focus on compressing project timelines rather than just allocating land. If the government can consistently deliver business-ready sites with clear permits and reliable infrastructure, India’s manufacturing pitch becomes far more credible.

title: Wafer-thin patience
text:
India will require all clean energy projects to use domestically manufactured solar ingots and wafers from 1 June 2028. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) announced the move on Wednesday, extending its Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) framework to the upstream solar supply chain.

The full chain: The move completes a phased localisation push backed by the government's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme. India already requires locally assembled solar modules in state-backed projects. Domestically made solar cells become mandatory across all projects from June 2026. Ingots and wafers are the latest entrant to this list.

The gap: India currently relies almost entirely on Chinese imports for cells, ingots, wafers, and polysilicon. Domestic ingot and wafer capacity sits at roughly 2 GW, all of it built under PLI. Progress has been slow, with visa restrictions on Chinese technicians and polysilicon price swings as key bottlenecks. The ALMM list won't be issued until at least three independent manufacturers with a combined 15 GW capacity are operational. Union Minister Pralhad Joshi said the move will ‘strengthen domestic solar manufacturing, reduce import dependence and improve supply chain resilience.’
sound_smarter: China is already challenging India's solar subsidies and ALMM framework at the WTO, calling them prohibited import substitution subsidies. India lost a near-identical case to the US in 2016 over domestic content requirements. The phased rollout may offer more legal cover, but with a fully made-in-India module still costing roughly double a Chinese one, the real test is whether domestic manufacturers can close the price gap fast enough.

title: Clearance sale stalls
text:
New Delhi is considering shelving the privatisation of three major state-run firms after a string of failed bids and lukewarm investor interest.

The hit list: Sales for IDBI Bank, Shipping Corporation of India (SCI), and HLL Lifecare may be scrapped. The IDBI deal collapsed last week after bids failed to meet the government’s minimum price, while SCI and HLL have been trapped in limbo since 2020-21.

Grand plans, lean results: PM Modi’s privatisation drive has struggled since its announcement in 2021. Beyond selling Air India to Tata, the program has been hobbled by red tape and a 2024 election result that forced a reliance on cautious coalition allies.

Investor cold feet: High reserve prices, unclear asset transfers, and unresolved liabilities like massive pension dues are scaring off private capital.
sound_smarter: State-run firms are fundamentally political assets, leaving buyers to grapple with decades of inefficiency and red tape. Until the government slashes its valuations or cleans up the balance sheets, smart money will bypass these legacy behemoths in favour of more nimble, private-sector companies.

title: Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with UAE President
text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, conveying advance Eid greetings and discussing the current situation in West Asia. Modi reiterated India’s strong condemnation of all attacks on the UAE that have resulted in loss of innocent lives and damage to civilian infrastructure. Both leaders stressed the importance of ensuring safe and free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and agreed to continue working together for the early restoration of peace, security and stability in the region.

title: Growing pains
text:
India is racing to lock in fertiliser from Russia, Belarus, and Morocco as the West Asia war and fresh Chinese export restrictions squeeze supply ahead of the summer planting season.

The squeeze: West Asia accounts for roughly half of India's diammonium phosphate (DAP) and urea imports. Meanwhile, China has quietly banned exports of nitrogen-potassium blends and certain phosphates, restricting between half and three-quarters of last year's shipments. International urea prices have risen around 40% from pre-war levels.

The buffer: India's current stockpiles are healthy. Urea and DAP inventories are up 10.7% and 105% respectively from a year ago. India sees a demand surge in June and July when farmers plant rice, corn, cotton, and oilseeds, and most shipments need to arrive between March and May.

Keeping the lights on: The government has prioritised gas supplies to fertiliser plants, ensuring at least 70% of average consumption, after LNG shipments from Qatar were disrupted by Strait of Hormuz threats, which we covered here.
sound_smarter: India's two fallback options pulled the rug at the same time – West Asia supplies the raw inputs; China fills in any gaps. With both constrained, New Delhi's subsidy-heavy fertiliser regime faces a direct hit as higher global prices mean a bigger bill for the government, right as it heads into an election-sensitive planting season.

title: Burning the midnight (imported) oil
text:
New Delhi is considering invoking emergency powers to force imported coal-based power plants to run at full throttle this summer as peak demand is projected to hit a record 271 GW.

The extraordinary clause: Under Section 11 of the Electricity Act, the Centre can direct any power plant to operate according to its directions during extraordinary circumstances, which includes threats to public order or for the sake of public interest. The government is reportedly targeting some of the 15 imported coal-based power plants that have 17 GW capacity in total to bridge an estimated 12 GW peak summer power demand shortfall.

The price of power: Imported coal is significantly pricier than domestic supply. To keep these coastal plants viable, the government will likely allow generators to pass higher fuel costs directly to consumers or offer a financial cushion to offset the hit under Section 11.

Role of gas: Usually, gas-based plants handle sudden surges. However, India has already reprioritised limited gas supplies toward households and fertiliser production, leaving the power sector without capacity to meet sudden surges in summer power demand.
sound_smarter: With the conflict in West Asia keeping gas markets on edge, New Delhi is choosing the high price tag of imported coal over the risk of widespread power failures

title: Bloatware or Big Brother?
text:
On Thursday, Reuters revealed that the Indian government is privately lobbing Apple, Google, Samsung, and leading smartphone manufacturers to pre-install the government’s biometric Aadhaar app on all new smartphones.

The pitch: The Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) wants the Aadhaar app preloaded into smartphones to enhance reach and skip the App Store download. Aadhaar is a unique 12-digit identity number tied to an individual's fingerprints and iris scans, held by nearly 1.34 billion residents, governing everything from banking to airport entry. Released in January, the updated Aadhaar app enables users to modify personal information, oversee family profiles, and secure biometric data against unauthorised use.

The pushback: Industry body MAIT is pushing back against the request. Manufacturers argue that forced pre-installation hikes production costs, requires India-specific assembly lines, and mirrors restrictive digital policies seen in Russia.

Security risk: Apple and Samsung have raised red flags over device security. New Delhi recently backtracked on a similar mandate for the Sanchar Saathi security app after a public outcry over privacy.
sound_smarter: This is New Delhi's second attempt at forced app pre-installation, after backing down on Sanchar Saathi following public outcry. The pattern matters more than the outcome — even if manufacturers win this round, India is clearly building toward a norm where government apps ship as default on every Indian handset.

title: Priced to protect
text:
India's trade ministry has recommended anti-dumping duties on Chinese imports of DASDA (4,4-Diamino Stilbene-2,2-Disulphonic Acid), an organic chemical used in textile dyes and optical brighteners, after finding evidence of dumped pricing.

The petitioner: Deepak Nitrite Limited, which controls roughly 60% of India's DASDA production, filed the complaint. Five smaller producers backed the petition during proceedings, though at least two were not producing DASDA during the investigation period.

The mechanism: The Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR), under the Commerce Ministry, proposed a reference-price duty: importers pay the difference between arrival price and USD 3,453 per ton if shipments fall below that threshold. The Finance Ministry has three months to decide whether to impose the duty.

The silent majority: DGTR sent questionnaires to nine downstream users, with only one responding. DASDA feeds into optical brightening agents used across India's textile and paper industries. Downstream manufacturers will absorb the higher input cost first.
sound_smarter: Anti-dumping duties protect capacity, but don't build competitiveness. Deepak Nitrite controls more than half of domestic DASDA production and just got the government to set a floor price on its main import competition. India wants a chemical industry that can compete globally; the risk is building one that can only survive behind tariff walls. Between 2020 and mid-2023, the Finance Ministry rejected over half of DGTR's duty recommendations, but since mid-2023, it has accepted nearly all of them.

title: Modi worked the phones on Thursday, speaking separately
text: Modi worked the phones on Thursday, speaking separately to France's Macron, Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, Qatar's Amir Sheikh Tamim, Jordan's King Abdullah II, and Malaysia's Anwar Ibrahim about the West Asia conflict. The message was consistent across all five calls: de-escalation, dialogue, diplomacy. Separately, India's Ministry of External Affairs called attacks on energy infrastructure across the region ‘deeply disturbing’ and ‘unacceptable.’

title: Crude control
text:
Prime Minister Modi chaired a high-level Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) meeting on Sunday to review India's energy, fertiliser, and supply chain resilience, amid sustained disruptions in sourcing.

The directives: Modi ordered a dedicated group of ministers and secretaries to coordinate across petroleum, power, fertilisers, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and MSMEs. He instructed states to crack down on hoarding and black-marketing of essential commodities. Operational details are expected in the coming days.

The exposure: The bulk of India's crude and almost all of its LPG imports transit the Strait of Hormuz. Crude import dependency sits near 89%, and domestic LPG cylinder prices have already climbed roughly 7%. The big three public sector refiners are configured for Gulf crude, and reconfiguring a refinery for different feedstock is a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar project.

The price shield: Retail prices have stayed steady since the start of the West Asia conflict. Industrial diesel, however, has climbed roughly 25%, the first significant increase since March 2024. Prices were deregulated between 2010 and 2014, though in practice, the government has directed oil marketing companies to hold the line. At USD 100–105 per barrel, they are running negative margins without subsidy backing. UBS has downgraded all three public sector refiners.

Supply push: Officials discussed alternative sources for fertilisers, chemicals, and industrial inputs ahead of disruptions to Gulf supply chains. India has already turned to Russia, Belarus, and Morocco for fertiliser supplies (we covered it here). New Delhi also signalled it may revisit fuel export plans to prioritise domestic consumption.
sound_smarter: Pump prices are technically market-determined, but the government is directing oil companies to absorb the gap, a de facto subsidy without the fiscal backstop. If Brent stays above USD 100, the trilemma sharpens: raise prices and stoke inflation, cut excise duty and widen the deficit, or let oil company margins collapse.
anchor: Prime Minister Modi chaired a high-level Cabinet Committee

title: A thirty-day breather
text:
On Saturday, Indian refiners signalled a return to Iranian crude after Washington issued a temporary sanctions waiver to soothe the global energy crunch triggered by the US-Israeli-Iranian conflict.

The waiver: The Trump administration announced a 30-day temporary waiver for purchasing Iranian oil already at sea, loaded on or before March 20 and discharged by April 19. Analysts say it covers roughly 170 million barrels currently on water, enough to plug holes but not to sink prices. This marks the third time the US has temporarily waived oil sanctions during this war, having previously issued temporary waivers for Russian oil already at sea.

Desperate times: India entered this conflict with a razor-thin 50-day reserve, which we covered here. With domestic industries buckling and fuel rationing already in effect (read our coverage here), New Delhi is scrambling for every drop of oil it can find.

Logistical hurdles: Three major Indian refiners are interested but still sweating the details. They are awaiting government guidance on payment mechanisms and clarity from Washington to ensure they don’t accidentally trip over remaining sanctions.
sound_smarter: The waiver offers immediate relief for India’s parched refineries. Supply stability remains a fantasy until regional energy infrastructure — currently being battered by Iranian strikes — is rebuilt and the Strait of Hormuz stabilises.

title: Unfasten the seatbelt
text:
India will scrap temporary domestic airfare caps starting today (March 23), ending a period of state-mandated pricing that began during IndiGo’s operational meltdown last December.

Market correction: While airfares are technically deregulated, New Delhi routinely intervenes during crises. The Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) now insists airlines exercise pricing discipline, but the real push is a return to pure market forces.

The West Asia squeeze: Indian carriers are bleeding. The regional conflict has spiked jet fuel prices, hammered the rupee, and disrupted lucrative Gulf routes. Lifting the caps allows airlines to pass these escalating costs to passengers rather than absorbing the hit.

Regulatory fine print: Despite the freedom, MoCA warned carriers to keep fares ‘commensurate with market conditions.’ Translation: don't gouge customers, or the caps come back.
sound_smarter: Allowing dynamic pricing helps carriers survive fuel spikes and rerouting costs, but also signals that geopolitical volatility is now a structural feature of India’s aviation economics.

title: Hormuz hits home
text:
The Indian rupee fell to 93.94 against the US dollar on Monday, a fresh all-time low, pressured by energy shocks from the West Asia conflict. India is the world’s third-largest oil importer.

The numbers: The rupee has weakened about 3% since US-Israeli strikes on Iran began. Foreign investors have pulled USD 9.6 billion from Indian equities this month alone. The rupee has actually fared better than peers – the Thai baht is down 4.9%, and the South Korean won 3.9% over the same period. The Reserve Bank of India's forward dollar sales of nearly USD 100 billion have done the heavy lifting, cushioning the fall.

Why it stings: The RBI spent 2025 cutting rates by 125 basis points to support growth, enabled by inflation running at historic lows. A sustained oil shock threatens to reverse that – a weaker rupee makes energy imports pricier. In a country where most logistics runs by road, that feeds directly into inflation, leaving the central bank in a bind.

The valuation question: Before the war, markets debated whether the rupee was overvalued. By late 2025, the RBI's own data showed it had crossed below the fair-value line for the first time in a decade. The current sell-off is pushing a fairly priced currency into genuinely weak territory.
sound_smarter: Six months ago, India had its best macro hand in years: inflation at historic lows, 125 basis points of rate cuts banked, trade deals with Washington and Brussels landing, and a currency no longer overvalued. The West Asia crisis has reshuffled the deck. If oil stays elevated, the RBI must choose between growth and the rupee. It cannot do both.

title: Faster deals, sharper watchdogs
text:
India is trying to make corporate dealmaking faster without loosening regulatory oversight.

What’s on the table: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman introduced the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, in the Lok Sabha on Monday. She then proposed referring it to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) for detailed scrutiny. The bill aims at easier compliance and smoother dealmaking.

Capital flexibility: Eligible firms may conduct two share buybacks annually, up from one, with a six-month cooling-off gap. The government also plans to decriminalise select compliance lapses, replacing jail risk with civil penalties.

Deal velocity: Fast-track mergers would get simpler where shareholders holding at least 75% in both firms sign off. The goal is to cut procedural drag that has long slowed consolidation.

Governance counterweight: The National Financial Reporting Authority would gain broader powers, including a wider definition of “professional misconduct” for auditors tied to company law violations.

Opposition pushback: Congress MP Manish Tewari opposed the bill, alleging excessive delegation of legislative power. Opposition members also raised concerns that it dilutes mandatory corporate social responsibility spending requirements. Sitharaman rejected the allegations, saying the bill followed two years of consultation.
sound_smarter: India is trying to free up capital while tightening supervision in one move. Faster buybacks and mergers could lift market efficiency, but stronger audit enforcement is the insurance policy. Should the bill pass, execution will decide whether India’s risk premium finally starts to narrow.
anchor: India is trying to make corporate dealmaking faster

title: Back to 100%
text:
On Monday, the Ministry of Commerce reinstated full export tax refunds, scrapping a 50% cap on the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products (RoDTEP) scheme weeks earlier than planned to offset surging maritime costs from West Asian instability. The reversal was backdated to February 23 to offset surging maritime costs stemming from the West Asia conflict.

The mechanism: Launched in 2021, RoDTEP is a WTO-compliant tool that neutralises domestic taxes – like electricity duty and VAT on fuel – incurred in the manufacturing and distribution of export goods.

The cap: In February, New Delhi halved RoDTEP benefits. The restoration unwinds that cut retroactively, but only through March 31. What applies after that remains unclear.

Exporter anxiety: Industry groups warned the 50% cap added 1-2% to price tags, enough to kill margins in price-sensitive global markets already suffering from slowing demands and protectionism.
sound_smarter: While restoring the rates provides a breather, it only marginally offsets rising costs from India's internal energy crunch and rising logistics costs that affect all inputs. More tellingly, the flip-flop within a single month signals a lack of predictability that may give long-term investors pause.

title: The cost of conversion
text:
The Supreme Court ruled that converting to Christianity or Islam strip an individual of Scheduled Caste (SC) status, terminating their access to affirmative action and specialised legal protections.

The ruling: Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Manmohan held that SC status is restricted to Hindus, Sikhs, and Buddhists under the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950. Once a person converts and practices another faith – as in the case of an Andhra Pradesh pastor who had been practising Christianity for over a decade – protections under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribe (Prevention of Atrocities) Act cease to apply. The court held that the caste system is alien to Christianity and Islam; legal remedies for caste-based discrimination cannot follow a convert.

Political firewall: The Modi government opposes extending SC status to Dalit Christians and Muslims, and has dismissed a 2007 commission's recommendation to delink SC status from religion as flawed. A new commission was appointed in 2022 to revisit the question; its report, due October 2025, has not been submitted.
sound_smarter: Dalits often convert to escape caste discrimination. By tying SC protections exclusively to Indic faiths, the state creates a steep material penalty for leaving the Hindu fold. India's most marginalised must choose between religious freedom and the safety net designed to address their marginalisation; a trade-off that keeps conversions in check and the Hindu demographic base intact.

title: Straight talk
text:
PM Modi and President Trump spoke on Tuesday to address the Middle East crisis, specifically the urgent need to keep the Strait of Hormuz functional. Their call was the first between the two leaders since the US and Israel launched coordinated strikes against Iran on February 28.

The five-day window: Trump postponed planned strikes on Iran's power plants on Monday, citing ‘productive’ talks with Tehran and claiming the two sides had reached ‘major points of agreement.’ Iran's parliamentary speaker Ghalibaf denied any negotiations had taken place, calling reports of talks an attempt to manipulate oil markets.

India's exposure: The near-closure of the Strait has throttled shipping and gas supplies. The Strait handles 40% of India's crude oil imports, and Modi told parliament on Monday that the crisis had triggered ‘unprecedented challenges.’

Modi's line: "India supports de-escalation and restoration of peace at the earliest. Ensuring that the Strait of Hormuz remains open, secure and accessible is essential for the whole world."
sound_smarter: India is the world's third-largest oil consumer, and Washington needs New Delhi's diplomatic channels with Tehran as much as its public backing. For India, a crisis that exposes dependence on a single chokepoint is the strongest argument yet for accelerating strategic reserves and alternative suppliers. Vulnerability, weaponised correctly, becomes leverage.
anchor: PM Modi and President Trump spoke on Tuesday

title: Harish Rana, the face of India's first passive
text: Harish Rana, the face of India's first passive euthanasia case, passed away on Tuesday after 13 years in a vegetative state. The Supreme Court permitted the withdrawal of life support on March 11, making his the first case to operationalise the court's 2018 recognition of the right to die with dignity. The Delhi High Court had initially denied his family's plea in 2024; the Supreme Court overturned that, ruling that clinically assisted nutrition constitutes medical treatment that can be withdrawn when it no longer serves the patient's interest.
anchor: Harish Rana, the face of India's first passive

title: Sunburnt
text:
India has delayed by a year its plan to force coal-fired power plants to reduce output when solar generation peaks, as regulators stall over who pays for the retrofit.

Stuck in neutral: Coal plants need expensive retrofits to cut their minimum use rate to 40% from 55%, but no one has agreed on who pays. The federal regulator has yet to approve the compensation framework, citing lack of operational data.

The cheap fix: Retrofitting would add just INR 0.28 to INR 0.60 per kilowatt-hour to tariffs, versus INR 5.76 to INR 6.04 for battery storage, making flexible coal at least ten times cheaper, according to the Central Electricity Authority.

The tab: When coal plants can't ramp down, grid operators curtail solar output instead and compensate solar generators for the lost revenue. Energy think-tank Ember estimates that the bill hit USD 76 million over eight months to December, funded through higher electricity tariffs.
sound_smarter: A grid that curtails solar because regulators can't agree on a compensation formula sends a specific message to investors, who India has been actively courting: the bottleneck in the country's transition is not technology or money, but the bureaucracy.
anchor: India has delayed by a year its plan

title: Underpromising, overdelivering?
text:
On Wednesday, the Union Cabinet approved India’s updated climate pledges, targeting a 47% reduction in emissions intensity by 2035 against 2005 levels.

The new targets: Beyond emissions intensity, India will commit to 60% non-fossil fuel power capacity and create a carbon sink of up to 4 billion tonnes by 2035 in its updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).

Focus on adaptation: Unlike previous updates, this NDC leans heavily into climate-resilient infrastructure. It explicitly prioritizes mangrove restoration, glacier monitoring in the Himalayas, and state-level Heat Action Plans to buffer the economy against extreme weather.

The ambition gap: Critics call the targets conservative. Moving the intensity goal from 45% by 2030 to 47% by 2035 is a marginal shift, especially compared to the EU’s binding 90% absolute reduction target for 2040 from 1990 levels.
sound_smarter: India hit its 2030 renewable capacity goal five years early, suggesting it may overdeliver again. But the modest 2% incremental bump in emissions intensity signals that policy ambition on clean energy may be lower than the rhetoric suggests.

title: Runway to nowhere
text:
India's Cabinet approved Modified UDAN on Tuesday, committing INR 28,840 crore (USD 3.4 billion) over the next decade to develop 100 airports from existing airstrips, build 200 helipads, and keep subsidising airlines to fly regional routes.

The track record: Since its launch in 2016, the original UDAN (Ude Desh Ka Aam Nagrik, or ‘let the common citizen fly’) scheme has a patchy record. A 2023 audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of the first three phases found that 52% of 774 awarded routes never started operations. Of those that did fly, only 7% survived beyond the three-year subsidy window. Fifteen airports went inactive during the period.

By the numbers: Over nine years, UDAN has operationalised 663 routes across 95 airports, carrying 16.2 million passengers. In a country of 1.4 billion, that works out to roughly one UDAN flight for every 86 Indians across the scheme's entire lifespan.

What's different this time: Modified UDAN extends viability gap funding from three to ten years, betting that longer subsidies will give routes time to build demand. The price tag is steep: INR 10,043 crore (USD 1.2 billion) in direct airline subsidies alone, with another INR 12,159 crore (USD 1.4 billion) for airport development, INR 3,661 crore (USD 430 million) for helipads, and INR 2,577 crore (USD 305 million) in operation and maintenance support for 441 aerodromes.

The monopoly problem: Even where UDAN routes survive, competition is thin. IndiGo operates nearly 80% of all domestic routes and is the sole carrier on more than 500 city pairs. The government issued licences to three new airlines in late 2025 to inject competition, but subsidised regional routes with low demand are unlikely to attract challengers.
sound_smarter: UDAN's problem was never the runways; it was the passengers. Extending subsidies from three to ten years buys time, but more tarmac won't close the gap if demand stays concentrated in a handful of metro airports.

text: India's consumer protection authority issued an advisory barring hotels and restaurants from adding default ‘LPG charges’, ‘gas surcharges,’ or ‘fuel cost recovery’ fees to bills. The CCPA ruled that fuel and energy costs are operational expenses that must be baked into menu prices, and warned that separate line items amount to unfair trade practices under the Consumer Protection Act.

text: India has secured crude oil supplies for the next 60 days, offsetting disrupted West Asian shipments with increased flows from the Western Hemisphere and Russia, the oil ministry said on Thursday. But crude is the easy part. The real pressure point is cooking gas.

title: Rupee for your thoughts
text:
India's markets are taking a direct hit from the Iran war. Foreign investors have pulled a record USD 12.14 billion from Indian equities since fighting broke out on February 28, sending the rupee to successive all-time lows.

The damage: The rupee has fallen 4.2% since the war began, now trading at 94.79 versus the USD. Goldman Sachs has slashed its 2026 growth forecast for India from 7% to 5.9%.

Why India hurts more: As a country that imports 85% of its oil, every escalation in West Asia is an Indian macro event. BNP Paribas estimates that a 10% rise in oil prices widens the current account deficit by 35 basis points and nudges inflation up by 30 basis points.

Policy response: New Delhi cut excise duties on petrol and diesel by INR 10 per litre to help out oil companies. The petroleum minister warned of a "huge hit" to tax revenues.
sound_smarter: Depreciation amplifies foreign investors' dollar losses, triggering more selling, weakening the rupee further. That’s a feedback loop the RBI can slow but not break. Until oil stabilises, India's macro story is Tehran's to write.
anchor: India's markets are taking a direct hit from

title: Closing the arbitrage window
text:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) moved to shield the rupee on Friday, ordering banks to cap net open onshore positions at USD 100 million by April 10, intending to kill the offshore-onshore arbitrage trade that is stressing the currency.

The context: A perfect storm of surging oil prices and war-driven capital flight has hammered the rupee. It hit a record low of 94.79 versus the USD this month, its worst slide in seven years.

Previous practices: Under existing rules, banks can set net open position limits up to 25% of total capital with the RBI able to set caps as needed. Banks would offset large onshore dollar buys with opposite positions in the offshore, non-deliverable forward (NDF) market. This netting allowed them to run massive arbitrage books – estimated between USD 10-18 billion – while remaining compliant.

Currency impact: This arbitrage actually hurts the INR. When banks rush to buy USD onshore to fuel this trade, they drive the domestic price of the USD up and the INR down.

New limit: The hard USD 100 million cap on the onshore leg will force banks to unwind these trades. To comply, banks must now sell dollars in the domestic market, which gives the RBI a boost in its efforts to defend the rupee without having to dip into its dollar reserves. Large banks – estimated to have USD 250-300 million net open positions each – are expected to incur losses as the rush to unwind their positions drives prices down. Banks are seeking relief and asking the RBI to apply the rules to positions taken after April 10.
sound_smarter: The RBI is signaling that while it generally allows market forces to work, it will not tolerate banks using its own domestic market to bet against the INR during a crisis.

title: Back to the hardware store
text:
India authorised Bharat Heavy Electricals (BHEL) and Steel Authority of India (SAIL) to procure critical equipment from China on Friday, the latest in a string of measures unwinding six years of commercial restrictions.

What's allowed: BHEL can now source 21 types of critical equipment from Chinese suppliers. SAIL received similar clearance for certain components, and other state firms can procure coal-gasification equipment. Chinese bidders in state contracts no longer need political and security clearance registration.

The sequence: New Delhi began easing power equipment import curbs in February, then relaxed FDI rules for Chinese-linked investments earlier this month. Friday's order moves from policy to named firms with specific procurement lists.

The wider thaw: Modi visited China last August for the first time in seven years. Since then, direct flights resumed and visa rules for Chinese professionals loosened.
sound_smarter: Each step has been framed as targeted and temporary, but the pattern is unmistakable. New Delhi is rebuilding commercial ties with Beijing sector by sector, driven less by diplomatic warmth than by supply chain arithmetic and the need to hedge against US tariff disruption.

title: Shopping around
text:
India approved USD 25 billion in military purchases on Friday, including Russian S-400 missile systems, transport aircraft, and strike drones, its second major defence splurge in as many months.

The shopping list: The Air Force gets S-400s, medium transport aircraft, unmanned attack drones, and Su-30 engine overhauls. The Army gets air defence systems, armour-piercing ammunition, Dhanush guns, and battlefield surveillance gear. A separate USD 47 million contract was also signed with Moscow, covering Tunguska air defence systems.

Record year: In all, India has approved 55 proposals worth 6.73 trillion rupees (USD 71 billion) and signed contracts for another 503 proposals amounting to 2.28 trillion rupees in this fiscal year, marking a historic high.

Why now: Last year's four-day clash with Pakistan, the worst case since 1971, exposed tactical gaps in drone saturation, battlefield communications, and rapid deployment.
sound_smarter: A USD 71 billion shopping spree across Moscow, Paris, and Washington is India's non-alignment doctrine made visible, but whether it holds is another question. Washington has already threatened CAATSA sanctions over the S-400s, and if forced to choose, no amount of diversification makes that choice disappear.
anchor: India approved USD 25 billion in military purchases

title: Keeping the lights on
text:
On Monday, the Ministry of Power rolled out an emergency playbook to prevent summer blackouts, insisting the grid is “adequately positioned to meet summer demand” despite gas shortages fueled by the West Asia conflict.

The gas gap: Gas provides only 2% of India’s power, but it provides 10 GW during peak-demand periods or heatwaves. With the regional conflict squeezing supplies, New Delhi is scrambling for alternatives.

The playbook: The government invoked Section 11 of the Electricity Act to force Tata Power’s 4,000 MW Mundra plant into action by April 1 (we covered Section 11 here). It is also deferring maintenance on thermal plants to keep 10,000 MW on the grid and pushing up coal inventory. To bridge the deficit, the Ministry is accelerating clearances to commission wind and battery energy storage systems while tweaking rules to encourage industries to use their own captive power.
sound_smarter: The West Asia conflict is a blunt reminder that energy security is impossible without decoupling from imported fuels. Accelerated renewable project clearances won't plug this summer’s gap – coal will still do the heavy lifting – but this conflict serves as a catalyst for more investments in renewable energy generation and storage to prevent every geopolitical tremor from threatening India’s power system.

title: Safe harbour, unsafe platforms
text:
India proposed changes to its IT law that would make government advisories and clarifications legally binding on internet platforms.

What changed: Under the current rules, the IT ministry's advisories on issues like deepfake labelling and content takedowns function as guidance without legal teeth. The proposed amendment would treat non-compliance as a failure to meet safe harbour conditions, the legal shield that protects platforms from liability for user-posted content.

The pattern: This follows a busy year of tightening the screws. In February, the Modi government compressed the content takedown window from 36 hours to three hours and introduced new disclosure and metadata requirements for AI-generated content (which we covered here).

The race for users: Global AI companies are pouring into India. At the AI Impact Summit in February, Sundar Pichai, Sam Altman, and Dario Amodei all showed up in New Delhi. OpenAI is giving away ChatGPT Go free for a year, Perplexity bundled with Airtel's 360 million customers, and Google's Gemini ships with Jio.

What's next: The ministry published the proposed rules for public feedback, with comments open until 14 April.
sound_smarter: By tying safe harbour to compliance with ministerial advisories, New Delhi has built a reusable lever to shape platform behaviour without passing new legislation each time. As AI companies race to acquire Indian users at any cost, the government is ensuring the price of entry includes obedience.
