title: From shell to soul
text:
India approved 29 proposals to manufacture the components it has never made at home. The INR 7,104 crore (USD 751 million) package under the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme covers PCBs, rare-earth magnets, capacitors, relays, and EV inductors.

The shift: Until now, India's electronics manufacturing has been concentrated in assembly of finished products. Vaishnaw said India is now building the “heart” of devices, with this round targeting the actual inputs.

The numbers: Domestic capacitor supply will jump from 35% to 61% of demand. Relays will hit 100% with export surplus. Rare-earth magnets will rise to 25% of domestic demand, up from near zero.

The China subtext: Every component on this list is one where Beijing currently holds leverage. A supply shock would constrain India’s defence and clean energy sectors first.
sound_smarter: India has approved ambitious electronics targets before, with limited results. What's different this time is the fine print: companies must now develop design and engineering capabilities in India to qualify for incentives. Earlier schemes rewarded production volume; this one ties subsidies to intellectual property. The goal is to make India a component supplier, not just an assembly floor.
anchor: India approved 29 proposals to manufacture the components

title: Planting season, war permitting
text:
New Delhi is scrambling to secure fertiliser supplies before kharif planting begins in June. The West Asia conflict has disrupted roughly half of India's DAP and urea imports, and the government is in talks with Russia, Belarus, and Morocco to fill the gap.

The exposure: India imports 60% of its DAP and roughly half its urea. Saudi Arabia is the top DAP supplier; Oman is the biggest urea source. Both ship through the Strait of Hormuz. China's phosphate export suspension, in place until at least August, has shut another door.

The hard deadline: Kharif planting begins in June. Most fertiliser shipments arrive in March–May. Ships from Russia and Belarus take weeks longer than Gulf routes.

The fiscal squeeze: Urea prices have surged roughly 50% since the war began. The government subsidises retail fertiliser prices, shielding farmers from global spikes. But the subsidy bill for 2026-27 was already set at INR 1.71 lakh crore (USD 20 billion) before the war; rising import costs will push it higher.
sound_smarter: Fertiliser is where the West Asia conflict meets India's voters. New Delhi subsidises retail prices, and a prolonged disruption threatens to inflate that ballooning budget even further.
anchor: New Delhi is scrambling to secure fertiliser supplies

title: Editor’s note
text:
India is holding elections in five assemblies this April, covering roughly 174 million voters. Kerala, Assam, and Puducherry vote on April 9. Tamil Nadu votes on April 23. West Bengal votes in two phases on April 23 and 29. Results across all five come on May 4.

Over the past fortnight, every major party and alliance has laid out its pitch.

- The common thread across ideological lines, across states, and across incumbents and challengers alike: cash transfers to women, free household goods, and pension hikes.
- What is almost entirely absent: jobs, manufacturing, education reform, or female labour force participation.

We go state by state.
anchor: India is holding elections in five assemblies this

title: Tamil Nadu: the industrial giant with a freebie habit
text:
The fiercest bidding war is in Tamil Nadu, where welfare politics has been the organising principle of elections since Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) patriarch M Karunanidhi promised free colour televisions in 2006.

The pitch:

- The ruling DMK's 525-promise manifesto offers an INR 8,000 (USD 95) coupon for homemakers to buy or replace appliances of their choice, from washing machines to microwaves. It doubles the existing monthly cash transfer for women to INR 2,000 (USD 24), pledges 35 lakh (3.5 million) free laptops, and promises health insurance cover of INR 10 lakh (USD 11,900).
- The opposition All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK)'s 297-promise manifesto counters with a free fridge for every ration-card family, INR 10,000 (USD 119) one-time cash for every household, three free LPG cylinders a year, and also INR 2,000 per month for women. Both parties promise the same paddy procurement price of INR 3,500 per quintal and the same sugarcane price of INR 4,500 per tonne.
- Actor Vijay's new Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) adds a third front, pledging anti-drug zones in schools and interest-free loans for young entrepreneurs.

The missing word: Strikingly, neither the DMK nor the AIADMK mentions liquor prohibition, a demand that has historically dominated Tamil Nadu elections. Both parties appear content to leave revenues from the state’s liquor monopoly, Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation Limited (TASMAC), untouched – a rare moment of fiscal honesty in an otherwise extravagant season.

The paradox: Tamil Nadu is India’s second-largest state economy and its most industrialised, which should, in theory, be able to afford a generous welfare floor. After all, It recorded 11.19% real gross state domestic product (GSDP) growth in 2024-25. Manufacturing expanded by 14.74%, over three times the national average. Merchandise exports doubled in four years to USD 52 billion. Chennai is India's automobile capital; Hyundai, Rolls-Royce, and Vietnamese EV manufacturer Vinfast have all committed to operations in the state.

- Yet the state's outstanding debt is projected to hit INR 10.71 lakh crore (USD 127 billion) by March 2027. Committed expenditure on salaries, pensions, and interest payments already eats between 60% and 68% of revenue receipts, and the share going to interest payments alone has risen from 27% to nearly 33% in four years. The fiscal deficit sits at 3% of GSDP, right at the statutory ceiling. Tamil Nadu's share of central tax devolution has also shrunk from 7.9% to 4.08% under the latest Finance Commission formula, squeezing the revenue side further.

No manifesto from any party explains how it plans to fund hundreds of new commitments within these constraints. Tamil Nadu's industrial engine generates the growth; the welfare machine absorbs it.
anchor: The fiercest bidding war is in Tamil Nadu,

title: Kerala: Gulf money dries up, promises flow
text:
Kerala votes on April 9 in a three-cornered fight between the incumbent Left Democratic Front (LDF), the Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF), and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA), which has never won more than a single seat in the assembly.

The pitch:

- The UDF is running on five Indira Guarantees (named after former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi): free Kerala State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC) bus travel for women, INR 1,000 (USD 12) monthly for college-going girls, welfare pensions for senior citizens hiked to INR 3,000 (USD 36), INR 25 lakh (USD 29,700) health insurance per household, and interest-free loans of up to INR 5 lakh (USD 5,950) for young entrepreneurs.
- The BJP released its manifesto today, promising an All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), high-speed rail from Thiruvananthapuram to Kannur, INR 2,500 (USD 30) monthly grocery and medicine cards for women, 20,000 litres of free water per household, and two free LPG cylinders a year timed to Onam (Kerala's biggest festival) and Christmas.
- The incumbent LDF, which broke Kerala's decades-long tradition of alternating governments by winning a second consecutive term in 2021, is running largely on its governance record.

The vulnerability: Kerala's economy has, for decades, run on remittances from the Gulf. The state accounts for roughly a fifth of all remittances flowing into India; in 2023-24, Gulf inflows totalled USD 26 billion, equivalent to roughly a fifth of the state's income. Remittances are 1.7 times the state's total revenue receipts.

This lifeline is now under direct threat. The ongoing West Asia conflict has strained energy supplies and Gulf economies, and India faces a "triple threat" of higher energy costs, falling remittances, and reverse migration. The GCC region hosts between eight and nine million Indian workers; if the conflict escalates, mass returns would hit Kerala hardest. Beyond the immediate crisis, the structural shift is already underway: the Gulf's share of Kerala's emigrants has fallen from 89.2% in 2018 to 80.5% in 2023, as younger Keralites increasingly head to the US, UK, and Canada. Post-2030 remittance inflows could decline by as much as 20%.

None of the three major fronts' manifestos addresses this structural exposure. Kerala has also breached the 3-3.5% fiscal deficit threshold, and the Centre has already clawed back borrowing limits for off-budget borrowing through vehicles like the Kerala Infrastructure Investment Fund Board (KIIFB). The UDF's five guarantees alone would cost an estimated INR 25,000 crore (USD 3 billion) annually.

The state's challenge is existential: how does an economy built on Gulf remittances fund a welfare expansion just as that money starts to dry up?

title: West Bengal: popular schemes, hollowed-out state
text:
West Bengal votes in two phases on April 23 and 29. Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee, of the Trinamool Congress (TMC), is seeking a fourth consecutive term.

The pitch:

- The TMC released its 10 pledges in March, centred on a INR 500 (USD 6) hike in the Lakshmir Bhandar women's monthly cash transfer to INR 1,500 (USD 18), INR 1,500 (USD 18) monthly for unemployed youth under Banglar Yuba-Sathi, a INR 30,000 crore (USD 3.6 billion) agriculture budget covering increased support for farmers, doorstep healthcare camps, and pucca (not a word international audiences know) homes and piped water for every household.
- The BJP has pivoted sharply from 2021, when it attacked these very handouts. It now promises INR 3,000 (USD 36) per month for women under a new Annapurna Yojana, effectively pledging to double Lakshmir Bhandar. This is the clearest illustration of how the competitive logic works: the party that mocked the scheme five years ago now promises more of it.

The decay: Mamata's welfare schemes are undeniably popular. Lakshmir Bhandar reaches millions of women and has been credited with consolidating the TMC's female voter base. But the state's broader economic indicators tell a grimmer story. West Bengal's outstanding debt is projected at INR 8.15 lakh crore (USD 97 billion) for 2026-27, with a debt-to-GSDP ratio of 38%, one of the highest among major states. The fiscal deficit sits at 3.6% of GSDP, above the recommended ceiling. Capital expenditure allocation is among the lowest in the country at roughly 10% of developmental expenditure. Welfare spending is crowding out long-term investment in roads, hospitals, and industrial infrastructure. The Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), has accused the TMC of pushing the state into a debt trap; the BJP's response is to promise even more transfers. The Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has also been a flashpoint, with opposition parties alleging it disproportionately affects minority voters, adding a volatile undercurrent to a state that has a fraught history of election-related tension.

title: Assam: identity, floods and the promise of jobs
text:
Assam votes on April 9. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma is seeking a second term for the BJP.

The pitch:

- The BJP released its Sankalp Patra today, mixing welfare with identity politics in a way the other states have not. Alongside INR 3,000 (USD 36) monthly for women, a figure that has become the going rate across BJP manifestos this cycle, and a pledge of 200,000 jobs, it promises a Uniform Civil Code, action against love jihad – a term Hindu nationalist groups use for alleged campaigns by Muslim men to convert Hindu women through marriage, and INR 18,000 crore (USD 2.1 billion) for flood mitigation.
- Congress has countered with five guarantees of its own, centring on cash support, health cover, and land rights.

Reform or polarisation? Assam's manifesto landscape reads differently from the southern states. The flood-proofing commitment and the jobs pledge at least gesture at structural problems. Assam faces annual devastation from Brahmaputra flooding, and 200,000 jobs would, if delivered, be a meaningful intervention in a state with limited industrial infrastructure. But the UCC and love jihad planks exist on a different axis entirely. In a state where the National Register of Citizens (NRC) process has already generated years of anxiety and legal limbo, and where the SIR of electoral rolls has triggered fresh accusations of selective disenfranchisement, these promises read as much as mobilisation tools as governance commitments. Assam's fiscal deficit has also breached the 3-3.5% threshold, though the state's lower absolute debt gives it marginally more room than West Bengal or Tamil Nadu.

title: What nobody is promising
text:
Across 824 seats and over a thousand pages of manifestos, some topics are conspicuous by their absence.

No major party in any state offers a serious plan for raising female labour force participation, which at roughly 35% is half the rate of men and well below the global average of 47%. Goldman Sachs estimates that closing this gap could add a full percentage point to India's potential growth.

No manifesto addresses the quality crisis in government schools or the mismatch between what universities produce and what employers need. Manufacturing strategy, where it appears, is limited to vague investment targets rather than specific policy reforms on land acquisition, labour laws, or ease of doing business.

- Tamil Nadu's own Economic Survey notes that the state should invest in youth skill development and promote women's workforce participation, but neither the DMK nor the AIADMK manifesto picks up the recommendation. The DMK promises 5 million jobs without explaining how; the AIADMK promises unemployment allowances, which concede the problem without solving it.
- In West Bengal, the Yuba-Sathi scheme pays youth INR 1,500 per month while they remain unemployed; the BJP promises to raise the amount. The incentive structure, in both cases, is to manage joblessness rather than eliminate it.
- Kerala, which prides itself on having India's most literate and skilled workforce, is perhaps the most glaring omission. With Gulf employment structurally declining and remittances under threat, the state urgently needs to create domestic jobs for returning workers and young graduates heading abroad.

No front's manifesto offers a plan to do so; all three would rather promise free bus rides than retool the workforce that pays for them.

title: The verdict
text:
The Supreme Court flagged the freebie problem in 2022 and asked the Election Commission to act. Four years on, the arms race has only accelerated.

What was once a Dravidian innovation in Tamil Nadu is now the default playbook from Guwahati to Thiruvananthapuram, and the most telling shift this cycle is the BJP's. The party that mocked cash transfers in Bengal in 2021 now promises to double them; the party that built its national brand on development and governance is, at the state level, competing coupon for coupon.

The freebie war is no longer Left versus Right. It is the price of entry.

Every manifesto promises to distribute more; none explains where the money comes from, how existing debt will be serviced, or what happens to the roads, schools, and hospitals that don't get built because the budget went to transfers instead. The voters get the freebies. The treasuries get the bill, and the bill will arrive long after the votes are counted.

title: India will deploy more than three million officials
text: India will deploy more than three million officials from tomorrow to begin the first phase of Census 2027, its first fully digital headcount. The houselisting phase runs from April to September, covering housing conditions and household assets, before a population enumeration in early 2027 that will include caste data for the first time since independence. The last census was conducted in 2011.

title: Busting retro tax ghosts
text:
India moved Wednesday to calm investor nerves after a Supreme Court ruling threatened decades of foreign investment protections.

Tiger’s tail: In January, the Supreme Court ruled Tiger Global’s Mauritius units were mere "conduits," stripping treaty protections from their USD 1.6 billion Flipkart stake sale to Walmart. The ruling sparked fears that tax officers would weaponise the precedent to reopen every legacy deal routed through tax havens.

The firewall, and the caveat: The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) clarified that investments made before April 1, 2017 are exempt from General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR). The change takes effect immediately. However, the protection covers the investment date, not the exit structure. If a post-2017 transaction lacks commercial substance, GAAR can still apply.

The ghost in the room: New Delhi is desperate to distance itself from its reputation for terrorising companies with massive tax bills. Vodafone spent a decade fighting a USD 2 billion retrospective bill, while Volkswagen is currently contesting a USD 1.4 billion demand spanning 12 years of scrutiny.
sound_smarter: This is damage control. The Tiger Global ruling rattled the same foreign investors India is courting for manufacturing and tech investment. By ringfencing legacy FDI, New Delhi is signalling that the past is settled.

title: Home base to the rescue
text:
India's export zones just got permission to sell at home. On Tuesday, the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) opened a one-year window for Special Economic Zone (SEZ) manufacturers to sell goods into the domestic market at concessional customs duty rates, a direct response to what the government called "global trade disruptions."

How it works: SEZ units that were operational by 31 March 2025 can now clear manufactured goods into the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) at reduced rates. A unit currently facing a 20% duty on domestic sales, for instance, would pay 12.5% instead. The concessions scale across brackets, with cuts of 1 to 10 percentage points depending on the product.

The guardrails: Domestic sales are capped at 30% of a unit's best export year over the previous three financial years. Goods must have at least 20% value addition over inputs. Sensitive sectors are excluded entirely. The window runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027.
sound_smarter: The 30% cap keeps the export orientation intact on paper. However, this is the first time New Delhi has formally let SEZ units redirect output homeward because export markets turned hostile. If trade conditions persist, extending the window becomes the path of least resistance. The relief keeps production lines running, but it is unlikely to become a comfortable alternative to exports.
anchor: India's export zones just got permission to sell

title: Squeeze play
text:
Three interventions in four days gave the rupee its best session since 2013. The currency surged 1.8% to 93.10 per dollar on Thursday after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) shut down speculative trades that had driven it to record lows.

The whack-a-mole: The RBI first capped banks' net open rupee positions at USD 100 million on Monday. When banks responded by offloading positions to corporates and hedge funds, the central bank followed up on Wednesday by banning rupee non-deliverable forwards and barring companies from rebooking cancelled forward contracts.

The bounce: The rupee hit 92.84 intraday, recovering from Wednesday's record low of 95.21. The last rally of this scale came in September 2013, when emergency RBI measures and a surprise pause in US Federal Reserve tightening steadied a currency hammered by current account fears.

The bill: Bank stocks paid the price. The Nifty Bank index fell 4.3% this week to a one-year low, with state-run lenders dropping hardest. Jefferies estimates sector-wide losses at INR 40–50 billion (USD 428–535 million).
sound_smarter: Each measure by the RBI closed one arbitrage route and opened another. The underlying stress, a current account squeezed by elevated oil prices amid the Iran conflict, remains beyond the central bank's reach.
anchor: Three interventions in four days gave the rupee

title: A gust of relief
text:
India’s power regulator (CERC) has pushed back stricter penalties for wind and solar generators to April 2027, granting the industry a one-year reprieve.

The friction: Under the Deviation Settlement Mechanism (DSM), generators are fined when actual power supply misses scheduled targets. Industry groups warned that the intermittent nature of renewables could lead to 48% revenue losses and kill fresh investment (we covered it here).

The compromise: Since the DSM Regulations were introduced in 2024, industry groups worried that penalties would immediately come into effect through an immediate reduction in the “X” value – a key penalty buffer – when the regulations commenced on March 31, 2026. The latest order from the CERC keeps the “X” value at 100% in FY2026-2027, then reduces the value until it hits 0% in 2031, exposing renewable projects to the same penalties as fossil-fuel power generators when they miss their promised supply targets. And unlike the stricter September 2025 proposal that outlined how the “X” value would fall, this new order slows the annual phase-down of this buffer and leaves the largest reduction for FY2030-2031.
sound_smarter: By back-loading the steepest penalty increases toward 2031, the regulator is buying time for renewable operators to sharpen their forecasting and for the domestic energy storage market to mature.

title: Guns, drones, and glory
text:
India’s defence exports hit an all-time high of INR 38,424 crore (USD 4.6 billion) in FY26, marking a 62.66% year-on-year jump.

State-led surge: Government-owned firms led the way, with exports leaping 151% to claim a 54.84% market share. Private firms grew 14%, supplying hardware ranging from armoured vehicles to drones.

Global footprint: India now ships to 80+ nations. While state firms focus on munitions and torpedoes, the number of active exporters grew to 145. As Defence Minister Rajnath Singh noted, India is "scripting an impressive defence exports success story."

The catalysts: Global volatility, specifically in Ukraine and the Caucasus, combined with India’s Atmanirbhar Bharat (self-reliance) push, has transformed India into a competitive global supplier.
sound_smarter: Volume and competitive pricing are embedding India in defence supply chains across both NATO-aligned states and the Global South. The more countries that depend on Indian hardware, the harder it becomes to switch suppliers.

title: A bitter shortage
text:
India’s sugar output is falling short of domestic demand for the second-year running as poor crops force mills to close early.

By the numbers: India expects just 28 million tons this season, 3 below the 31 million tons predicted. The country consumes 29 million tons annually, leaving no surplus.

The world stage: As the world's second-largest producer, India's crunch is driving up global prices. Brazil and Thailand are positioned to fill the gap.

The export mistake: The government recently greenlit 2 million tons in exports, betting on a surplus that never arrived. The national stockpile is now shrinking.

Empty mills: In the sugar-rich states of Maharashtra and Karnataka, almost all mills have already shut down for the season weeks ahead of schedule.
sound_smarter: India's sugar policy is built around a predictable monsoon that is becoming less reliable. The buffer the government uses to control prices and meet ethanol blending targets is thinning. If output keeps falling short of forecasts, the planning model underpinning both food security and energy policy faces serious strain.

title: Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov called
text: Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov called on PM Modi on Wednesday, briefing him on progress in trade, fertilisers and connectivity following the December 2025 India-Russia summit. Separately, a parliamentary delegation led by Vladimir Yakushev, First Deputy Chairperson of Russia's Federation Council, met Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman Harivansh. The two sides discussed restarting the Inter-Parliamentary Commission, which last met in 2018, and flagged artificial intelligence, space research and clean energy as new areas for cooperation. India will host the BRICS Parliamentary Forum this year as the bloc's chair.

title: Hormuz or high water
text:
Indian shares slid Monday morning after President Donald Trump threatened "hell" if Iran fails to reopen the Strait of Hormuz by Tuesday.

The ultimatum: Trump warned Tehran it would be "living in Hell" if the waterway remains blocked past 8 pm Eastern Time Tuesday. Iran refused to budge until its demands are met. Brent crude hit USD 109.77, roughly 50% higher than when the conflict started on February 28.

The damage: The Nifty 50 and Sensex both dropped over 0.4% at the open, with losses across fifteen of sixteen major sectors. The Nifty has fallen roughly 10% since the conflict began. March saw a record Rs 1.22 lakh crore (USD 12 billion) exodus by foreign portfolio investors.

The squeeze: India imports 85% of its crude, with 40-50% of its energy needs transiting Hormuz. Forex reserves have fallen USD 30.5 billion since late February as the RBI intervened to defend the rupee. Last week, the central bank capped banks' rupee positions and banned non-deliverable forwards to crush speculative trades (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Indian markets are now reactive to geopolitical rhetoric rather than domestic fundamentals. The RBI can defend the rupee with reserves and regulation, but it cannot price out the risk premium investors charge when energy security is under threat. As long as the Strait remains closed, the Nifty will move on headlines from Washington and Tehran rather than corporate earnings.

title: Higher costs for hedging
text:
The central bank (RBI) crackdown on rupee speculation has sent dollar hedging costs soaring by the most since the 2008 financial crisis.

The squeeze: One-year dollar hedging costs jumped 30 basis points to 3.96% on Monday, following a massive 70-bp surge last Thursday. The spike comes after the RBI moved to kill arbitrage, forcing a panicked scramble among importers to lock in dollar exposure.

RBI’s heavy hand: To rein in the rupee, the central bank capped banks' net open positions at USD 100 million and banned companies from rebooking cancelled forward contracts, which we covered here and here. This effectively trapped corporations, forcing them to hedge beyond their immediate needs to avoid being caught without cover later.

Market reaction: The rupee rallied 2% toward the 93 level. But by banning non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) and rebooking, the RBI has reduced market liquidity.
sound_smarter: The RBI’s latest moves may help stabilise the rupee in the short term but they do so by making the hedging channel less efficient and raising the cost of business for importers.
anchor: The central bank (RBI) crackdown on rupee speculation

title: Growing pains
text:
India's services sector grew at its weakest pace in 14 months in March as the West Asia conflict weighed on domestic demand, though foreign orders surged to near-record levels.

By the numbers: The HSBC India Services Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) fell to 57.5 from February's 58.1, still comfortably above the 50-mark separating expansion from contraction. The broader Composite PMI dropped to 57.0 from 58.9, its weakest reading in nearly three and a half years.

Under the hood: New business grew at its slowest rate since January 2025, with firms citing competition and fading domestic appetite. International orders, however, climbed to their second-highest level since the index began tracking them in 2014. Input costs rose at their sharpest since mid-2022. Firms passed some of that on to clients but absorbed the widest gap between costs and prices in nearly three years. However, hiring expanded for a third straight month at its strongest pace since June 2025, and business confidence hit a near 12-year high.
sound_smarter: The West Asia conflict is producing opposite effects across sectors. Services exporters are thriving on foreign demand while their domestic business slows. Manufacturing exporters face the reverse, with weak global orders prompting the government to let SEZ units sell domestically at concessional duties for a year (we covered it here). If both trends persist, that temporary measure starts looking permanent, and India's growth model quietly reshuffles around whichever markets are still buying.
anchor: India's services sector grew at its weakest pace

title: Tarmac over targets
text:
New Delhi is evaluating austerity measures to preserve its 4.3% fiscal deficit goal for FY27 as the Middle East conflict drives up energy costs.

Hold the line: The government sees "no immediate risk" to budget targets, stating projections will only change if global pressures last beyond three months. Private analysts are less certain, and Standard Chartered predicts a potential fiscal slippage of up to 0.9% due to rising oil prices.

Targeted curbs: To bridge the gap, the government plans to trim budgets for ministries with low spending capacity. These savings will protect high capital expenditure in growth-critical sectors like roads, railways, and airports.

The political cost: With four state assembly elections this month, the government is absorbing high crude prices via subsidies rather than raising retail rates. This shields consumers but adds an INR 1.83 trillion burden to the federal budget.
sound_smarter: New Delhi is reshuffling its budget to protect credit ratings and bond inflows. By starving administrative budgets to fund infrastructure, New Delhi is betting that economic growth can outrun the fiscal pressure, even as election-year subsidies and war-driven oil spikes tighten the squeeze.

title: Off the boil
text:
India's cooking gas crisis is dragging down sugar and edible oil consumption as restaurants and street vendors scale back or shut down.

The numbers: Edible oil imports fell nearly 9% in March to 1.2 million tonnes. Sugar consumption dropped by 200,000 tonnes over the same period, with a similar decline expected in April. Lower demand could ease India's import bill for vegetable oils, especially palm oil and sunflower oil.

Street-level damage: Roadside eateries and restaurants, workhorses of India’s vast informal sector, are bearing the brunt. Commercial LPG cylinders remain capped at 50% of pre-crisis supply, and vendors are unsure when their next delivery will arrive.

Policy hold: Food Secretary Sanjeev Chopra said India has no plans to curb sugar exports or cut import duties on edible oils, despite output falling short of forecasts for a second consecutive year (we covered it here). Chopra also ruled out diverting sugar toward ethanol production to offset crude oil disruption from the West Asia conflict. India's sugar output is expected to fall below its 29 million tonne annual consumption for a second straight year.
sound_smarter: Suppressed demand from shuttered kitchens is closing the supply-demand gap that weaker harvests created. If gas supplies recover before the next crushing season and consumption snaps back, the sugar deficit returns with no export buffer left to absorb it.
anchor: India's cooking gas crisis is dragging down sugar

title: Campbell Wilson has stepped down as Air India
text: Campbell Wilson has stepped down as Air India CEO and Managing Director, four years into a five-year term. Wilson, who joined from Singapore Airlines subsidiary Scoot in 2022, led the Vistara merger and launched the Vihaan.AI turnaround plan, but exits with combined losses of INR 10,859 crore (USD 1.3 billion) in FY25 and a USD 400 million fleet retrofit running two years behind schedule. The June 2025 Ahmedabad-London crash, which killed 260 people, intensified regulatory scrutiny. Tata Sons is expected to finalise a successor by May.

title: Damming the divide
text:
On Wednesday, New Delhi approved INR 40,175 crore (USD 4.7 billion) for two hydroelectric projects in Arunachal Pradesh: the 1,720 MW Kamala and 1,200 MW Kalai-II plants.

Grid stabiliser: The two plants will help manage peak electricity demand and steady a national grid increasingly reliant on intermittent solar and wind. The Kamala project also provides flood moderation in the Brahmaputra Valley, with a dedicated budget of INR 4,744 crore for that component alone.

Local buy-in: Arunachal Pradesh holds a 26% equity stake in the Kamala project and receives 12% free power from both plants, plus an additional 1% earmarked for a Local Area Development Fund. New Delhi is also funding over 225 km of roads and bridges across the two project sites.

The Brahmaputra race: Kalai-II is the first hydropower project on the Lohit river, opening an entirely new basin. Following the 2024 and 2025 clearances of the Tato-I and Tato-II projects, these latest approvals extend India's push to establish prior use across the Brahmaputra system, countering Beijing's upstream dam-building.
sound_smarter: Beyond the green energy optics, these dams are infrastructure as sovereignty. Kalai-II sits in Anjaw, a border district where China claims the entire state. By planting high-capex engineering in these areas, New Delhi is asserting effective control. In Himalayan hydro-politics, whoever builds first establishes prior use on shared rivers, and India is racing to get there before Beijing does.

title: Iranian oil is back
text:
India is set to receive its first Iranian oil shipment since 2019 after Washington issued a 30-day waiver last month to ease global supply crunches.

The details: State-run Indian Oil Corp (IOC) snagged the cargo aboard the VLCC Jaya, which was originally headed for China and is currently heading to India’s east coast. A second carrier, Jordan, is also signalling India as its destination.

The waiver: Washington issued a 30-day waiver for countries to purchase Iranian oil already at sea – roughly 170 million barrels loaded by March 20 and discharged by April 19 (we covered it here). It’s a temporary band-aid designed to plug supply holes caused by the ongoing West Asia conflict.

Energy anxiety: India entered this regional crisis with a razor-thin 50-day reserve, which we covered here. Having been forced to ditch Tehran’s crude five years ago under US pressure, New Delhi is now scrambling to stabilize domestic prices.
sound_smarter: While these shipments provide brief breathing room, India’s depleted reserves leave it dangerously exposed. Expect New Delhi to use its economic pain as leverage to push Washington toward a more permanent diplomatic – or at least longer – de-escalation with Iran when negotiations start on Friday in Islamabad.

title: The Congress party attacked PM Modi's foreign policy
text: The Congress party attacked PM Modi's foreign policy after Pakistan brokered a two-week ceasefire between the US and Iran in the ongoing West Asia conflict. Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh called Pakistan's role a "severe setback" to Modi's "highly personalised diplomacy," arguing that the "self-styled Vishwaguru" (world teacher, a title Modi uses to frame India's global leadership) "stands thoroughly exposed." Ramesh pointed to Modi's visit to Israel just two days before the war began on February 28, and accused the government of staying silent on both Israeli military action and Trump's rhetoric. The opposition argued that New Delhi's failure to play any mediating role, while Pakistan stepped in, undercuts years of efforts to isolate Islamabad internationally.

title: Relationship context: No surprises here that Pakistan would
text: Relationship context: No surprises here that Pakistan would be in a better position than India to broker a ceasefire between Iran and the US. Pakistan shares a long border with Iran and according to Asif Durrani, Pakistan’s former ambassador to Tehran, Pakistan is “the only country in the region enjoying good relations with the US and Iran.” Pakistan has also represented some Iranian diplomatic interests in Washington, where Tehran has no embassy.

text: Millions of voters across Assam, Kerala, and Puducherry are casting ballots today in the opening phase of the 2026 elections to five legislative assemblies – Assam, Kerala, Puducherry, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal. title: India's Civil Aviation Ministry has cut landing and
text: India's Civil Aviation Ministry has cut landing and parking charges at all domestic airports by 25% for three months, the latest in a series of measures to shield carriers from the West Asia crisis. Aviation fuel prices have surged over 100% globally since the conflict began, but New Delhi has capped the pass-through to domestic airlines at 25%. The landing charge reduction, effective immediately, is expected to save airlines roughly INR 400 crore over the three-month window. The Airports Economic Regulatory Authority will adjust any airport revenue shortfalls in the next five-year tariff cycle.

title: Crisis management, cylinder by cylinder
text:
India laid out its crisis playbook for the Hormuz disruption at an inter-ministerial briefing on Wednesday, spanning fuel rationing, pharmaceutical supply chains, maritime operations, and the evacuation of Indian nationals from the region.

Crisis footing: Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) booking intervals have been stretched from 21 to 25 days in cities and up to 45 days in rural areas. Commercial LPG allocation sits at 70% of pre-crisis levels, conditional on industries applying for piped natural gas (PNG) connections. New Delhi cut excise duty on petrol and diesel and imposed export levies on diesel and aviation fuel to keep domestic supply intact. Retail prices remain unchanged, a pattern we have been tracking since March. Over 116,000 raids against LPG hoarding have been conducted nationwide. Customs duty has been zeroed on 40 petrochemical products to protect pharmaceutical inputs.

Abroad: Indian missions have been facilitating the movement of nationals out of the region, including through Armenia and Azerbaijan for those stranded in Iran. Airspace remains closed in Kuwait and Israel. Bahrain has just reopened, while the UAE and Qatar are running limited flights. Saudi Arabia and Oman are operating normally.

Diplomatic front: External Affairs Minister Jaishankar visits the UAE on 11-12 April, his first trip there since the conflict began, announced hours after the US-Iran ceasefire. Petroleum Minister Puri is in Qatar today to press for priority Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) delivery after QatarEnergy declared force majeure on long-term gas contracts last month, following Iranian strikes that knocked out roughly 17% of Qatar's export capacity.
sound_smarter: Six weeks into the Hormuz crisis, this briefing is a stress test scorecard. Crude oil has alternatives: over 40 suppliers, flexible spot markets, and refineries running above capacity (which we covered here). Pharma inputs can be rerouted with duty cuts and domestic substitution. Evacuations are functioning through third countries. LPG remains the one dependency India cannot engineer around, and New Delhi is using the crisis to try to wean its populace off imported cooking gas and onto domestically supplied piped natural gas, closing a gap the crisis has finally made urgent.

title: World Bank raises growth forecast to 6.6%
text: The World Bank raised India's FY27 growth forecast to 6.6%, up from its October estimate of 6.3%, citing robust domestic demand and recently signed free trade agreements with the EU and UK. The upgrade still marks a slowdown from FY26's 7.6%, with the West Asia conflict the primary drag. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is bullish at 6.9%; Moody's more cautious at 6.0%.
anchor: The World Bank raised India's FY27 growth forecast

title: Taxing the flight to profits
text:
The Ministry of Finance more than doubled windfall taxes on diesel and aviation turbine fuel (ATF) exports on Saturday, escalating efforts to shore up domestic stocks as regional supply chains wobble.

The price hike: Effective immediately, the tax on diesel jumped from 21.5 to 55.5 rupees per litre, while ATF rose from 29.5 to 42 rupees. This follows the initial levy introduced on March 26 to curb a massive export surge.

Chasing margins: Indian refiners boosted diesel exports by 20% in March, primarily to Southeast Asia.

Energy instability: With the West Asia crisis throttling global oil flows, the government is in full intervention mode. Alongside export taxes, New Delhi has cut excise duties and capped monthly ATF price hikes to shield the domestic economy from a volatile energy market.
sound_smarter: The April 8 ceasefire between Iran, Israel, and the US have not stopped these hikes three days later. For Indian refiners, the export incentive remains attractive. Expect the Finance Ministry to tighten the screws further if outbound tankers don't start staying home.
anchor: The Ministry of Finance more than doubled windfall

title: Rice paper trail
text:
India is cutting red tape to feed the rest of Europe. Last Friday, New Delhi renewed a six-month waiver on mandatory inspection certificates for rice exports to non-EU European countries, extending a policy first introduced in October 2025.

The divide: The Export Inspection Council (EIC) certificate remains compulsory for EU member states, the UK, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland. All other European countries are exempt.

Export surge: Rice exports hit USD 12.95 billion in 2024–25, up 62% since 2014. Removing the EIC bottleneck for markets that never required the certification clears the way for faster shipments to buyers across Eastern Europe and Eurasia.
sound_smarter: The geography of this exemption is the real story. By waiving requirements specifically for Eurasia and the Balkans, India is courting markets that don't demand Brussels-level paperwork. These are low-friction entry points designed to test whether simplified access can meaningfully shift volumes.

title: India mourns playback singer Asha Bhosle
text: Legendary playback singer Asha Bhosle died on Sunday from multi-organ failure, at the age of 92. Bhosle recorded over 12,000 songs across multiple Indian languages in a career spanning eight decades and held the Guinness World Record as the most recorded artist in history. In a moving tribute, Prime Minister Modi called her "one of the most iconic and versatile voices India has ever known."
anchor: Legendary playback singer Asha Bhosle died on Sunday

title: Reserved seating
text:
Parliament convenes a special three-day session on Wednesday to pass amendments to the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (Women's Reservation Act), the 2023 constitutional amendment that reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies.

The backstory: The law passed unanimously in September 2023 but tied implementation to a future census and delimitation exercise, pushing enforcement to roughly 2034. The government's amendment delinks implementation from the upcoming 2027 Census, using 2011 Census data instead to get women's reservation in place for the 2029 general election.

The big structural shift: To carve out women's seats without displacing incumbents, the Lok Sabha expands from 543 to 816 seats (a uniform 50% increase across states). Of those, 273 go to women. Seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (India's constitutionally recognised disadvantaged communities) also increase, from 84 to 136 and 47 to 70 respectively, with one-third of each reserved for women.

Why the opposition objects: Congress, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), and southern chief ministers support women's reservation but oppose the bundle. They are concerned that using 15-year-old census data for delimitation is procedurally flawed; a population-based seat increase widens the gap between high-growth northern states and southern states that controlled their populations; the absence of reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBC) sidesteps a caste census; and scheduling the session during West Bengal and Tamil Nadu legislative assembly election campaigns smacks of political timing.

The squeeze: The amendment needs a two-thirds majority in both houses plus ratification by at least half of state legislatures. Modi has written to all floor leaders urging consensus, and separately addressed a women’s empowerment rally calling this "one of the biggest decisions of the 21st century." The opposition's bind is obvious: voting against women's reservation during election season is politically toxic, but voting for the package means accepting a delimitation framework that could reshape India's parliamentary geography for decades.
sound_smarter: No party can afford to vote against women's reservation. Modi has used that fact to bundle it with delimitation based on 15-year-old census data, reshaping parliamentary geography before updated numbers can rebalance the map. If the package passes, the north-south seat gap widens permanently and the window for an OBC quota tied to a fresh caste census narrows considerably. The opposition has been handed a reform it must support and a framework it cannot unpick.
anchor: Parliament convenes a special three-day session on Wednesday

title: All dressed up with nowhere to glow
text:
Rajasthan, India’s solar powerhouse, has 60 GW of clean energy projects stuck in limbo because the national grid can't keep up with the pace of construction.

The bottleneck: In an April 10 filing, the Central Transmission Utility (CTUIL) admitted it lacks the infrastructure for nearly half of the 130 GW of connectivity applications in the state. While generation is booming, transmission planning has not.

Hold on: The crunch is so severe that regulators recently told one developer, Saurya Urja, they could simply withdraw their application and claw back their bank guarantees.

The national gap: This isn't just a Rajasthan problem. CTUIL warns that while the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has identified 450 GW of renewable potential nationwide, transmission plans only cover 240 GW.
sound_smarter: India’s 500 GW renewable target for 2030 is a vanity metric if the transmission infrastructure isn’t there to carry the load. Transmission isn't sexy like massive solar farms, but without it, the green transition risks becoming a graveyard of stranded assets.

title: Pass the Rupee
text:
India's central bank now suspects its own clampdown created a workaround and plans to investigate the matter. Rather than closing USD 40 billion in speculative rupee positions, some banks may have quietly handed them to corporate clients instead.

Why it matters: Corporations are permitted to hedge FX exposure. If banks dressed up these trades as hedges and passed them along, that's market abuse.

What the RBI is doing: Since March 27, banks have been capped at USD 100 million in net onshore rupee positions, which we covered here. The RBI has now contacted treasury divisions at several large banks, demanding transaction records, client data, and deal documentation from the unwinding period.

The result so far: The win on paper was clear. The rupee has recovered from near 95.20 to around 92.50 per dollar. But the investigation suggests the underlying positions may simply have migrated.
sound_smarter: The central bank is not addressing the deeper problem: India’s relatively shallow FX market struggles to absorb geopolitical shocks without blunt intervention. Yet, every time the regulator leans in with a heavy hand, it fractures the trust that liquid markets depend on.

title: When the gas runs out
text:
Police fired tear gas to disperse factory workers in Noida, an industrial suburb of Delhi, as protests over rising living costs entered their fourth day. Vehicles were torched, stones pelted, and protesters blocked the Chilla Border connecting Delhi and Noida.

What they want: The protests are driven by a wage gap with neighbouring Haryana, which last week ordered a 35% hike in minimum wages after similar unrest in the auto hub of Manesar. Noida's factory workers earn around INR 13,000 (USD 155) per month; Haryana's new floor is INR 19,000 (USD 225). Workers are demanding parity.

The trigger: India is the world's second-largest LPG importer, and the US-Israeli war on Iran has choked fuel supplies. Prices at street eateries have doubled in some areas, hitting migrant factory workers hardest. The government has cut industrial gas allocations to protect household cooking supplies, squeezing businesses and workers simultaneously.

Labour flight: A growing number of migrant workers are heading back to their villages as food costs spiral. Auto suppliers in Manesar reported disrupted production this week. Employers say getting the migrant workers back is difficult once they leave.
sound_smarter: Haryana's wage hike bought temporary peace but pushed costs onto an auto industry already absorbing higher raw material prices from the Iran conflict. If Noida follows the same playbook, the pattern becomes a template: unrest, concession, cost pass-through.
anchor: Police fired tear gas to disperse factory workers

title: Iranian oil reached Indian ports
text: Two very large crude carriers (VLCC) loaded with Iranian oil have reached Indian ports for the first time in seven years, as refiners use a temporary US sanctions waiver to resume purchases from Tehran. India stopped buying Iranian crude in May 2019 under US pressure. Separately, Iran's ambassador to New Delhi confirmed that Indian tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz did not pay tolls to Tehran, after Trump vowed to block passage for vessels making payments to Iran. The US began enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports on Monday; the sanctions waiver expires April 19.

title: The long goodbye
text:
Nitish Kumar resigned as Bihar's chief minister on Tuesday, completing a choreographed transition that hands the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) direct control of India's third most populous state for the first time. Deputy CM Samrat Choudhary was unanimously elected BJP legislature party leader and takes oath as Bihar's chief minister today.

The sequence: The handover has been weeks in the making. After the National Democratic Alliance's (NDA, the BJP-led ruling coalition) landslide in the 2025 state elections, the BJP emerged as the single largest party with 89 of 243 seats but kept Nitish as CM for alliance continuity. In March, Nitish announced he would move to the Rajya Sabha (upper house of Parliament). He was elected on March 16, took his oath on April 10, and resigned as CM yesterday.

Who is Choudhary: Positioned as the BJP's Other Backward Classes (OBC) face in Bihar, Choudhary, 57, started in Lalu Prasad Yadav's Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) in 1999, switched to the Janata Dal (United), or JD(U), in 2014, then joined the BJP in 2017. He once vowed to wear a turban and remove it only after dethroning Nitish Kumar. He ended up serving as his deputy instead.

What JD(U) gets: Nitish, 75, has been promised continued influence and plans to spend most of his time in Bihar. His son Nishant, who joined JD(U) just a month ago, is being floated for a role in the incoming cabinet.
sound_smarter: For two decades, the BJP governed Bihar as a junior partner content to let Nitish run the show. Choudhary's appointment gives the BJP direct control ahead of 2029 and ends the party's dependence on an alliance partner whose loyalties have shifted multiple times.

title: PM Modi inaugurates Delhi-Dehradun Expressway
text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Delhi-Dehradun Expressway on Tuesday, a landmark project designed to cut travel time between the national capital and Uttarakhand from 6 hours to 2.5 hours. The 210-km corridor, built at a cost of approximately ₹13,000 crore ($14mn), features Asia’s largest 12-kilometre elevated wildlife corridor to protect the Shivalik forest ecosystem. The expressway is divided into four sections and includes a 340-meter tunnel near Dehradun to improve connectivity to the Himalayan foothills while minimising environmental impact.
anchor: Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Delhi-Dehradun Expressway

title: Shrinking for the wrong reasons
text:
India’s trade deficit narrowed to a nine-month low of USD 20.67 billion in March.

The March numbers: Exports rose slightly to USD 38.92 billion, while imports fell sharply to USD 59.59 billion. Despite this monthly dip, the financial year 2025-2026 (FY26) deficit sits at a three-year high of USD 119 billion, as annual imports (+6.5%) continue to outpace export growth (+4.22%).

The American tailwind: Shipments to the US jumped 17.4% to USD 8.02 billion. This surge in textiles and engineering goods follows a US Supreme Court ruling that slashed punitive 50% tariffs down to 10%, which we covered here.

Geopolitical friction: Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal attributed the shift to regional instability: "Our exports to [the] Middle East in the month of March have dipped by USD 3.5 billion... a decline of 57.95 per cent. There has been a decline of import[s] also... around USD 8.7 billion."
sound_smarter: The deficit shrank because of a sharp drop in imports – primarily energy (-35.91%) and raw materials – that outpaced the export slump, making this an artificially compressed deficit rather than an indication of growth in Indian export competitiveness.
anchor: India’s trade deficit narrowed to a nine-month low

title: All that glitters
text:
India's gem and jewellery exports fell 3.32% to USD 27.72 billion in the financial year 2025-2026 (FY26), marking the sector's worst performance since 2011.

Why it happened: US tariff pressure was the main cause, compounded by global inventory corrections, sluggish consumer demand, and luxury shoppers drifting toward experiences over earrings.

The reshuffle: The UAE has overtaken the US as India's top jewellery export market. UAE exports grew 22%, and Australia surged 38%, both propped up by free trade agreements.

Bright spot: Silver jewellery took the trend, surging 52% on rising affordability and global demand. Studded gold jewellery also held firm, up 6.27%.

Outlook: The India–US trade framework restores gems and jewellery tariffs to 18%, with zero duty on diamonds and coloured gemstones. Industry bodies project up to USD 3 billion in near-term export recovery.
sound_smarter: The 18% tariff restoration looks like a win until you note that is still nearly triple pre-tariff-war levels. The USD 3 billion recovery projection assumes US retailers, currently running lean inventory, rush straight back to Indian suppliers. The assumption is plausible, but competitors won't hand the market share back quietly.

title: Wholesale headache
text:
India’s wholesale prices are surging as global energy shocks hit the factory gate. In March, Wholesale Price Index (WPI) based inflation jumped to 3.88%, up from 2.13% in February and more than double the January print. This is the highest reading since January 2023.

The fuel fire: Energy costs are the primary culprit. The fuel and power index climbed 4.13%, supercharged by an 8.77% spike in mineral oils. A 5.07% dip in electricity prices provided only a minor cushion against rising crude and gas costs.

Manufacturing pain: The pressure is broad-based. The manufacturing sub-index, comprising over 64% of the WPI, saw 16 of 22 industrial groups post hikes. Metals, chemicals, and textiles led the gains.

A silver lining: Food and non-food articles eased slightly month-on-month. While annual comparisons remain high, this suggests near-term softening for consumers even as industrial overheads skyrocket.
sound_smarter: WPI has now overtaken the Consumer Price Index, an indicator that retail prices will follow in the next quarter. The 8.77% spike in mineral oils confirms India’s exposure to global energy shocks remains structural. With wholesale inflation more than doubling in ninety days, the Reserve Bank of India’s room to cut rates has effectively vanished.

title: Full steam behind
text:
A high-pressure steam tube ruptured at Vedanta's coal-fired power plant in Chhattisgarh's Sakti district on Tuesday, killing at least 17 workers and injuring 36 others.

What happened: The blast struck Unit 1 of the 1,200 megawatt (MW) Singhitarai plant when a steel tube carrying superheated steam from the boiler to the turbine burst, causing severe burns and triggering a fire. Four workers died on the spot; the rest succumbed to their injuries later. Operations at the unit have been suspended.

The fine print: Vedanta said the affected workers were employed by its subcontractor NTPC GE Power Services (NGSL), a joint venture between the National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) and General Electric (GE). The company announced INR 3.5 million (USD 41,000) per family of the deceased and INR 1.5 million (USD 17,600) for the injured. Chief Minister Vishnu Deo Sai has ordered an inquiry; a separate magisterial probe is also underway.

Troubled history: The plant, originally owned by Athena Chhattisgarh Power, broke ground in 2009 but sat idle from 2016 to 2022. Vedanta acquired it in 2022 and commissioned Unit 1 only last August. The second unit remains under construction.
sound_smarter: The timing stings. Just last week, the Power Ministry deferred scheduled maintenance on 10 gigawatts (GW) of coal capacity to compensate for gas-fired generation lost to West Asia's disruptions, and invoked emergency powers under the Electricity Act to keep plants running. India's coal fleet is being asked to do more with less downtime, and Singhitarai is now a case study in what happens when ageing infrastructure meets political pressure to keep the lights on.

title: Hard rocks
text:
India has hit pause on Zambian critical mineral investment, refusing to commit further capital until Lusaka guarantees long-term mining rights.

The sticking point: Zambia allocated India a 9,000 square kilometre block last year for cobalt and copper exploration. Geologists have completed initial fieldwork and returned with samples, but New Delhi refuses to move the project into private-sector extraction without guaranteed tenure.

Strategic hunger: India's copper imports rose 4% to 1.2 million tonnes in the fiscal year ending March 2025. The 2018 closure of Vedanta's Sterlite Copper smelter flipped India from copper exporter to vulnerable importer of a metal critical to EVs and power grids. Cobalt dependence is even starker as nearly all supply is imported.

The leverage game: New Delhi is pursuing parallel government-to-government deals across Africa and Latin America, including an initial agreement with the Democratic Republic of Congo, to reduce exposure to a tightening global market.
sound_smarter: India is resisting the exploration trap, where countries fund years of mapping and sampling only to watch host governments shift terms once extraction turns profitable. Withholding capital now signals to other resource-rich partners that future New Delhi deals require binding commitments before private investment flows.

title: Linked bills fail to pass
text:
The Indian Parliament’s special session concluded on Saturday following the collapse of a high-stakes legislative package. At the center was a proposed amendment to the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (Women’s Reservation Act), which we covered here. The government attempted to pull forward the implementation of women's representation in the national legislature by tethering it to a controversial delimitation exercise – the redrawing of voting boundaries to expand the legislature.

- The amendment to the Women’s Reservation Act would pull forward the implementation of a 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha (lower house) and state assemblies so that it’s in place for the 2029 general election. Else, enforcement would have to wait until roughly 2034.
- The delimitation exercise would expand the Lok Sabha from 543 to 815 seats and allow for the increased women’s representation without displacing incumbents.

This combined legislative push failed to clear the lower house. While there was broad, theoretical support for women’s representation, the bill was fundamentally tethered to the more controversial proposal to expand the House. This linkage proved to be the poison pill that led to the bill’s defeat.

- The government’s logic was to present a legislative package that modernized the size of the parliament while ensuring gender parity – all while avoiding displacing mostly male incumbents.
- However, the opposition viewed this as a tactical maneuver to force through a redistribution of political power under the popular guise of women's empowerment because it would grant the legislature discretionary power over delimitation beyond simply unfreezing it (we cover it in more detail below).

Struggle for greater female political representation

The struggle for a women’s reservation bill in India is nearly three decades old. First introduced in 1996, the bill has historically faced fierce resistance, often from regional parties who feared it would displace established male leaders or disproportionately benefit upper-class women over those from marginalized castes. Despite India having high-profile female leaders – including Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and multiple female Chief Ministers – female representation in the Lok Sabha has remained stubbornly low. In recent years, it has hovered around 14-15%, significantly below the global average and far behind many of India’s neighbors.

The Women’s Reservation Act is a 2023 constitutional amendment that reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies. The law passed unanimously in September 2023 but tied implementation to a future census and delimitation exercise, pushing enforcement to roughly 2034. The government's proposed amendment delinks implementation from the upcoming 2027 Census, using 2011 Census data instead to get women's reservation in place for the 2029 general election.

There is overwhelming public support for the bill. Indian women are becoming an increasingly influential voting bloc, often outvoting men in several state elections. While almost every major party claims to support women’s reservation in their manifestos, internal party hierarchies remain male-dominated. The failure to pass the bill on Friday is being framed by the opposition as a betrayal by the government for making the quota conditional on the contentious delimitation process, rather than passing it as a standalone bill.

Redrawing voting boundaries and expanding the legislature

The second, and more contentious, half of the failed legislation involved redrawing voting boundaries and increasing the number of Members of Parliament (MPs). The number of seats in India’s Parliament has been frozen since the mid-1970s. In 1976, during the Emergency, the government froze the seat allocation based on the 1971 Census to ensure that states which successfully implemented population control (primarily in the South) were not punished by losing seats to states with higher birth rates (primarily in the North). This freeze was later extended until 2026.

The failed bill sought to end this freeze and expand the legislature based on the 2011 census data (or potentially more recent estimates).

- Southern states like Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka argue that because they have achieved lower fertility rates and better development outcomes, a population-based expansion would drastically reduce their proportional influence in the capital.
- Opposition groups warned that if passed, the bill would overwhelmingly benefit the BJP, which draws significant support from the several high population growth northern states, including Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Madhya Pradesh.

The Modi government claims that the delimitation bill would provide a uniform 50% increase in seats across all states. They claimed this would maintain the relative power balance between states while accommodating India’s massive population growth.

Critics, however, pointed out that the draft legislation lacked language to guarantee this proportional protection. Under Article 81 of the Constitution, the delimitation of constituencies and readjustment of seats is to be done after every census using population data. However, the proposed bill would remove this obligation and instead leave it to parliament to determine when to conduct delimitation and which census is to be used as the basis. It says nothing about protecting the share of seats allocated to each state. If anything, this move would leave significant power in the hands of the parliament, which is expected to be increasingly dominated by the BJP given the support they enjoy from high population growth regions, which will gain more seats. This would inevitably reduce the influence of southern states’ voice in electing the Parliament and in central government decisions.

The logic of linking the two bills

The BJP’s decision to link the Women’s Reservation Bill with the Delimitation Bill was a calculated, albeit risky, political strategy.

By tying a highly popular social reform (women’s seats) to a controversial structural reform (delimitation), the government hoped to make it politically impossible for the opposition to vote against the package. They essentially framed it as: if you want women’s seats, you must accept the expansion of the legislature.

- In theory, bundling the two together makes sense. One of the greatest internal hurdles to women’s reservation is that current male MPs fear losing their seats. By expanding the total number of seats in the House, the government could theoretically carve out 33% for women without significantly reducing the total number of seats available for men, thus neutralizing internal dissent. To carve out women's seats without displacing incumbents, the Lok Sabha expands from 543 to 816 seats. Of those, 273 go to women. Seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (India's constitutionally recognised disadvantaged communities) also increase, from 84 to 136 and 47 to 70 respectively, with one-third of each reserved for women.

But the opposition have reason to fear that passing the two as a package would allow the BJP to advance its long-term goal of re-aligning the electoral map to reflect current population realities, which favours their electoral strongholds, while simultaneously claiming the title of the party that finally delivered for Indian women.
sound_smarter:
Despite widespread support to implement the quota, a standalone amendment to fast-track the implementation of the Women’s Reservation Act remains unlikely. The government will likely maintain that expanding the House is the only painless path to reservation, one that avoids a mass displacement of sitting male MPs. Conversely, the opposition will continue to demand a clean bill that applies to the current 543 seats.
Alternatively, the BJP may pivot by reintroducing a delimitation bill that explicitly guarantees a uniform 50% seat increase for every state. This manoeuvre would require a constitutional amendment, necessitating a special parliamentary majority and ratification by half of India’s states. While this proportional guarantee might satisfy opposition concerns regarding Southern representation, it would represent a compromised victory: the government would bring forward women’s representation but fail to reap the political benefits of shaping delimitation exercises.
anchor: The Indian Parliament’s special session concluded on Saturday

title: Hull and high water
text:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) fired on two Indian-flagged vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, forcing both to turn back despite having received prior clearance from Iranian authorities to transit. New Delhi summoned the Iranian ambassador and flagged its "deep concern." No injuries were reported.

The ships: The Sanmar Herald, a supertanker carrying roughly two million barrels of Iraqi crude, and the Jag Arnav, sailing from Saudi Arabia's al-Jubail, were intercepted by IRGC gunboats using small-arms fire and deck guns. Audio from the Sanmar Herald captured a crew member telling the Iranian navy: "You gave me clearance to go. My name is second on your list. You are firing now. Let me turn back." A third Indian tanker, the Desh Garima, made it through the Strait the same day.

Why now: The attack came hours after Iran reversed its Friday announcement that the Strait was open to all commercial shipping. Tehran blamed the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, which Iran considers a violation of the Pakistan-brokered April 8 ceasefire, which expires on Wednesday. Talks between the US and Iran failed last weekend, and Trump has threatened to resume bombing if no deal is reached.

Why India: In late March, Iran granted transit rights to five countries: China, Russia, India, Iraq, and Pakistan. China and Russia are aligned with Tehran. Pakistan is mediating the ceasefire. Iraq sits within Iran's sphere of influence. The attack was calibrated: coercive enough to send a signal, restrained enough to avoid fatalities or an irreparable diplomatic rupture. That the Sanmar Herald was carrying Iraqi crude on an Indian-flagged ship adds another dimension; Iran exerts significant influence over Iraq's oil sector, making the cargo's origin as much a part of the message as its destination.

The Dena shadow: On March 4, a US submarine torpedoed the Iranian frigate IRIS Dena in international waters off Sri Lanka, killing at least 87 sailors. The Dena had just left India's MILAN 2026 naval exercise in Visakhapatnam as New Delhi's guest (we covered it here). India never publicly criticised the US for sinking a ship that had been under its hospitality days earlier.

Same-day shield: Hours after the attack, India approved an INR 129.8 billion (USD 1.4 billion) government-backed guarantee for a maritime insurance pool covering hull, cargo, and war risk for ten years. Several major reinsurers, including India's own government-owned GIC Re (General Insurance Corporation of India), have either pulled cover or hiked premiums as the Iran conflict and Western sanctions on Russia squeeze the market. Member insurers will issue policies with combined underwriting capacity of about INR 9.5 billion (USD 110 million).
sound_smarter: Saturday distilled India's Hormuz problem into a single day – its ships are under fire in the same waters where its insurers are retreating. Of the five nations Iran trusted enough to let through, India was the only one worth shooting at: close enough to Washington to deliver a message, important enough to Tehran to do it without sinking the ship. India stayed silent when the US torpedoed Iran's guest off Sri Lanka. It responded to Saturday's attack with "deep concern," not condemnation. Both restraints point to the same calculation: India needs the Strait open, Iran needs the US blockade lifted, and New Delhi knows it is being asked to bridge the gap.

title: Blink and you'll miss it
text:
India has shelved its plan to pre-install the Aadhaar biometric ID app on all smartphones sold in the country, after pushback from the industry.

What's Aadhaar: A 12-digit biometric ID linked to fingerprints, iris scans, and personal data for all 1.34 billion residents and used for banking, telecom, and airport access. It is in many ways India's everything-ID.

Why it failed: Apple and Samsung flagged security risks and compatibility concerns. Manufacturers warned of India-specific assembly lines and higher production costs, which we covered here. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) reviewed the proposal and decided against it, with no official reason given.

The pattern: This is the sixth time in two years the government has sought mandatory pre-installation of state apps on phones. All six were opposed by the industry. December 2025's Sanchar Saathi telecom app mandate lasted days before being rolled back.
sound_smarter: India's manufacturing ambitions and its digital governance ambitions are quietly eating each other. A 0-for-6 record on app preloads tells foreign manufacturers something reassuring: when digital sovereignty bumps against foreign direct investment (FDI), FDI wins.

title: No more extensions
text:
India's competition regulator has set a final hearing date of May 21 in its antitrust case against Apple, after the company went silent on the investigation for six months.

The case: Competition Commission of India (CCI) investigators found in 2024 that Apple abused its dominant position in the app market by forcing developers to use its proprietary in-app payment system. Apple denies wrongdoing.

The standoff: Apple has not submitted financials or responded to the investigation report since October 2024. Instead, it challenged India's antitrust penalty law in the Delhi High Court, which allows the CCI to calculate fines based on global turnover. Apple has said this could expose it to penalties of up to USD 38 billion. It also asked the CCI to pause proceedings pending the court challenge. The CCI refused.

The stakes: Apple's India footprint is growing fast. iPhone shipment share hit a record 9% in 2025, up from 4% two years prior. One in five iPhones globally is now assembled in India.
sound_smarter: New Delhi has spent years courting Apple's manufacturing investment with tax breaks and tailored incentives. A multibillion-dollar antitrust fine complicates that courtship. However, backing down would gut the CCI's credibility on big tech cases before it has properly built any.
anchor: India's competition regulator has set a final hearing

title: Loosening the grip
text:
India's central bank is partially standing down. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Monday lifted its April 1 ban on rupee non-deliverable forward (NDF) contracts and restored the ability to rebook cancelled forward contracts.

Why the ban: In late March, the rupee hit an all-time low of INR 95.22 to the dollar as the Iran conflict pushed Brent crude above USD 110 a barrel. Banks had built up an estimated USD 30 to USD 40 billion in arbitrage positions, buying cheap dollars onshore and selling at higher offshore rates.

The fix: On March 27, the RBI capped banks' net open positions at USD 100 million. When banks shifted positions to corporates, the RBI banned NDF contracts outright on April 1 (we covered it here). The rupee posted its biggest single-day gain in 12 years, recovering to USD 93.10.

What stays: The USD 100 million position cap remains.
sound_smarter: The conditions that broke the rupee in March have not disappeared. Brent is still above USD 95, the Iran conflict remains unresolved, and the ceasefire is fragile. This rollback restores normal hedging for corporates, but the NDF ban stays in the RBI's toolkit for the next oil shock.

title: Seoul-mates
text:
On Monday, Indian Prime Minister Modi and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung pledged to double bilateral trade to USD 54 billion by 2030, anchored by a 250+ person business delegation and an upgrade of their 2010 trade pact.

The upgrade: Both nations agreed to fast-track talks to upgrade the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA). India wants to narrow its trade deficit, while Seoul seeks deeper access to the world’s fastest-growing economy. The ​two countries also established a ministerial-level economic cooperation committee for the first time.

Meeting of the minds: South Korea’s POSCO and India’s JSW finalised a USD 1.09 billion joint venture for a steel plant in Odisha. Beyond metals, 20 other MOUs were signed covering shipbuilding, semiconductors, and green energy.

Energy jitters: With the Iran conflict tightening global oil taps, both leaders prioritised stable supplies of naphtha and raw materials, alongside new cooperation in nuclear power.
sound_smarter: Seoul is de-risking China by shifting its advanced manufacturing to take advantage of India’s scale, while New Delhi is looking past simple trade volumes to secure the specific industrial know-how required to build a credible counterweight to Chinese manufacturing dominance.

text: A fire broke out at the HPCL Rajasthan Refinery (HRRL) in Balotra, Rajasthan on Monday, just 24 hours before Prime Minister Narendra Modi was scheduled to inaugurate the facility. Officials confirmed the blaze is under control with no casualties reported. HRRL aims to help the country slash import dependency by processing local Mangala crude and producing high-value petrochemicals.

title: Code breaker
text:
Over 700 citizens filed a complaint to the Election Commission alleging that Prime Minister Modi's April 18 national address violated the Model Code of Conduct (MCC), which is in force ahead of the Tamil Nadu and West Bengal elections on April 23.

The speech: A day after the women's reservation bill was defeated in the Lok Sabha (which we covered here), Modi addressed the nation on state media, calling the opposition's vote a "sin" and naming the Indian National Congress (INC), Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), Trinamool Congress (TMC) and the Samajwadi Party. All four are contesting in Tamil Nadu and West Bengal.

The signatories: Filed on April 20, the complaint carries names including former Delhi Lieutenant Governor Najeeb Jung, activist Yogendra Yadav, and economist Jayati Ghosh. The Communist Party of India and Communist Party of India (Marxist) have lodged separate complaints. They allege Modi used publicly funded platforms for partisan electioneering, giving the ruling party an undue advantage days before polling.

The ask: The complainants want the Election Commission (EC) to investigate and, if Modi's speech was pre-approved, grant opposition parties equal airtime on public broadcasters.
sound_smarter: Tamil Nadu votes in two days. Modi's speech put opposition parties on the defensive over women's reservation in front of the exact voters they are trying to win, using the state's own airwaves. The political damage is already done, and any EC ruling will arrive after the ballots are cast.
