title: Das Boot, made in Mumbai
text:
India and Germany inked a Defence Industrial Cooperation Roadmap in Berlin on Tuesday, moving the 25-year-old Strategic Partnership from handshakes into factory floors.

The paperwork: Raksha Mantri Rajnath Singh and German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius signed two agreements: a roadmap for co-developing and co-producing defence equipment in niche technologies, and a separate arrangement for cooperation in UN Peacekeeping Training.

Brussels blueprint: Singh pointed to the India-EU Security and Defence Partnership, signed in January, as the wider frame. Both ministers agreed to use it bilaterally and across Europe to deliver "tangible outcomes" in joint capabilities and regional stability.

Boots and jets: Pistorius welcomed the institutionalisation of service-level staff talks and bilateral military exercises. Singh invited the German Air Force to join Tarang Shakti, India's multilateral air exercise, this September. The 2024 edition drew air forces from 11 countries including France, the UK, the US, Australia, Japan and the UAE, with 18 others as observers.
sound_smarter: The roadmap formalises co-production as the operating logic of the relationship. India has bought European defence equipment for decades. A structured framework for joint development, plugged into the January EU defence pact, turns Germany from a vendor into a manufacturing partner. That fits squarely into Atmanirbhar Bharat's (India’s self-reliance push) defence logic: absorb foreign technology, build domestically, and keep the production capability permanently.
anchor: India and Germany inked a Defence Industrial Cooperation

title: Made in India or left in the dark
text:
India will require all solar PV projects to use domestically made cells from June 1, 2026. The rule covers government-backed schemes, net-metering, and open-access projects. Projects already bid out are exempt, but all future bids must comply.

The background: India's renewable energy ministry (MNRE) amended its Approved Models and Manufacturers framework, which has been in place since 2019, to extend local sourcing rules from modules to cells. Cells are the core component that converts sunlight into electricity.

The supply gap: India has 80 GW of module-making capacity but only 7 GW of cell capacity. The rest is imported, mostly from China, which accounts for roughly 70% of India's installed solar base. Developers are already filing petitions, citing short-term supply constraints and cost pressures.

Scaling up: Tata Power has commissioned a 4.3 GW cell plant. Reliance has a 20 GW integrated facility in the pipeline. Adani operates 4 GW. The government expects domestic capacity to rise substantially before the deadline.

The bigger picture: The mandate sits within a broader localisation push. Modules are already required domestically, and ingots and wafers follow in 2028. India's target is 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030, up from 156 GW today.
sound_smarter: By mandating domestic cells before supply catches up, New Delhi is deliberately creating conditions that force capital into Indian cell manufacturing. The short-term cost to developers is the price of building the industry.

title: Chasing the sun (and taxing it)
text:
The US Commerce Department on Thursday hit Indian solar imports with a staggering 123.04% preliminary antidumping duty, signaling a hardening stance against alleged dumping from Southeast and South Asia.

The price of entry: India’s rate dwarfs its peers, with Indonesia facing 35.17% and Laos just 22.46%. When combined with existing countervailing duties imposed in February, the total tax burden on Indian solar exports now exceeds 200%. The US accounts for over 95% of India’s solar cell and module exports.

The backstory: A group of US manufacturers petitioned for the probe in July 2025, claiming firms relocated to India and Indonesia to dodge tariffs previously slapped on Cambodia and Vietnam. The United States International Trade Commission (ITC) had ruled in August that these imports "materially injured" the US domestic industry.

Diplomatic friction: This bombshell dropped while an Indian delegation was in Washington trying to finalize an interim trade deal (we covered the trade deal here). New Delhi has been hesitant to sign since the US replaced reciprocal tariffs with a flat 10% duty and launched Section 301 investigations against several countries, including India (we covered here).
sound_smarter: Washington is putting pressure on India’s solar industry to force New Delhi into a trade deal. But the deal itself is a bad bargain because it sets a higher tax rate (18%) than what India currently pays (10%) on other goods. Unless the US offers a significant rollback on these duties, expect India to keep its pen in its pocket.

title: Ctrl+Alt+Decline
text:
India's IT giants just had their worst week in years. The Nifty IT index, already 2026's worst-performing sector, shed roughly USD 26 billion in market value after Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) and Infosys delivered disappointing earnings.

The damage: TCS recorded its first annual revenue decline in more than two decades. Infosys guided fiscal 2027 growth at just 1.5-3.5%. HCLTech and Wipro also trimmed their forecasts. Across the top five firms, analysts expect near-term revenue growth of only 3–4%.

Where it hurts: The US, which accounts for more than half of revenue at most large firms, is showing softer deal pipelines as clients delay long-term technology spending amid tariff uncertainty and geopolitical risk. The sharpest pain is in banking, financial services, and insurance (BFSI), a key revenue driver for the sector.

The AI bind: AI-driven revenue is growing fast but still sits at roughly 5% of total revenue. Worse, agentic AI is compressing pricing on legacy contracts, the bread and butter of the USD 315 billion industry (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: The sector that built India's middle class on offshore labour arbitrage is being squeezed from both ends. Clients are spending less and the technology that was supposed to drive the next growth wave is cannibalising existing contracts faster than it creates new ones.

text: India’s largest renewable energy company by installed capacity, Adani Green Energy, is slowing the pace at which it builds new solar and wind power projects, even though it has the resources to expand faster. Company executives said they could add about 7-8 gigawatts of new capacity each year, but are limiting this to roughly 4.5-5 gigawatts to avoid producing power that cannot be delivered to users due to grid bottlenecks.

title: Stealing the playbook
text:
Seven Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) Rajya Sabha members, led by Raghav Chadha, defected to the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Friday, cutting AAP's upper house presence from ten seats to three. The BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) coalition already held a simple majority in the 245-member chamber. The coalition now holds 146 seats, 17 short of the two-thirds majority needed for constitutional amendments, including the stalled delimitation bill to expand the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850 seats (we covered it here).

The trigger: AAP stripped Chadha of his deputy leader post on 2 April, citing prolonged absence from party events. Chadha called AAP a "toxic work environment" run by "corrupt and compromised" people. The Enforcement Directorate (ED), India's financial crimes investigation agency, raided two AAP leaders' homes in Punjab the week before, and the AAP accuses BJP of running what the opposition calls a "raid-defect-reset" strategy, using central investigative agencies to pressure opposition politicians into switching sides.

The legal irony: Seven is exactly two-thirds of AAP's ten Rajya Sabha seats, the minimum for a recognised party merger under the Tenth Schedule, India's constitutional anti-defection law. In 2022, Chadha introduced a bill to raise this threshold to three-fourths. Had it passed, he'd have needed eight defectors.

The Punjab play: Six of the seven defectors hold Punjab seats, including former cricketer Harbhajan Singh and Sandeep Pathak, the strategist behind AAP's 92-of-117 seat sweep in 2022. BJP holds just two Punjab assembly seats. Its alliance with the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) collapsed in 2020 over the farm laws, and the party has announced it will contest the 2027 state elections alone.
sound_smarter: Chadha and Pathak give BJP the architects of AAP's biggest electoral win. Nevertheless, BJP's brand in Sikh-majority Punjab remains damaged by the 2020-21 farm law protests, the labelling of Sikh farmers as separatists, and the fallout from the assassination of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada. The party won 6.5% of the Punjab vote in 2022. Turncoats can build party infrastructure where none exists – whether rural Sikh voters follow them into a party they associate with all of the above remains to be seen.

title: Keeping it cool
text:
India’s peak power demand hit a record 256.1 GW last weekend, forcing New Delhi to trigger an emergency fossil-fuel surge to stave off blackouts during a brutal heatwave.

The surge: Grid data shows coal-fired generation ramped up to 187 GW, supported by 9.6 GW of gas-fired capacity.

The playbook: The Ministry of Power released its emergency playbook to prevent summer blackouts in March, with measures including deferring maintenance on 10,000 MW of thermal plants until July and invoking Section 11 of the Electricity Act to force plants to come online, which we covered here. Beyond fossil fuels, the Ministry is accelerating wind and battery storage clearances while tweaking rules to let industries tap into their own captive power plants.

Fuelling the gap: NTPC, India’s top thermal power producer, is aggressively procuring gas via the Indian Gas Exchange. While the Ministry of Power previously insisted the grid is "adequately positioned," the looming El Niño – the strongest in a decade – threatens to push demand toward 270 GW later this year.
sound_smarter: Fossil fuels remain India’s ultimate insurance policy. While the green transition is the long-term goal, renewable capacity and transmission lag (we covered it here) behind the immediate, climate-driven spikes in demand. This makes fossil fuels an indispensable backstop. The West Asia crisis has reframed the need for renewable energy as energy security, not just an environmental need, which is great news for the long-term green energy transition.

title: Gears, fears, and arrears
text:
India's automakers are heading into earnings season with record sales and a growing cost problem. Industry-wide wholesale volumes jumped 13.2% year-on-year in Q4 FY26, up from 2.4% in the previous quarter, driven by the September 2025 GST cuts that slashed tax on small cars and two-wheelers from 28% to 18%.

The pecking order: SUVs and exports are separating the winners. Maruti Suzuki leads with roughly 25% revenue growth, powered by SUV demand and a 34% jump in exports. Mahindra posted its highest-ever SUV volumes. Tata Motors surged 37% in Q4 after a cyberattack-related production halt at Jaguar Land Rover earlier in the year. Hyundai trails at around 8.7% growth, squeezed by marketing costs and a model lineup that skews away from the SUV segment dominating buyer preference.

The margin squeeze: Steel prices rose nearly 10% and aluminium jumped about 20% year-on-year in Q4. Lower discounting has provided temporary relief, but analysts expect margins to soften from here. Several manufacturers have already pushed through price increases of up to 2% from April, with more likely needed.
sound_smarter: The sector's demand outlook remains healthy. The bigger risk is on the cost side. A West Asia escalation would hit Indian automakers through multiple channels at once: disrupted exports to the region, higher freight rates, and elevated steel and fuel input costs. A sector riding a GST-fuelled demand wave could see those gains partially eaten by an energy shock beyond its control.

title: Swiss Air flight aborts takeoff at Delhi after engine fire
text: A Swiss International Air Lines flight bound for Zurich aborted takeoff at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport on Sunday after the crew detected an engine failure and fire alert during the takeoff roll. All 228 passengers, four infants, and 13 crew members were evacuated via emergency slides on Runway 28, which was subsequently closed until the aircraft could be removed. Six passengers sustained injuries during the evacuation. The airline said it had established a task force to investigate the incident.

title: The accused chairs the jury
text:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh told the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) defence ministers' meeting in Bishkek that Operation Sindoor, India's military strikes on Pakistani targets in response to the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack proved "terror epicentres are no longer immune to justifiable punishment," demanding action against states that shelter terrorists.

Without naming names: Singh said the SCO "should not hesitate in seeking appropriate action against those who abet, shelter and provide safe havens to terrorists." Pakistan, an SCO member since 2017, was the unmistakable target. Pakistan currently chairs SCO’s Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS).

Sideline diplomacy: Singh met Chinese Defence Minister Admiral Dong Jun for talks on regional security, conditions along the India-China de facto border known as the Line of Actual Control (LAC), and strengthening military communication channels. He also held talks with Russian Defence Minister Andrei Belousov.

The precedent: Last September's declaration at the summit in Tianjin explicitly condemned the Pahalgam attack and rejected "double standards" on terrorism, with Pakistan's PM Shehbaz Sharif at the table. The same declaration also condemned attacks on Pakistan's Jaffar Express train and in Khuzdar, Balochistan. India has leaned into the even-handed framing to escalate its language at each subsequent SCO meeting.
sound_smarter: The Tianjin summit condemned Pahalgam alongside Pakistani attacks, giving New Delhi the cover to treat counter-terrorism as a settled consensus rather than a bilateral grievance, and it now cites Sindoor as proof of follow-through. Each summit makes it harder for Pakistan to use the same forum for legitimacy. The bilateral with Dong Jun, meanwhile, signals that India-China defence engagement is quietly normalising, even as New Delhi uses a China-founded forum to corner Islamabad.

title: Grounded by fuel
text:
India's three largest airlines have warned the government they are "on the verge of closing down or stopping operations" unless aviation fuel costs are brought under control.

The SOS: The Federation of Indian Airlines (FIA), representing Air India, IndiGo and SpiceJet, sent an urgent letter to aviation secretary Samir Sinha last week. Aviation turbine fuel (ATF) now accounts for 55-60% of airline costs, up from 30-40% before April's price hike. The West Asia conflict and the rupee's slide have compounded the squeeze.

The political wrinkle: With state assembly elections underway, the government capped April's domestic ATF base price hike at 25% while international fuel prices rose by over 100%. A monthly revision for May is due this week.

Tax pile-up: Airlines want the 11% excise duty on ATF temporarily suspended and state Value Added Tax (VAT) rates cut. Delhi charges 25% VAT on ATF, Tamil Nadu 29%. India’s six largest hubs, covering over half of airline operations, levy between 16% and 29%.

The export irony: ATF makes up just 4% of India's refinery output. Domestic airlines consume only 30% of that, with the rest marked for export.
sound_smarter: The government shielded domestic passengers from April's full price shock for electoral reasons, but pushed the burden onto international routes. That distortion undermines the model where carriers cross-subsidise domestic legs with international revenue. The May revision will show whether Delhi treats this as a structural problem or keeps managing it month to month.

title: Nowhere to hide
text:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Monday ordered banks to report all offshore rupee derivative trades executed by their group entities, significantly increasing its view into the currency’s global movements.

The mandate: Banks must now report both deliverable and non-deliverable over-the-counter FX contracts to the Clearing Corporation of India. While trades under USD 1 million are exempt, the rules close a massive loophole by requiring foreign lenders to disclose trades from offshore units, not just their Indian branches.

The timeline: Implementation will be phased. Lenders must report 70% of notional value by July 2027, hitting 100% by July 2028.

Regulatory context: This follows a series of aggressive RBI moves to manage the rupee, including capping net open positions at USD 100 million (we covered it here) and a brief, chaotic ban on non-deliverable forwards in April (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: While the RBI claims this supports efficient price discovery, the move is clearly about increased oversight. The RBI is laying the groundwork for future intervention so it can use the data to see who is shorting the rupee abroad, making its market defences faster and more targeted.

title: Sugar rush
text:
India's transport ministry published draft rules on Tuesday night to formally recognise E85 and E100 fuels, the next leap in a blending programme that has already reshaped the country's agriculture, energy imports, and political landscape.

What changed: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) proposed amendments to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules adding E85 (85% ethanol, 15% petrol) and E100 (nearly pure ethanol) to India's regulatory framework. The draft is open for 30 days of public comment. This follows the mandatory nationwide rollout of E20 (20% ethanol) on 1 April 2026, which India achieved a year ahead of its original target.

What it doesn't mean: E85 will not appear at fuel pumps tomorrow. The amendment creates a legal basis for type-approval testing and eventual commercialisation of vehicles built for higher blends. The government wants to begin a phased E85 rollout by late 2026, starting with select fuel stations offering it as a separate grade alongside E20.

Your car, your problem: Existing vehicles engineered for E10 or E20 cannot run on E85. Ethanol at high concentrations corrodes standard seals, hoses, and fuel lines, and risks permanent engine damage. Running on E85 or E100 requires a flex-fuel vehicle (FFV) with specialised sensors that adjust fuel injection and ignition timing based on the ethanol-petrol mix. No mass-market FFV is currently sold in India. The government is considering tax incentives to push buyers toward the more expensive flex-fuel engines.

The mileage trade-off: Ethanol carries roughly 27-30% less energy per litre than petrol. A vehicle running on E100 will travel significantly fewer kilometres per tank. Whether E85 saves consumers money depends entirely on final retail pricing, which the government has not yet set. NITI Aayog, India’s apex public policy think tank, recommended in 2021 that higher-blend fuels be priced below regular petrol to compensate for the energy loss. That recommendation has not been implemented for E20.

The oil import case: India spends roughly INR 10.5 lakh crore (USD 125 billion) annually importing crude oil. The E20 programme saved an estimated USD 19.3 billion in foreign exchange. With crude prices surging nearly 80% in early 2026 amid West Asia tensions (which we covered here), the strategic argument for higher blending has strengthened. Union Minister for Road Transport and Highways, Nitin Gadkari, has long framed domestically produced ethanol as insulation from West Asian energy volatility.

Follow the sugarcane: India's ethanol comes from two main feedstocks: sugarcane and grain. Grain-based ethanol now accounts for 60% of production. But sugarcane remains the crop that shapes politics. Maharashtra's political economy runs on the sugar lobby, where politicians own or control sugar mills across the state. The industry engages roughly 50 million farmers and 2 million mill workers nationwide. In Marathwada, one of India's most water-stressed regions with average rainfall of 800mm, sugarcane cultivation expanded from 167,000 hectares in 1970-71 to over 1 million hectares. The crop requires 1,500-3,000mm of water, and farmers in Marathwada compensate by drilling borewells deeper than 1,000 feet, further depleting groundwater supplies. Gadkari himself has attributed farmer suicides in Vidarbha and Marathwada to water scarcity.

The capacity question: Indian distillers have capacity to produce roughly 20 billion litres of ethanol annually. Domestic demand under E20 sits at approximately 11 billion litres. Moving to higher blends would absorb this surplus, benefiting the roughly 500-550 distilleries that supply the programme and the sugarcane and maize farmers who feed them.

Declared interests: Gadkari is the ethanol programme's most vocal champion. He has been photographed driving a Toyota flex-fuel prototype around Delhi running on pure ethanol. His sons Nikhil and Sarang run Cian Agro Industries and Manas Agro Industries respectively. Cian Agro's revenue rose from INR 18 crore (USD 2.1 million) in June 2024 to INR 523 crore (USD 62 million) in June 2025. Its stock price rose 2,184% in eight months. The Indian National Congress has demanded an investigation by the Lokpal, India’s anti-corruption body. Gadkari has said the companies account for less than 0.5% of the country's total ethanol supply and that the sugar factory predated the ethanol programme. The petroleum ministry has called the criticism an attempt by vested interests to create confusion.

The verdict

- E85 at scale is years away. The vehicle base does not exist, the pricing framework is not set, and nationwide distribution requires separate dispensers at fuel stations. Expect a slow, niche rollout concentrated in sugar-producing states.
- The immediate beneficiary of higher blending targets is the distillery industry, which is sitting on capacity nearly double the current demand. Higher blends solve a surplus problem as much as an energy security one.
- The water contradiction will sharpen. Every litre of sugarcane-derived ethanol deepens the groundwater crisis in regions already losing farmers to drought and debt. The policy routes water from food crops to fuel tanks in some of India's driest districts. For a country sitting at the epicenter of global warming and changing climate patterns, this will prove to be a considerable stress test.
anchor: India's transport ministry published draft rules on Tuesday

title: Oil shock, capital flight
text:
Foreign investors have pulled over USD 20 billion from Indian equities in the first four months of 2026, surpassing last year's full-year record. Of that, USD 19 billion has exited since the Iran war began.

Why India: India imports 90% of its energy and depends heavily on West Asian supply. A war-driven oil spike hits the current account, the rupee, and corporate margins simultaneously. The Nifty 50 and Sensex are both down sharply year-to-date. The rupee has hit record lows.

Hardest hit: Financial stocks have borne the brunt of foreign selling. IT services face a separate pressure as investors increasingly question the sector's resilience to AI-driven automation.

The floor, for now: Domestic institutions bought a record USD 15.4 billion in March alone, offsetting the highest-ever monthly foreign outflows of USD 12.7 billion.
sound_smarter: Domestic capital can absorb selling and prevent a crash, but what it cannot do is drive a sustained rally. Indian markets have historically needed foreign inflows to set direction, with local institutions following rather than leading, with the trigger for that reversal in West Asia.

title: Loosening the cap
text:
India cut export duties on diesel and aviation turbine fuel (ATF) on Thursday, partially unwinding the sharp hikes imposed less than three weeks ago.

The rollback: Export duty on diesel dropped to INR 23 per litre from INR 55.5, while ATF fell to INR 33 from INR 42. Domestic fuel duties remain unchanged. The government more than doubled these same levies on April 12 to curb an export surge by refiners chasing better margins in Southeast Asia (we covered it here).

Shielding consumers: Indian refiners have been forced to not raise retail petrol or diesel prices in four years, even as crude import costs hit USD 120 per barrel this month amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis. At current prices, state-owned refiners are losing INR 20–30 per litre on fuel sales. Separately, the government capped monthly ATF price increases for domestic carriers at 25% – jet fuel accounts for up to 40% of airline operating costs.
sound_smarter: The duty cut is a balancing act. State-owned refiners are already losing INR 20–30 per litre on domestic sales. Squeeze their export earnings too hard and they cut throughput, shrinking the very supply New Delhi is trying to protect. Meanwhile, Reliance Industries operates its Jamnagar refinery from a Special Economic Zone (SEZ), exempting it from these duties altogether. Public sector refiners like the Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) absorb the domestic price freeze and the export restrictions. Reliance faces neither.

title: Apple is dragging India’s antitrust watchdog to court
text: Apple is dragging India’s antitrust watchdog to court, accusing the regulator of "usurping" judicial authority by demanding financial data for a potential USD 38 billion penalty. Since 2024, the Competition Commission of India (CCI) has been investigating Apple for abusing its dominant position in the iPhone app market. This month, the CCI gave Apple an ultimatum to submit financial records ahead of a final May 21 hearing (we covered it here).

title: New plan for the planners
text:
India has completed the most sweeping overhaul of NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) since it replaced the Planning Commission in 2015, swapping the vice-chairman and nearly all full-time members in two rounds over ten days.

The new roster: On April 24, former Chief Economic Adviser (CEA) Ashok Lahiri replaced Suman Bery as vice-chairman. Lahiri, a Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) legislator from West Bengal's Balurghat, is the first vice-chairman with elected political experience. He served as CEA under both BJP and Congress governments. Five full-time members were named alongside him: economist K V Raju, All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Director M Srinivas, molecular scientist Gobardhan Das (who also contested as a BJP candidate in West Bengal's 2021 elections), Department of Science and Technology Secretary Abhay Karandikar, and former Cabinet Secretary Rajiv Gauba, the only holdover. On Saturday, two more joined: R Balasubramaniam, a development scholar and author of Power Within: The Leadership Legacy of Narendra Modi, and Arunachal Pradesh academic Joram Aniya, the first woman from the Nyishi community to earn a doctorate. Total membership now stands at seven.

The pitch: Officials say the reshuffle signals a shift from policy design to delivery. Most of the new members have run large institutions rather than theorised about them. A Prime Minister's Office (PMO) official told India Today this was a team assembled to implement policy, not debate it.

The institution: NITI Aayog replaced the Nehruvian-era Planning Commission in 2015, but inherited none of its teeth. The Planning Commission controlled plan funds and had allocation leverage over states; NITI Aayog is purely recommendatory, with no budget, no statutory authority, and no enforcement power. Several opposition-ruled states already boycott its meetings, and ministries routinely sideline its reports.
sound_smarter: The new roster has genuine technical weight. But turning a recommendatory body into an execution engine requires execution tools it does not have. The political colouring of the appointments may compound this; opposition chief ministers are unlikely to treat a body led by a BJP MLA and staffed with party-linked appointees as a neutral platform for cooperative federalism.

title: Wrapping paper and gifts
text:
Ecuador's Foreign Minister Gabriela Sommerfeld Rosero wrapped up a visit to New Delhi, leaving with a trade roadmap, a development grant, and a warm invite to India's digital governance model.

On the table: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal and Sommerfeld discussed a Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA) framework, expanded Indian pharmaceutical exports, and supply-chain partnerships in copper and gold. Bilateral trade stood at USD 1.26 billion in 2023–24, with India exporting pharmaceuticals, vehicles, and steel and importing crude oil, gold, and cocoa.

The rest of the haul: Ecuador joined the International Solar Alliance (ISA) and the International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA). India pledged INR 12 crore (USD 1.4 million) in development grants over five years. Sommerfeld toured Jan Aushadhi drug centres and got a demo of the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and Aadhaar, with both sides discussing potential replication in Ecuador.
sound_smarter: Ecuador sits on the southern extension of the Andean metallic belt, with world-class copper and gold deposits. India is using trade frameworks and goodwill diplomacy to lock in upstream resource access. But Beijing got there first — Chinese state-owned companies already operate Ecuador's largest copper mine and acquired its Cangrejos gold deposit last year. India is arriving at a table where China already has the biggest seat. The PTA is the wrapping paper; the minerals are the gift.

title: India's GalaxEye launches world's first optical-radar satellite
text: Bengaluru-based startup GalaxEye launched Mission Drishti on Saturday aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9. The 190 kg satellite is the world's first to combine optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imaging on a single platform, allowing all-weather, day-and-night Earth observation. It is also India's largest privately built satellite. Founded by IIT Madras alumni in 2020, GalaxEye has partnered with NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), the Indian Space Research Organisation's (ISRO) commercial arm, for global distribution of the imagery. Prime Minister Modi called the launch a milestone for India's private space sector. The company plans a full constellation by 2029.

title: Editor’s note
text:
India held elections across five state assemblies this April, covering roughly 174 million voters. Results came in today. Kerala, Assam, and Puducherry voted on April 9. Tamil Nadu voted on April 23. West Bengal voted in two phases on April 23 and 29.

Two results stand out.

- In West Bengal, the BJP has won its first ever government in the state, sweeping over 200 of 293 seats and ending 15 years of Mamata Banerjee's Trinamool Congress (TMC) rule.
- In Tamil Nadu, actor Vijay's Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), a party that did not exist two years ago, has emerged as the single largest party in its debut election, pushing the state towards a hung assembly and shattering the six-decade Dravidian duopoly. Chief Minister M.K. Stalin lost his own seat.

Elsewhere, the BJP secured a third consecutive term in Assam, and the Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) returned to power in Kerala, ending the Left Democratic Front's (LDF) decade-long tenure. No Left party now governs any Indian state for the first time since 1977.

All five states were part of the freebie arms race we covered ahead of polling (we covered it here). Today we look at what the voters decided and what comes next.

We go state by state.

title: West Bengal: Fortunes reversed
text:
The BJP has secured a resounding victory in West Bengal, unseating the Trinamool Congress (TMC) after 15 years of rule. Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee, one of Prime Minister Modi’s most vocal critics, saw her party’s dominance collapse in a historic shift for the state.

The tally: The BJP won 206 out of 294 seats, securing a commanding 70% of the assembly. The ruling TMC plummeted to 81 seats (28%), followed by the Indian National Congress and Aam Janata Unnayan with two seats each, and the Communist Party of India (Marxist) and All India Secular Front with one each. This marks a dramatic reversal from the last election, where the TMC held 215 seats to the BJP's 77.

Voter roll controversy: The election followed a contentious special intensive revision of voter rolls. Unlike routine updates, the SIR required every voter to be re-verified, a process the TMC alleged was a targeted effort to disenfranchise voters. Mamata Banerjee personally petitioned the Supreme Court in February to halt the exercise (we covered it here); however, the Court only granted a timeline extension, allowing the revision to proceed. (we covered it here)

The collapse: Experts attribute the shift to deep-seated anti-incumbency and corruption allegations that crippled the TMC’s standing. The BJP accelerated this momentum by shedding its “outsider” label and running a more culturally attuned campaign that avoided past friction with Bengali identity. The BJP also capitalised on national outrage over the rape and murder of a Kolkata doctor by fielding the victim’s mother, who secured a symbolic victory.

Leadership outlook: Suvendu Adhikari, a former Banerjee ally who defected to the BJP in 2020, is the frontrunner to lead the new government. Adhikari’s platform focused heavily on stricter measures against illegal migration, specifically targeting Bangladeshi and Rohingya populations.

The Bangladesh front: West Bengal shares a 2,216 km border with Bangladesh, the longest of any Indian state. Adhikari has made illegal immigration a central plank, mirroring Sarma's approach in Assam. With both border states now under BJP chief ministers running on anti-infiltration platforms, New Delhi's room to moderate the rhetoric narrows further. Dhaka summoned India's acting High Commissioner over Sarma's remarks last month; a second front from Kolkata adds pressure.

The verdict:

- The BJP’s resounding victory in West Bengal builds on BJP’s already strong power base and gives it more power to shape the national political landscape without substantial opposition.
- With Adhikari likely to become leader, relations with Bangladesh are likely to remain frosty (we covered it here), with every step forward threatened by escalatory actions from Adhikari.
- Both TMC and BJP promised significant handouts ahead of the election (we covered it here), but the state's broader economic indicators tell a grim story of debt, fiscal deficit, and low capital expenditure needed to develop the state. Industrialisation and job creation will be critical for the BJP to retain its newly attained hold on West Bengal.

title: Tamil Nadu: Intermission
text:
Matinee idol Vijay's Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) has emerged as the single largest party in Tamil Nadu's 234-seat assembly in its very first election, pushing the state towards a hung assembly and breaking a political duopoly that has held since 1967.

The tally: TVK won 108 seats with 38% of the vote share, ten short of the 118-seat majority mark. The ruling Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) won 59, and the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) won 47. The Indian National Congress (INC) holds 5, Pattali Makkal Katchi (PMK) 4, and smaller parties including Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi (VCK), Communist Party of India (CPI), Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI(M)), and Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) hold 2 each. The BJP won a single seat. Turnout hit 85.1%, the highest in the state's history.

The scalp: Chief Minister M.K. Stalin lost his own constituency of Kolathur to TVK's V.S. Babu. His son and deputy Chief Minister Udhayanidhi Stalin held Chepauk-Triplicane but only after a scare. The DMK's losses cut across Chennai and the southern districts, traditionally its strongest ground.

The paradox: Tamil Nadu is India's closest thing to a Make in India success story. Back-to-back double-digit real GSDP growth, per capita income at 1.77 times the national average, and USD 52 billion in merchandise exports. Hyundai, Rolls-Royce, and Vietnamese EV manufacturer Vinfast all committed new operations during the DMK's term. The state borrows heavily, but unlike states where debt crowds out investment, Tamil Nadu has kept industrial policy stable regardless of who governs. That continuity is what makes the state attractive to global manufacturers.

The freebie front: None of it saved the DMK. Tamil Nadu has run competitive welfare politics since the DMK pioneered the playbook in 1967, and TVK outbid it on its own turf: INR 2,500 (USD 30) monthly for women against the DMK's INR 2,000 (USD 24), six free LPG cylinders, and INR 4,000 (USD 48) monthly for unemployed graduates (we covered the full manifesto arms race here). Vijay called DMK graft the '30% commission.' Turnout surged from 72.7% in 2021 to 85.1%, the highest in the state's history – the extra voters did not go to the DMK. Growth built the economy; it did not build loyalty.

Breaking the binary: Since C.N. Annadurai led the DMK to power in 1967, ending Congress rule, Tamil Nadu has alternated exclusively between the DMK and AIADMK. The closest parallel to today is 1977, when M.G. Ramachandran (MGR) split from the DMK and swept to power with the AIADMK in his first election. Vijay has done something similar, only without splitting from either party. TVK was founded in February 2024. Vijay announced that TVK would contest all 234 seats solo in March 2026.

Government formation: TVK needs 10 more seats to cross the 118-seat majority mark. With 19 seats held by smaller parties outside the DMK and AIADMK blocs, there are multiple paths. TVK has repeatedly signalled it will not ally with the BJP (1 seat). Congress (5), VCK (2), CPI (2), CPI(M) (2), and DMDK (1) are potential partners; Congress plus any two others would get Vijay over the line. A tie-up with the AIADMK is arithmetically possible but would likely require the AIADMK to exit the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), a move with significant national implications. Vijay himself won Tiruchirappalli East by over 26,000 votes.

The verdict:

- TVK's 38% vote share on record turnout confirms this was a genuine anti-incumbency wave channelled through a new vehicle, not a celebrity vanity project that split votes and got lucky.
- The question for investors is whether Tamil Nadu's industrial policy continuity survives a party with zero governing experience. Every government since 1967 has kept the state's manufacturing framework broadly intact. If TVK breaks that pattern, the consequences extend well beyond state politics.
- The Dravidian binary is broken but not buried. Both the DMK and AIADMK retain significant vote shares and organisational depth. Whether TVK becomes a permanent third pole or a one-cycle disruption depends entirely on how it governs.
- TVK's no-BJP stance limits its options but opens a door for Congress to rebuild relevance in a state where it has not independently held power since 1967. The coming days of negotiation will shape Tamil Nadu's political alignment for years.

title: Kerala: Nothing Left
text:
The Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) has swept Kerala's 140-seat assembly, crossing the majority mark with over 90 seats and ending the Left Democratic Front's (LDF) decade-long hold on the state.

The tally: The Indian National Congress (INC) won 63 seats, the Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) added 22, and Kerala Congress (KEC) contributed 7. The Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI(M)) crashed to 26 from 62 in 2021. The Communist Party of India (CPI) holds 8, and the Revolutionary Socialist Party (RSP) 3. The BJP won 3 seats. Majority mark is 71.

The pattern snaps back: Kerala has alternated between the UDF and LDF at every election since 1982. The LDF broke that rhythm in 2021 by winning a rare second consecutive term under Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan. Voters have corrected the anomaly. Vijayan himself held his Dharmadam constituency, but at least 12 of his cabinet ministers were trailing or lost their seats.

The last domino: With Kerala gone, no Left party governs any Indian state. The CPI(M) held West Bengal for 34 years until 2011, Tripura until 2018, and Kerala until today. The last time India had no Communist chief minister was 1977.

Saffron breakthrough: The BJP won three seats, including Nemom in Thiruvananthapuram, where state president Rajeev Chandrasekhar defeated sitting CPI(M) minister V. Sivankutty. The party now has elected legislators in Kerala's assembly for the first time. In a state where the BJP has historically struggled to break single digits, three seats and a growing vote share represent a foothold rather than a breakthrough, but a foothold is all they needed to start.

The top job: V.D. Satheesan, the outgoing Leader of the Opposition and five-time MLA from Paravur, is the front-runner for Chief Minister. Veteran leader Ramesh Chennithala and Congress general secretary K.C. Venugopal are also in contention. The Congress high command will make the final call.

The verdict:

- The CPI(M) has now lost its last state government, capping a decline that saw it reduced to four Lok Sabha seats in 2024. Kerala was the last proof that Communist parties could still win elections in India. Without it, the Indian Left faces an existential question: governing force or permanent opposition?
- Kerala's economy runs on Gulf remittances, which account for roughly a fifth of the state's income. The Gulf's share of Kerala's emigrants has already fallen from 89% in 2018 to 80% in 2023. The UDF's five Indira Guarantees alone would cost an estimated INR 25,000 crore (USD 3 billion) annually, and the state has already breached fiscal deficit ceilings (we covered it here). Whoever governs inherits shrinking revenue and expanding commitments.
- The BJP's three seats matter more than the number suggests. Kerala has been one of the party's weakest major states. A legislative presence, however small, gives it a platform to build from in a state where the Congress-Left binary has defined politics for decades.
- Watch the chief minister race. The Congress will try to balance community and factional considerations. The choice will signal whether the party sees Kerala as a launchpad for a broader national revival or simply a state to administer.

title: Assam: Settled
text:
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) has locked down Assam for a third consecutive term, crossing the two-thirds supermajority mark in the 126-seat assembly.

The tally: The BJP won 82 seats on its own, well past the 64-seat majority mark. Coalition partners Asom Gana Parishad (AGP) and Bodoland Peoples Front (BOPF) added 10 each, bringing the NDA total to 102. The Indian National Congress (INC) won 19. The All India United Democratic Front (AIUDF) and Raijor Dal (RJRD) hold 2 each. The All India Trinamool Congress (AITC) won 1.

Opposition collapse: The result cements the INC's decline in Assam. Once dominant after 1947, the party lost power in 2016 and has failed to rebuild since. The AIUDF, which held 20 seats in 2021, has been reduced to 2.

Growth delivered: Assam is India's third fastest-growing state at 7.94% real GSDP growth. The state economy nearly tripled from INR 2.54 lakh crore in 2016-17 to INR 6.43 lakh crore (USD 75 billion) in 2024-25. Guwahati has been the centrepiece: an Asian Development Bank (ADB)-backed USD 125 million urban services project, water-metro plans, and three high-speed road corridors have all been announced. The debt-to-GDP ratio sits at a relatively healthy 25%.

The infiltration card: Illegal immigration from Bangladesh has shaped Assam's politics since the Assam Agitation of 1979-85. Sarma has leaned into it harder than any predecessor. Last month, his remarks about "pushing back Bangladeshi infiltrators" triggered a diplomatic row. He also said he "prays" India-Bangladesh relations do not improve. The rhetoric plays well domestically but complicates New Delhi's efforts to stabilise ties with Dhaka.

The verdict:

- A two-thirds supermajority gives the BJP legislative room to push through contentious measures flagged in its manifesto, including a Uniform Civil Code and action on the National Register of Citizens (NRC), without needing opposition support.
- Sarma runs a dual-track approach: anti-Bangladesh rhetoric for domestic consumption alongside Act East connectivity initiatives with Dhaka. A supermajority makes this harder to challenge internally, but each diplomatic incident erodes the trust New Delhi needs to operationalise its eastern corridor strategy.
- With the INC at 19 and AIUDF at 2, Assam has effectively become a one-coalition state. The opposition's challenge is existential: rebuild organisationally before the next cycle or risk permanent irrelevance in the state.
anchor: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led National Democratic Alliance

title: Puducherry: Small and stable
text:
The National Democratic Alliance (NDA) has held Puducherry, returning Chief Minister N. Rangaswamy to power in the 30-member assembly.

The tally: Rangaswamy's All India N.R. Congress (AINRC) won 12 seats. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) added 4, bringing the NDA core to 16 in an assembly where the majority mark is 16. The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) won 5, the Indian National Congress (INC) 1, and the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) 1. Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) picked up 2 seats. Three independents round out the chamber.

A familiar script: Puducherry has long flipped between INC-led alliances and regional players. That changed in 2021, when Rangaswamy's AINRC aligned with the BJP to form the government. This result confirms the shift was more than a one-off, though the razor-thin majority leaves little room for floor crossings or factional dissent.

The verdict:

- The NDA holds Puducherry but without a cushion. Any defection changes the arithmetic. Rangaswamy's ability to keep the coalition intact will define the term.

title: Old medicine, new crisis
text:
The Cabinet on Monday approved the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) 5.0, reviving a pandemic-era lending backstop to cushion businesses against the West Asia conflict. The scheme targets INR 2.55 lakh crore (USD 26.8 billion) in additional credit flow, including INR 5,000 crore (USD 526 million) earmarked for airlines.

The playbook: ECLGS was first launched in May 2020 under the Aatmanirbhar Bharat (self-reliant India) package to keep MSMEs afloat during COVID lockdowns. Versions 1.0 through 4.0 eventually issued INR 3.61 lakh crore (USD 38 billion) in guarantees to 11.9 million borrowers before the scheme wound down in March 2023. Version 5.0 dusts off the same architecture for a different shock.

How it works: The government-owned National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company Limited (NCGTC) provides 100% guarantee coverage for Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) and 90% for non-MSMEs and airlines. Eligible borrowers can access additional credit of up to 20% of their peak working capital usage during Q4 FY26, capped at INR 100 crore (USD 10.5 million). Airlines get up to 100% additional credit, capped at INR 1,500 crore (USD 158 million) per borrower. There is no guarantee fee, and loans run for five years with a one-year moratorium. Airlines get seven years with a two-year moratorium.

Who qualifies: MSMEs and non-MSMEs with existing working capital limits, and scheduled passenger airlines with outstanding credit facilities as of 31 March 2026, provided they are current on repayments. Accounts classified as non-performing by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) are excluded. The scheme runs until 31 March 2027.
sound_smarter: ECLGS worked during COVID because the problem was demand destruction: businesses had viable models but no customers. The West Asia shock is a supply-side problem, with rising input costs, disrupted shipping routes, and spiking energy prices. Cheap credit helps with cash flow, but it cannot fix broken supply chains or absorb a 30-50% jump in packaging and petrochemical costs.

title: Back in business (mostly)
text:
Indian traders have begun exporting wheat for the first time in four years, ending a hiatus triggered by weather shocks and domestic price surges. Conglomerate ITC is currently loading 22,000 metric tons at Kandla port destined for the UAE.

The policy pivot: After banning overseas sales in 2022 to protect local supply then extending the ban to 2023 and 2024, New Delhi relented this year following a robust harvest in 2025. The government has cleared a total of 5 million tons for export across two recent tranches.

Price parity: Don’t expect a flood of grain. Indian wheat is about $20 more expensive than rival supplies from Australia or the Black Sea.

Niche appeal: Because of the price gap, Indian exports are currently limited to buyers with immediate supply gaps or geographic proximity, like the Middle East. Most global buyers will stick with cheaper Australian, Argentine or Black Sea supplies.
sound_smarter: India’s return to the wheat market is opportunistic. Because domestic prices remain the government’s priority, exports will stay opportunistic and prone to sudden bans the moment domestic prices rise too much.

title: Picking up the thread
text:
The Union Cabinet approved a INR 5,659 crore (USD 594 million) five-year mission on Tuesday to rescue India’s wilting cotton sector from a 17-year production low.

The crisis: Yields have hit a wall. Outdated seeds, erratic monsoons, and the Pink Bollworm’s growing immunity to Bt cotton have forced India – traditionally an exporter – into record-high imports to feed its domestic mills.

The toolkit: The mission focuses on improved cotton production technologies and climate-resilient seeds to boost density and durability. It also targets contaminants in the supply chain by modernizing 2,000 ginning and processing facilities and expanding the Kasturi Cotton Bharat branding for better traceability.

Beyond the boll: In a bid to diversify the fiber base, the plan allocates resources for alternative natural fibers like flax, bamboo, and even banana fiber to align with global shifts toward sustainable textiles.
sound_smarter: By focusing on process upgrades, branding, and traceability, New Delhi is attempting to move India from a bulk commodity supplier to a high-trust origin, which is essential for MNCs facing tightening ESG and traceability audits in the US and EU.

title: The Cabinet approved the final two projects under India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) 1.0
text: a Gallium Nitride (GaN) display panel facility in Dholera and a chip packaging plant in Surat. The two assembly-tier facilities bring a combined INR 3,936 crore (USD 414 million) in investment and close out ISM 1.0 at 12 approved projects worth INR 1.64 lakh crore (USD 17.3 billion). Six of the twelve projects are in Gujarat. The Supreme Court of India is set to grow from 33 to 37 judges, excluding the Chief Justice of India, after the government cleared a bill to add four seats. Over 90,000 cases are currently pending. The government can create seats but cannot choose who fills them: appointments are made by the collegium, a five-judge panel led by the Chief Justice of India. Four extra judges will do little to dent a backlog that has been growing for decades, but the expansion signals there is acknowledgement of the problem.

title: Middle powers united
text:
President To Lam of Vietnam wrapped up his India visit today, elevating bilateral ties to an Enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership to insulate both nations from superpower friction.

More trade: Leaders set a USD 25 billion trade goal by 2030. Key to this is a critical minerals pact and linking India’s UPI with Vietnam’s Fast Payment System. They also pledged to finish the ASEAN India Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA) review by year-end to fix trade imbalances.

South China Sea signals: The duo committed to expanding oil and gas exploration "in accordance with international law." In diplomatic speak, that’s a direct nod to resisting Beijing’s maritime claims.

Defence co-production: Moving beyond buyer-seller roles, the two will now co-produce military tech. This includes regular joint hydrographic surveys and increased naval port calls to boost maritime awareness.
sound_smarter: As US-China tensions remain elevated, middle powers like India and Vietnam are building a third way. By locking in trade ties, high-tech defence, critical mineral supply chains, they are gradually creating a middle-power bloc capable of navigating the Indo-Pacific without picking a side.

title: Musical censors
text:
The Centre on Wednesday appointed Shashi Shekhar Vempati as chairperson of the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) for a three-year term, replacing Prasoon Joshi, who has been elevated to chairman of Prasar Bharati, India’s public broadcaster.

The swap: Joshi led the CBFC since August 2017, succeeding the controversy-prone Pahlaj Nihalani. His tenure focused on digitising the board's certification process. On May 2, the Information and Broadcasting (I&B) Ministry moved him to head Prasar Bharati, creating the vacancy Vempati now fills.

The new chair: An IIT Bombay alumnus, Vempati spent 16 years at Infosys before running Niti Digital and India272, platforms tied to Modi's 2014 campaign. He previously served as CEO of Rajya Sabha TV and Prasar Bharati, and received a Padma Shri, India’s fourth-highest civilian honour, in January 2026.

Track record: Under Joshi, the CBFC drew fire from both directions. In January 2026, the board delayed certification of actor Vijay's Jana Nayagan weeks before the Tamil Nadu elections over reported concerns about political dialogues, prompting Chief Minister Stalin to call the CBFC "a new weapon of the BJP government." Vijay's Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) went on to win the election (we covered it here). Meanwhile, both instalments of The Kerala Story, widely accused of communal fearmongering, sailed through certification.
sound_smarter: Joshi and Vempati have effectively traded chairs across the same two institutions, keeping familiar hands on India's media and cultural gatekeeping infrastructure. The more interesting question is what a digital-first operator does at the helm of the censor board. The CBFC's mandate currently stops at theatrical releases, leaving streaming platforms outside its reach. Joshi has publicly acknowledged this gap, and Vempati's tech background makes him a natural pick to close it.

title: The hand that stabs
text:
Congress on Tuesday night agreed to support Vijay's Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) to form a government in Tamil Nadu, triggering a furious backlash from its own INDIA bloc ally, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK).

The numbers: TVK won 108 of 234 seats, ten short of the 118 needed for a majority. Congress holds five. Vijay submitted support letters from 112 MLAs to Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar on Wednesday, who told him to return with proof of 118.

Congress's reasoning: General secretary K.C. Venugopal said Vijay had personally requested support. "The INC is clear that the mandate in Tamil Nadu is for a secular government," he said, adding the party was "determined not to have the BJP and its proxies run the government."

DMK's response: Spokesperson Saravanan Annadurai called Congress "backstabbers," noting the party's five seats came entirely from its DMK alliance. "Otherwise, they would have drawn a blank," he said. Another spokesperson, TKS Elangovan, warned: "Congress is doing it in every state, and ultimately, they are losing in all of them."

The AIADMK wildcard: The BJP's central leadership is reportedly pushing the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK, 47 seats), its alliance partner, to back TVK rather than allow a Congress-backed government in Chennai. Senior AIADMK leader Leema Rose Martin confirmed her party was in talks with TVK.
sound_smarter: Prior to the election, Congress said there was "not even a 1% chance" of allying with TVK. Twenty-four hours after the results, it reversed course. The calculation is rational: five seats buy influence in a new government rather than irrelevance in opposition. But the cost is a fracture in the INDIA bloc. The DMK is one of the opposition alliance's strongest regional pillars, and its spokesperson has already warned that this move will erode trust with partners.

title: West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee has refused
text: West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee has refused to resign despite the BJP's landslide victory (we covered it here), claiming about 100 seats were "forcibly taken" and calling the election "rigged." She provided no evidence. The state's Chief Electoral Officer called the allegations "baseless." Banerjee's term expires on Thursday, after which the new assembly will be sworn in and the BJP will form its first ever West Bengal government. Two of her chief advisors have already resigned.

title: The Board of Control for Cricket in India
text: The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) has moved the Indian Premier League (IPL) final from Bengaluru to Ahmedabad, citing requirements from local authorities that were "beyond the scope of BCCI's established guidelines." The shift follows last year's stampede outside Bengaluru’s Chinnaswamy Stadium that killed 11 people after Royal Challengers Bengaluru's maiden IPL win. The Karnataka State Cricket Association said it was disappointed and had not been given specific reasons. The 132,000-seat Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad will now host its fourth IPL final in five years. The venue, in the Prime Minister's home state, has become India's default stage for marquee cricket, hosting both the 2023 ODI and 2024 T20 World Cup finals, despite Ahmedabad not being a top-tier metro.

The ship, MV Gautam, was carrying seven crew members, six Indian and one Indonesian, en route from Oman to India. Pakistan dispatched a naval ship that provided food, medical assistance, and technical support.

title: Votes counted, battles not
text:
India held elections. But many didn’t accept the results.

Blood on the ballot: At least four people were killed after the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) secured West Bengal for the first time, winning 206 of 294 seats. Both parties reported workers beaten to death and offices ransacked. The Election Commission's "zero tolerance" directive arrived after the damage was done.

Lawyer up: Mamata Banerjee is refusing to leave office despite losing her seat and her majority, calling it a deliberate act of protest. She's heading to the Supreme Court, personally resuming legal practice to challenge the result, while keeping her eye on Delhi and the 2029 general elections.

Short of the finish line: In Tamil Nadu, Vijay's two-year-old Tamilaga Vetri Kazhagam (TVK) made history. TVK became the first non-Dravidian party to top the assembly since the 1960s. But it fell short of a majority, forcing a hasty coalition with Congress, poached from the rival Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK)-led alliance. On May 6, Vijay met the Governor to stake his claim.
sound_smarter: Banerjee's Supreme Court gambit keeps Trinamool Congress (TMC) alive as a national opposition force. In Tamil Nadu, the real question is whether a novice coalition can govern India's second-largest state economy without stalling investment. At least for the coming weeks, uncertainty in these states is written on the wall.

title: Playing ball (mostly)
text:
The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports issued a memo on Tuesday clearing the way for Pakistani teams to compete in multilateral events hosted by India.

The distinction: New Delhi is drawing a hard border between bilateral and multilateral play. India will still refuse to play one-on-one series against Pakistan or host them for standalone matches. However, for international tournaments, the government will now follow global sporting norms, allowing Indian athletes to compete in events with Pakistani athletes.

The freeze: Bilateral cricket has been on ice since 2012, with a military skirmish exactly one year ago hardening the freeze further. During this year’s India-hosted T20 World Cup, Pakistan played its matches in Sri Lanka to avoid the optics of crossing the border.

Host ambitions: India is aggressively bidding for the 2030 Commonwealth Games, 2036 Olympics, and 2038 Asian Games. With Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) officials visiting Ahmedabad soon, New Delhi cannot afford to look like an unreliable or exclusionary host.

Packed schedule: Indian and Pakistani athletes are expected to face each other in the upcoming Commonwealth Games and the Asian Games that are just months away.
sound_smarter: By decoupling bilateral beef from multilateral events, New Delhi avoids being the difficult host that disrupts international events. Alienating the same global sporting bodies India needs to approve its 2036 Olympic bid would be a self-inflicted wound.

title: Below the bench
text:
Government schools in India now enrol fewer than half the country's students for the first time. A NITI Aayog report released on Wednesday maps a decade of decline across the world's largest school system, covering 1.47 million schools and 247 million students.

The exodus: Government school enrolment has fallen from 71% in 2005 to 49.24% in 2024-25, despite government institutions making up 68.1% of all schools. Private schools, at 23.1% of institutions, now account for 38.8% of enrolment. Parents increasingly associate private schools with better English-medium instruction and employability. The report's own data suggests the perception has some basis: over a third of schools have fewer than 50 students, more than 100,000 run with a single teacher, nearly 98,600 lack functional girls' toilets, and 61,500 have no usable toilets at all. Only 5.4% of schools offer continuous education from Grade 1 to 12, forcing families to navigate transitions between institutions at every stage.

The dropout cliff: The Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) drops from 90.9% at primary level to 58.4% at higher secondary. Nearly four in ten children leave before finishing school. The report also flagged nearly 8,000 schools with zero student enrolment that continue to receive funding and staffing due to outdated records.

The prescription: Thirteen recommendations including composite school complexes to consolidate fragmented institutions, teacher workforce planning, competency-based assessments, and AI integration into pedagogy. The report maps 33 implementation pathways with over 125 performance indicators.
sound_smarter: The report's own data undermines India's demographic dividend pitch. A country banking on its young workforce cannot afford four in ten students dropping out before higher secondary. The recommendations are sound, but NITI Aayog is a purely advisory body with no power to allocate funds or compel states to act. Its recent reconstitution under new Vice Chairman Ashok Lahiri (which we covered here) is designed to change that, but the body's track record suggests the gap between diagnosis and delivery will persist.

title: Gold can wait
text:
New Delhi is asking citizens to treat fuel conservation as a national duty. Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday asked Indians to stop buying gold for a year, cut fuel consumption, and postpone foreign travel to conserve foreign exchange amid the West Asia crisis.

Covid playbook: Speaking at a Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) rally in Hyderabad, Modi called for reviving pandemic-era practices, including work from home, online meetings, and video conferences, this time to conserve fuel rather than contain a virus. He pushed for public transport and carpooling in cities, electric vehicle adoption, and a shift to Made-in-India products. He also urged farmers to halve chemical fertiliser use and move to solar-powered irrigation.

The pressure: Crude oil prices have spiked from USD 70 to over USD 120 per barrel since the conflict began. India's state-owned Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs), Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum Corporation, and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation, are absorbing under-recoveries of INR 1,600–1,700 crore (USD 190–200 million) per day. Total losses over ten weeks have crossed INR 1 lakh crore (USD 12 billion). Retail petrol and diesel prices remain unchanged.
sound_smarter: Modi's appeal is the clearest signal yet that fuel price hikes are coming. State-owned oil companies cannot absorb INR 30,000 crore a month in losses indefinitely, and the timing, days after election results were declared and new governments are taking shape, matches what analysts had predicted. Framing conservation as patriotic duty softens the ground before the numbers hit the pump.

title: 29 laws walk into a bar
text:
India has finally closed the paperwork gap on its biggest labour reform in decades. On Friday, the central government notified the implementing rules for all four labour codes. This is the last procedural step before enforcement could begin.

What they replace:The Code on Wages (2019), Industrial Relations Code (2020), Code on Social Security (2020), and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code (2020) consolidate 29 existing labour laws into a single framework. All four came into force on November 21, 2025, but lacked the rules needed to actually function. Draft rules were published on December 30, 2025, for stakeholder feedback before legal vetting and final gazette notification.

What changes: Basic pay must now be at least 50% of total salary, overtime triggers double pay, and every worker gets a mandatory appointment letter. Gig and platform workers enter the social security net for the first time. Workers aged 40 and above are entitled to free health check-ups, and weekly working hours are capped at 48.
sound_smarter: India has attempted labour consolidation before, and the codes themselves sat on the shelf for years after parliamentary passage. The rules are now published, removing the legal ambiguity that let employers and states sit on their hands. For anyone hiring at scale in India, the 50% basic pay floor and mandatory appointment letters materially change payroll structuring and contractor risk. State-level follow-through will be the real signal to watch, because enforcement lives in the detail.

title: Suvendu Adhikari was sworn in as West Bengal's
text: Suvendu Adhikari was sworn in as West Bengal's first Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) chief minister on Saturday after the party won 207 of 294 seats. Mamata Banerjee refused to resign despite her Trinamool Congress being reduced to 80, prompting Governor RN Ravi to dissolve the assembly. In Tamil Nadu, actor-turned-politician Vijay took oath on Sunday after days of coalition arithmetic. His Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) won 108 seats but needed backing from the Indian National Congress, the Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi (VCK) and the Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) to cross the 118-seat majority. Himanta Biswa Sarma will be sworn in in Assam on Tuesday for a second term after the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) won 102 of 126 seats. In Keralam, Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) won 102 of 140 seats but has yet to pick a chief minister a week after results, with supporters of the three contenders holding rival rallies and running duelling social media campaigns.

title: The post-FTA parade
text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi flies out on Thursday for a six-day, five-nation tour spanning the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the Netherlands, Sweden, Norway, and Italy, days after asking Indians to save fuel, skip gold, and stay home.

United Arab Emirates: Modi meets UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on May 15. MBZ visited New Delhi in January, signing a 10-year liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply deal between ADNOC Gas and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) and setting a USD 200 billion bilateral trade target by 2032. The return visit comes as the Strait of Hormuz crisis chokes the supply lines those agreements depend on. The UAE is India's third-largest trade partner and hosts over 4.5 million Indian nationals, and energy cooperation now sits squarely in crisis-management territory.

The Netherlands: Modi visits from May 15–17, his second trip (after 2017), meeting Prime Minister Rob Jetten early in Jetten's tenure. The Netherlands is India's fourth-largest source of foreign direct investment (FDI) with USD 55.6 billion cumulative, and bilateral trade hit USD 27.8 billion in 2024–25. Semiconductors give the visit an edge: Dutch firm ASML, the world's sole maker of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, is already supplying equipment to India's Tata-PSMC mega-fab in Gujarat and actively seeking partnerships with Indian companies under India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 (ISM 2.0). India's recent entry into Pax Silica, the US-led initiative to ringfence chip supply chains from China (we covered it here), makes the ASML relationship both commercially and geopolitically significant. The agenda also covers green hydrogen, defence, critical minerals (we covered it here), and a Strategic Partnership on Water.

Sweden: Modi heads to Gothenburg on May 17–18 to meet Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. The two will co-address the European Round Table for Industry alongside European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a signal of where New Delhi sits in Europe's post-FTA economic calculus. Swedish FDI in India stands at USD 2.83 billion.

Norway: Modi arrives on May 18 for the first Indian prime ministerial visit in 43 years. He meets Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and addresses the India-Norway Business and Research Summit. The commercial backdrop is the India-European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA), which entered into force in October 2025 and commits the EFTA bloc (Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein) to USD 100 billion in FDI over 15 years. Norway's Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), the world's largest sovereign wealth fund, already holds close to USD 28 billion in Indian capital markets. The 3rd India-Nordic Summit follows on May 19 in Oslo, bringing together the leaders of Norway, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, and Sweden. Previous summits in Stockholm (2018) and Copenhagen (2022) focused on climate, the blue economy, and Arctic cooperation. This edition adds green hydrogen, defence, and a new commercial layer: three of the five Nordic participants (Sweden, Denmark, and Finland) fall under the India-EU FTA, while the remaining two (Norway and Iceland) are covered by the India-EFTA TEPA.

Italy: Modi wraps up in Rome on May 19–20, meeting Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. Defence dominates the agenda. In February, Adani Defence and Italy's Leonardo signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to build an integrated helicopter manufacturing ecosystem in India (we covered it here). Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto visited New Delhi on April 30, exchanging a 2026–2027 bilateral military cooperation plan with his counterpart Rajnath Singh. The same day, Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri's military naval vessel division met the Indian Coast Guard to discuss collaboration with Indian shipyards on modular ship design, hybrid propulsion, and counter-drone systems. Bilateral trade reached USD 16.77 billion in 2025.
sound_smarter: Every stop on this tour sits on top of a recent agreement that exists on paper but hasn't yet delivered results. The ADNOC LNG deal, the ASML partnerships under ISM 2.0, the India-EFTA TEPA, the Adani-Leonardo helicopter MOU. Modi is flying to five countries in six days because signing deals and operationalising them are two different things, and the West Asia crisis has turned the gap between the two from an inconvenience into a vulnerability.

title: retail inflation climbs to 3.48%
text: India's retail inflation rose to 3.48% in April, undershooting the 3.8% forecast, as the Centre absorbed most of the oil price shock rather than raising prices at the pump. Food inflation climbed to 4.2%. Economists expect the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to hold rates at its June review, but warn that fuel price increases are likely in Q2, which could push inflation toward 5% for FY27.

title: The lithium courtship
text:
Chile’s Foreign Minister Francisco Pérez Mackenna led a high-level delegation to New Delhi this week, as India and Chile push to upgrade their two-decade trade relationship into a full Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).

What's on the table: The proposed CEPA would replace a Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA) signed in 2006 and expanded in 2017. Negotiations were formally launched during Chilean President Gabriel Boric's visit to India in April 2025, following a Joint Study Group report finalised in April 2024. The deal would cover digital services, investment promotion, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), and critical minerals.

The mineral prize: Chile holds the world's largest lithium reserves and is the leading global copper producer. Both are essential inputs for batteries, electric vehicles, and clean energy infrastructure. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal signalled that the deal's fate hinges on minerals, telling reporters the agreement could be finalised “if we get a good deal around critical minerals and other important mining concessions.”

The pattern: Chile is the latest stop on India's critical minerals shopping spree. New Delhi is already in talks with Brazil, Canada, France, and the Netherlands to jointly explore, extract, and process lithium and rare earths (we covered it here). External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar held a separate meeting with Mackenna, framing the visit around “diversifying markets and sourcing.”
sound_smarter: India's bilateral trade with Chile is small (around USD 1.15 billion in exports in 2024–25), but the CEPA isn't really a trade deal – it is a minerals access play. Chile's reserves give India another card as it builds supply chain alternatives to Chinese-controlled mineral processing.

title: A Seoul-ful shipyard in Tamil Nadu
text:
India is getting its first mega greenfield shipyard. On Wednesday, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW) announced that National Shipbuilding & Heavy Industries Park and Sagarmala Finance Corporation had signed a tripartite MoU with South Korea’s HD KSOE earlier in April to build a massive facility in Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu.

The specs: The yard targets an annual capacity of 2.5 million gross tonnage (GT). This is the first major win for ‘VOYAGES,’ a new maritime framework launched during South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s state visit (we covered it here).

The ambition: New Delhi wants India in the world's top five shipbuilders by 2047. To get there, they’ve already overhauled the Merchant Shipping Act, established a Maritime Development Fund worth USD 2.9 billion for the country’s shipbuilding and repair industry, and launched a Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Programme to slash contract costs.

Market demand: The MoPSW projects that India needs 437 new vessels by 2042. Under a new structured model, the government will allow some imports provided the vast majority are built domestically to force-feed local tech and skills.
sound_smarter: South Korean yards are losing their lead to China due to high labor costs and a shrinking workforce; India has the hands but lacks the high-end tech. India is using this alignment of factors to boost its shipbuilding capacity and, in the process, drive large-scale employment.
anchor: India is getting its first mega greenfield shipyard.

title: Runways to nowhere
text:
Air India will temporarily suspend and reduce flights on several international routes between June and August, citing airspace restrictions and record jet fuel prices. The airline, which has been without a permanent CEO since Campbell Wilson resigned in April, has pulled around 100 daily flights from its network.

What's cut: Air India has suspended the Delhi–Chicago, Mumbai–New York, Delhi–Newark, Delhi–Singapore, and Delhi–Shanghai routes, and reduced frequencies to San Francisco, Paris, Milan, Rome, Toronto, Melbourne, and Sydney.

The squeeze: Two overlapping airspace closures are driving costs up. Pakistan banned Indian carriers from its airspace in April 2025 after military tensions, forcing longer westbound routings on every flight to Europe and North America. The Iran conflict has since closed additional corridors and pushed global jet fuel prices from USD 99 per barrel in late February to USD 163 per barrel as of May 8.

Not just Air India: IndiGo, India's largest carrier, has suspended all flights to Tbilisi, Almaty, Baku, and Tashkent since January after Iranian airspace closures made its narrow-body A320neo fleet unable to reroute. It has also cut frequencies on London and Copenhagen services.

The paradox: India is opening mega-airports at pace. Navi Mumbai International Airport (NMIA) began commercial operations in December 2025 and is preparing to launch international flights this month. Noida International Airport in the Delhi-National Capital Region (NCR) was inaugurated in March and begins commercial services in June. Both are designed as global hubs with eventual capacity exceeding 70 million passengers each. The infrastructure is arriving. The flights to fill it are going the other way.
sound_smarter: India's aviation ambitions rest on becoming a global transit hub, a connector between East and West. But that pitch depends on geography, and geography currently works against it. With Pakistan and Iran airspace closed, Indian carriers face longer routes and higher costs than Gulf and Southeast Asian rivals on the same corridors. The new airports in Mumbai and Delhi are world-class facilities. The question is whether airlines can afford to use them.
anchor: Air India will temporarily suspend and reduce flights

title: NTA scraps medical entrance exam after paper leak
text: The National Testing Agency (NTA) scrapped India's National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), the sole gateway to undergraduate medical programmes, after discovering the exam's questions had been leaked. Around 2.3 million students sat the test on May 3. The Centre immediately handed the investigation to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), which has already arrested five people across Jaipur, Gurugram, and Nashik. The case was filed under the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, a law passed after NEET questions were similarly leaked in 2024. That time, the government did not cancel the test.
