title: Diplomatic waters
text:
India condemned an attack that sank an Indian-flagged cargo vessel off the coast of Oman on Thursday, calling it "unacceptable," as BRICS foreign ministers gathered in New Delhi for their annual meeting.

The attack: The Haji Ali, a wooden dhow carrying livestock from Somalia to the UAE, caught fire after a suspected drone or missile strike in Omani waters in the early hours of Wednesday. All 14 crew were rescued by the Omani coast guard. No one has claimed responsibility, and India did not name an attacker.

Mounting toll: The Haji Ali is the second vessel sunk since the US-Israeli war with Iran began on February 28. At least two other Indian-flagged ships have been attacked. Last month, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) gunboats fired on two Indian tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz despite both having received prior Iranian clearance (we covered it here). New Delhi summoned the Iranian ambassador and flagged its "deep concern" over that incident.

Meanwhile, in Delhi: External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar opened the two-day BRICS Foreign Ministers' Meeting on Thursday, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in the room. Jaishankar called for "safe and unimpeded maritime flows through international waterways, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea," without naming any party responsible for the disruption. Iran and the UAE, now on opposing sides of the conflict and both BRICS members, have made a joint statement difficult. An earlier deputy-level meeting in April ended without consensus for the same reason.
sound_smarter: India's language on Thursday was carefully split. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) statement on the Haji Ali named no attacker; Jaishankar's BRICS address named no aggressor. New Delhi is threading a needle familiar from prior conflicts – condemning the act while preserving the relationship with every party in the room. The question is how long that formula holds when Indian ships keep sinking.

title: Sweet nothings
text:
India pulled the plug on sugar exports on Wednesday, banning all shipments of raw, white, and refined sugar until September 30, or until further notice.

What went wrong: New Delhi had cleared mills to export 1.59 million tonnes earlier this year, confident domestic supply would hold. It won't. India now risks consuming more than it produces for the second straight season, with weakening cane yields in major growing states. El Niño-linked monsoon disruptions could make next season worse.

Stuck in the middle: Of the approved quota, around 800,000 tonnes were contracted. Over 600,000 tonnes have already been shipped, leaving roughly 200,000 tonnes of committed orders stranded. Traders who signed deals on the back of February's expanded quotas are now exposed.

Market reaction: New York raw sugar futures jumped over 2%, and London whites surged 3%. Brazil and Thailand stand to capture the windfall.
sound_smarter: The sugar ban reads as currency defence first, commodity management second. With the rupee at a record low of 95.75 and a crude import bill inflated by the Strait of Hormuz closure, New Delhi cannot afford food inflation on top of everything else. Sugar joins gold duty hikes as part of a broader effort to stem FX bleeding. Each new restriction signals the pressure is sharper than official statements let on.

title: All that glitters just got discounted
text:
On Wednesday, India hiked import duties on gold and silver from 6% to 15%, a drastic move to shore up foreign exchange reserves as geopolitical instability rattles the rupee.

The Modi mandate: The hike follows PM Modi’s plea on Sunday for citizens to pause gold purchases, curb fuel use, and skip foreign vacations for a year to conserve foreign exchange (we covered it here).

Market mayhem: Local prices spiked instantly, but demand did not follow. Instead, Indian gold discounts hit a record USD 207 per ounce as investors rushed to offload holdings and lock in gains.

By the numbers: India is the world’s second-largest gold consumer, with demand largely driven by investments and jewellery.
sound_smarter: These record discounts are a short-term distortion caused by domestic players rushing to cash in on price gains. While the tax hike creates a temporary chill, gold's status as a safe-haven asset and its role in jewellery remain deeply entrenched in Indian culture. Expect the market to absorb the shock and for discounts to normalise over time.
anchor: On Wednesday, India hiked import duties on gold

title: Satheesan named Kerala’s new CM
text: The Indian National Congress (INC) named V.D. Satheesan as Kerala's new Chief Minister on Thursday, ending 11 days of internal jockeying after the Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) swept the April assembly elections with 102 of 140 seats. The result ended a decade of Left Democratic Front (LDF) rule under Pinarayi Vijayan. Satheesan, a six-time legislator from Paravur and Leader of the Opposition since 2021, beat out Congress general secretary K.C. Venugopal and veteran Ramesh Chennithala for the post. Grassroots cadre support and sustained backing from the Indian Union Muslim League (IUML), the UDF's most influential alliance partner, tilted the decision in his favour.

title: Gulf insurance
text:
India and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) signed a raft of defence and energy agreements during Modi's Abu Dhabi visit on Thursday, the first stop on his five-nation tour.

On defence: The framework covers defence industrial cooperation, joint military training, maritime security, cybersecurity, secure communications, and advanced technology collaboration.

On energy: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) will store up to 30 million barrels of crude on Indian soil, expanding an existing strategic petroleum reserve arrangement. The Indian Oil Corporation also secured an increased liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supply under the package. The deals follow the HPCL-ADNOC 10-year LNG supply agreement signed during UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan's visit to New Delhi in January (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Thirty million barrels of Abu Dhabi crude stored on Indian soil is a quiet but significant hedge. With the Strait of Hormuz under stress and the rupee under pressure from an inflated import bill, locking in physical reserves through a supplier-side arrangement removes one variable India cannot afford to leave to the market.
anchor: India and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) signed

title: The Hague chips in
text:
Tata Electronics and Dutch semiconductor giant ASML signed an MoU on Saturday to build India's first front-end 300-millimetre chip fabrication plant in Dholera, Gujarat, during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's two-day visit to the Netherlands.

The deal: ASML, Europe's largest tech company by market capitalisation and the world's sole maker of advanced lithography machines, will supply its chipmaking tools and help ramp up production at the Dholera facility. Tata Electronics plans to invest USD 11 billion in the plant, which will manufacture chips for AI, automotive, and mobile applications. The two companies will also collaborate on workforce training and supply chain development.

The upgrade: Modi and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten elevated the bilateral relationship to a Strategic Partnership, adopting a five-year roadmap (2026–2030) covering semiconductors, defence, green hydrogen, critical minerals, water management, and migration. The Netherlands is India's fourth-largest source of foreign direct investment (FDI). Over 300 Dutch companies operate in India.

The backdrop: The visit follows the India–EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) which concluded in January (we covered it here). The Netherlands, home to Europe's largest port in Rotterdam, serves as a gateway to the EU single market for Indian exporters. Both sides also signed a customs mutual administrative assistance agreement to smooth trade under the new arrangement.

Water and energy: Modi and Jetten visited the Afsluitdijk, a 32-kilometre dam protecting the Netherlands from the North Sea, drawing parallels with India's Kalpasar project in Gujarat. Both sides signed a Letter of Intent for Dutch technical cooperation on Kalpasar and launched an India-Netherlands Roadmap on Green Hydrogen Development. An MoU on critical minerals was also signed, covering exploration, supply chain resilience, and ESG standards.
sound_smarter: The ASML deal caps a remarkable five months for India's tech ambitions. In February, New Delhi hosted the AI Impact Summit. The Union Budget announced a 21-year tax holiday for foreign data centre operators and launched India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) 2.0. In March, India joined Pax Silica, the US-led initiative to ringfence semiconductor and AI supply chains. Now comes ASML. Taken together, it’s clear India wants to move from consuming chips to making them.
anchor: Tata Electronics and Dutch semiconductor giant ASML signed

title: Disjoint statement
text:
BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement after two days of talks in Delhi on Friday, leaving host India to issue a chair's statement that acknowledged "differing views" on the conflict in West Asia (we covered the opening of the meeting here).

The split: Iran wanted BRICS to condemn the US-Israeli war on Iran and accused a fellow member, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), of direct involvement in military operations. Tehran has struck the UAE with missiles and drones multiple times since the conflict began on 28 February. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said a BRICS member blocked parts of the statement, adding he hoped differences would resolve before the leaders' summit later this year.

The pushback: The UAE categorically rejected Iran's allegations. Deputy Foreign Minister Khalifa Shaheen Al Marar called Iran's strikes "terrorist attacks" targeting civilian and critical infrastructure, accused Tehran of obstructing international maritime routes including the Strait of Hormuz, and said the UAE was "fully capable of deterring unprovoked aggression."

The timing: As Araghchi sat in Delhi, Modi was in Abu Dhabi telling UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan that "the way the UAE was targeted is unacceptable in any form." An India-flagged ship was sunk in the Strait of Hormuz the same week.
sound_smarter: India's BRICS chairmanship was always going to be tested by the West Asia conflict. New Delhi managed to hold the meeting and produce a document, but the absence of a joint statement exposes the limits of a bloc that now includes both the aggressor and the target.

title: Solar state says no to coal (again)
text:
Rajasthan’s power regulator has doubled down on its refusal to approve a 3.2 GW coal-fired project, snubbing state utilities despite surging heatwave demand across North India.

The standoff: For the second time since November, the Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory Commission (RERC) blocked the proposal, directing state utilities to conduct rigorous resource planning to prove that new coal capacity is actually necessary over cleaner alternatives.

The utility’s plea: State power utility Rajasthan Urja Vikas & IT Services Ltd argued that coal is essential for round-the-clock power. With temperatures in Delhi and the North set to spike 5°C above normal this week, the pressure to maintain baseload power is high.

The context: Rajasthan became the first Indian state to have solar exceed 50% of its installed power capacity in 2024. The state now has roughly 47 GW of renewable energy installed, second only to Gujarat. Adding 3.2 GW of coal would lock in fossil fuel infrastructure for decades in a state already proving that renewables can anchor the grid.

National backdrop: While Rajasthan holds the line, the Ministry of Power is in emergency mode. It recently invoked Section 11 of the Electricity Act, forcing plants running on expensive imported coal, such as Tata's Mundra facility, to operate at full capacity to avoid summer blackouts (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Despite the coal lobby’s structural might — anchored by massive public undertakings and millions of workers — regulators in India’s top solar state aren’t backing down. They recognize that renewables paired with storage now offer reliable, round-the-clock power. More importantly, they know that approving new coal projects today only sabotages the transition to clean energy tomorrow.

title: New mantris in town
text:
In case you missed it, the results of five state assembly elections came out earlier this month with historic upsets in West Bengal and Tamil Nadu. We covered the results in-depth here.

Today, we give you an overview of the new chief ministers of each state and who they’ve chosen for their cabinets.

West Bengal's new chief Minister is Suvendu Adhikari, a former Trinamool Congress (TMC) politician and architect of the Nandigram movement that catapulted Mamata Banerjee – the founder and president of TMC and the chief minister that Adhikari replaces – to the center of West Bengal politics. Adhikari defected to the BJP in 2020.

Adhikari has allocated portfolios to five ministers:

- Dilip Ghosh: Panchayat & Rural Development, Animal Resources, and Agricultural Marketing
- Agnimitra Paul: Women and Child Welfare, Urban Development, and Municipal Affairs.
- Nisith Pramanik: North Bengal Development, Youth Affairs and Sports.
- Ashok Kirtania: Food and Supplies, and Co-operation.
- Khudiram Tudu: Tribal Development, Backward Classes Welfare, and Minority and Madrasa Education

Tamil Nadu’s new Chief Minister is C. Joseph Vijay, the Kollywood superstar who transitioned his massive fan base into a political force by turning his Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), a party that did not exist two years ago, into the single largest party in its debut election.

Vijay has allocated portfolios to nine ministers, with key portfolios going to:

- K.A. Sengottaiyan: Finance and Pensions
- N. Anand: Rural Development and Water Resources
- Aadhav Arjuna: Public Works and Sports Development
- C. T. R. Nirmal Kumar: Energy Resources and Law
- Dr. K.G. Arunraj: Health, Medical Education, and Family Welfare
- S. Keerthana: Industries and Investment Promotion

Kerala’s new Chief Minister is V.D. Satheesan, a five-term member of the legislative assembly and former Leader of Opposition. Satheesan and his new ministry will be sworn in later today.

Assam’s new Chief Minister is Himanta Biswa Sarma, also known as the “Chanakya of the Northeast” for being the architect behind the BJP’s rapid growth in a region where smaller parties and Congress once dominated politics, will lead Assam for his second consecutive term. Sarma defected to the BJP from Congress in 2015.

Sarma has allocated key portfolios to four ministers, of which only Rameswar Teli is a new addition, signaling that policy continuity is expected.

- Ajanta Neog: Women and Child Development, and Tourism
- Rameswar Teli: Transformation and Development, and Labour Welfare
- Atul Bora: Panchayat and Rural Development, Implementation of Assam Accord, and Excise
- Charan Boro: Transport, and Welfare of Bodoland

Puducherry’s new Chief Minister is N. Rangaswamy, a veteran of Puducherry politics who began his fifth term as chief minister last week. While A. Namassivayam and Malladi Krishna Rao have been sworn in, specific portfolios remain unconfirmed. Both previously held senior roles in Industries and Health, respectively.
sound_smarter: The delay in assigning a full slate of portfolios is a standard, albeit complex, feature of Indian politics. While the Chief Ministers have taken their oaths, the full cabinet is rarely announced in one go, especially when the government is formed by alliances. Plum portfolios – Finance, Revenue, and Industries – are subject to intense negotiations.

title: India's free trade deal with Britain has hit
text: India's free trade deal with Britain has hit a hurdle over the UK's new steel import curbs, delaying a rollout initially expected by May. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said the UK's stricter steel safeguards, announced in March and set to take effect from July 1, were not factored into negotiations. The new regime will sharply reduce tariff-free quotas and impose steep duties beyond those limits, potentially diluting the market access gains Indian steelmakers expected from the deal. Agrawal said both sides are working on a "creative solution" to operationalise the agreement.

title: On Saturday, India reclassified silver imports from "free"
text: On Saturday, India reclassified silver imports from "free" to "restricted" with immediate effect, requiring importers to obtain prior government approval before bringing in shipments. The new rules cover silver bars with 99.9% purity and all other semi-manufactured forms of silver, two categories that accounted for more than 90% of the country's silver imports last fiscal year. The measure follows a duty hike on gold and silver from 6% to 15% announced earlier in the week (we covered it here), as New Delhi moves to curb precious metals imports amid pressure on foreign exchange reserves from the Strait of Hormuz crisis.
anchor: On Saturday, India reclassified silver imports from "free"

title: The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) is preparing
text: The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) is preparing to drop criminal fraud charges against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, while a related civil case brought by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is set to be settled subject to court approval. The SEC alleged that Adani and his nephew, Sagar Adani, concealed a scheme involving about USD 265 million in alleged bribes to Indian officials to secure solar power contracts, charges the Adani Group has denied. Under the proposed settlement, the two men would pay a combined USD 18 million in penalties without admitting or denying wrongdoing. Adani had pledged USD 10 billion in US energy investments shortly after Trump's election win in November 2024.

title: The Netherlands returned 11th-century Chola dynasty copper plates
text: The Netherlands returned 11th-century Chola dynasty copper plates to India during Modi’s visit. The Anaimangalam Copper Plates, a set of 21 large and three small sheets held at Leiden University since the mid-19th century, record grants by Chola emperor Rajaraja I to a Buddhist monastery at the port town of Nagapattinam in Tamil Nadu. India had pursued their restitution since 2012.
anchor: The Netherlands returned 11th-century Chola dynasty copper plates

title: The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) seized 227 kilograms
text: The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) seized 227 kilograms of Captagon in the country's first-ever interception of the drug, uncovering an international syndicate using India as a transit corridor to funnel the stimulant into Gulf nations. The haul, valued at INR 182 crore (USD 21 million), was recovered across Delhi and Mundra port in Gujarat over four days under Operation RAGEPILL, a multi-agency initiative targeting the consignment. Captagon is a psychotropic stimulant that gained notoriety during the Syrian civil war, where combatants used it to suppress fear and fatigue, and is now at the centre of a consumption epidemic across the Gulf.
anchor: The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) seized 227 kilograms

title: Babies for ballots
text:
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu announced cash incentives for families who have a third or fourth child on Saturday, part of a growing push by Modi allies to reverse India's declining fertility rate.

The offer: Naidu's scheme, dubbed "Children Are Wealth," will pay families INR 30,000 (USD 312) for a third child and INR 40,000 (USD 415) for a fourth. It revises an earlier proposal that offered INR 25,000 for a second child. Naidu, who once championed population control, told a rally in Srikakulam that "children should be seen as wealth."

The southern problem: Andhra Pradesh's total fertility rate (TFR) sits at roughly 1.5 children per woman, well below the national average of 2.0 and far from the 2.1 replacement level. All five southern states now report TFRs between 1.3 and 1.6. Meanwhile, Bihar (2.8), Uttar Pradesh (2.7), and Madhya Pradesh (2.4) remain well above replacement.

The political stakes: This fertility divide feeds directly into India's most contentious constitutional fight. Last month, the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill proposed expanding the Lok Sabha from 543 to 850 seats and reallocating them by population using 2011 Census data. Southern states objected: population-based redistribution would reward northern states for higher birth rates while punishing the south for successful family planning. The bill fell 54 votes short of the required two-thirds majority (we covered it here).

Not alone: Sikkim in Northeastern India provides year-long maternity leave, month-long paternity leave, and financial support for in-vitro fertilisation (IVF). Former Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M.K. Stalin urged newlyweds to have more children last year, citing delimitation fears explicitly.

Ideological backing: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu nationalist organisation from which Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) emerged, has made bigger families a stated priority. General Secretary Dattatreya Hosabale warned last week that "demographic imbalances will create tensions." The RSS has long framed declining Hindu birth rates as a demographic security concern. Government survey data shows Hindu TFR at 1.94 and Muslim TFR at 2.36, though the gap has narrowed sharply from 1.1 children per woman in 1992 to 0.42 today. Researchers attribute the remaining difference primarily to income and education levels rather than religion.
sound_smarter: Naidu's baby bonus doubles as parliamentary survival strategy. Under any future delimitation exercise, seats will flow to states with bigger populations. Southern leaders know the 131st Amendment will return in some form, and when it does, every additional birth in the south is a vote against seat erosion. Nevertheless, cash incentives of INR 30,000 will not reverse a demographic transition driven by education, urbanisation, and contraceptive access.
anchor: Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu announced cash

title: Going with the float
text:
Major Indian non-bank lenders are changing how they borrow. ICICI Home Finance, Tata Capital, Mahindra & Mahindra Financial Services, and HDB Financial Services plan to raise INR 85.5 billion (USD 888 million) this week through three-year floating-rate bonds, rather than their usual fixed-rate debt.

Why now: Markets have quickly moved from expecting Reserve Bank of India (RBI) rate cuts to pricing in at least 100 basis points of hikes over the next 12 months. The shift reflects rising inflation concerns as higher oil prices linked to the West Asia conflict feed into India’s import bill.

How they work: Floating-rate bonds pay interest at a spread over the three-month Treasury bill yield and reset every quarter. This lowers the initial borrowing cost for issuers while allowing investors to benefit if interest rates rise.

Market signal: Some issuers have struggled to raise their target amounts through fixed-rate bonds, suggesting investors are demanding higher yields to compensate for inflation risk.
sound_smarter: When high-grade borrowers abandon fixed-rate debt, it usually means investors no longer trust today's yields to compensate for tomorrow's inflation. Now India's credit market is telling the RBI that "higher for longer" may arrive before the central bank formally announces it.

title: Slick defiance
text:
India will keep buying Russian crude regardless of US sanctions waivers, a top petroleum ministry official confirmed Monday.

The stance: "Whatever waiver or no waiver, it will not affect," said Joint Secretary Sujata Sharma. She noted that "commercial sense" dictates India’s energy security, regardless of Washington’s shifting red lines.

The pivot: Hours after New Delhi’s blunt declaration, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reversed course. He announced a 30-day extension for "energy-vulnerable" nations, walking back a previous plan to let the grace period expire last weekend.

By the numbers: Russian imports are expected to hit 1.9 million barrels per day this month – near record highs. After a brief dip last year under US pressure, Indian refiners are back to business as usual.

The backdrop: The US initially issued the waiver in March to keep global prices stable (we covered it here) and later expanded it through an authorization valid until May 16. India had asked the US to extend its waiver on Russian oil.
sound_smarter: India’s stance sent a clear signal to Washington that Russian oil remains on its shopping list regardless of US waiver extensions. This puts the US in a difficult spot. By extending the waiver, the US maintains a diplomatic status quo that keeps all parties satisfied. Had it refused, the US would have been forced to confront India’s defiance, a move it is unlikely to make while a critical trade deal remains on the line (we covered it here)

title: Fjords meet the Global South
text:
India and Norway used the Nordic summit to add more substance to a steadily warming relationship. On Monday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre upgraded ties to a Green Strategic Partnership and signed a pact to jointly fund projects in the Global South.

The deal that matters: Both sides signed a triangular development cooperation agreement to jointly roll out India's digital public infrastructure (DPI) in Global South countries, with Norway co-funding projects while India exports the model.

The rest of the basket: The Indian Space Research Organisation signed an MoU with the Norwegian Space Agency, and health and digitalisation pacts followed. Norway joined India's Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative, sending a meaningful signal from a NATO member with Arctic interests.

Reading between the fjords: Norwegian PM Gahr Støre called on both nations to "stand up to those who weaponise trade and technology," echoing language from the Pax Silica declaration India signed earlier this month (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: India's DPI stack is the likely export: UPI-style payment rails, Aadhaar-equivalent digital ID systems, and DigiLocker-style document infrastructure are the three modules New Delhi has already piloted in countries from Sri Lanka to the Pacific Islands.

text: India and Sweden elevated bilateral ties to a Strategic Partnership during Modi's visit to Gothenburg on Sunday, with a joint action plan (2026–2030) covering AI, critical minerals, defence, and clean energy. The two sides endorsed a joint AI corridor (SITAC) and set a target of doubling bilateral trade and investment within five years. Sweden awarded Modi the Royal Order of the Polar Star, its highest civilian honour for a foreign leader. A day later in Oslo, Norway's King Harald V conferred the Grand Cross of the Royal Norwegian Order of Merit, bringing Modi's tally of international honours to 32.

title: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh departed for Vietnam and
text: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh departed for Vietnam and South Korea on Sunday for a four-day visit focused on military cooperation, defence industrial partnerships, and maritime security. The Vietnam leg marks 10 years of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, recently upgraded to an Enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership during Vietnamese President To Lam's state visit to India earlier this month (we covered it here). In South Korea, Singh will hold talks with Defence Minister Ahn Gyu-back and chair an India-Korea business roundtable.

title: Five flags, one fjord
text:
The 3rd India-Nordic Summit wrapped up in Oslo on Monday, with Prime Minister Modi holding bilateral meetings with the leaders of Finland, Denmark, Iceland, and Norway on the sidelines (we covered the tour here). The summit follows previous editions in Stockholm (2018) and Copenhagen (2022).

Finland: India and Finland elevated ties to a Strategic Partnership in Digitalization and Sustainability, committing to double bilateral trade by 2030. The two countries will jointly host the World Circular Economic Forum in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, in September 2026. Both leaders also backed the early entry into force of the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA).

Denmark: Modi and Acting Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen reviewed progress under the India-Denmark Green Strategic Partnership, launched in 2020. Modi invited Danish companies to set up in Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City) and highlighted a joint Smart Laboratory on Clean Rivers in Varanasi.

Iceland: Modi met Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, the youngest prime minister in Iceland's history, for their first bilateral. Both leaders highlighted the India-European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA), which entered into force in October 2025, as a framework for expanding trade and investment.

Norway: India's Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) signed five agreements with Norwegian research bodies covering offshore wind, clean energy, geosciences, and academic exchanges. The centrepiece is a collaboration on floating offshore wind technology with SINTEF, Norway's largest independent research organisation.
sound_smarter: Three of the five Nordic participants (Sweden, Denmark, and Finland) fall under the India-EU FTA; the remaining two (Norway and Iceland) are covered by the EFTA TEPA. Oslo is the one table where both trade frameworks sit side by side, giving New Delhi a single room to push implementation across both. With the India-EU FTA still awaiting ratification and the EFTA TEPA's USD 100 billion FDI pledge barely a year old, the Nordic bloc is where India can test whether Europe's trade promises translate into actual capital flows.
anchor: The 3rd India-Nordic Summit wrapped up in Oslo

title: RSVP from the Kremlin
text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi on 12-13 September, according to Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov. It will be his second trip to India in less than a year.

Diplomatic drumbeat: Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was in New Delhi last week for the BRICS Foreign Ministers’ Meeting and reaffirmed Russia’s commitment to its “privileged strategic partnership” with India.

Awkward backdrop: Last week’s ministerial meeting ended without a joint communiqué after members failed to agree on language on the US-Iran conflict. India, as chair, issued a summary instead.

Why it matters: Hosting Putin underscores the durability of India-Russia ties. It also ensures New Delhi’s BRICS year will be closely watched as divisions inside the bloc become harder to hide.
sound_smarter: Don't mistake BRICS’ lack of consensus for Indian diplomatic failure. New Delhi’s goal isn't to turn the bloc into a monolith, but to ensure India has a seat at every major table. By hosting Putin while finalizing deals with Europe, India is navigating an increasingly multipolar world without picking a side.
anchor: Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the BRICS

title: Kerala’s new Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government
text: Kerala’s new Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government announced a special committee on Tuesday to draft a White Paper on the state’s financial condition. The UDF majority ends a decade of Left Democratic Front (LDF) rule (we covered it here). Throughout the campaign, the UDF frequently alleged that the previous LDF administration had severely mismanaged the state's finances.
anchor: Kerala’s new Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government

title: Union Home Minister Amit Shah announced that India
text: Union Home Minister Amit Shah announced that India was finally free from Maoism on Monday during a landmark visit to the former insurgent stronghold of Bastar. Attributing this achievement to the bravery of security forces, the Minister detailed a comprehensive plan to reintegrate 3,000 surrendered Naxals – the Left-wing extremist who sought to overthrow the state – into mainstream society through "respectable" roles and development initiatives. He further pledged to bridge the region's historical infrastructure gap within three to five years, transforming remote security camps into public service centers to ensure tribal communities receive the same rights and facilities as major cities.

title: No Roman holiday
text:
Prime Minister Modi and Italian Prime Minister Meloni elevated India-Italy relations to a Special Strategic Partnership in Rome on Tuesday, setting a EUR 20 billion bilateral trade target by 2029 and signing agreements on defence, critical minerals, and innovation.

Trade snapshot: Bilateral trade stood at EUR 14.2 billion in 2024, with Italy acting primarily as a machinery supplier to India (EUR 2 billion, nearly 40% of Italian exports) while importing Indian steel, electronics, and chemicals. The EUR 20 billion target would require roughly 40% growth in five years.

What was signed: MoUs on critical minerals and agriculture, a defence industrial roadmap covering co-production of helicopters, naval platforms, and electronic warfare systems, and a Joint Declaration of Intent on nurse mobility from India to Italy. The two sides also announced INNOVIT India, an innovation hub covering sectors from semiconductors to quantum computing.

The corridor and the FTA: Both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) and called for the first IMEC Ministerial meeting to take concrete steps in 2026. They also pushed for early implementation of the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA), whose negotiations concluded earlier this year.
sound_smarter: Modi publicly thanked Meloni for Italy's role in getting the India-EU FTA across the line. By pairing that with a Special Strategic Partnership upgrade and an IMEC push, he's investing in a relationship that gives India a reliable interlocutor inside the EU's biggest economies.
anchor: Prime Minister Modi and Italian Prime Minister Meloni

title: Bulletproof
text:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh signed three defence agreements with South Korea in Seoul on Tuesday, wrapping up a two-nation tour that began in Vietnam (we covered it here).

What was signed: The Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) cover defence cyber cooperation, training exchanges between India's National Defence College and Korea National Defence University, and peacekeeping operations.

The bigger play: Beyond the MoUs, both sides discussed operationalising KIND-X (India-Korea Defence Innovation Accelerator Ecosystem), a joint platform for co-developing and co-producing defence systems. L&T and Hanwha also signed two commercial agreements on defence technology at a business roundtable Singh chaired in Seoul.

By the numbers: India recorded approximately INR 1.54 lakh crore (USD 18 billion) in defence production and nearly INR 40,000 crore (USD 4.7 billion) in exports in FY 2025-26. Singh said exports will reach INR 50,000 crore (USD 5.9 billion) within two years.
sound_smarter: South Korea builds world-class defence platforms, India has factories and cost advantages but needs the technology. KIND-X and the L&T-Hanwha deals suggest both sides see the complementarity clearly enough to let the private sector lead while governments set the framework.
anchor: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh signed three defence agreements

title: DC calling
text:
Washington is sending its top diplomat. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will visit India from 23–26 May, the highest-level U.S. trip since Donald Trump returned to the White House.

On the agenda: Rubio will visit Kolkata, Agra, Jaipur, and New Delhi. Talks are expected to cover trade, defence cooperation, and energy security as the West Asia conflict pushes up oil prices.

Trade overhang: Trump’s tariffs strained ties earlier this year (we covered it here). Many were later rolled back, and both sides are now working toward a broader trade agreement.
sound_smarter: Cabinet-level visits are a useful indicator of priorities. Rubio’s trip suggests Washington now sees India less as a “China hedge” and more as a co-architect of a hard-edged economic security order in the Indo-Pacific. The two sides may argue over market access, but the strategic logic of the relationship remains intact.

title: Paving the way with paper
text:
Close to a dozen Indian cities are set to issue debut municipal bonds this year, fuelled by a regulatory push to fix India’s crumbling urban infrastructure.

The Maharashtra cluster: At least seven cities in Maharashtra – including those ringing Mumbai like Navi Mumbai and Thane – are prepping issues totalling INR 33 billion (USD 341 million). Other debutants include Shimla, Ujjain, and Gorakhpur. Notably, Greater Mumbai, the nation's richest, remains on the sidelines.

Carrots and sticks: To move the needle on a stagnant market – only INR 45 billion (USD 465 million) raised in nine years – the government is offering INR 1 billion (USD 10 million) incentives for large issues and 2% interest subsidies. Regulators are also tightening financial disclosure rules to soothe investor nerves regarding opaque local accounting.

Investor appetite: Key players like the state-backed National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development and commercial banks are stepping in as anchor investors. New rules will also allow refinancing of old loans and higher rates for retail investors to broaden the pool.
sound_smarter: With rapid urbanisation and climate change demanding massive capital, these bonds are the only way to fund India’s future-ready cities without blowing the union budget.
anchor: Close to a dozen Indian cities are set

title: Second date for the trade deal
text:
US trade negotiators are expected in India next month to resuscitate a trade deal. Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal confirmed the visit on Thursday, signaling a push to finalise terms after months of legal and political gridlock.

The backdrop: Negotiations stalled after the US Supreme Court scrapped the "Liberation Day" tariffs – the original basis for the deal (we covered it here). Washington pivoted to a 10% flat duty under Section 122 and launched Section 301 investigations into Indian trade practices (we covered it here).

Legal limbo: A recent US Court of International Trade ruling declared those 10% duties unlawful, but the win is narrow. US Customs continues to collect the tax from everyone except the specific plaintiffs.

The Rubio factor: While negotiators arrive in June, Secretary of State Marco Rubio lands first on May 23. His four-day visit focuses on trade, defence, and energy, setting the stage for the technical teams following behind him.
sound_smarter: Both sides are sprinting because the clock is ticking on Section 301 investigations, which carries no expiry and no ceiling. Trump needs a tangible trade win, while a newly emboldened BJP has the domestic political capital to make concessions. Expect India to trade a few market-access wins for a significant reduction in those unpredictable tariff rates.
anchor: US trade negotiators are expected in India next

title: Open for (serious) business
text:
America is no longer window-shopping in India. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal announced that US companies have committed over USD 60 billion in investments over the last six months, concentrated in data centres, digital infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing.

Beyond the cheque: Road Transport Minister Nitin Gadkari urged Indian firms to stop treating foreign capital as a cash injection and start treating it as a classroom. His push for joint ventures with US companies is explicitly about absorbing American know-how in infrastructure, mobility, and logistics, not just booking the investment.

The deal on the table: A US trade delegation is expected in India next month for fresh negotiations, with both sides keen to close a broader agreement after months stalled by tariff disputes.
sound_smarter: What separates this wave from earlier rounds of US-India trade optimism is that the geopolitical incentive is now structural, not rhetorical. India is no longer pitching itself on cheap labour. Instead, it is pitching political alignment and supply-chain resilience to companies actively reducing China exposure. That gives New Delhi unusual leverage, provided it can actually deliver on absorption, not just attraction.

title: India-Africa summit postponed over Ebola outbreak
text: India and the African Union (AU) have postponed the fourth India-Africa Forum Summit, which was scheduled for May 28–31 in New Delhi, citing an "emerging public health situation" in Africa. The summit was set to cover trade, investment, digital technology, and global governance. The move follows a World Health Organization (WHO) warning that the Democratic Republic of Congo's ongoing Ebola outbreak has recorded 600 suspected cases and 139 suspected deaths over the past two months, involving a rare strain for which no vaccine exists. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) has said that new dates will be finalised in due course.

title: Making up is hard to do
text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his Indian counterpart S. Jaishankar in New Delhi on Sunday, attempting to stabilise a relationship currently at a two-decade low.

The friction: Ties have frayed under President Trump’s global tariff offensive, which hit Indian exports hard. Rubio framed the move as "global perspective" economics rather than a targeted snub, hoping to pivot back to strategic alignment.

The backdrop: Both countries have not finalised the terms of their trade deal; US trade negotiators are expected in India next month (we covered it here). Negotiations stalled after the US Supreme Court scrapped the "Liberation Day" tariffs – the original basis for the deal (we covered it here). Washington pivoted to a 10% flat duty under Section 122 and launched Section 301 investigations into Indian trade practices (we covered it here).

The Quad factor: Rubio heads into a Quad ministerial meeting on Tuesday with counterparts from India, Australia, and Japan. Despite the trade spat, the security imperative in the Indo-Pacific remains the glue holding the partnership together.

Energy as an olive branch: Rubio pitched US energy as the solution to India’s energy security problem, specifically as a hedge against Iran, during his meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday.
sound_smarter: By swapping Iranian or Russian barrels for American ones, India can satisfy its energy security needs and shrink the trade surplus that constantly irritates Trump. New Delhi is likely to use any commitment to purchase energy to secure continued sanctions waivers or tariffs rates lower than the 18% initially agreed to in February, which we covered here.

title: The Mediterranean shortcut
text:
India and Cyprus elevated their relationship to a Strategic Partnership on Thursday, with the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) emerging as the centrepiece of the visit. Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides arrived in New Delhi days after Modi wrapped a tour of the Netherlands, Sweden, Norway, and Italy, the latest in a string of bilateral engagements with individual EU member states aimed at underpinning the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA).

The IMEC play: Cyprus is pushing to build out the Mediterranean leg of the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), proposing itself alongside Greece and Italy as the corridor's European entry point. IMEC's eastern segment, connecting India to the Gulf, broke ground in April 2025. But the northern corridor, designed to run overland through Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Israel to European ports, remains stalled: Haifa port is under threat from Iranian strikes, Jordan is reluctant to serve as a transit corridor, and Saudi-Israeli normalisation has been frozen since 2023. During its EU Council presidency, Cyprus has formed an IMEC friends group within the EU to keep the project alive in Brussels, and officials say they are building port and logistics infrastructure now so the Mediterranean end is ready when the overland route becomes viable. Both sides established a bilateral connectivity dialogue to take this forward.

The package: Six MoUs were signed covering counter-terrorism, diplomatic training, innovation, search and rescue, higher education, and culture. Separately, both sides announced a defence cooperation roadmap for 2026–2031, a cyber security dialogue, a joint task force on shipping and infrastructure, and Cyprus' entry into the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (IPOI). Cyprus also plans to open a trade centre in Mumbai.

Why Cyprus: The island currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union (EU) and ranks among India's top 10 foreign investors. Cypriot investment into India has nearly doubled over the past decade. Modi said both sides aim to double it again within five years. Cyprus has been divided since Turkey's 1974 invasion, with the northern third controlled by the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), recognised only by Ankara. India reiterated its support for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and unity of the Republic of Cyprus. In return, Cyprus backed India's bid for a permanent seat on a reformed UN Security Council.
sound_smarter: Modi visited Cyprus last June, toured four European capitals last week, and elevated Italy to a Special Strategic Partnership. Cyprus fits that pattern, but its specific pitch as IMEC’s first gateway into Europe gives it a competitive edge the other partners lack. Cyprus is betting that whoever builds the Mediterranean entry point first gives it access to India’s diplomatic weight when the rest of IMEC catches up.

title: Goyal heads to Canada for CEPA talks
text: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal will visit Canada from May 25–27 for the next round of India-Canada Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) negotiations, accompanied by representatives from over 100 Indian businesses. Goyal will meet Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and call on Prime Minister Mark Carney. Bilateral trade stood at around USD 8 billion in FY2025–26, with both sides targeting USD 50 billion by 2030. The CEPA negotiations were launched during Carney's visit to India in March (which we covered here).

title: India signs WTO accession protocol with Ethiopia
text: India and Ethiopia signed a bilateral accession protocol in Geneva on Thursday supporting Ethiopia's membership of the World Trade Organization (WTO). India is Ethiopia's second-largest trading partner, and bilateral relations were elevated to a Strategic Partnership during Modi's visit to Ethiopia in December 2025. Ethiopia's WTO Working Party met for its seventh round in April.

title: India test-fires Agni-1, flags off new rocket system
text: India successfully test-launched the nuclear-capable Agni-1 short-range ballistic missile from Chandipur, Odisha on Thursday, validating all operational parameters under the Strategic Forces Command. The Agni-1 has a range of 700–1,200 km. Separately, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh inaugurated a private-sector defence manufacturing complex at Shirdi, Maharashtra, and flagged off India's first 300 km Universal Rocket Launching System, Suryastra. Singh cited Operation Sindoor as proof that future conflicts will be decided by munitions and automation, not troop numbers.

title: One code, zero consensus
text:
The Assam government tabled the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), Assam, 2026 Bill on Monday, proposing a single legal framework for marriage, divorce, succession, and live-in relationships that would replace religion-specific personal laws for all residents except Scheduled Tribes. If passed, Assam would become the third Indian state to enact a UCC, after Uttarakhand in 2024 and Gujarat in March this year.

What's in it: Parliamentary Affairs Minister Atul Bora tabled the Bill on behalf of Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma during the inaugural session of the new Assam Legislative Assembly. The legislation mandates monogamy, with bigamy and polygamy carrying up to seven years' imprisonment. It sets the minimum marriage age at 21 for men and 18 for women, requires compulsory registration of all marriages and divorces, and introduces gender-equal inheritance rules that place spouses, children, and parents within the same top-tier category of heirs.

The live-in clause: The Bill requires all live-in relationships to be registered within one month. Children born from such relationships will be considered legitimate, and deserted partners will be entitled to seek maintenance through the courts. Penalties apply for non-registration.

The bigger project: The UCC has been a cornerstone demand of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its ideological parent, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) for decades. The argument is that religion-specific personal laws create a parallel legal system that undermines national cohesion.

Why it matters: India currently governs personal matters like marriage, divorce, and inheritance through separate legal codes for different religious communities. Hindu, Christian, and Parsi personal laws already broadly enforce monogamy and relatively standardised succession rules. Muslim personal law permits polygamy, follows distinct divorce procedures, and applies different inheritance rules where daughters typically receive half the share of sons. A UCC replaces all of these with a single code. The BJP-led central government has long promised a national UCC, enshrined as a directive principle under Article 44 of the Constitution, but has never tabled one in Parliament.
sound_smarter: By routing the UCC through states, the BJP avoids the political cost of a national debate while creating precedents that could eventually make a central law feel inevitable. Assam is the first state where a UCC would affect a large Muslim population, making it the real test of enforceability. Most Muslim-majority countries that reformed practices like polygamy and triple talaq simply made them legally void. India has chosen a hardline stance by criminalising these practices.
anchor: The Assam government tabled the Uniform Civil Code

title: Partners, not packages
text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio drew a clear line on Pakistan on Monday, midway through a four-day India visit that concludes with the Quad foreign ministers' meeting today. Speaking before flying to Agra, Rubio said India's concerns about Pakistan on cross-border terrorism never came up in the context of Islamabad's mediation role in the US-Iran conflict. "Their issue with Pakistan is different," he said.

The reassurance on record: At a joint press conference with External Affairs Minister Jaishankar on Saturday, Rubio addressed the question of whether US-Pakistan engagement was coming at India's expense. "I don't view our relation with any country in the world as coming at the expense of our strategic alliance with India," he said. Jaishankar was notably guarded on Pakistan's mediation role, saying only: "As to who all are involved in the matter which Secretary Rubio addressed, I think it's for the parties to work out."

The escalation: Washington's language on Pakistan's Iran role has been steadily upgrading. In July 2025, Rubio praised Islamabad's "constructive role" in mediating conversations with Tehran. Three days before landing in India, he called Pakistan the "primary interlocutor" at the NATO foreign ministers' meeting in Helsingborg. Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir was in Tehran the same day.
sound_smarter: Rubio's framing decouples India and Pakistan into separate lanes: one a strategic alliance, the other a functional channel for the Iran talks. The distinction is tidy on a podium, but Pakistan's mediation role is giving Islamabad real diplomatic capital at a time when Delhi would rather it had none.

title: Breaking the cylinder habit
text:
The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas barred households with piped natural gas (PNG) connections from refilling LPG cylinders on Monday to protect dwindling fuel stocks.

The mandate: If you have piped gas, you’re done with tanks. Consumers must surrender their LPG connection or take a "transfer voucher" within 30 days. The voucher allows for a future connection if a household moves to an area without piped infrastructure.

War footing: The move is a direct response to the West Asia crisis. India is the world's second-largest LPG importer, and the US-Israeli war on Iran has choked fuel supplies. Almost all of India's LPG imports come from Qatar and the UAE, and there’s no way to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

Supply crunch: While New Delhi is scrambling to source from the US, Canada, and Norway, the Middle Eastern shortfall has already forced supply cuts to several industrial sectors. The central government has stretched minimum LPG booking intervals and conducted raids on LPG hoarding nationwide (we covered it here).

Official line: Despite the squeeze, the Ministry claims distributors are not out of inventory, even reporting 17.2 million cylinder deliveries against 16.6 million bookings in the last four days.
sound_smarter: By mandating the decoupling of households from LPG supplies, the regulator is ensuring a permanent shift toward domestically produced PNG. This move prioritizes LPG for rural and unconnected areas to reduce supply strains on the national gas system as a result of the West Asia crisis.

title: Finance Minister flags fuel, fertiliser, forex as West Asia crisis bites
text: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman flagged fuel, fertiliser, and foreign exchange as the economy's three critical pressure points amid the West Asia crisis, framing PM Modi's earlier call to conserve forex and avoid gold purchases as "very important." Crude has surged from around USD 70 to over USD 115 per barrel since the Strait of Hormuz disruptions began in late February, fertiliser costs have hit what she called "unimaginable" levels, and excise duty cuts on petrol and diesel are already costing the exchequer INR 1 lakh crore (USD 11.7 billion). Sitharaman maintained that India's domestic fundamentals "remain positive and resilient," insisting the challenges are externally driven.

title: Quad squad directives
text:
The Quad wants to prove it can do more than talk. On Tuesday, the foreign ministers of Australia, India, Japan, and the United States met in New Delhi and launched a package of Indo-Pacific initiatives backed by real commitments. Rubio said the grouping must move beyond dialogue and deliver concrete outcomes. Officials are now working toward a leaders' summit later this year.

What launched: The ministers announced the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration (IPMSC), the Quad’s first initiative to pool maritime surveillance. They also rolled out a Quad Critical Minerals Initiative Framework with the intent to mobilise USD 20 billion in government and private sector support to strengthen critical mineral supply chains, alongside a separate Indo-Pacific energy security initiative. The group also rolled out their first infrastructure project, a port in Fiji.

Hormuz front and centre: The joint statement condemned attacks on commercial shipping and explicitly opposed the imposition of tolls on the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed the group on ongoing negotiations with Iran. Australia's Penny Wong said the closure directly threatens regional energy security.

The fine print: The statement flagged "dangerous and coercive actions" in the East and South China Seas, citing water cannons, flares, and ramming by coast guard and militia vessels, and welcomed Pax Silica as a "pillar of shared economic security." It also called for action against cross-border terrorism, explicitly condemning the attacks at Pahalgam and Bondi Beach. China was not explicitly mentioned.
sound_smarter: The Hormuz crisis handed the Quad something it has lacked: urgency. Previous meetings produced frameworks and working groups. This one launched initiatives because disrupted shipping lanes and volatile energy prices gave every member a reason to act now, not next quarter. After years of communiques, the Quad is finally trying to build capabilities.

title: Hundred-company handshake
text:
India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal landed in Ottawa on Sunday leading the largest Indian business delegation ever sent to Canada, over 100 companies strong, to accelerate free trade talks between the two countries.

The visit: Goyal met Prime Minister Mark Carney, Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, Agriculture Minister Heath MacDonald, and Foreign Minister Anita Anand across a packed first day. Carney called the proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) a "game changer." Both sides want to conclude it by the end of 2026.

By the numbers: Bilateral trade in goods currently sits at around USD 8.5 billion. The target is USD 50 billion by 2030. The delegation spans energy, mining, automotive, pharmaceuticals, telecom, AI, leather, and textiles.

Negotiation timeline: Terms of Reference were signed in March 2026 during Carney's visit to India (which we covered here). Two rounds of talks followed. A third round is running in parallel with Goyal's visit in Ottawa this week, with negotiators from both sides working through May 29.

The bigger arc: Ties froze in 2023 after then-PM Justin Trudeau alleged Indian involvement in the killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar. Carney's March visit, a uranium deal, and Canada's move to revoke the citizenship of Pakistani-Canadian terrorist Tahawwur Rana (which we covered here) cleared the diplomatic path. Three months later, both sides are already deep in trade text.
sound_smarter: Speed is the story. India and Canada went from frozen ties to a third round of free trade negotiations in under a year. Trump's tariffs have made Canada's US-dependence a vulnerability, and India offers the scale to hedge. For New Delhi, a CEPA unlocks critical minerals, uranium, and a USD 2 trillion economy that needs diversification just as badly as India does.
anchor: India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal landed in Ottawa

title: Central government establishes high-level committee on ‘unnatural’ demographic change
text: The central government has constituted a high-level committee to study demographic changes resulting from illegal immigration and other ‘unnatural’ reasons, as announced by Home Minister Amit Shah on Tuesday. Headed by retired Supreme Court Judge Prakash Prabhakar Navlekar, the panel is tasked with analysing population shifts across religious and social communities and recommending a permanent mechanism for the identification, detention, and deportation of illegal immigrants. Additionally, the committee will propose institutional measures to strengthen border management, address national security concerns, and promote population stabilisation. The group has been directed to submit its comprehensive report and recommendations within one year, with a potential extension of up to six months if necessary.

title: Feeding the machine
text:
India is wiring AI into the world's largest food welfare programme. On Wednesday, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) approved SARTHAK-PDS, an INR 25,530 crore (USD 3 billion) overhaul of the Public Distribution System (PDS) running through March 2031.

The stack: The scheme introduces three AI-powered platforms. NIRMAL is a real-time beneficiary registry with cross-ministry integration. ASHA handles grievance redressal across calls, WhatsApp, IVRS, and multilingual chatbots. SAKSHAM covers vehicle tracking, QR-code traceability, route optimisation, and demand forecasting to cut waste in food grain transport.

The fine print: SARTHAK-PDS merges two existing schemes under one umbrella, pairing financial support for state-level grain transport with a technology layer. The government expects food grain travel distances to fall by 15–50%, saving roughly INR 280 crore annually.
sound_smarter: Feeding roughly 800 million people, India’s public distribution system is a massive undertaking. At this scale, even minor leakage reductions yield significant fiscal savings. By integrating AI into this digital public infrastructure (DPI), India has created a powerful proof of concept for global adoption. These successes bolster India’s strategy to export its DPI framework, a move recently formalised through a new partnership with Norway (we covered it here).

title: Goyal co-chairs investment roundtable in Toronto, Canada announces trade mission
text: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal moved to Toronto for Day 2 of his Canada visit, co-chairing an investment roundtable with Canadian pension funds and banks alongside Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu. Sidhu announced a Team Canada Trade Mission to India in November, the first such delegation since the diplomatic reset earlier this year. Goyal also held one-on-one meetings with leading Canadian firms across insurance, banking, food processing, and critical minerals. We covered Day 1 of the visit here.

Beyond finalising the interim trade agreement, both sides are expected to build towards a comprehensive bilateral trade agreement.

title: Indian Railways approves first indigenous hydrogen-powered train
text: Indian Railways has approved its first indigenous hydrogen fuel cell trainset, a 10-car, 1,200 KW unit set to run on the Jind–Sonipat section in Haryana at up to 75 kmph. A locally built hydrogen storage and refuelling facility is already licensed and in place at Jind. The train emits only water vapour, placing India alongside Germany, Japan, China, and the United States in the small group of countries piloting hydrogen-powered rail.

title: Six months of overtime
text:
Siddaramaiah resigned as Karnataka Chief Minister on Thursday, ending a six-month standoff over a power-sharing deal that should have handed the job to Deputy Chief Minister DK Shivakumar last November. Karnataka, home to Bengaluru and India's largest tech economy, is Congress's most prized state government.

The deal: When Congress swept Karnataka's 2023 assembly elections, the party brokered a 2.5-year rotational arrangement between the two rivals. Siddaramaiah, a veteran administrator, took the first innings. Shivakumar, widely credited as the party organiser who delivered the election victory, stayed on as the Deputy Chief Minister. The handover date passed in November 2025 without action, sparking months of public jockeying.

The exit: Siddaramaiah said the Congress high command directed him to step down two days ago. He submitted his resignation, though it only takes effect once the state Governor formally accepts it. Siddaramaiah endorsed Shivakumar as successor, who is expected to take oath on May 30.

Hanging over it all: The Mysuru Urban Development Authority (MUDA) land scam has dogged Siddaramaiah's second term. The Governor sanctioned his prosecution in August 2024, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) attached properties worth INR 300 crore (USD 35 million), and the Lokayukta, Karnataka's anti-corruption ombudsman, continues to investigate.
sound_smarter: Shivakumar inherits the top job with just two years until the next state election with opinion polls already showing the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) comfortably ahead. The smooth handover proves Congress can manage internal transitions without creating new factions, though addressing Karnataka's stretched finances after years of welfare guarantees will be an uphill task.

title: Albanese praises India in Parliament ahead of Modi visit
text: Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Parliament that India is "one of the largest growing economies" and called the Indian Australian community the country's fastest-growing migrant group. He confirmed he will host Prime Minister Modi for a second visit to Australia soon. The remarks cap a busy week for the bilateral relationship: earlier, Foreign Minister Penny Wong met Prime Minister Modi on the sidelines of the Quad Foreign Ministers' Meeting in New Delhi, which we covered here.

title: Anchor management
text:
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called India a "critical anchor" for Indo-Pacific stability at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore on Saturday, praising its military build-up and rising weight in the Indian Ocean. "In South Asia, India is a critical anchor to hold the line," Hegseth said, adding that "a powerful India acting in its own self-interest advances our shared goal of maintaining a balance of power across the region."

The hardware: He credited India with modernising its forces to carry more of the regional security burden, and with building the industrial capacity to repair and sustain shared platforms, including support for US Navy vessels operating forward in the theatre.

The China subtext: Hegseth urged Asian partners to lift defence spending and warned of Beijing's military build-up, but dropped the Taiwan warnings that dominated his 2025 address. China's defence minister stayed away for a second year, with Beijing sending a lower-ranking delegation.
sound_smarter: Washington's wording – "in its own self-interest" – gives the game away. It is asking no one to join an anti-China bloc, because it is not assembling one. A strong and independent India works in Washington's favour and validates New Delhi's doctrine of strategic autonomy, especially a fortnight after Trump's detente with Xi.
anchor: US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called India

title: Shore thing
text:
India confirmed the sale of its BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles to Vietnam, its largest arms-export deal in Southeast Asia to date.

The reveal: Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh let it slip at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, telling a Vietnamese delegate the contract with Hanoi had already been signed, though not yet publicly announced. Officials say it was concluded quietly last fiscal year.

The package: Vietnam is buying the land-based coastal defence variant, built to strike ships at sea. The deal, reportedly worth around INR 58 billion (USD 630 million), bundles mobile launchers, radars, command systems, missiles, training, and logistics. BrahMos flies at nearly three times the speed of sound, with a range of about 290 kilometres.

The neighbourhood: The Philippines became the first export buyer in 2022, and Indonesia entered its own agreement to procure the missile in March (we covered it here). All three are locked in maritime disputes with China in the South China Sea.
sound_smarter: New Delhi is quietly arming China's maritime rivals. Sales to Vietnam, the Philippines, and Indonesia are ringing the South China Sea with supersonic anti-ship missiles pointed at Chinese shipping, a mirror of the encirclement India has long felt from Beijing. The secrecy around the Vietnam contract, signed months ago and admitted only now, shows how carefully India is managing the provocation.
anchor: India confirmed the sale of its BrahMos supersonic

title: Scan and deliver
text:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the State Bank of Vietnam have signed an agreement to connect their digital payment systems. The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) covers information sharing, regulatory coordination, and the plumbing for cross-border QR-code merchant payments.

The pitch: New Delhi frames the tie-up as a way to make trade and tourism payments faster, cheaper, and real-time, while positioning India as a regional fintech hub. India has been exporting its Unified Payments Interface (UPI) one country at a time, with links already running or agreed across Singapore, the UAE, France, and Sri Lanka. Vietnam, with its own fast-growing QR-payment habit, is the latest target.
sound_smarter: Each linkage plants India's payment standards in another market before Western card giants or rival state-backed systems entrench themselves, turning UPI into quiet infrastructure diplomacy. Vietnam matters because it is chasing the same China-plus-one factory orders as India, so wiring the two economies together greases a trade corridor both want to grow.

title: Keyword warriors
text:
In a landmark ruling, the Delhi High Court has held that Google infringes trademarks, by auctioning rivals' brand names as ad keywords.

The case: Bathroom-fittings maker Hindware sued after rivals bought its name as a Google Ads keyword, so that searches for "Hindware" surfaced their adverts instead. On 22 May, Justice Mini Pushkarna agreed, permanently barring Google from auctioning the trademark and awarding INR 3 million (USD 31,600) in damages.

Google's defence, rejected: Google argued that keywords are invisible backend triggers and that it is a passive intermediary. The court held that even "invisible use" of a trademark to divert traffic counts as use under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, and that Google actively sells the marks.

The backers: The ruling gained traction after two of India's best-known tech founders, Zerodha's Nithin Kamath and Zoho's Sridhar Vembu, backed it publicly, arguing that businesses are forced to pay to stop rivals hijacking searches for their own names.
sound_smarter: Google's core ad-auction model is now on notice in one of its biggest markets by users, after the court found that even invisible keyword bidding infringes trademarks, and handed every Indian trademark holder a precedent to fence off its own name.

title: General Subramani takes over as Chief of Defence Staff
text: General NS Raja Subramani took charge as India's third Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) on 31 May, succeeding General Anil Chauhan. A four-decade Army veteran, he was most recently Vice Chief of the Army Staff and Military Adviser at the National Security Council Secretariat. He pledged to push greater jointness across the services and faster induction of home-built weapons under India's self-reliance drive. The CDS post anchors India's tri-service integration, including its long-planned theatre commands.

title: India lifts cotton import duty for the off-season
text: The Centre has lifted the 11% import duty on cotton from 1 June to 31 October, easing input costs for textile mills through the lean months. The levy bundles the Basic Customs Duty and the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess (AIDC), and imports will be free of both for the five-month window. The exemption lapses on 1 November, just as the new crop reaches market, a timing that eases mill costs now while protecting growers at selling time.

title: Gulf course
text:
The India–Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) entered into force yesterday, giving Indian exporters duty-free access on 99.38% of goods shipped to Oman, a significant increase from 15.33% under the previous Most Favoured Nation (MFN) regime.

What’s in it: Bilateral trade in goods hit USD11.18 billion in FY 2025-26. Oman's total import market is worth around USD28 billion, leaving Indian exporters substantial room to grow. The CEPA covers goods, services, investment, and regulatory cooperation. Oman has opened 127 services sub-sectors to Indian providers, the most comprehensive offer any Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) country has made to India. Oman's ports at Sohar, Duqm, and Salalah – away from the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf – give Indian exporters a logistics corridor into the wider GCC and East African markets.

Win-win: Oman is mid-pivot away from hydrocarbon dependency, as it builds out special economic zones in Duqm and Salalah as international logistics and manufacturing hubs. That expansion needs engineers, healthcare professionals, IT specialists, and supply chain experts that Oman's domestic workforce cannot yet supply at scale.

The mobility piece: The CEPA raises the cap on company-transferred workers from 20% to 50% of a firm's workforce. Oman has also made binding commitments for specific professional categories: engineers, doctors, IT professionals, teachers, and consultants, legally granting market access to Indian professionals.
sound_smarter: India's real win is in services, where it runs a USD 447 million surplus with Oman on just a 5.31% share of Oman's services imports. The bigger prize is precedent – Oman is the first GCC state to grant India binding professional access, and New Delhi will use it as the template in pending talks with the other five Gulf members, where millions of Indian workers and far larger remittance flows are at stake.
anchor: The India–Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) entered

title: Courting the general
text:
Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi yesterday. It was the former junta chief's first foreign trip since taking the presidency this year.

Why now: The election that handed Min Aung Hlaing the presidency was widely dismissed as a sham staged to legitimise military rule. China endorsed the result almost immediately. While India did not go that far, hosting him weeks later for a high-profile state visit hands the general the international respectability he has been chasing since the 2021 coup.

On the table: A pillar of India's Act East policy, Myanmar is a crucial node in both the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport project and the India-Myanmar-Thailand trilateral highway. Both sides committed to completing the projects, though the government in Naypyidaw is battling an armed insurgency across several parts of the country. India raised its Mekong Ganga scholarships for Myanmar students from 36 to 100, and both governments backed expanding the Rupee-Kyat settlement mechanism that has handled bilateral payments since May 2024. New Delhi also has its eye on Myanmar's rare-earth deposits, concentrated in the northern frontier where China currently dominates extraction and processing.

The security ask: General Hlaing reiterated that Myanmar's territory would not be used against India's security interests, a commitment that matters given insurgent activity along the shared northeastern border. India reaffirmed support for Myanmar's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
sound_smarter: China has bankrolled and shielded the junta for years, leaving Myanmar lopsidedly dependent on Beijing. The General is in Delhi to manufacture a counterweight. India's problem is that its two real prizes both sit in rebel hands, not the junta's. The Kaladan corridor's final stretch runs through territory held by the Arakan Army, and the rare-earth deposits India covets lie in the same contested northern frontier. New Delhi has already begun courting those rebels directly. Min Aung Hlaing offers legitimacy; the rebels hold the ground. India is courting both.
anchor: Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing met Prime Minister

title: Pest problem
text:
Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the viral "Cockroach Janta Party" (CJP), announced he will return to India on June 6 to lead an offline protest demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The infestation: The CJP was born by accident last Friday after Chief Justice Surya Kant compared unemployed youth to "cockroaches attacking the system." Within five days, the movement’s Instagram following hit 18 million – double that of the ruling BJP (we covered it here).

The protest follows a catastrophic run for India’s testing agencies:

- NEET-UG: Cancelled after a nationwide paper leak; 2.2 million students affected.
- CBSE: Result delays and a portal mix-up where students were served the wrong answer sheets; 1.7 million students affected.
- SSC-GD: Canceled shifts across Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, including in Kanpur after authorities issued 819 admit cards for a 399-seat center.
- CUET: Delayed by technical glitches, affecting another 1.6 million candidates.

Accountability deficit: Dipke claims over 10 million students are victims of these systemic failures. "If Pradhan fails to resign, it would imply there is no accountability left in India," Dipke stated, citing 800,000 signatures on his petition.
sound_smarter: The CJP could become a nightmare for the government because it lacks a traditional political body that would allow for negotiation and assimilation. By leaning into an insult, the CJP has become a non-partisan rallying point for Indian youths to protest systemic incompetence without the baggage of joining an opposition party they likely already distrust.
