title: Priced out of the past
text:
India is replacing its 15-year-old wholesale price yardstick. On June 15, the government will release a new Wholesale Price Index (WPI) series with a 2022–23 base year, alongside a new suite of Producer Price Indices (PPIs) covering outputs, inputs, and seven service sectors including banking, telecom, and aviation.

Closing the gap: The US, EU, and Japan abandoned WPI-style indices for PPIs years ago. PPIs are also the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) preferred standard. The old WPI gets a five-year sunset before it's discontinued entirely.

What shifts: The tracked basket grows from 697 to 957 items. Solar, wind, and nuclear power enter the energy group for the first time. Crude petroleum and gas migrate from "Primary Articles" to "Fuel and Power." Weights now reflect domestic production rather than net trade, giving a more accurate picture of what India actually makes.
sound_smarter: The methodology overhaul is largely welcome, but the five-year WPI sunset is the practical risk hiding in plain sight. Any long-dated contract with price escalation clauses referencing WPI needs a relook, starting now.
anchor: India is replacing its 15-year-old wholesale price yardstick.

title: Slick diplomacy
text:
Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez arrives in India today for a five-day visit, just as New Delhi cements its position as the world’s second-largest buyer of Venezuelan crude.

The agenda: Rodriguez will meet PM Modi in Delhi before heading to Mumbai to huddle with energy industry leaders. Discussions cover the "full spectrum" of ties, from pharma to renewables, though oil remains the undisputed priority.

Supply crunch: The West Asia crisis has blocked 40% of India’s usual crude imports, and Caracas offers a vital, albeit distant, lifeline. In May, India gobbled up 427,000 barrels per day, second only to the US.

The Trump factor: India halted Venezuelan purchases last year after Washington imposed a 25% tariff on countries buying Venezuelan crude. Imports resumed in February after Washington eased sanctions following the capture of Nicolás Maduro. Under the current arrangement, the US Treasury controls the proceeds and sets commercial terms.
sound_smarter: Ramping up Venezuelan imports allows India to stabilise its inflation-hit energy supplies while aligning with the Trump administration’s broader push to revive Venezuela’s oil production. New Delhi is certain to use this alignment as a chip in its ongoing trade negotiations with Washington.
anchor: Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez arrives in India

title: Keeping the wings on
text:
New Delhi approved a 100 billion rupee (USD 1.05 billion) jet fuel stabilization fund on Wednesday, a cushion for airlines battered by soaring costs from the ongoing West Asia conflict.

The mechanism: The government will provide interest-free advances to oil marketing companies (OMCs). These funds cover under-recoveries – the gap between expensive global market rates and the capped prices charged to carriers.

The fine print: This isn't a permanent subsidy. The support lasts for 36 months or until the cash is recovered. When international prices eventually drop, OMCs must pay the differential back into the Consolidated Fund of India until the advance is settled.

Operational strain: Jet fuel accounts for up to 40% of airline operating costs. Major players like Air India and IndiGo have already slashed frequencies as West Asian airspace closures force longer routes and higher fuel burn (we covered it here).

Official line: The government claims the move will "protect and sustain domestic and international air connectivity" during the volatility.
sound_smarter: While this provides immediate liquidity to OMCs, the state is deferring the losses instead of absorbing it. Although fuel prices are impacting domestic routes, the long-term trajectory of India’s domestic aviation industry to increase regional connectivity remains unchanged, though prolonged cost pressure on carriers may reduce demand for slots in newly opened airports in the short-term.

title: Forced into a corner
text:
The United States Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed an additional 12.5% tariff on Indian imports, naming India among 60 economies it says have failed to curb goods made with forced labour. The proposal landed mid-visit, as a US delegation met in New Delhi to finalise the interim trade agreement struck in February, which we covered here.

The charge: A USTR report found India had failed to impose and enforce a ban on imports made with forced labour, calling its policies unreasonable and a burden on US commerce. Washington's concern is with what India lets in rather than what it ships out: it says forced-labour goods, often Chinese inputs, pass unchecked into India and then move through its supply chains to the US. The report singles out cotton from China’s Xinjiang region, which the US already bars under its Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA).

Delhi's response: The Commerce Ministry stressed the tariffs are not final, with public comments due by 6 July and a hearing on 7 July.
sound_smarter: Washington opened a second front precisely as both sides sat down in New Delhi, building leverage for the bigger trade deal it actually seeks. The finding rests on shaky ground, since it penalises India's import screening rather than anything in its exports, and Delhi will push hard to keep Section 301 and the bilateral negotiation on separate tracks.

title: A massive fire at an illegal bed and
text: A massive fire at an illegal bed and breakfast in South Delhi’s Malviya Nagar killed 21 people on Wednesday, including 12 foreign medical tourists. The establishment lacked a fire safety certificate and operated 26 rooms despite a legal limit of six, leading to the arrest of the owner for culpable homicide. title: Apple has agreed to hand over its India
text: Apple has agreed to hand over its India financials to the Competition Commission of India (CCI), ending a months-long standoff and moving a long-stalled antitrust case toward a penalty ruling. A 2024 CCI investigation found Apple had abused its dominant position in the iPhone apps market, a finding Apple denies. The company had withheld financials and taken the regulator to court, accusing it of judicial overreach. At a 21 May hearing, Apple's lawyer secured a final extension to file India-specific figures by 25 June, while the Delhi High Court has barred the CCI from issuing a ruling before 15 July. The dispute centres on India's updated competition law, which lets the CCI calculate fines on global rather than Indian turnover.

title: Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Rabi Lamichhane, founder
text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Rabi Lamichhane, founder of Nepal's ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) on Wednesday. The RSP had swept March elections in a landslide, the first since last year's GenZ uprising. Modi called Nepal a priority partner under India's Neighbourhood First policy, and the visit is a move to signal continuity in relations between the two countries.

title: Crude calculations in Caracas
text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez met on Thursday to secure a long-term energy lifeline amidst ongoing West Asia chaos.

The backdrop: Rodríguez is running Venezuela after US troops captured Nicolas Maduro in January. She lands in New Delhi as Venezuela becomes India's third-largest oil supplier, filling the void left by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Perfect complementarity: India wants crude while Venezuela has the world’s largest proven reserves. New Delhi is aggressively chasing Venezuelan oil for its long-term energy security, spanning both upstream extraction and downstream refining.

Little hiccup: The Indian side raised the issue of a government-owned oil and gas explorer struggling to repatriate over USD 500 million in frozen dividends after investing in two oil exploration projects in Venezuela.

Beyond oil: The duo discussed low-cost Indian generic drugs and joint exploration of Venezuelan gold, diamonds, and critical minerals. Rodríguez will cap her trip by visiting Reliance Industries’ Jamnagar refinery, the top buyer of Venezuela’s dense crude.
sound_smarter: India needs Venezuela for its oil but Venezuela also desperately needs India as a customer. Venezuelan crude is dense and contains high levels of sulphur, meaning only select specialised refineries worldwide can process it. India is one of the few buyers equipped to take in discounted Venezuelan oil, process it efficiently, and still make a profit. That makes trade relations with India critical for rebuilding Venezuela and gives India leverage in subsequent investment negotiations.
anchor: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Venezuela’s acting President

title: Common ore, uncommon delays
text:
India and the UK launched a critical minerals intelligence platform on Thursday and used the occasion to paper over a trade deal running behind schedule.

What launched: The Critical Minerals Global Supply Chain Observatory (GSCO) is a joint initiative of IIT (ISM) Dhanbad, TEXMiN, and the University of Cambridge. The Observatory went live in New Delhi, co-inaugurated by the Minister of Coal and Mines G Kishan Reddy and UK Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper.

What does it observe: The platform monitors global critical mineral supply chains, flags supply risks, and generates market intelligence for policymakers and industry. First announced at the India–UK PM bilateral in October 2025, it was formalised by the Research Collaboration Agreement in March 2026.

The awkward backdrop: The India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), signed in July 2025, is stalling. Two UK measures are the problem: steel import quotas tightening by 60% from July 1, and a Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism arriving in 2027. India has signalled it may revisit Scotch whisky tariff concessions if those proceed. Speaking after returning from talks in Delhi on Wednesday, UK Trade Minister Peter Kyle said London has no intention of reopening the deal, though he acknowledged implementation may slip beyond earlier expectations.
sound_smarter: For India, supply-chain intelligence on critical minerals matters more than the FTA's timeline, since it feeds the same rare-earth diversification push driving its bilateral mineral deals elsewhere. The deal can slip without stalling the strategic agenda underneath it.

title: Deadly hospital fire and water contamination expose civic safety gaps
text: Two civic safety failures struck within a day, days after a fire killed 21 at an illegal South Delhi bed and breakfast (we covered it here). On Thursday, a fire broke out in the intensive care unit (ICU) of the private Prasad Hospital in Muzaffarpur, Bihar, killing at least five people and forcing the rescue of more than twenty patients, with a short circuit suspected as the cause. Separately, in Ahmedabad, around fifty residents of the Ghatlodia area, part of Union Home Minister Amit Shah's Lok Sabha constituency, fell ill with diarrhoea and vomiting after drainage water entered a drinking water pipeline during repair work, leaving seven still hospitalised.

title: Boomerang diplomacy
text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin warned the United States that sanctioning India would backfire. He then used the same breath to pitch a fighter jet.

What was said: Speaking at the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum last Friday, Putin declared that any attempt to pressure India through sanctions would "boomerang immediately" under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership. The remarks were a direct response to questions about the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA), the United States law penalising significant transactions with Russia, and whether India risked exposure by procuring the Su-57 stealth fighter or S-500 air defence system.

The personal touch: Putin invoked Modi's pre-2014 US visa ban as evidence of hardened resolve. "I know PM Modi will never forget about it," he said.

The sales pitch: Russia is ready to sell the Su-57, which Putin called "probably the most modern aircraft in the world." A joint development programme was proposed earlier but never materialised.

The backdrop: Last week, US trade officials were in New Delhi negotiating the first tranche of a bilateral trade deal, with Commerce Minister Goyal signalling a mid-July close. The 50% US tariff on Indian goods, partly a penalty for Indian purchases of Russian oil, is the central grievance New Delhi wants resolved. Putin's speech landed squarely in the middle of those talks.
sound_smarter: CAATSA is losing its teeth. India bought the S-400, kept buying Russian oil, and faced no sanctions. Every time Washington blinks, the credibility cost compounds and Moscow is keeping score.
anchor: Russian President Vladimir Putin warned the United States

title: Sprinting for the close
text:
India closed FY2025–26 with a sprint. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 7.8% year-on-year in the January–March quarter, pushing full-year growth to 7.7%, ahead of most forecasts.

What drove it: Private investment led the charge, up 10.8%, the fastest pace in roughly three years. Construction picked up to 8.4% on the back of infrastructure spending and real-estate activity. Agriculture recovered to 3.6% growth, supporting rural incomes. Government expenditure contributed a steady 4.9%.

The caveat: These are the cleanest numbers India will post for a while. Inflation, elevated oil prices, geopolitical friction, and monsoon risk all cloud the FY2026–27 outlook. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sees growth slowing to 6.6% this fiscal year. Household consumption, the economy's broadest engine, has yet to fully fire.
sound_smarter: 7.8% is a strong number, but read it carefully. Private investment and construction are doing the heavy lifting, while consumption is still punching below its weight. India entered the new fiscal year with real momentum, but sustaining near-8% growth means converting investment into jobs and wages, and hoping the monsoon cooperates.

title: Zero tax, please stay
text:
The Ministry of Finance exempted Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) from income and capital gains taxes on Government Securities (G-Secs) on Friday to halt capital flight and shore up a sliding rupee.

The bond bonanza: The government expanded its Fully Accessible Route (FAR) – which allows investment without caps for non-resident investors – to include 15-, 30-, and 40-year bonds alongside Sovereign Green Bonds. It also merged the "general" and "long-term" investment categories, stripping away concentration limits.

Tax holiday: FPIs previously faced 12.5% long-term capital gains tax on listed ​shares and bonds held for more than ​12 months, ⁠and a 20% withholding tax on interest earned from government bonds. This complete waiver aims to align India with competing global bond markets.

The panic button: Foreign investors have dumped USD 27.6 billion in Indian equities this year, outpacing 2025's total outflows. Paired with high oil prices, this exodus has hammered the rupee.
sound_smarter: The move joins New Delhi’s growing defences of the rupee (we covered some moves here and here). Instead of hiking interest rates and choking domestic growth like its peers, New Delhi is trying to bribe foreign capital back and limit outflows by replacing volatile, flighty equity capital with sticky, passive institutional debt. It will cushion the currency against high oil prices but it avoids the real conversation about why foreign investors are dumping Indian equities: they still trade at a premium in comparison to their Asian peers.
anchor: The Ministry of Finance exempted Foreign Portfolio Investors

title: Balen of power
text:
Nepal agrees to rule out foreign mediators to resolve the border dispute. Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal said on Sunday that Nepal wants to resolve its border dispute with India through bilateral mechanisms alone, the final step in a week-long retreat from Prime Minister Balen Shah's suggestion in parliament that China and the United Kingdom (UK) be brought in.

The disputed ground: India and Nepal contest the Kalapani, Limpiyadhura, and Lipulekh region, a stretch of high-altitude territory at the trijunction with China. New Delhi maintains the area belongs to the state of Uttarakhand. The row hardened in 2020, when a previous Nepali government published a revised political map claiming the territories after India opened a road through Lipulekh.

How it started: On 31 May, in his first parliamentary address, Shah said Kathmandu had raised the border issue with China and the UK, the latter over its colonial-era role in the region. Within hours, Nepal's Foreign Ministry recast the remarks as a narrow technical point about cross-border occupation.

Delhi's line: On 3 June, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said established bilateral mechanisms cover all boundary matters and there is no role for any third party. Khanal later clarified that the UK reference concerned only historical documents held in British libraries and museums.

The climbdown: Speaking after meeting External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Saturday, Khanal said no boundary is too complex to settle when both sides meet with an open heart, a rational mind, and mutual respect. He said Nepal refuses to view India through a hyper-sensitive lens and wants a single agenda of economic transformation.
sound_smarter: A four-year-old party with a landslide mandate is learning that campaign-trail nationalism collides with the economics of a landlocked country dependent on Indian trade and transit. The walk-back was visible in its choreography: a same-day ministry clarification, a RSP’s founder meeting Modi in Delhi (which we covered here), and now the foreign minister closing ranks behind Jaishankar.

title: Hooked in
text:
India will keep exporting animal-origin food to the European Union past a September deadline. New Delhi has been added to the EU's updated authorised-exporter list for aquaculture, honey, eggs, and animal casings, securing market access under tightened rules.

Why September mattered: The EU tightened Regulation (EU) 2021/405 over Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) concerns, raising the bar for all animal-origin imports. Countries left off the revised list lose access. India's fish and fishery exports to the EU alone are worth USD 1.59 billion.

How the pass was earned: The Department of Commerce and Export Inspection Council (EIC) upgraded India's inspection, testing, and certification systems to satisfy Brussels' new standards. The Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA) will continue working with EU-approved establishments on compliance.
sound_smarter: The mechanism matters more than the reprieve. Upgrading official control systems to meet EU AMR standards lifts every food and agri exporter who clears Brussels' bar, making them credible suppliers to any market that mirrors EU biosafety expectations. The harder work is extending that compliance from the large EU-approved processors down to the thousands of smaller suppliers that feed the export chain.

title: No bloc, no opposition
text:
The opposition INDIA bloc gathered in New Delhi on Monday for its first formal meeting since June 2024, convening to repair an alliance fractured by a brutal round of May assembly elections.

Who showed up: Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, Trinamool Congress (TMC) chief Mamata Banerjee, Samajwadi Party's Akhilesh Yadav, and Shiv Sena (UBT)'s Uddhav Thackeray were in attendance. The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) boycotted over Congress abandoning their Tamil Nadu partnership to back actor-politician Vijay's Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK). The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) stayed away, having quit the bloc after the 2024 general election.

Power reshuffle: Banerjee lost not only her state in May but her own constituency, and is now battling a revolt at home where two-thirds of TMC legislators have broken with her leadership. Congress, buoyed by its Kerala win and holding its ground in Karnataka bypolls, now carries more political weight within the bloc than it did a year ago.

The empty chair: The same week, the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) gathered nearly 800,000 signatures demanding Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resign over examination irregularities. The organisation staged a protest in New Delhi on Saturday to press its demands.
sound_smarter: The opposition's deepest problem is relevance, or the lack of it. Rahul Gandhi and Abhishek Banerjee attacked Pradhan over the very same exam chaos, yet the crowds and the signatures gathered behind a movement that cannot contest elections. When a satirical outfit out-organises the formal opposition on a grievance they share, the governing party can keep governing as if no opposition exists.
anchor: The opposition INDIA bloc gathered in New Delhi

title: Crude interception
text:
A US missile has disabled a tanker crewed entirely by Indians. On Monday, United States forces struck the Palau-flagged MT Marivex off Masirah, Oman. The 24-member crew of the ship, all Indian nationals, were rescued by the Royal Navy of Oman. No casualties have been reported. The ship remains anchored off the coast of Masirah.

The strike: US Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed that the vessel had been hit after the crew did not comply with US directions. The Marivex was sanctioned by the US Treasury in December 2025 over alleged involvement in transporting Iranian oil, and India's Coast Guard rescue centre in Mumbai, alerted by a crew member's relative, coordinated the evacuation with Oman within hours.

The blockade: Marivex was not an isolated target. CENTCOM says it was the seventh vessel disabled since blockade enforcement against Iran began on 13 April 2026. The operation polices the waters around the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, through which a large share of the world's seaborne crude passes.

India's careful words: New Delhi has not named the United States as responsible. The official press release made no mention of the US, framing the episode instead around international maritime cooperation and the Indian Coast Guard's commitment to safeguarding Indian seafarers. Answering questions at his press briefing, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal also declined to name Washington, saying: "The ship MT Marivex was disabled off the coast of Oman. We have learned that it is a Palau-flagged vessel. We also understand there was some exchange of communication between the ship and the US Navy before the incident." India thanked Oman warmly for the rescue and said nothing critical of Washington.
sound_smarter: CENTCOM claimed the strike openly, while India described the same event in the passive voice and reserved its gratitude for Oman. That restraint is a choice. India buys discounted Iranian-origin crude and is deepening defence and technology ties with the United States at the same time, the same Hormuz tightrope we walked through in March. Naming the US as the party that fired on a ship full of Indian sailors would force a public position India has spent the entire crisis avoiding.
anchor: A US missile has disabled a tanker crewed

title: Still at the helm
text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi has set a new record. On 10 June 2026, Modi completed 4,399 consecutive days in office to become India's longest continuously serving elected Prime Minister.

The fine print: Jawaharlal Nehru remains India's longest-serving Prime Minister by total tenure, having governed from 1947 until his death in 1964. The record Modi has broken counts continuous days as an elected leader, measured from the first general election. Modi has held office without interruption since 26 May 2014, winning three consecutive mandates in 2014, 2019, and 2024.

The framing: The occasion is being celebrated under the banner "12 Years of Seva," with Modi stating that his government's tenure has been dedicated to trust, development, and public welfare.

The congrats: Three Global South leaders sent congratulations. President Anura Kumara Dissanayake of Sri Lanka called the milestone a testament to the trust placed in Modi's leadership. Prime Minister James Marape of Papua New Guinea credited him with lifting over 200 million people out of poverty. Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar of Trinidad and Tobago said India had become a leading global voice under him.
sound_smarter: The choice of who congratulated Modi is the message. All three congratulations came from the Global South, the constituency India has worked to lead as an alternative pole to both Beijing and the West. The milestone itself rests on continuity, the one asset coalition-era India lacked and the quality that lets a government commit to decade-long bets on infrastructure and digital public goods. That same continuity now defines the central question of a fourth term: a leader who has faced no electoral interruption in twelve years has also had no external check to force course correction.

title: Farewell MGNREGA, hello fiscal discipline
text:
Rural Development Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan held a high-level meeting on Tuesday to prepare states for the 1 July launch of the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB–G RAM G), which officially replaces India's historic Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) scheme.

The upgrade: The new law increases guaranteed annual wage employment from 100 to 125 days per rural household for unskilled manual labour. It also strengthens the unemployment allowance owed when no work is provided and adds compensation for delayed wages.

The catch: Unlike MGNREGA, which was demand-driven with the Centre funding any surge in work, the new model sets a normative allocation determined by the Centre. States must now bear at least 40% of the cost, compared to the previous model where New Delhi footed the entire wage bill. Expenditure beyond sanctioned limits falls entirely on state budgets.

Smoothing transitions: Anticipating friction, Chouhan told state ministers via video conference that "not a single worker should remain without work even for a day," demanding zero disruption in wage payments or statutory rights.
sound_smarter: By capping central funds and forcing a 60:40 cost-sharing model, New Delhi is passing the fiscal buck to the states. Localised planning and funding limits may reduce waste, but stripping the open-ended, demand-driven safety net means states will struggle to protect vulnerable citizens during droughts or economic shocks.

title: Piercing the winter wall
text:
Union Minister Nitin Gadkari witnessed the main tunnel breakthrough at the Zojila Tunnel Project on Monday, marking a massive milestone for India’s Himalayan infrastructure.

The project: The 13.15-km, INR 6,800-crore (USD 715 million) bi-directional tunnel connects Baltal and Minamarg on National Highway-1. Sitting above 2,900 meters, it is scheduled to open in 2028.

Weatherproofing defense: The Zojila Pass currently shuts for weeks every winter – including 73 days in 2026 – cutting off Ladakh. The tunnel ensures year-round civilian and military access to the strategic frontier.

Kargil lessons: This highway is the primary supply route for troops along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and the Siachen Glacier. During the 1999 Kargil war, Pakistan targeted this exact route to choke Indian logistics.

The broader frontier: This is one of 31 border tunnels under construction in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. The infrastructure push accelerated after the 2020 Galwan clash to match rapid Chinese troop mobilization.
sound_smarter: While the tunnel eliminates a massive winter blind spot for New Delhi, China still holds the upper hand in overall logistics and transport capacity along the border, which is further complicated by the rugged and steep terrain on the Indian side of the LAC.
anchor: Union Minister Nitin Gadkari witnessed the main tunnel

title: Modi condemns strikes on Kuwait in call with Emir
text: Modi telephoned Kuwait's ruler after Iranian strikes hit the Gulf state. On 9 June, Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with the Emir of Kuwait, His Highness Sheikh Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al Sabah, condemning attacks on Kuwait's sovereignty and territorial integrity and repeating India's call for de-escalation, dialogue, and diplomacy. title: Jaishankar and Modi to court Europe on back-to-back trips
text: India is courting Europe across back-to-back trips. External Affairs Minister Jaishankar travels to Bulgaria on 10 June and Finland on 11 June, the latter for the 14th Kultaranta Talks, Helsinki's flagship foreign-policy forum. Days later, Prime Minister Narendra Modi begins a 13 to 18 June visit to France and Slovakia. In France, he will hold a bilateral meeting with President Emmanuel Macron and launch the "Bharat Innovates" event in Nice, before joining the G7 Summit at Évian-les-Bains on 16 to 17 June as an invited partner. The Slovakia leg marks the first visit by an Indian Prime Minister to the country since its 1993 independence.

title: Capacity for disagreement
text:
India pushed back on Washington yesterday, rejecting United States Trade Representative (USTR) allegations that its textile and steel sectors carry structural excess capacity. Additional Trade Secretary Amitabh Kumar was blunt, stating "Overcapacity is a country's perspective. We don't think we have overcapacity in anything."

The US charge: In March 2026, the USTR opened Section 301 investigations into 16 economies over alleged manufacturing overcapacity, India among them. Washington cites India's USD 42 billion goods trade surplus from 2025 and flags sectors from textiles and steel to solar modules and petrochemicals. A separate tariff targeting alleged textile overcapacity is also under consideration, on top of the 12.5% forced-labour tariff Washington proposed last week, which we covered here.

India's rebuttal: Delhi's argument is methodological. Output must be measured against population, domestic demand, and development needs, not absolute volumes. The Cotton Textiles Export Promotion Council (TEXPROCIL) told the USTR that over 80% of India's cotton textile production is consumed at home, and that output across cotton, yarn, and fabric segments is flat or declining, the opposite of the expansion an overcapacity claim implies. India's formal submission called Washington's notice short on evidence and shorter on logic.

The bind: Kumar acknowledged the probe targets a "particular country", meaning China, while serving broader aims. India is the collateral. Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal had earlier stated that a bilateral trade deal tranche could close by mid-July.
sound_smarter: India's per-capita defence is economically sound but legally weak. Trade disputes are adjudicated on volumes, price effects, and market share, not on a country's development stage. The deeper danger is positional. Washington is now running three pressure tracks against India at once – overcapacity, forced labour, and the broader Section 301 review, and each one folds India into an enforcement architecture built for China. That is the precise outcome Delhi has spent two years trying to avoid, selling itself to Washington as the alternative to Beijing rather than a smaller version of it.

title: Cockroach Janta Party threatens indefinite sit-in over exam crisis
text: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) will launch an indefinite peaceful sit-in at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi from June 20 unless Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns. The group plans a touring agitation first, starting in Pune on June 11 and moving through Lucknow, Amritsar, Bengaluru, Jaipur, and Hyderabad, with founder Abhijeet Dipke saying activist Sonam Wangchuk would join the Pune leg. The CJP frames the exam irregularities as a national accountability failure affecting millions of families, and has vowed to continue until Pradhan steps down. title: The wrong flag
text:
The US military has killed three Indian sailors in a strike on a tanker off Oman, the first deaths since Washington began enforcing its blockade of Iranian ports in April. The Palau-flagged MT Settebello was hit on 10 June off Oman’s coast, with 24 Indian crew aboard, of whom 21 were rescued.

The strikes: US Central Command (CENTCOM) said one of its aircraft fired precision munitions into the Settebello's engine room after the crew repeatedly failed to follow directions. It was the second of three vessels with Indian crews struck in the Gulf of Oman within a week. On 8 June, US forces hit the Palau-flagged tanker Marivex, whose 24 Indian crew were rescued by the Omani military before the ship sank (we covered it here). On 11 June, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged MT Jalveer came under attack, with all 20 crew evacuated safely by the Royal Navy of Oman. All three ships were foreign-flagged but crewed mainly by Indians.

The blockade: Washington sealed off Iran's ports on 13 April after Tehran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas passes. CENTCOM says it has disabled eight vessels and redirected 134 others since the blockade began.

Delhi's response: India lodged a strong protest, summoning the US chargé d'affaires to convey its concerns over the attacks. Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the targeting of commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure in the region must end. The exposure is large: the shipping ministry counts 562 Indian seafarers on Indian-flagged vessels alone, including 233 in the Gulf of Oman, with more than 18,000 across the wider Gulf, and the Directorate General of Shipping (DGS) has advised those on both Indian and foreign-flagged vessels in conflict-affected waters to exercise the highest caution.

The warhead: The strain reached Indian shores on 11 June. The Indian Navy recovered an unexploded missile warhead from the crude oil tanker MT Olympic Life off Kochi, a projectile that had pierced the Marshall Islands-flagged vessel's hull off Oman on 26 May and lodged inside a fuel tank. An Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team isolated the detonation mechanism and extracted it for examination.
sound_smarter: Indians crew a large share of the world's commercial shipping, which means a US campaign aimed at Iranian oil flows kills Indian nationals regardless of intent, and Delhi absorbs the casualties of a war it is not party to. India's protest stops at summoning a diplomat because its options are thin: it will not break with Washington over crews on foreign-flagged ships, and it cannot police the Strait of Hormuz itself.
anchor: The US military has killed three Indian sailors

title: Payment rails over mountain trails
text:
India and Nepal have connected their payment systems. On 6 June, the two countries launched a peer-to-peer cross-border remittance link connecting India's UPI and Nepal's National Payments Interface (NPI), allowing users to send money instantly across the border through mobile apps and digital wallets.

How it works: The integration was built by NPCI International Payments Limited and Nepal Clearing House Limited. Transfers move directly between the two national payment systems without correspondent banks or separate foreign exchange processes, enabling real-time settlement.

Who benefits: The main beneficiaries are Indian tourists and Nepali workers sending money home. Users no longer need to carry cash or rely on traditional remittance channels. Nepali merchants also gain easier access to India's vast digital payments ecosystem.

More than QR codes: UPI is already accepted in nine countries, including Singapore, United Arab Emirates, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Bhutan, Qatar, Sri Lanka and Cambodia. Most of those arrangements centre on merchant payments through QR codes. This new linkage goes further, enabling full person-to-person remittances between the two national systems.
sound_smarter: UPI's international expansion is as much geopolitical as technological. Every country connected to India's payment rails becomes more tightly integrated with New Delhi's financial ecosystem. In Nepal, where China has steadily expanded its economic footprint, embedding UPI into daily remittance flows is a subtle but durable strategic play. Infrastructure can be rebuilt. Payment habits, once entrenched, are much harder to replace.
anchor: India and Nepal have connected their payment systems.

title: Goyal heads to Switzerland to push EFTA pact rollout
text: Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal will visit Berne, Switzerland, on 12 June 2026 to meet Swiss government officials and pharmaceutical industry leaders, with talks focused on implementing the India-European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA). The pact, which covers Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein, took effect in October 2025 and is the first Indian trade agreement to carry a binding investment target, committing the EFTA bloc to USD 100 billion in investment and one million direct jobs over 15 years. The trip follows Modi's Nordic summit in Oslo last month, where Norway and Iceland, the two EFTA members under TEPA, featured in his bilaterals (we covered it here).Goyal is scheduled to meet State Secretary for Economic Affairs Helene Budliger Artieda and Federal President Guy Parmelin, and will court Swiss companies and investors in Zurich on the sidelines.

title: Nice work if you can get it
text:
India and France pulled their partnership a notch tighter in Nice on Saturday, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Emmanuel Macron signing off on 13 outcomes spanning defence, critical minerals, space, and trade.

The headline: This was the first Modi-Macron meeting since the two countries elevated their relationship to a Special Global Strategic Partnership earlier this year (we covered it here). The leaders agreed to a High-level Mechanism to double bilateral trade within five years and pushed for early implementation of the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (we covered it here).

The hard deliverables: A new Economic Security Dialogue commits both sides to supply-chain resilience, with an explicit focus on critical minerals. A General Security Agreement on the exchange and protection of classified information deepens the defence relationship, which the leaders agreed to push further into co-design, co-development, and co-production of platforms and advanced technologies.

The longer game: India's new SHANTI Act opens civil nuclear cooperation, including small and advanced modular reactors. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and France's Centre National d'Études Spatiales signed a letter of intent on human spaceflight, and the two sides issued a declaration of intent on high-speed rail in India. On the sidelines, the leaders jointly inaugurated Bharat Innovates, India's first deep-tech showcase held abroad, putting 120 start-ups in front of more than 350 global investors.
sound_smarter: As India hunts alternatives to Chinese supply of critical minerals, Paris offers both processing technology and African mining access without the strings the United States attaches. The visit also lands days before Modi meets Donald Trump at the G7 in Evian, a sequence that lets New Delhi bank a frictionless European win before sitting down with a far less predictable American counterpart.
anchor: India and France pulled their partnership a notch

title: Grounded ambitions
text:
One year after Air India Flight AI-171, the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau's (AAIB) interim report has still not reached a conclusion on what caused the crash that left 260 people dead. The flight, a Boeing 787-8 operating from Ahmedabad to London, crashed shortly after take-off on June 12, 2025.

The non-answer: The AAIB marked the anniversary with an interim statement confirming the probe has reached its final integrated analysis, while declining to name a cause, citing pending international reviews and consultations. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) rules require an interim statement when no final report lands within twelve months.

What we do know: The preliminary report from July 2025 had found both engine fuel control switches were moved from RUN to CUTOFF one second apart, soon after take-off. The cockpit voice recording captured one pilot asking the other why he cut off the fuel, and the other denying it. The switches were flipped back, but the engines could not recover. A year later, whether that sequence was deliberate, accidental, or a fault remains undetermined.

The cost of silence: Air India is now in talks with Airbus and Boeing to defer hundreds of jet deliveries from its near-500 aircraft orderbook. That book was built on the 2023 deal for 470 jets, the largest commercial aircraft order ever placed at the time, meant to anchor the carrier's revival under Tata Group. The carrier cited roughly USD 3 billion in annual losses, the Iran conflict, Pakistan's airspace ban, record fuel prices, and a crisis of confidence traced directly to the crash. The airline is also without a permanent leadership, with chief executive Campbell Wilson having resigned earlier this year and no successor yet named, which we covered here.
sound_smarter: The deeper strain is structural. India recently opened two greenfield mega-airports, Navi Mumbai in December and Noida in March, on a bet that it could become the connecting hub between Europe and Southeast Asia. However, the two major Indian carriers: IndiGo and Air India, are pulling back, with both airlines trimming international flights and suspending European and Asian routes. The terminals are being built faster than the carriers can fill them, and a year of fuel shocks, airspace closures, and unresolved crash questions has stalled India's hub ambitions for now.

issue_title: Nice work if you can get it
title: Hotter, but under the bar
text:
India’s retail inflation crept up to 3.93% in May, hitting its highest level under the newly revamped consumer price index series.

The drivers: State-owned oil firms hiked fuel prices four times in May, pushing transport inflation to 1.75%. Food inflation also accelerated to 4.78% from April's 4.20%.

The geopolitical tax: The escalation of the US-Iran conflict has battered the rupee, which bottomed at a record 96.96 against the US dollar on May 20. A weaker currency is actively importing inflation into the economy, forcing the government and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to roll out dollar-attracting liquidity measures, including exempting foreign portfolio investors from income and capital gains tax on government securities (we covered it here).

What to watch: A developing El Niño threatens the crucial June–September monsoon season, which provides 70% of India's annual rain. The government barred retail diesel sales for commercial buyers after trucking companies flooded retail stations to avoid higher bulk-supply prices, causing shortages in some areas.
sound_smarter: While this reading sits just below the RBI's 4% target, West Asian energy shocks and a weak monsoon could easily breach the central bank's ceiling by autumn. Nevertheless, the RBI is expected to hold interest rates steady, as officials believe further hikes would do little to support the rupee while actively hurting economic growth.

issue_title: Nice work if you can get it
title: Rockets and rhetoric
text:
India wants its missile shield to move faster. On June 12, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh inaugurated a new Advanced Weapon System Complex at the Defence Research and Development Laboratory (DRDL) in Hyderabad, part of the Defence Research and Development Organisation's (DRDO) Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Missile Complex.

Operation Sindoor effect: Singh explicitly linked the inauguration to the performance of Indian missile systems during Operation Sindoor. Citing platforms such as Akash and BrahMos, he argued that India has proven its ability to compete in the global defence technology ecosystem.

The shield plan: The minister used the event to reaffirm Mission Sudarshan Chakra, a multi-layered missile defence programme first announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Independence Day 2025. The proposed three-tier architecture aims to protect military facilities, critical infrastructure, and civilian population centres simultaneously.

Beyond the ribbon-cutting: Singh's broader message was that resilience and deterrence now define India's security doctrine in an era of hypersonic weapons, AI-enabled warfare, and shifting alliances. He also stressed that production capacity matters as much as R&D, calling for tighter coordination between DRDO, the armed forces, public sector firms, private industry, start-ups, and academia.

Aatmanirbhar, weaponised: Singh framed defence indigenisation as a strategic necessity rather than a political slogan, pointing to more than a decade of investment in domestic defence innovation and manufacturing.
sound_smarter: Singh's repeated focus on production suggests New Delhi increasingly sees manufacturing bottlenecks, not research gaps, as the main obstacle to military self-reliance. If Mission Sudarshan Chakra can shorten the journey from laboratory to deployment, it could mark a genuine shift in India's defence ecosystem. If not, it risks joining the long queue of ambitious programmes that remain permanently under development.
anchor: India wants its missile shield to move faster.

issue_title: Nice work if you can get it
title: IAF transport crash kills five in Assam
text: Five Indian Air Force (IAF) personnel were killed on Saturday when an An-32 transport aircraft crashed during a routine sortie near Jorhat in Assam. The aircraft went down while attempting to land at the Rowriah Air Force Station. The IAF confirmed the deaths of all five personnel on board, expressed condolences to their families, and said crash site management and preliminary inquiries were underway. A court of inquiry has been ordered to determine the cause of the accident.
anchor: IAF transport crash kills five in Assam

issue_title: Nice work if you can get it
title: US Navy rescues 14 Indian sailors off Oman
text: A United States Navy patrol aircraft helped rescue all 14 Indian crew of the Indian-flagged sailing vessel Virat 1 on Sunday, after the ship suffered engine failure and began sinking about 80 nautical miles off Oman's Ras Al Hadd. A US Navy P-8 Poseidon dropped a life raft and monitored the evacuation before the crew transferred to a passing merchant ship bound for Mumbai. The rescue involved no attack, the vessel simply lost power, but it came days after the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) protested US strikes on commercial ships carrying Indian seafarers in the same waters, a campaign that killed three Indian sailors aboard the Settebello last week.
anchor: US Navy rescues 14 Indian sailors off Oman

title: Racing the tariff clock
text:
The US is sending in its top trade negotiator. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will visit India on June 23–24 for talks with Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal aimed at closing an interim trade deal before a key tariff deadline.

Final stretch: Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said both sides will focus on putting the finishing touches on a framework agreement while continuing work on the broader Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA). The visit follows negotiations earlier this month covering goods trade, non-tariff barriers, customs cooperation, trade facilitation, and economic security.

The clock: The real deadline is July 24 when Washington's 150-day pause on higher reciprocal tariffs expires. Both governments want an interim deal in place before then. The draft framework also includes a reciprocal safeguard clause allowing either side to adjust tariffs if the other changes its commitments.

The trade-off: India has reportedly offered to eliminate or reduce tariffs on most US industrial goods and a broad range of agricultural products. Goyal said on June 5 that negotiators are narrowing the remaining gaps.

G7 waypoint: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump are expected to review progress during the G7 summit, but officials on both sides have signalled that negotiations will continue afterwards.
sound_smarter: Senior officials only get on planes when negotiators think a landing zone exists. The question is whether that landing zone includes agriculture. Every major India–US trade negotiation eventually runs into the same obstacle: Washington wants greater access for farm products, while Delhi sees farm tariffs as politically radioactive. What India concedes on agriculture over the next six weeks will tell you far more about the eventual deal than any headline tariff cuts on industrial goods.
anchor: The US is sending in its top trade

title: Selling more, spending more
text:
India's exports reached a record in May, but the import bill climbed faster. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry estimated total exports of merchandise and services at USD 81.96 billion for May 2026, up 15.83% on a year earlier, even as the combined trade deficit widened to USD 10.51 billion from USD 6.79 billion.

By the numbers: Merchandise exports rose to USD 45.20 billion, led by petroleum products (up 54.89%) and engineering goods (up 24.48%). Services exports added USD 36.76 billion. Imports outpaced both, climbing 19.23% to USD 92.47 billion.

Where the gap opens: The merchandise deficit alone reached USD 28.21 billion for the month. Russia, China, and the United States led the rise in import sources, while Singapore and several African markets drove export gains. The Centre had raised the effective gold and silver import duty to 15% from 6%, aimed at curbing dollar outflows on bullion, which we covered here.
sound_smarter: The record export figure is the wrong number to watch. India's external pressure now runs through two channels the government can only partly control: gold imports, where price rather than volume drives the bill, and electronics, where rising imports track the manufacturing base New Delhi is deliberately building. With crude above USD 100 and West Asia unsettled, the petroleum cushion that quietly held the FY26 deficit down has now flipped into a third source of strain.

title: Bratislava, and the art of the hedge
text:
Modi became the first Indian Prime Minister to visit Slovakia since the country's independence in 1993, using the trip to elevate bilateral ties to a Comprehensive Partnership. On Sunday, he held talks with Prime Minister Robert Fico, capping a state visit that produced eleven agreements and a host of new dialogue mechanisms.

What was signed: The two sides exchanged Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) on labour migration, digital technologies, higher education, audio-visual creation, and quantum communication, plus a Letter of Intent on defence cooperation. India will set up its first Indian Council for Cultural Relations (ICCR) Chair in Artificial Intelligence at the Technical University of Kosice.

The institutional scaffolding: Both leaders announced a Joint Working Group on Counter-Terrorism and a Consular Dialogue. Slovakia reaffirmed support for India's permanent United Nations Security Council (UNSC) seat and its bid to join the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG).

The EU angle: The leaders welcomed the India-European Union (EU) Free Trade Agreement concluded in January (we covered it here) and pressed for its early signing. Slovakia, with its automotive and advanced-manufacturing base, was framed as a Central European entry point for Indian industry.
sound_smarter: Fico is the EU's most openly pro-Moscow, pro-Beijing leader, and has built his foreign policy on hedging between West, Russia, and China. For New Delhi, which prizes strategic autonomy, courting Bratislava buys a sympathetic ear inside Brussels precisely when India wants the FTA ratified and its options kept open.

title: AI, space, and a dash of French connection
text:
India and France officially adopted the Innovation Roadmap 2030 on Monday, focused on technology sovereignty.

The focal point: "Trusted AI" is the star of the roadmap. The duo will collaborate on child safety online, risk-based AI governance, and privacy-preserving data frameworks. France is matching India’s Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) with its own health data platforms to facilitate secure, consent-based research sharing.

Boots on the ground: Paris is chasing an ambitious target to welcome 30,000 Indian students by 2030, backed by an expanded Mutual Recognition of Qualifications framework. On the industrial front, the deal sets up an aeronautical training campus in Kanpur and a bilateral startup corridor called the InnoXchange Bridge.

Space race: In September, the two will sync calendars, hosting back-to-back space summits in Bengaluru and Paris to align Earth observation and low-Earth orbit space station designs.

Upgraded ties: The two countries upgraded ties to a “Special Global Strategic Partnership” in February this year and launched the “India-France Year of Innovation 2026,” focusing on AI in health and digital science. (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Through mobility, industrial cooperation, and policy alignment, New Delhi and Paris are building a highly practical tech ecosystem independent of both Washington and Beijing – one designed to secure their strategic autonomy.
anchor: India and France officially adopted the Innovation Roadmap

title: Modi welcomes US-Iran understanding to end West Asia conflict
text: Modi welcomed the understanding reached between the United States and Iran to end the conflict in West Asia on Sunday, his first comment since the truce. In a post on X, he said: "I welcome the understanding reached between the United States and Iran on ending the conflict in West Asia, which has caused serious economic disruption across the world and led to loss of life in many countries." He added that India hopes implementation will restore regional stability and ensure freedom of navigation and commerce, and looked forward to a sustainable final agreement on remaining issues.
anchor: Modi welcomes US-Iran understanding to end West Asia conflict

title: ASI, Denmark to survey 1619 Danish shipwreck
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's Underwater Archaeology Wing and the National Museum of Denmark signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on Sunday to locate and document the Oresund, a Danish ship wrecked off Karaikal in Puducherry in 1619. The first Danish vessel known to have reached India, it sank shortly after arrival. The non-invasive survey marks the Wing's first international collaboration.
anchor: ASI, Denmark to survey 1619 Danish shipwreck

title: Credit where its due
text:
India and Japan formally adopted the Rules of Implementation for their Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM), a Japanese-run crediting scheme that pays for emission cuts abroad. The JCM will be the operational layer that turns last year's bilateral carbon market agreement into an investment instrument.

What the JCM does: Under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, Japan funds low-carbon projects in India. The resulting emission reductions are verified and converted into carbon credits known as Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs). Japan counts a share toward its own climate targets; India keeps the rest without it touching its own commitments.

What changed on June 8: The Memorandum of Cooperation signed in 2025 established intent. The Rules of Implementation add the mechanics, setting out project eligibility, verification methodology, a Joint Committee, registry systems, and anti-double-counting rules. The architecture is now live.

What flows through it: Japanese investment and technology into Indian renewables, industrial efficiency, clean mobility, and waste management. Japan needs high-integrity credits, India needs capital and technology, and the JCM converts that into a rulebook-backed flow.
sound_smarter: India is quietly building a bilateral carbon market architecture that positions it to become one of the largest Article 6.2 credit suppliers at exactly the moment the US has left the Paris Agreement and COP30 is about to stress-test whether the rulebook holds. The country that controls high-integrity carbon credit supply in a demand-constrained market holds real leverage, and the Union Cabinet has now authorised the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) to strike similar deals with other countries.

title: Rice and wheat stocks hit multi-year highs
text: Government rice reserves climbed 15% year-on-year to a record 68.43 million tonnes as of 1 June, while wheat stocks reached a five-year peak of 53.41 million tonnes, official data showed on Tuesday. Both figures far exceed federal targets, giving New Delhi room to sustain exports and tame any domestic price spikes through open-market sales later this year. India, which supplies around 40% of global rice exports, removed its last export curbs on the grain in March 2025. The cushion matters because the weather office has forecast below-average monsoon rainfall for 2026, which traders had feared could squeeze production.
anchor: Rice and wheat stocks hit multi-year highs

title: MeitY restricts Telegram ahead of NEET-UG re-examination
text: The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) temporarily blocked access to the Telegram messaging app on Tuesday ahead of the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test for Undergraduates (NEET-UG) re-examination on 21 June. The restriction runs until 22 June, with the platform's message-editing feature disabled in India until 30 June. The National Testing Agency (NTA), which administers the exam, said fraudsters had run Telegram channels demanding money from candidates and their families in exchange for fake re-examination papers. The re-examination stems from the exam-fraud crisis that spawned the Cockroach Janta Party, which we covered here.
anchor: MeitY restricts Telegram ahead of NEET-UG re-examination

title: Modi works UAE, UK, Canada at G7 outreach
text: Modi addressed the G7 outreach session in Evian, France, on rebuilding international solidarity, then held bilaterals with the UAE, the United Kingdom, and Canada. The meetings reaffirmed existing trade and defence tracks: early entry into force of the India-UK trade deal, launching India-Canada security-of-information talks, and BRICS Summit invitation to the UAE president.
anchor: Modi works UAE, UK, Canada at G7 outreach

title: No duty, more savings
text:
New Delhi and London announced on Wednesday that their hard-fought Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) and a companion social security agreement will take effect on July 15, 2026.

The big prize: The deal grants India zero-duty access on roughly 99% of its exports to the UK. High tariffs on Indian textiles (12%), leather (16%), and marine products (21.5%) will drop to absolute zero on day one.

White-collar windfall: The UK opened up 137 services sub-sectors, providing predictable mobility routes for IT workers and professionals. Crucially, the social security agreement exempts temporary Indian workers from paying double social security contributions for up to five years, saving 75,000 professionals from a bureaucratic tax trap.

Defensive shielding: India protected its sensitive agricultural sector, keeping dairy, grains, and oilseeds completely off the liberalization table. It also negotiated carved-out exemptions to protect 85% of its steel exports from the UK's upcoming steel import restrictions. The agreement previously stalled due to two UK measures: steel import quotas tightening by 60% from July 1, and a Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism arriving in 2027 (we covered it here). It is unclear whether the latter has been addressed.
sound_smarter: The favourable terms and exemptions India has secured highlight its growing leverage as the world’s fourth-largest economy, especially at a time when foreign businesses face mounting market and regulatory hurdles in both China and the US. Capitalizing on this shift, New Delhi is actively negotiating and signing a string of free trade agreements, leveraging its unique position to secure critical exemptions in the final stages of talks.

title: Stop the leaks, break the messenger
text:
New Delhi temporarily restricted Telegram until 22 June, citing cheating networks targeting the NEET-UG re-examination after last month's paper leak scandal affecting 2.3 million students.

Scam economy: Authorities said channels such as "Paper leaked NEET" and "Private Mafia" sold fake leaked papers and guaranteed success. Telegram was also ordered to disable message editing for Indian users until 30 June.

Telegram fights back: The company sued, calling the restrictions unconstitutional and "grossly disproportionate." It warned the case could legitimise blanket suspensions of digital platforms used by millions.

Durov escalates: Telegram founder Pavel Durov said the ban punished 150 million users while fraudsters simply moved elsewhere.
sound_smarter: While blocking channels makes for an interesting headline, it does nothing to fix the systemic vulnerabilities and insider collusion that allowed the papers to be compromised at the source in the first place.
anchor: New Delhi temporarily restricted Telegram until 22 June,

title: EU to sign India trade deal by end-2026, Modi meets Merz
text: The European Union will formally sign its landmark free trade agreement with India by the end of 2026, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday after meeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Group of Seven (G7) summit. Von Der Leyen said the two sides had moved fast since concluding the "mother of all trade deals” and a signing by year-end could bring it into force in 2027. Modi also met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on the sidelines of the summit, where both sides marked 75 years of diplomatic ties and discussed trade, defence, and green cooperation.
anchor: EU to sign India trade deal by end-2026, Modi meets Merz

title: Exchange of hands
text:
India's largest stock exchange is finally going public. On Wednesday, the National Stock Exchange (NSE) filed draft papers for an initial public offering, ending a listing saga that began in 2016 and stalled for years under regulatory enquiry and litigation with the markets regulator.

Not a fundraise: The offering is a pure offer-for-sale of 148.9 million shares, around 6% of NSE's equity. Existing shareholders, including domestic banks, state insurers, Singapore's Temasek, and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, are the ones selling. At an unlisted-market valuation of roughly USD 55 billion, NSE would rank among India's ten most valuable companies.

The business: NSE is the world's most active derivatives exchange and India's dominant bourse. It reported total income of INR 187 billion (USD 1.98 billion) and net profit of INR 103 billion for the year to March 2026, a 53% net margin, with transaction charges making up about 82% of revenue. The NSE has a unique retail base of around 130 million investors, against the institution-led models of Nasdaq or the New York Stock Exchange.

The overhang: NSE's listing was frozen for years by the co-location case, an investigation into whether the exchange gave some high-frequency traders unfair early access to its price feed between 2010 and 2014. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) fined NSE INR 11 billion (USD 117 million) in 2019 over the lapse, then cleared the listing this January. NSE has now applied to settle the remaining charges for around USD 158 million.
sound_smarter: Foreign investors spent early 2026 pulling more than USD 20 billion out of Indian equities, the outflows we covered here, and Indian markets have historically needed foreign money to set direction. A marquee listing is exactly the kind of asset that draws them back. But this one is a sell, not a buy: Temasek and the Canadians are taking money off the table, not putting it in. The rupee has clawed back from its May record low on cheaper oil, yet remains down nearly 9% over the year, so any dollar that left a year ago is returning to a more expensive entry. NSE will list comfortably on domestic demand. Whether it attracts foreign capital back into India is the question this offer-for-sale cannot answer.
anchor: India's largest stock exchange is finally going public.

title: Trust, but ratify
text:
Prime Minister Modi met President Trump on the margins of the G7 Summit. This was their first meeting since February 2025, marking a thaw after a year of strained ties.

The deliverable: The two instructed officials to finalise an interim Bilateral Trade Agreement "at the earliest," with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer travelling to India next week to take the talks forward. Trump told reporters a deal was close.

The warm-up: Modi opened by commending Trump on the understanding to end the conflict in West Asia, then raised freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the safety of seafarers, the same crews caught in last week's US naval strikes that we covered here. The two also reviewed progress under the India-US COMPACT (Catalyzing Opportunities for Military Partnership, Accelerated Commerce and Technology), the defence and technology framework agreed in Washington in February 2025.

Next door: Modi also met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Evian. Both agreed to restore trade ties to pre-war levels, with Zelenskyy flagging "good industrial and other projects" the two could pursue
sound_smarter: Last week India was summoning the US ambassador over Indian sailors; yesterday Modi was commending Trump on regional peace. The trade deal explains the pivot. India needs the interim agreement to lift the punitive tariffs still hanging over its exporters, and Greer's visit next week puts a date on it. Modi raised the seafarers, but as a line item inside a friendly meeting, not a grievance. New Delhi has decided the deal is worth more than the protest.

title: Building bridges, literally
text:
Prime Minister Modi called for "balanced, shared and sustainable growth" at the G7 Summit, arguing that global prosperity should be measured by inclusion and well-being.

The pitch: Modi positioned India as a bridge between developed and developing economies. He highlighted the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) as a model for strengthening supply chains, creating jobs, and fostering innovation across regions.

A bigger ambition: Modi proposed a new initiative, the International Mobilization Partnership for Accelerating Connectivity and Trade (IMPACT), combining G7 capital, Indian talent, and Global South ownership to finance connectivity projects across Africa, Latin America, and the Pacific island countries. It builds on the same trade-integration push that has India chasing agreements with G7 members, including the interim deal with Washington now nearing the finish line.
sound_smarter: IMEC was India's answer to China's Belt and Road, a Western-aligned corridor to move goods from India to Europe. IMEC stalled when war broke out across the route it depended on. IMPACT scales that bet rather than hedging it, wagering that a stabilised West Asia reopens the connectivity map. India is offering to be the executor the G7 funds and the Global South trusts. The pitch only works if the guns stay quiet.
