title: 40-year Kiwi thaw
text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and New Zealand counterpart Christopher Luxon elevated bilateral ties to a Strategic Partnership in Auckland, in the first visit by an Indian prime minister to New Zealand in 40 years.

The deliverables: The two governments signed ten agreements and issued eight announcements. On defence, they inked a maritime cooperation arrangement, a mutual logistics support pact between the two navies, and a hydrography deal, plus a Joint Working Group on Counter-Terrorism. A Roadmap to 2030 frames five pillars covering political, security, trade, cultural, and multilateral cooperation.

By the numbers: Both sides set a target to double two-way trade in goods and services to NZD 7 billion (USD 4 billion) by 2030, anchored on the India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) concluded this year in nine months. New Zealand pledged USD 20 billion in Indian investment over 15 years and joined the Global Biofuels Alliance, an initiative launched at the 2023 G20 New Delhi summit.

Indo-Pacific tilt: New Zealand nominated maritime security as its priority pillar under India's Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (IPOI). Both leaders backed a rules-based order and peaceful dispute resolution under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).
sound_smarter: After forty years without a prime ministerial visit, signing ten agreements and a logistics pact in a single day underscores a sudden urgency to elevate ties. Historically, New Zealand kept India on the margins while courting China on trade. That dynamic is shifting as Wellington seeks to reduce its economic dependence on Beijing, a pivot accelerated by regional security anxieties, including a recent Chinese ballistic missile test in the South Pacific that deeply rattled New Zealand. By naming maritime security as its priority pillar under India’s Indo-Pacific initiative, Wellington signals that India is now firmly on its strategic map, even if the immediate pact covers only fishing patrols.
anchor: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and New Zealand counterpart

title: Better late than never
text:
Quick-commerce apps promise groceries in minutes. India's food regulator has spent years struggling to check whether that food is safe. This week, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) hit Swiggy Instamart with nine notices over expired whey protein, rotten eggs, spoiled ready-to-eat meals and unsafe infant formula reaching customers' doors.

The ask: FSSAI wants documented proof of quality checks, stock rotation, storage hygiene and grievance handling, plus a root-cause analysis. Miss the deadline, and the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 kicks in. Instamart says it is reviewing the listings.

Growth outran governance: Quick-commerce, apps like Instamart, Blinkit and Zepto promising ten-to-twenty-minute delivery from local "dark stores" (small, customer-inaccessible warehouses), has been one of Indian retail's fastest-growing categories. The combined dark-store count across the top three players jumped from 3,405 to over 5,000 in the past year alone, with the segment growing roughly 40% annually. Oversight did not scale at the same pace. Blinkit faced near-identical complaints in May, over eggs described as smelly and rubber-textured. FSSAI is now insisting e-commerce platforms own compliance for everything they list, third-party seller or not, a standard the sector's breakneck expansion had largely outrun.

A related, milder case: Heritage Foods, part of the same broader FSSAI push into packaged food, faces a show-cause notice over calling its paneer "fresh." A labelling dispute, not a spoilage one.
sound_smarter: The gap between "eggs delivered in ten minutes" and "eggs stored safely for ten minutes" was always going to close, and closing it costs more than a compliance memo. Expect slower dark-store throughput and higher operating costs precisely where investors have been pricing in neither.

title: Goyal leads business delegation to Spain, Belgium, Finland
text: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal will lead a business delegation to Spain, Belgium, and Finland from July 13 to 17, pushing India-European Union (EU) trade ties ahead of the proposed India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA). In Brussels, Goyal will co-chair the third India-EU Trade and Technology Council (TTC) Ministerial, the highest institutional mechanism for India-EU cooperation on trade and technology, with meetings expected with the Presidents of the European Commission and the European Council. The delegation spans advanced manufacturing, clean energy, gems and jewellery, and healthcare. Navy commissions sixth indigenous stealth frigate at Visakhapatnam: The Indian Navy commissioned INS Mahendragiri, the sixth Project 17A stealth frigate, into its Eastern Fleet at Visakhapatnam on Saturday, July 11. Designed by the Navy's Warship Design Bureau and built by Mazagaon Dock Shipbuilders Limited (MDL), the 6,670-tonne warship carries over 75% indigenous content and can be fitted with the BrahMos cruise missile. It is the sixth ship of the series inducted in 18 months. MDL cut launch-to-delivery time by roughly half, from 63 to 31 months, and cleared the vessel in a single sea trial rather than the usual five to seven.
anchor: Goyal leads business delegation to Spain, Belgium, Finland

title: Fifteen Indian tourists killed in Vietnam boat capsize
text: A tourist boat carrying 32 Indian nationals capsized off Vietnam's Phu Quoc island on Saturday, killing 15. The vessel overturned about 400 metres from shore while returning from Hon May Rut island to An Thoi port, in rough seas with large waves. Twenty-one people have been rescued. The Embassy of India in Hanoi said it was monitoring the incident and had set up emergency response centres in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi to assist families.
anchor: Fifteen Indian tourists killed in Vietnam boat capsize

title: Gold couldn’t wait
text:
The Commerce Ministry reported India's June merchandise trade deficit widening to USD 30.43 billion, a five-month high and up 59% on the USD 19.10 billion gap a year earlier, as imports outran exports.

The trend: This is the second straight month the gap has widened. May's merchandise deficit was USD 28.21 billion (we covered it here). Merchandise exports rose 15.5% year-on-year in June to USD 40.41 billion, led by gems, jewellery, and engineering goods. Imports climbed almost twice as fast, up 31% to USD 70.84 billion.

What drove it: Petroleum imports rose 23% to USD 19.32 billion, gold jumped 47% to USD 1.96 billion, and electronics climbed 43.8% to USD 13.36 billion. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal repeated the government's line that higher global prices for crude and precious metals, not rising volumes, drove the bill.

The levers already pulled: In May, Modi asked citizens to pause gold purchases and foreign holidays for a year, framing forex conservation as economic patriotism (we covered it here). Two days later, the Centre raised the gold import duty from 6% to 15%. The World Gold Council expects the hike to soften demand, but Indian gold buying peaks in the October festival and wedding season, months away.
sound_smarter: The Prime Minister's appeal and the import duty both target household demand, yet the strain sits in prices driven by the West Asia crisis. Whether Indian consumers defer their purchases will not show until festival buying arrives in the autumn.
anchor: The Commerce Ministry reported India's June merchandise trade

issue_title: If you can’t sell them mangoes, take their cash
title: If you can’t sell them mangoes, take their cash
text:
India is reviewing its trade agreement with Japan, according to government sources, after the bilateral trade deficit nearly tripled to USD 15.4 billion over the last decade.

Trade agreement: The India-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) was signed and took effect in 2011. The two sides held the 7th India–Japan CEPA Joint Committee Meeting in Tokyo in March 2026, where the Indian side “underscored the need to enhance and diversify bilateral trade and investment” and the need for “a more balanced bilateral trade relationship.”

By the numbers: Indian imports from Japan skyrocketed from USD 9.8 billion in 2015-16 to USD 21.43 billion in 2025-26, while India's exports crawled from USD 4.6 billion to just USD 6 billion.

The hurdle: Stringent non-tariff barriers, such as Japanese quality and sanitary standards, make the market tough to crack. Tokyo recently banned Indian mangoes over pest-control lapses.

Pivoting to capital: Realizing it cannot easily sell goods to Tokyo, New Delhi is leveraging the FTA review to get more Japanese investment instead. Japan is India's fifth-largest FDI source and has pledged JPY 10 trillion (~USD 62 billion) over the next decade.
sound_smarter: Boosting Japanese investment in India's domestic manufacturing is crucial to shrinking the trade deficit. By shifting Indian production from low-value agricultural goods to high-value manufactured items, India can export more lucrative products to Japan. However, because these investments take years to yield results, the massive trade deficit is unlikely to shrink anytime soon.

title: Not so fast
text:
Trade secretary Rajesh Agrawal said talks on the India-US trade deal are progressing well and the framework agreement is ready, and that the deal will be signed at the “right time.”

Not a rejection: Commerce minister Piyush Goyal and US ambassador Sergio Gor both pushed back on reports that India had rejected a quick deal. They sang in unison that talks remain constructive, both sides are engaged, and nobody has walked away.

Framework déjà vu: The interim pact in February involved India lowering trade barriers and buying more American goods, while Washington offered an 18% tariff track for Indian exports (we covered it here). The Supreme Court ruling in March unwound it weeks later, and a temporary 10% tariff now lapses on July 24.
sound_smarter: It does not take a commerce minister and a US ambassador both going on record to dismiss an anonymously sourced report unless it landed close enough to true to move markets. From the look of it, both sides agree on the deal but not on the terms. India can offer tariff cuts and big-ticket purchase pledges only if Washington can guarantee Indian exporters will be better off than their competitors. Until the US tariff machine stops shape-shifting, signing fast is riskier for New Delhi.

title: Modi to launch India's first hydrogen train on July 17
text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will flag off India's first hydrogen-powered train from Jind in Haryana on July 17. Commercial operations will begin on the 89-kilometre Jind–Sonipat section under Northern Railway, following months of trials. Indian Railways approved the 10-car, 1,200 KW trainset in May (we covered it here), which runs on hydrogen fuel cells and emits only water vapour. The launch is the first under the "Hydrogen for Heritage" programme, which plans 35 such trains for heritage and hill routes at roughly INR 80 crore (USD 8 million) per train, plus INR 70 crore (USD 7 million) in route infrastructure. Modi will flag off the train during a Jind visit that will be his first to the Jat-dominated district in nearly a decade, ahead of Punjab's assembly elections next year.
anchor: Modi to launch India's first hydrogen train on July 17

title: Payoneer to open a global capability centre in India
text: US fintech Payoneer is opening a new global capability centre (GCC) in Gurugram and plans to hire around 300 engineers in India by the end of 2026. The Nasdaq-listed payments firm said the hub will focus on artificial intelligence (AI) and platform engineering, making India its second-largest technology and research centre globally. Payoneer already employs around 400 staff in Bengaluru handling domestic sales. The move deepens a broader trend of global fintechs building product, payments, and AI operations in India rather than treating it as a back office.
anchor: Payoneer to open a global capability centre in India

title: Strait into the crossfire
text:
India summoned Iran's deputy ambassador yesterday after an Indian seafarer was killed and ten injured in missile attacks on two tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz.

What happened: The vessels MT Al Bahiyah and MT Mombasa were struck during transit through the strait, carrying 30 Indian seafarers among a combined crew of 46. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said one Indian national aboard Al Bahiyah died and one was injured, while nine of the 18 Indians on Mombasa were hurt, two of them critically. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) Defence Ministry attributed the strike to two Iranian cruise missiles fired while the tankers sat in Omani waters.

India's response: The MEA lodged a strong protest with Iran's Deputy Chief of Mission and called for an immediate cessation of violence. It condemned the attacks without publicly naming Iran, a gap with the UAE's open accusation. India's mission in the UAE is assisting the affected crew.

The backdrop: The strikes followed fresh US action against Iran and a renewed threat to blockade the strait. Indian sailors have now died on both sides of the escalation. A US strike on the tanker MT Settebello last month killed three Indian crew (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: In June, India summoned the United States chargé after a US strike killed three Indian sailors aboard the Settebello. One month on, it has summoned Iran's envoy over the same category of death in the same Strait. India's posture lets it protest to Washington and Tehran in the same breath, but it also means both sides' ordnance kills Indian crews, and a summons is the ceiling of what Delhi will do in either direction. India left the attribution to the UAE and named nobody, which keeps intact a relationship it has spent decades nurturing.

title: A forced hand
text:
India's Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) prohibited the import of goods produced wholly or partly through forced labour on Monday, amending the Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) 2023 five weeks after Washington proposed fresh tariffs against India over the same issue.

How the ban works: The notification inserts a new clause into the FTP defining forced labour by borrowing the International Labour Organization (ILO)'s 1930 Forced Labour Convention wording, and empowers the Centre to block specific goods once an inquiry finds evidence they were made with forced labour. The rule takes effect 30 days after gazette publication. Nothing stops at the border yet so far. DGFT must investigate and name products first, with procedures to follow the Handbook of Procedures, 2023.

The USTR probe behind it: The United States Trade Representative (USTR) is running Section 301 investigations into 60 economies, India included, over failures to block forced-labour imports. On 3 June, the USTR proposed a 12.5% tariff tied to this failure (we covered it here). India currently faces a flat 10% US tariff, and this is one of two separate USTR probes, the other into industrial overcapacity, that could push that rate higher.
sound_smarter: The true test of this prohibition lies in the upcoming inquiry mechanism and implementation framework slated for the Handbook of Procedures. Until Delhi defines how it will actually identify, investigate, and verify forced labour in complex supply chains, this is a placeholder rather than an active enforcement tool. Furthermore, once operationalized, this mechanism could put New Delhi in bind, as Washington is bound to pressure India to block imports from China, its largest trading partner, based on US allegations of forced labour, risking a severe diplomatic and economic backlash from Beijing.
anchor: India's Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) prohibited

title: India and Maldives conclude first round of FTA negotiations
text: India and the Maldives have concluded the first round of Free Trade Agreement (FTA) talks, covering eight policy areas. On July 8, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal met his Maldivian counterpart, Mohamed Saeed, and the two reaffirmed a commitment to expedite both the FTA and a parallel Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT), alongside cooperation on tourism, startups, digital payments, and micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). India is the Maldives' second-largest trading partner, with bilateral trade reaching USD 771.76 million in 2025-26, up 13.54 per cent from USD 679.70 million the year before.
anchor: India and Maldives conclude first round of FTA negotiations

title: Duty free, at last
text:
The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) took effect on Wednesday, a year after signing. The UK scraps duties immediately on 96.8% of tariff lines, covering 97.7% of trade value.

India's side of the ledger: New Delhi removes duties at once on 64.1% of tariff lines and phases out tariffs on a further 21%. Dairy, grains, and oilseeds stay off the table entirely, the same defensive basket India has protected in every recent trade agreement. Textiles, leather, footwear, marine products, gems, and jewellery gain duty-free entry against UK tariffs that ran from 4% to 20%.

The UK's asks: India opens its automobile market on a phased quota, allowing 37,000 completely built UK vehicles a year at preferential tariffs, alongside openings in procurement, financial services, education, and insurance. India's procurement market opens to UK suppliers at around USD 114 billion. The UK's own runs to roughly USD 120 billion.

The white-collar clause: The linked Double Contribution Convention exempts eligible Indian professionals and employers from the UK's National Insurance contributions for stays of up to five years, covering roughly 75,000 workers and 900 employers. Services access spans 137 sub-sectors.

By the numbers: India shipped USD 13.44 billion of goods to Britain and imported USD 11.68 billion in 2025-26. Services trade hit USD 35.44 billion in 2024, with India running a surplus of nearly USD 7.9 billion.

The road here: The deal stalled twice, first over the UK's steel import quotas tightening 60% from July 1, and then over an incoming Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: India runs a USD 1.76 billion goods surplus with the UK, small enough to be noise, but nearly USD 8 billion in services, and the Double Contribution Convention protects exactly that flow by removing a five-year payroll tax on the professionals who generate it. The UK won concessions – cars and Scotch give London something to hold up at a press conference. India got a treaty-bound floor under its largest export earner, at a moment when its IT majors are guiding to 3% growth and Washington is opening tariff fronts on its goods.
anchor: The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA)

title: Crude timing
text:
India’s Russian oil purchases could complicate the timing of its US trade deal. A bipartisan Senate bill would let President Donald Trump impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian energy. India is firmly on that list.

By the numbers: India’s imports of Russian oil surged by 34% in June to a record USD 5.2 billion, making it the world’s second-biggest buyer of Russian oil behind China.

Still prohibitive: Cutting the ceiling from 500% to 100% is not a restraint that it looks. A 100% tariff would effectively close the US market to many Indian goods. But the bill is not yet law, and Trump could waive the measure in the US national interest.

Deal within reach: The India-US framework is ready but unsigned as both sides confirmed the willingness to sign earlier this week (we covered it here). New Delhi wants the final pact to leave Indian exporters better off than their competitors and protection from Washington’s next tariff turn.

New uncertainty: The sanctions bill would create a separate tariff power outside the trade framework. Washington could use it to press India over Russian oil, although no such linkage has been formally made.
sound_smarter: The presidential waiver is the real story. It turns a Russia sanction into potential trade leverage. For India, that reinforces the case for waiting on the timing and signing is risky if Washington cannot guarantee the tariff advantage will last.
anchor: India’s Russian oil purchases could complicate the timing

title: Chips with everything
text:
India is turning its phone-assembly boom into a semiconductor launchpad. On Wednesday, the Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0, a USD 13.3 billion (INR 1.275 trillion) programme spanning chip design, equipment, materials, fabrication, packaging, research and skills.

Second time around: The 2021 semiconductor mission has approved 12 manufacturing units and 24 design projects; three facilities are already producing commercially. Semicon 2.0 shifts the focus from landing factories to building the ecosystem around them.

Built-in buyer: The Cabinet also approved USD 6.5 billion (INR 625 billion) over five years for mobile-phone manufacturing. Firms can receive 2.25%–5% of eligible sales, plus up to 1.5% for sourcing key components locally.

Scale, not depth: India is the world’s second-largest mobile-phone manufacturer. Production reached USD 56.9 billion (INR 5.45 trillion) and exports USD 20.9 billion (INR 2 trillion) in FY2024–25. Domestic value addition across electronics remains just 18%–20%.
sound_smarter: Pairing chip subsidies with phone incentives is smart industrial policy: one builds supply, the other creates demand. Success is now measured by more Indian chips, components and intellectual property inside them.

title: Gadkari says drivers wanting pure petrol must pay more
text: Union Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari told the Times of India that motorists who do not want ethanol-blended petrol can buy 100% petrol at a higher price, as complaints mount over the Centre's blending push. India has hit 20% ethanol blending, with E20 now sold at every fuel station in the country. When asked whether pumps should dispense multiple blends, he said the question sits with the Petroleum Ministry and declined to comment. He repeated the government's position that E20 does not damage engines and that every E10-compliant vehicle can run on it, calling the campaign against the fuel politically motivated.
anchor: Gadkari says drivers wanting pure petrol must pay more

title: All hands off deck
text:
India has ordered shipowners, ship managers, and recruitment firms to stop deploying Indian seafarers on any vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with the ban running until further orders.

The trigger: The circular names five vessels struck in recent days: Mombasa, Al Bahiyah, GSV Galaxy, Settebello, and AS Revattas. Indian crews died on two of them. A US strike on the Settebello off Oman killed three in June, and one seafarer was killed aboard the Al Bahiyah on July 14, after which India summoned Iran's deputy ambassador without publicly naming Tehran as responsible (we covered it here).

The order: Issued late Wednesday by the Directorate General of Shipping, the directive says recent attacks have raised the risks to seafarers and commercial ships "significantly". Masters of vessels must stay vigilant on the security situation across the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, and adjoining waters, with continuous monitoring of navigational warnings.
sound_smarter: India is the world's third-largest supplier of seafarers, with more than 300,000 sailors crewing global fleets. Roughly a fifth of world oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz, and the vessels carrying it are disproportionately staffed by Indians. Owners now have to choose between finding replacement crews at a premium or idling tonnage, and New Delhi has found a lever on the Gulf without firing anything.
anchor: India has ordered shipowners, ship managers, and recruitment

title: Securing the (fertiliser) bag
text:
The Cabinet approved a new investment policy for urea on Wednesday, aiming to finally plug the gap between domestic demand and costly imports.

By the numbers: India imports 26% of its annual urea requirement. Oman is the biggest supplier and shipments go through the Strait of Hormuz. Unsurprisingly, the West Asia conflict has disrupted supplies and caused prices to surge to nearly double the pre-conflict price at one point.

The upgrade: The National Investment Policy for Urea-2026 (NIPU-2026) replaces a 2012 framework that expired in 2019. It targets new gas-based plants to expand India's existing 33-unit manufacturing footprint.

The sweet spot: To lure private capital, the government is offering a guaranteed 12% to 16% return on equity and shielding investors from currency volatility by converting fixed costs to rupees after four years. The tweaks should save over INR 250 crore (~USD 26 million) per plant compared to the old policy, according to the government.
sound_smarter: India’s massive agricultural sector is its most powerful political constituency, where any threat to farming interests triggers large-scale protests, such as the demonstrations in June over rising fuel prices and urea shortages. By offering guaranteed returns and hedging foreign exchange risks, New Delhi can attract private players to curb import reliance and stabilize prices, ultimately reducing the likelihood of future input-driven unrest.

title: Mileage may vary
text:
India's Ministry of Power circulated draft fuel economy norms for passenger cars on Thursday, replacing fines for missed targets with a published price at which carmakers can buy their way to compliance.

What CAFE is: Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) rules cap the average emissions of everything a carmaker sells, rather than judging each model. A company can keep selling thirsty SUVs provided enough small cars, hybrids, or electric vehicles pull the fleet average down. India has run two cycles: CAFE-I from 2017 capped fleets at 130 grams of carbon dioxide per kilometre, and CAFE-II from 2022 tightened that to 113. CAFE-II expires on March 31, 2027.

The new ceiling: The draft cuts the fleet target to 94.76 grams per kilometre in 2027-28, then steps down each year to 78.90 by 2031-32. Compliance is measured over two blocks, three years then two. Each manufacturer's specific target is scaled to the weighted unladen mass of what it sells, so a fleet of heavy SUVs earns a looser limit than a fleet of small hatchbacks, before any powertrain offsets are counted. Makers below 1,000 units a year are exempt.

The buyout: Carmakers running a deficit can purchase credits from the Bureau of Energy Efficiency at INR 2,500 (USD 26) per gram of carbon dioxide per kilometre in 2027-28, rising to INR 4,500 (USD 47) by 2031-32. They can also trade credits with each other on privately agreed terms inside a 30-day window each year. Ninety per cent of the proceeds go to state governments. Electric vehicles count 3.0 times their actual sales volume in the compliance maths, plug-in hybrids 2.5 times, and strong hybrids 1.6 times. Ethanol flex-fuel vehicles get a 22.3 percent discount on declared emissions.

The dispute behind it: In FY22 all 19 carmakers met their targets. In FY23, the first year of the tighter 113 gram cap, eight missed: Hyundai, Kia, Mahindra, Honda, Renault, Nissan, Skoda, and Force Motors, though no penalty was ever levied. The companies argued the Energy Conservation Act's penalty provisions only took effect on January 1, 2023, three quarters of the way through the assessment year, so applying them across all of FY23 would be retrospective. Weeks ago the Centre dropped the matter entirely.
sound_smarter: The compliance path Delhi has drawn runs through hybrids, not batteries. A strong hybrid counts 1.6 times its sales volume with no charging infrastructure required, which makes it the cheapest way to move a fleet average and explains why every maker without one is now late. The flexibilities cluster at the front: nine bolt-on technologies worth a gram each, a credit buyout priced lowest in year one, and super credits on volumes that are still small. The target does not flex. It lands at 78.90 grams in 2031-32, roughly 30 per cent below today, and no amount of LED lighting gets a fleet there. Delhi has given the industry five cheap years to build expensive capability. The makers who spend them buying credits instead will have to greet 2032 with the same engines and a much larger bill.
anchor: India's Ministry of Power circulated draft fuel economy

title: Navy to commission second Mahe-class anti-submarine craft
text: The Indian Navy will commission Malvan, the second Mahe-class Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft (ASW-SWC), on July 22. Built at Cochin Shipyard Limited in Kochi with over 80 per cent indigenous content, the craft is designed for anti-submarine work in shallow coastal waters, where larger warships cannot operate effectively.
anchor: Navy to commission second Mahe-class anti-submarine craft

title: Codex adopts three India-led spice standards
text: The Codex Alimentarius Commission adopted international quality standards for large cardamom, coriander, and vanilla at its session in Geneva from July 6 to 10. The standards were finalised at the Codex Committee on Spices and Culinary Herbs, which India hosts, at a meeting in Guwahati in October 2025. Codex, run jointly by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Health Organization, sets the food safety benchmarks that governments and importers reference. India is among the world's largest producers of cardamom and coriander, and harmonised standards ease market access for its exporters.
anchor: Codex adopts three India-led spice standards

title: Control issues
text:
Parliament opened its Monsoon Session on Monday with new controls on foreign funding ready for debate, while a plan to remove detained ministers remained stuck in committee.

Follow the money: The Foreign Contribution Regulation Act, or FCRA, governs how Indian organisations receive and use overseas donations. The proposed amendment cuts the maximum prison sentence for violations from five years to one. It also allows a government appointed authority to control and dispose of foreign contributions and assets created from them when an organisation’s FCRA registration ends.

Thirty days: The Constitution Amendment Bill would remove ministers, including the Prime Minister and Chief Ministers, after 30 consecutive days in custody over an alleged offence carrying a maximum sentence of at least five years. A committee draft proposed suspension instead, with restoration after acquittal or stalled prosecution. Last Friday, the panel deferred its report for further consultation.
sound_smarter: Political cost prevails in the decision-making process for both bills here. Giving the government control over foreign funded assets affects individual organisations, while removing a PM or CM before conviction could change an entire government. That consequence makes the custody bill far more contentious, helping explain why the FCRA rewrite is moving forward while the removal proposal remains stuck in committee.

title: Fast-tracking accountability
text:
After three weeks on a hunger strike over national exam paper leaks, activist Sonam Wangchuk was forcibly hospitalised by Delhi police over the weekend, escalating youth-led protests against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government.

The spark: Wangchuk, known for campaigning on issues affecting his home region of Ladakh, joined forces with the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) to demand the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Wangchuk is best known for building artificial glaciers to store winter water for irrigation use in the summer and fighting for statehood for Ladakh (which is a federally controlled territory), which got him jailed in 2025.

Ongoing protests: The CJP has been protesting at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi since June 6, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and reforms in the examination system (we covered it here). Wangchuk joined the protests on June 28 and started an indefinite hunger strike, which increased the size and diversity of crowds.

The government’s predicament: Pushing a revered, Gandhian-style figure into a hospital bed rarely plays well on social media, especially when he's fasting on behalf of millions of furious student voters.
sound_smarter: Despite mounting nationwide protests and intense pressure from opposition parties, the BJP is unlikely to give in and ask Dharmendra Pradhan to resign, who continues to enjoy strong backing from the BJP leadership. The government is unwilling to set a precedent where public protests force a minister out of office.

title: Skyroot completes India’s first private orbital rocket launch
text: India’s private space industry has reached orbit. On Saturday, Hyderabad based Skyroot Aerospace launched Vikram 1, the country’s first privately developed orbital rocket, from the Indian Space Research Organisation’s Satish Dhawan Space Centre. The 22 metre vehicle carried customer satellites and technology experiments into a 450 kilometre low Earth orbit within 15 minutes on its maiden Mission Aagaman. Vikram 1 can carry up to 350 kilograms. The launch goes beyond Skyroot’s Vikram S test in 2022, which reached space but did not enter orbit, and makes India the third country after the US and China where a private company has achieved orbital launch capability.
anchor: Skyroot completes India’s first private orbital rocket launch

title: Battery not included
text:
On Tuesday, the government updated Parliament on two Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, part of the Atmanirbhar Bharat (self-reliant India) drive, launched in 2021 to build an advanced automotive supply chain at home.

Cars accelerate: Under the INR 25,938-crore (USD 2.7-billion) Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for automobiles and auto components, manufacturers had invested INR 44,326 crore (USD 4.6 billion) and created 67,820 jobs by March 31, 2026. The government has disbursed INR 2,386 crore (USD 248 million) in incentives across 225 units.

Missing cell: The companion Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) battery programme has an INR 18,100-crore (USD 1.9-billion) budget and targets 50 GWh of domestic capacity. Four firms hold allocations totalling 40 GWh, but none has claimed an incentive, which requires the production and sale of qualifying Indian-made cells.

Latest report: Beneficiary firms reported INR 5,180 crore (USD 538 million) in investment by May 31, 2026, far below the INR 45,000 crore (USD 4.7 billion) the government originally envisaged. When capacity was awarded in March 2022, beneficiaries were given two years to establish their factories. A February 2026 update reported just 1 GWh of installed capacity, entirely belonging to Ola.
sound_smarter: PLI is proving better at deepening an established industry than building a new one from scratch. India's automakers can draw on mature supplier networks, skilled workers, and export infrastructure, while battery-cell producers still need to assemble the technology, equipment, raw-material supply chains, and expertise. The result is an EV industry developing from the outside in, with vehicle and component production advancing faster than the cells that power them, leaving India dependent on imports at the most strategic point in the supply chain.

title: The third summons
text:
India summoned Russia's top diplomat in Delhi on Tuesday after a missile strike on the MV Golden Leo killed four Indian crew members leaving Ukraine's Odessa port.

What happened: On the evening of July 19, 2026, the cargo vessel Golden Leo was attacked while departing Odessa. Of 17 crew on board, five were Indian nationals. Four were killed and one is hospitalised in a critical condition. Ukraine's Navy said Russian forces launched three cruise missiles at the ship.

India's response: The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) summoned Russian Chargé d'Affaires Vladimir Ladanov and conveyed India's "grave concerns and unequivocal condemnation". The MEA told Ladanov that targeting commercial shipping and the resulting loss of civilian lives are "unacceptable and must be avoided".

A pattern forms: This is the third time in six weeks India has protested a foreign power over dead seafarers. New Delhi summoned the United States twice and Iran once over crew losses during the Iran war (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Russia is India's steadiest partner, the supplier of most of its arms and a large share of its crude, and New Delhi has never condemned the Ukraine invasion outright. Summoning Moscow's envoy shows the ceiling on that friendship: India will call out its closest partner when its own citizens die, even as it shields the wider relationship from the war it refuses to take sides on.
