title: A shot in the arm
text:
India cleared its first dengue vaccine on Monday, granting marketing authorisation to Takeda's Qdenga for use in people aged 4 to 60.

The approval: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), India's drug regulator, authorised the Dengue Tetravalent Vaccine (Live, Attenuated), manufactured by Germany's Takeda GmbH and imported by its Indian arm. The schedule is two doses given three months apart.

The evidence: Clearance followed trials across more than eight countries, including Brazil, Thailand, and Sri Lanka, plus a Phase III study in the Indian population. Qdenga already holds approval in 42 countries and World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification, with more than 24 million doses distributed globally.

The burden: Dengue is endemic across India, with large seasonal outbreaks that strain hospitals through the monsoon months. The vaccine will run alongside existing vector control, surveillance, and case management under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme.
sound_smarter: A foreign-made import filling a first-in-country gap points to where India's vaccine strategy is heading next. Domestic developers, including Panacea Biotec and the Indian Council of Medical Research, have their own dengue candidates in trials, and today's approval sets the regulatory and pricing benchmark they will have to beat to justify a homegrown alternative.
anchor: India cleared its first dengue vaccine on Monday,

title: Small capitals, big map
text:
President Droupadi Murmu met North Macedonian President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova in Skopje on Tuesday, the first visit there by an Indian president.

The Skopje offer: The leaders agreed to double bilateral trade, without setting a deadline. India will also double North Macedonia’s training places under its Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) programme and welcomed its interest in three India-backed climate and infrastructure groupings. No binding deals were announced.

First stop: Murmu visited Moldova on Monday, another first for an Indian president. She met President Maia Sandu and addressed a business forum with an Indian corporate delegation, pitching cooperation in digital technology, energy, agriculture and pharmaceuticals.

Why these three: Moldova and North Macedonia are EU candidates, while Romania, Murmu’s final stop, is already a member.
sound_smarter: High-level visits, training programmes and access to India-backed groupings offer New Delhi low-cost influence in overlooked capitals. Trade returns may remain modest, but these relationships can produce multilateral support and more routes into European policymaking.
anchor: President Droupadi Murmu met North Macedonian President Gordana

title: Cockroaches in the capital
text:
Thousands of youth continued to protest in Delhi on Tuesday, turning widespread anger over leaked medical entrance exams into Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s biggest third-term crisis.

The catalyst: The leak affected two million students and sparked a movement led by the satire-born Cockroach Janta Party (we covered it here). Violent clashes with police left 180 injured on Monday during a march demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resign.

Modi responds: Modi broke his silence, promising a "foolproof system" and strict punishment for culprits. Protesters aren't buying it, continuing demonstrations while calling off another march to parliament to avoid police batons.

Opposition strikes: Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was detained outside Modi’s home after lying on the road in protest. Meanwhile, the Delhi High Court permitted hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk to move to a private hospital (we covered Wangchuk’s forced hospitalisation here).
sound_smarter: Exam leaks are a flashpoint for deeper Gen Z fury over systemic job shortages. Modi can promise clean tests, but unless New Delhi addresses youth unemployment, student despair will keep fueling political volatility.
anchor: Thousands of youth continued to protest in Delhi

title: India joins WTO fisheries subsidies agreement
text: India deposited its instrument of acceptance for the World Trade Organization (WTO) Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies on Monday, becoming the 123rd member to join. The agreement, the first WTO pact with an environmental sustainability objective, bans subsidies tied to illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing and to overfished stocks. Aquaculture and inland fisheries stay outside its scope, which shields India's shrimp exports, the bulk of its seafood trade.
anchor: India joins WTO fisheries subsidies agreement

title: India faces 900+ member questions at WTO trade review
text: India's 8th Trade Policy Review at the World Trade Organization (WTO) opened on Tuesday, running across two sittings on July 21 and 23, with Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agarwal leading the delegation. The review, conducted every five years, covers 2021 to 2025. Members filed more than 900 written questions for India to answer, and over 40 countries will deliver oral statements during the sessions.
anchor: India faces 900+ member questions at WTO trade review

title: Paper trail
text:
The US-India trade deal could be signed within three to four months, a senior US official said, with negotiations effectively complete.

The holdup: Speaking anonymously on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Foreign Ministers' meeting in Manila, the official said "The deal... is there. We literally have the paper." The remaining delay stems from Washington's own Section 301 trade investigations, which cover unfair trade practices and can trigger tariffs, rather than any unresolved bilateral dispute.

The sequencing: One Section 301 probe covering 60 countries concerning forced labour is expected to conclude this week or next. Washington has separately proposed tariffs of up to 12.5% on dozens of nations, India included, over goods made with forced labour (we covered the ban here).

The pharma wrinkle: President Trump said generic drugs will stay tariff-free for two years from August 1, then face 100% tariffs for a year and 200% thereafter, a schedule meant to push manufacturers to reshore. The United States buys USD 9.7 billion of Indian pharmaceutical exports, nearly 38% of India’s USD 25.8 billion in pharmaceutical exports.
sound_smarter: A finished deal that India cannot sign on its own timeline is a finished deal on Washington's terms. The signing waits on a probe that could raise India's tariff rate first, so New Delhi may end up initialling the agreement from a weaker position than where it started.
anchor: The US-India trade deal could be signed within

title: Balancing the books
text:
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar told his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi that the two sides must tackle market access and their lopsided trade balance, as New Delhi works to repair ties with Beijing. The two met in Manila on the sidelines of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on Wednesday.

The ask: Jaishankar flagged fair market access, supply-chain predictability, and the trade imbalance. He restated that border calm is the precondition for normal relations, pointing to engagement since October 2024.

The thaw: Ties began recovering after Modi met President Xi in October 2024, ending friction that dated to the 2020 border clash. Direct flights have resumed, business visas for Chinese professionals have been eased, and land border trade is set to restart on August 1 after a six-year gap. India's imports from China still hit USD 132 billion in fiscal year 2025/26, its highest from any nation, leaving a deficit above USD 100 billion within total trade of USD 151.10 billion.
sound_smarter: India is opening the door to Chinese investment and machinery because its factories depend on them, which weakens its hand on the deficit it wants to shrink. Pressing Wang Yi on market access shows how New Delhi wants the thaw to pay off in trade terms, treating border calm as the floor rather than the prize.
anchor: External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar told his Chinese

title: Private capital, public atom
text:
The Atomic Energy Commission approved Tarapur in Maharashtra for India’s first 220 MW and 55 MW small modular reactors.

Prototype push: The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), India’s main nuclear research agency, is developing both models and a high-temperature reactor for hydrogen production. India wants at least five indigenous small reactors operating by 2033, backed by INR 200 billion (USD 2.3 billion). Its wider goal is to lift nuclear capacity from 8.8 GW to 100 GW by 2047.

Rules rewritten: India’s 2025 nuclear law (SHANTI Act) permits licensed private participation in plant operation, generation and manufacturing. But fuel-cycle activities, nuclear waste and security remain under government control. Adani, Tata Power and Reliance have shown interest, although none has joined the Tarapur projects.
sound_smarter: Although there is a technical challenge involved in advancing India’s nuclear sector, the other pressing challenge is regulatory. The government needs to provide predictable licensing, pricing, fuel supply and liability rules that can turn public prototypes into repeatable, investable projects for the private sector.
anchor: The Atomic Energy Commission approved Tarapur in Maharashtra

title: Ministry reprimands aviation regulator over conflict-of-interest controls
text: India's Ministry of Civil Aviation has reprimanded the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) for failing to stop officials influencing jobs for their relatives in the sector. The ministry has challenged the safety body repeatedly since mid-2025, including a case where a DGCA engineering official handled approvals affecting Air India while his sister worked in its quality department. As of January 31, 51 DGCA officials had disclosed 59 relatives working in aviation. The rebuke lands as the DGCA faces staffing shortages, a police bribery investigation, and a routine US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) safety audit due within months.
anchor: Ministry reprimands aviation regulator over conflict-of-interest controls

title: Fast track, slow burn
text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced fast-track courts to prosecute those behind exam paper leaks on Thursday, his first public comment since protests escalated this week (we covered it here).

The announcement: Modi posted on X that the courts would deliver swift and stringent punishment, and said he had directed the concerned departments to act. In a video address later on Thursday he went further, promising a tougher law against paper leaks and saying the Cabinet would take up the issue on Friday. He called the leaks a matter of great pain for students without naming Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Fast-track courts are dedicated benches designed to bypass India's overburdened judicial system, previously used for terrorism, money laundering, and crimes against women and children. No start date, court count, or draft legislation was published.

The movement: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as online satire after Chief Justice Surya Kant compared unemployed youth to cockroaches (we covered its origins here), has demanded Pradhan's resignation for 25 days over medical entrance exam leaks that forced millions of students to retake the test and have been linked to several student suicides. Founder Abhijeet Dipke says the sit-in continues until Pradhan goes.

The hunger strike: Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended a 26-day hunger strike late on Thursday, shortly after Modi's video address. Wangchuk, 59, had fasted since June 28 in solidarity with the CJP, and said on X that he stopped after a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country.

The response: The CJP said it would continue, with spokesman Ashutosh Ranka arguing that fast-track courts do not address systemic problems in the education system and repeating the demand that Pradhan be removed. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi also rejected the announcement.

The containment: Delhi Metro Rail Corporation shut 16 central stations yesterday, the second consecutive day of closures. Mobile internet was suspended around the Jantar Mantar protest site on Monday during the blocked Parliament march, and again on Wednesday. Delhi Police ordered personnel at the site into full uniform on Tuesday evening, after footage from Monday showed men in plain clothes striking protesters alongside uniformed officers without name badges.

The legal gap: The Internet Freedom Foundation notes that no suspension order has been published by the Home Ministry, the Department of Telecommunications, the Delhi government, or Delhi Police. An earlier Supreme Court ruling requires every such order to be published with written reasons.
sound_smarter: Modi has offered a procedural fix to a demand for a political scalp, which is why the courts landed without settling anything. The Centre would rather absorb repeated shutdowns in central Delhi than concede a resignation, which tells investors how much political capital the government thinks it would lose by giving the protesters their win.
anchor: Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced fast-track courts to

title: No country for old cars
text:
India is locking in E20 petrol. The government stated that it will not restore E10 or ethanol-free petrol and says supplying several blends nationwide would be too costly and complex. No decision has been made on moving above 20%.

Backlash background: E20, containing 20% ethanol and 80% petrol, has faced protests over lower mileage, possible damage to older vehicles and the lack of consumer choice (we covered it here).

Government defence: New Delhi says service records covering over 200 million two-wheelers and 30 million cars show no widespread engine damage. It concedes a 3% to 5% mileage loss in some vehicles designed for E10, which contains 10% ethanol.

The ledger: Blending reached 20% between November 2025 and June 2026, five years ahead of the original target. The programme has saved INR 1.97 lakh crore (USD 20.5 billion) in foreign exchange, displaced 31.6 million tonnes of crude, and transferred INR 1.66 lakh crore (USD 17.3 billion) to farmers.

The awkward bit: India’s 2021 roadmap recorded the automobile industry’s insistence that E10 remain available as a “protection grade” during the transition.
sound_smarter: The government rushed ethanol blending before the fleet was ready, then dropped the safety net the industry asked for. Drivers of older cars now absorb a permanent mileage penalty so the Centre can bank the foreign exchange savings.
anchor: India is locking in E20 petrol. The government

title: Adani takes to the skies
text:
Billionaire Gautam Adani wants to crash India’s aviation duopoly, if the government lets him rewrite the rules first.

The manoeuvre: Adani has asked New Delhi to dilute a clause capping airport operators at a 10% stake in scheduled airlines. Adani operates eight airports, including both Mumbai and Navi Mumbai, which together serve India's financial capital. GMR Airports, which runs Delhi and four others, would get the same latitude under any rule change.

Market squeeze: IndiGo and Air India control roughly 90% of domestic traffic. After recent operational meltdowns and safety scrambles (we covered it here and here), New Delhi is quietly nudging deep-pocketed conglomerates to jump in.

Turbulence ahead: Rival carriers fear conflicts of interest over slot allocation. The Airports Economic Regulatory Authority sets aeronautical tariffs, but slot coordination and ground handling sit outside its remit. Adani-owned CSMIA (Mumbai’s primary airport) has already fought IndiGo and Air India over payment terms while operating as a neutral landlord. Kingfisher, Jet Airways, and Go First all crashed into bankruptcy in this notoriously price-sensitive market.
sound_smarter: Owning both the runways and the planes would give Adani leverage over the two things every competitor needs and cannot substitute. GMR moves more passengers through Delhi and Hyderabad than Adani does through Mumbai, and only one of the two has the balance sheet to fund an airline through years of losses. A rule written for both delivers for one, which is fine for Adani and a nightmare for everyone else at the gate.
anchor: Billionaire Gautam Adani wants to crash India’s aviation

title: DRDO flight-tests Kusha long-range air defence missile
text: The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) conducted the maiden flight-test of the Kusha long-range surface-to-air missile from APJ Abdul Kalam Island off Odisha on July 23, 2026, intercepting an electronic target simulating a high-speed, high-altitude aerial threat. DRDO says the system can engage fighter jets, missiles, unmanned aerial vehicles, and large aircraft, with the missiles, radars, and command and control centre all developed by DRDO laboratories and industry partners.
anchor: DRDO flight-tests Kusha long-range air defence missile

title: Resign, reassign, repeat
text:
India's youth protesters won the scalp they wanted. Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday, and their month-long agitation over alleged exam paper leaks ended hours later.

The settlement: President Droupadi Murmu accepted Pradhan’s resignation immediately. He acknowledged young people’s “legitimate expectations”, while saying his exit would stop “anti-national forces” exploiting the unrest. The government also agreed to reform examinations, withdraw cases against demonstrators and compensate families of students who died by suicide following the leaks. The Cockroach Janta Party declared victory, ended its agitation “in good faith” and told supporters to disperse peacefully. Internet access and metro services around central Delhi have been restored.

The month behind it: The leak affected two million students. Delhi police hospitalised a fasting Sonam Wangchuk, clashes injured 180, Rahul Gandhi was detained outside Modi's residence, and the city shut 16 metro stations and suspended mobile internet twice. On Friday, day 25, Modi offered fast-track courts and a tougher law without naming Pradhan. We tracked the week here.

New desk: Pralhad Joshi took charge of the education ministry on Sunday and opened with a review meeting. He continues to hold Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, and New and Renewable Energy.

Back to the test: Modi named Nandan Nilekani, Infosys co-founder and architect of the Aadhaar identity system, to head a six-member task force on examination reform. Members include former ISRO chairman S. Somanath and former Intelligence Bureau director Tapan Deka. Nilekani sat on a Supreme Court-appointed panel in 2019 after alleged irregularities in the Staff Selection Commission's 2017 recruitment exams, and that report was never made public.
sound_smarter: India convened the same expertise in 2019 and never published what it found, which is the gap Nilekani's panel inherits. What differs now is that the Prime Minister announced this one himself after a month of protest, which makes burying the report a political cost he has to absorb personally.
anchor: India's youth protesters won the scalp they wanted.

title: Tiers of joy
text:
More than half of India's exports to America got more expensive. The United States imposed an additional 10% duty on July 23 over forced-labour enforcement, 2.5 points below the level it proposed in June (we covered it here).

The complaint: The United States Trade Representative (USTR) investigated 60 economies under Section 301 of the US Trade Act, 1974, over failures to block imports made with forced labour. USTR says forced-labour goods, singling out cotton from China's Xinjiang, enter India unchecked and then reach the US inside Indian products.

The scope: Roughly 45% of India's exports to the US fall outside the new duty, including generic pharmaceuticals, smartphones, and goods already covered by Section 232 measures on steel, aluminium, and auto parts.

Delhi's move: USTR set 10% for economies that already prohibit forced-labour imports and 12.5% for those that do not, publishing the distinction on June 2. India's Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) notified such a prohibition on July 13, four days after the hearings closed. Nothing stops at the border yet, as the DGFT has still to open investigations and name products (we covered it here).

The company India keeps: Seventeen economies made the 10% tier, among them Bangladesh, Cambodia, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Indonesia, and Malaysia. USTR also exempted certain products of a group that includes Bangladesh and Cambodia, and leaves out India.

The textile bargain: USTR will set up tariff-rate quotas for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia, running an initial three years. Each country's quota depends on how much American cotton and textile input it buys. India is not on the list, and the Commerce Ministry states that it is pursuing the mechanism inside Bilateral Trade Agreement talks.
sound_smarter: Four of India's apparel rivals can now buy cheaper access to the American market by importing American cotton. Washington did not extend the offer to Delhi, so the lower tier the Commerce Ministry is presenting as a win leaves India matching its competitors on the headline rate while they hold a quota India has to now negotiate its way into.
anchor: More than half of India's exports to America

title: Solvent states
text:
India is buying its chemical industry a plumbing upgrade. The Union Cabinet cleared INR 30.3 billion (USD 314 million) on July 24 for three chemical parks under Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojana Rasayan (BHAVYA Rasayan).

The split: The scheme allocates INR 30 billion (USD 311 million) for common infrastructure and utilities inside the parks, with an additional INR 300 million (USD 3 million) earmarked for administration. The scheme runs until 2031, and was announced in the 2026 Union Budget.

The terms: The Centre grants up to INR 10 billion (USD 104 million) per park, conditional on the host state contributing at least INR 5 billion (USD 52 million). States compete for the three slots through a Challenge Route, and each site needs a minimum 8 sq km (2,000 acres) of contiguous, encumbrance-free land. The release does not set out how bids will be scored or who picks the winners.

What gets built: The grant covers shared infrastructure inside each park: common effluent treatment, hazardous waste treatment and disposal, water supply, solvent recovery and distillation, steam networks, interconnected pipelines, and warehousing. The Centre calls the model plug-and-play, and states that it will lower costs, tighten environmental compliance, and help Indian producers substitute imports and move up the value chain.
sound_smarter: The scheme sets two gates and the same states clear both. A host must assemble 2,000 contiguous acres free of encumbrance and find INR 5 billion of its own, which rules out the densely settled, the ecologically constrained, and the fiscally stretched states before a single proposal is judged. A contest presented as open competition is set to hand chemical capacity to the states that already have it.
anchor: India is buying its chemical industry a plumbing

title: UNESCO inscribes Sarnath as India's 45th World Heritage site
text: UNESCO inscribed the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath on the World Heritage List on July 25, 2026, at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan, South Korea. It is India's 45th property on the list. The site covers the Chaukhandi Stupa and the archaeological remains at Sarnath, including the Dhamekh Stupa and the Ashokan Pillar, within Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh. Sarnath is where the Buddha delivered his first sermon in the 6th century BCE, and the Mauryan lion capital excavated there became India's national emblem. India now ranks 6th globally and 2nd in the Asia-Pacific by number of UNESCO World Heritage sites.
anchor: UNESCO inscribes Sarnath as India's 45th World Heritage site

title: India and Israel close second FTA negotiating round
text: India and Israel concluded the second round of negotiations for a proposed free trade agreement (FTA) on July 23, 2026, after four days at New Delhi. Technical teams covered trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade, intellectual property rights, customs procedures, and economic cooperation. The terms of reference signed in November 2025 continue to frame the talks, and both sides committed to an early conclusion without setting a date. Merchandise trade between the two countries stood at USD 3.93 billion in the last financial year.
anchor: India and Israel close second FTA negotiating round

title: The cost of cheating
text:
The Centre introduced a bill in the Lok Sabha to drastically raise penalties and fast-track trials for paper leaks and public exam malpractices on Monday.

Background: The proposed amendments to the 2024 Public Examinations Act double down on offenders following years of high-profile paper leaks that disrupted millions of job-seeking candidates. Most recently, this led to nationwide protests over the alleged National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET-UG) paper leak (we covered the latest developments here).

The deets: Individual cheaters face 5–10 years in prison (up from 3–5) and the maximum fine rising fivefold to INR 50 lakh (~ USD 52 thousand). Complicit service providers would face fines of up to INR 5 crore (~USD 518 thousand) and an 8-year ban from public-examination work, double the current four. Organised offences would carry at least seven years and fines of up to INR 10 crore (~ USD 1 million).

Express lane: Investigations would have to finish within two months, with Courts of Session designated as Special Fast Track Courts running day-to-day trials and a three-month deadline from charge sheet to verdict.
sound_smarter: Stiffer penalties won't solve a problem rooted in institutional failure and extreme desperation. Millions of youths spend their prime years retaking exams for a shot at a secure job, and the 2024 law already made paper leaks non-bailable but still we see cheating. Increasing fines does little when the testing agencies themselves remain untouched and unexamined.
anchor: The Centre introduced a bill in the Lok

title: On your own watch
text:
India has summoned both sides of the Ukraine war. On Monday, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) called in Ukraine's ambassador Oleksandr Polishchuk over the attack on MV Omorfi, which killed an Indian national on July 18.

What the ministry said: The MEA condemned attacks on commercial shipping in the strongest terms, citing the effect on safety of navigation, freedom of navigation, and international commerce. Polishchuk was asked to tell Kyiv that such actions are "unacceptable and must be avoided". The release does not name Ukraine as responsible for the strike. New Delhi had called in Russian chargé d'affaires Vladimir Ladanov on July 21 over the strike on MV Golden Leo, which killed four Indians leaving Odesa (we covered it here).

The advisory, a day earlier: On July 26, the MEA warned that the security situation around the Black Sea remains "highly volatile", with commercial vessels facing missile and drone attacks. Incidents have risen since April 2026, killing five Indians. Sailors are told to weigh the risks before accepting assignments, and to obtain the vessel's route, ports of call, security arrangements, insurance coverage, and emergency response procedures from employers. Contracts should cover medical care, evacuation, repatriation, and compensation.

The Hormuz precedent: On July 15, the Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) barred shipowners, ship managers, and recruitment firms from deploying Indian seafarers on any vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz until further orders (we covered it here). The same regulator's Black Sea circular, dated July 23, carries no equivalent restriction.
sound_smarter: India keeps losing sailors to wars it has stayed out of, and protests to four governments have not stopped the count from escalating. New Delhi is at the ceiling of what diplomacy can do here, so it has shifted to what it can control. It has told its seafarers the Black Sea is dangerous enough to turn the work down, and for those who take the assignment anyway, their safety is now their own to manage.
anchor: India has summoned both sides of the Ukraine

title: Not my blend
text:
A Union minister is suing three American platforms over AI fakes of himself. On Monday, the Bombay High Court granted Nitin Gadkari leave to sue Meta, Google, X, and unnamed accounts over deepfakes he says brand him the architect and beneficiary of India's ethanol-blending programme.

The ask: Gadkari has flagged at least 24 posts as defamatory and is seeking INR 11 crore (USD 1.14 million) in damages, plus their removal. His filings allege the posts were published maliciously and without any basis, accusing him of corruption, nepotism, and abuse of office. He says the suit is confined to fabricated claims and does not touch criticism of his record.

Not my portfolio: Gadkari says that despite holding the Road Transport and Highways portfolio since 2014, he has no role in decisions on E20, the 20 per cent ethanol-blended petrol standard. He argues the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas administers the Ethanol Blending Programme, launched in 2003, and issues its own statements on progress.

On record: Gadkari has been the policy's most vocal public defender. He told the Lok Sabha in December 2025 that blending had saved over INR 1.40 lakh crore (USD 14.5 billion) in foreign exchange, signed rules for 100 per cent ethanol fuel in June, and this month dared critics to name a single vehicle harmed by E20.

Street pressure: The Centre ruled out any return to E10 last week (we covered it here). The suit lands six days before Delhi's transport unions are due to march on Parliament over E20, on August 4.
sound_smarter: Gadkari's defence is technically sound but strategically thin. A year spent claiming credit for E20's savings and daring critics to prove harm built the public association the deepfakes now exploit. A favourable order can remove the posts; it cannot undo the ownership of the policy he spent that year building in public.
anchor: A Union minister is suing three American platforms

title: Gyan Bharatam logs 11.9 million manuscripts for AI digitisation
text: Gyan Bharatam, the Ministry of Culture's flagship manuscripts mission, has logged more than 11.9 million texts, through a national survey documenting holdings, repositories, and custodians across every state and union territory. The mission's web portal applies artificial intelligence (AI) to make them searchable, translatable, and easier to study online, combining optical character recognition, handwritten text recognition, script identification, semantic search, and machine translation. Three tools sit on it: Gyan Mitram for interpretation and exploration, Pandulipi Darpan for transliteration and translation of uploaded pages, and BharatiyaGPT, which takes text, audio, and voice queries through a Talk to Manuscript feature.
anchor: Gyan Bharatam logs 11.9 million manuscripts for AI digitisation

title: Sight unseen
text:
India's Supreme Court has ordered every under-18 protester released, barring coercive action against demonstrators and requiring police to preserve all footage of the crackdown.

The order: Chief Justice Surya Kant told authorities to keep every recording from drones, body cameras, and closed-circuit television, and to hold protesters' personal data without publishing it. Kant is the judge whose comparison of unemployed youth to cockroaches gave the movement its name. He was hearing petitions from students and activists alleging that police and paramilitary forces used excess force and pellet guns.

The pellet trail: The Rapid Action Force (RAF), the federal anti-riot unit deployed at Jantar Mantar, issued pellet guns to at least a dozen personnel on the morning of July 20, according to an internal inquiry. The force stopped using them on July 23, once the allegations surfaced. Delhi Police have denied issuing them at all. The RAF sits under separate central command.

A second front: Student activist Aishe Ghosh is separately pressing the Delhi High Court to declare the surveillance unconstitutional and have the data destroyed. Demonstrators had photographed a police van, branded Ikshana, mounted with 360-degree cameras. India currently has no law governing police use of facial recognition.

Where it stands: The protests ended on July 25 after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned and the Centre met the movement's three remaining demands: reform of the exam system, withdrawal of the police cases filed against protesters, and compensation for the families of students who died by suicide after the leaks. The Cockroach Janta Party says hundreds of students have since been arrested across several states, in breach of that commitment. The party has threatened to resume the protests unless the cases are dropped, and says its members remain under surveillance.
sound_smarter: Top-level political concessions rarely dismantle youth-led movements while core issues of reform remain unresolved. Although recent government gestures have helped calm immediate tensions, a lack of swift, tangible progress could easily reignite protests.
anchor: India's Supreme Court has ordered every under-18 protester

title: IT ministry summons Meta after Modi's video briefly removed
text: Facebook briefly removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's July 23 video message on exam paper leaks, showing Indian users a notice that access had been withheld in the region following a legal request. Meta, Facebook’s parent company, restored the post, apologised, and attributed the takedown to a technical glitch in its automated filters. According to reports, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has since summoned Meta's global affairs chief Joel Kaplan. Delhi Police ordered platforms last week to remove around 450 posts targeting Modi during the protests.
anchor: IT ministry summons Meta after Modi's video briefly removed

title: India runs first direct container freight train into Nepal
text: India’s first direct commercial container freight train to Nepal has reached Biratnagar, Nepal’s industrial hub near the border with Bihar, from Kolkata Port. The 40-wagon train, carrying canola, travelled under the revised India–Nepal Rail Transit Protocol without requiring transshipment at the border. The service uses the Jogbani–Biratnagar broad-gauge link inaugurated in 2023 and follows a revised bilateral agreement signed in November 2025. New Delhi expects the direct route to reduce cargo handling, transit times and logistics costs.
anchor: India runs first direct container freight train into Nepal

title: The speed test
text:
The Lok Sabha has put paper-leak trials on a clock. It passed the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026 by voice vote on Wednesday, the same day a fast-track court took the first chargesheet in the exam-leak investigation on record.

The route to appeal: Appeals against a Special Fast Track Court order will go only to the High Court, heard by a bench of two judges and disposed of within three months. No other appeal or revision is available. The higher penalties, the two-month investigation limit, and the three-month trial deadline came with the bill's introduction on Monday (we covered it here). The bill still needs the Rajya Sabha and presidential assent.

The test case: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) charged 13 people on Tuesday over the leak of the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) paper, among them three subject experts, two people linked to coaching centres, middlemen, and candidates who gained from it. All 13 are in judicial custody. Special Judge Anu Grover Baliga took the chargesheet on record at Rouse Avenue on Wednesday, noting that the witness statements and the lists of documents and articles had not come with it. The CBI cited 360 witnesses, 422 documents, and 43 material objects, and said the full record runs to about 20,000 pages, still being scanned, which then has to be supplied to each accused. It has three days. The court considers the chargesheet on August 3.
sound_smarter: The complexity and scale of this case make a three-month deadline very tight. But with political pressure mounting and the threat of renewed protests, the government is likely to push this case along.
anchor: The Lok Sabha has put paper-leak trials on

title: Clearing the ground
text:
India's longest insurgency has no leadership left. Security forces arrested Misir Besra, the last absconding member of the Communist Party of India (Maoist) politburo, in Jharkhand on Tuesday.

What it was about: The insurgency began in 1967 with a peasant uprising in Naxalbari, a West Bengal village that gave the movement its Naxal name. The state crushed that first wave within a few years and the movement splintered. It regrouped through a forested belt across eastern and central India, drawing its cadre largely from tribal communities with grievances over land, access to forests, and displacement by mining. That belt holds much of India's iron ore. Its two largest armed groups merged in 2004 to form the Communist Party of India (Maoist). The violence peaked in 2010, when more than a thousand civilians and security personnel were killed.

The man and the hunt: Besra sat on both the politburo and the central committee, the party's two top decision-making bodies, and carried a bounty of more than INR 10 million (USD 104,000). He had been in the field since the early 1980s. State police and the Central Reserve Police Force's Commando Battalion for Resolute Action flushed him out of the Saranda forest in West Singhbhum in Jharkhand.

The Centre's ledger: Home Minister Amit Shah declared the country free of Maoism from Bastar in May (we covered it here). The Home Ministry told the Rajya Sabha on Wednesday that no district is now classed as Naxal-affected, down from eight in December 2025. Thirty-seven cleared districts sit on a watch list the Centre calls Legacy and Thrust, where security and development spending continues. Two-thirds of the security camps in cleared areas are staying put. The single district still listed as a District of Concern is West Singhbhum, the district Besra was taken from.
sound_smarter: No company was willing to commit billions to a mine in a place with no roads, where it could not keep its staff safe. That has changed. The roads are built, the security camps are staying, and the men who ran the insurgency are dead, jailed, or surrendered. Mining companies will start looking at this land. The people living on it now hold title deeds, so when they need to object, they can do it in court instead of the forest.
anchor: India's longest insurgency has no leadership left. Security

title: Fast track, same track
text:
India’s tougher anti-paper-leak bill is one signature away from becoming law.

Across the line: The Rajya Sabha passed the amendment on Thursday, a day after the Lok Sabha (We covered the tougher penalties, compressed timelines and the ongoing NEET case here). It now requires presidential assent.

Head start: The government says six special fast-track courts are already operating, with more planned. But the bill does not create a new judicial system. It requires every state and union territory to designate an existing Sessions Court and appoint special prosecutors.
sound_smarter: The bill nationalises the promise but localises the burden. Calling existing Sessions Courts “fast track” changes which cases jump the queue in India’s overburdened court system; it does not add judges. New Delhi gets credit for speed, while states and high courts absorb the caseload, and the blame if other trials slow down.
anchor: India’s tougher anti-paper-leak bill is one signature away

title: Watt a waste
text:
Transmission bottlenecks forced India’s grid to waste over 8,000 GWh – or 11% – of its solar output from April to June, according to deputy power minister Shripad Yesso Naik.

Bottlenecked sun: About 12 GW of India’s 162 GW solar fleet cannot run at full capacity, while another 21 GW relies on temporary grid hookups while dedicated lines are built.

Summertime squeeze: The massive curtailments occurred just as scorching heatwaves drove air conditioning use and electricity demand to record highs.

The root cause: Solar parks are being commissioned far faster than utilities can construct high-voltage transmission lines to evacuate the power. That structural delay threatens New Delhi’s ambitious target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity. Earlier this year, the Central Transmission Utility (CTUIL) admitted it lacks the infrastructure for nearly half of the 130 GW of connectivity applications in Rajasthan, India’s solar powerhouse (we covered it here). New Delhi is deploying an USD 83 billion transmission roadmap through 2036 to address the gap between generation and grid capacity.

Developer danger: Curtailments directly undercut developer revenues, threatening capital inflows right as India aims to expand clean capacity from 296 GW to 500 GW by 2030.
sound_smarter: Like many countries, India's energy transition is no longer constrained by capital or power supply, but by transmission capacity. Because high-potential wind and solar sites are often far from major demand centers, and existing infrastructure was not designed for intermittent power, substantial investment in transmission hardware and energy storage are needed.
anchor: Transmission bottlenecks forced India’s grid to waste over

title: Set sail insured
text:
India is bringing maritime risk onto its own balance sheet. New India Assurance issued the first sovereign-backed Protection and Indemnity (P&I) policy under the Bharat Maritime Insurance Pool (BMIP) to Shipping Corporation of India on Thursday.

Cover story: Hull insurance protects the ship; cargo insurance protects its goods. P&I covers third-party liabilities including crew injuries, cargo damage, pollution and wreck removal. The policy provides up to USD 1.5 billion in cover.

From plan to policy: The Cabinet approved BMIP in April after the West Asian war drove insurers from Gulf routes (we covered it here). Since May, the pool has issued 1,608 cargo and hull war-risk policies. The government says premiums have fallen 35–40% from the conflict peak, without disclosing its benchmark.

Risk returns: War-risk premiums on some Red Sea routes have climbed to 1–2% of vessel value following renewed Houthi attacks.
sound_smarter: BMIP is trying to make maritime chokepoints insurable. Domestic insurers absorb manageable claims, while the sovereign guarantee carries the catastrophic layer. India is replacing dependence on foreign insurers with dependence on its own balance sheet.
anchor: India is bringing maritime risk onto its own

title: The long churn
text:
The Centre is paying to hunt for oil and gas under India's seabed. The Union Cabinet approved Samudra Manthan, the National Offshore Exploration Scheme, on Friday, with an outlay of INR 840.84 billion (USD 8.81 billion) running to FY 2030-31.

Where it goes: Seismic surveys across India's offshore basins, deepwater and ultra-deepwater exploratory drilling, and scientific drilling in frontier basins. Funds have also been allocated for shared production and evacuation infrastructure, plus a manufacturing and services zone for offshore equipment.

The churn: Prime Minister Modi trailed the scheme from the Red Fort on Independence Day 2025, naming it for the myth in which the gods churn the ocean for the nectar of immortality. With the scheme, India aims for more than 600 million tonnes of oil equivalent in fresh reserves. India's crude output last year was 28 million tonnes.

Why the Centre is paying: Almost all offshore acreage is already open to explorers, the contract framework has been rewritten, and the National Data Repository of exploration data is built out. Import dependence still climbed to a record 88.7% in FY 2025-26 on provisional figures, the Petroleum Ministry told the upper house of parliament on July 27, up from 85.5% four years earlier.
sound_smarter: Open acreage has been available for years. Private explorers would not fund the surveys and dry holes that come before a commercial find, and Samudra Manthan moves that bill onto the state. The next licensing round will open with the mapping and viability already paid for. The scheme aims to find reserves – the import bill is settled in barrels produced, and those are years apart.
anchor: The Centre is paying to hunt for oil

title: Surface tension
text:
The Centre wants eight times more solar floating on India's reservoirs. The Union Cabinet cleared the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY) on Friday, an INR 50.7 billion (USD 531 million) scheme for 5,000 MW of floating solar photovoltaic (FSPV) capacity with storage attached.

The terms: Developers get INR 10 million (USD 104,800) per MW, paid only after commissioning, plus up to INR 5 million (USD 52,400) per project for feasibility work including surveys that require studying the floor of water bodies. Every project carries at least two hours of storage. Sanctions run to FY 2030-31, with money flowing to FY 2032-33.

What exists: The National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE) puts India's reservoir potential at about 102 GW. Roughly 700 MW is built, most of it in the Omkareshwar park on the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh, awarded at 600 MW in 2022 and generating 278 MW. NISE’s assessment has been unable to arrive at India-specific cost figures, instead citing a 2021 United States benchmark that puts floating plants about 25% above ground-mounted ones.

The ask and the award: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) Secretary Santosh Kumar Sarangi told a Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) event in December 2025 that the ministry had sought INR 70 to 80 billion in viability gap funding for a floating solar and storage scheme. Friday's approval came in at INR 50.7 billion, paid as a flat grant per MW.

The wider fleet: India's solar capacity stands at 162 GW. Between April and June, grid operators curtailed 8,133 gigawatt-hours of solar output, around 11% of the total, because transmission could not carry it (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: The five gigawatts barely register against total electricity generation, but what is more important is what comes attached. At midday every solar plant in a region generates at once, the power lines run out of room, and the extra electricity is thrown away. Two hours of storage lets a project hold that surplus and sell it after dark, and this scheme will be judged on how much power India stops throwing away.
anchor: The Centre wants eight times more solar floating

title: Crop and paste
text:
India has locked in five more years of farmer payments. The Cabinet approved INR 3.16 trillion (USD 33.1 billion) to continue the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN) scheme through FY2030–31.

What is PM-KISAN: Launched in 2019, it is New Delhi’s nationwide income-support programme for eligible landholding farmer families. Each receives INR 6,000 (USD 63) annually through three direct bank transfers to help cover agricultural expenses.

Scale of delivery: The scheme has transferred over INR 4.47 trillion (USD 46.9 billion) through 23 instalments. Its latest payment reached more than 94.9 million farmers, while women account for nearly one-quarter of beneficiaries.

Government’s case: New Delhi says the money supports purchases of seeds, fertiliser and equipment while reducing informal borrowing. A NITI Aayog evaluation found that over 92% of surveyed beneficiaries used it for agricultural purposes.
sound_smarter: The five-year allocation looks transformative, but each family still receives only INR 500 (USD 5.25) per month, which is the same nominal payment offered in 2019. Inflation will keep shrinking what each instalment can actually buy. However, the scheme’s political value lies not only in the money transferred, but in maintaining a direct payment channel to nearly 95 million rural households.
anchor: India has locked in five more years of

title: Maldivian payments system goes live with UPI
text: The Maldives Monetary Authority (MMA) switched on a live link between its instant payment system, Favara, and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), on July 30. Senders in the Maldives can now move money to UPI-enabled bank accounts in India in real time, initiating in Maldivian rufiyaa and landing in Indian rupees. In the first phase, the corridor is restricted to person-to-person transfers.
anchor: Maldivian payments system goes live with UPI

title: India-China border trade resumes at Nathu La after six years
text: India and China reopened border trade through the Nathu La pass in Sikkim on Saturday, ending a suspension of more than six years. The list of 36 approved commodities is unchanged, and each registered trader is capped at INR 200,000 (USD 2,100) a day. Trade stopped in early 2020 during the pandemic and stayed shut through the Galwan standoff.
anchor: India-China border trade resumes at Nathu La after six years

title: Power regulator proposes transmission fee waivers for delayed clean energy projects
text: India’s power regulator has proposed reinstating interstate transmission fee waivers for renewable energy and battery storage projects stalled by grid delays (we covered the impacts of transmission bottlenecks here and here). The draft policy reverses a planned phase-out to assist developers who missed deadlines, provided they hold long-term power sale contracts through 2026.
anchor: Power regulator proposes transmission fee waivers for delayed clean energy projects

title: Out of sight
text:
India wants every new vehicle on its roads talking to the ones beside it. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has issued a draft notification amending the Central Motor Vehicles Rules to require Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication systems in all new two- and three-wheelers, passenger vehicles, and goods vehicles.

How it works: Each fitted vehicle broadcasts its position, speed, direction, and braking status to every other fitted vehicle within a few hundred metres. Because it works over radio, it reaches vehicles that cameras and radar cannot see, including those behind a truck or around a bend.

Two dates: The draft proposes that vehicles manufactured on or after October 1, 2027 that carry a V2V system must conform to India’s Automotive Industry Standard (AIS) 230. From October 1, 2028, fitment becomes compulsory. Comments on the draft will be examined after 30 days, with a final notification to follow.

What the standard covers: AIS-230 sets minimum requirements for the hardware, its positioning accuracy, and its cybersecurity, and specifies Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything (C-V2X), which runs on the 5.9 GHz band that the Department of Telecommunications had earlier exempted from licensing. It enables safety functions including emergency brake alert, forward collision warning, wrong-way driving, and emergency vehicle alert.

The casualty base: India recorded 172,890 road deaths in 2023, with two-wheeler riders accounting for 44.8 per cent of them, the largest share of any vehicle category. Last year, two-wheelers made up 21.7 million of the 28.3 million vehicles sold domestically.

Not the only two-wheeler rule: The same day, the ministry proposed a first regulatory framework for two-wheeled road ambulances, adopting standard AIS-209 for L2-category machines fitted with a stretcher or patient-conveyance unit, also from October 1, 2027. These are aimed at rural, remote, and hilly areas where conventional ambulances struggle to reach, with each state deciding where they may operate.
sound_smarter: The crashes that kill riders are usually the ones they never see coming: a truck turning across a blind curve or a car braking three vehicles ahead. Helmets, seat belts, and airbags all work on what a crash does to the body once it has happened, and this is the first Indian mandate aimed at the information a rider is missing before it does.
anchor: India wants every new vehicle on its roads

title: Book ’em, cloud
text:
India is dragging a 135-year-old banking evidence law into the cloud. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman introduced the Bankers’ Books Evidence Bill, 2026 in the Lok Sabha on Monday. It would replace the 1891 Act governing how bank records are used in legal proceedings.

What changes: Existing law already lets certified copies serve as evidence without producing the originals. The Bill would extend the same treatment to digital, virtual, cloud, backup, and disaster-recovery records.

Proof standard: Banks must certify records came from regularly operated systems, were handled by authorised personnel and show no detected tampering. Certificates may use manual, digital or electronic signatures.

Wider reach: Government may extend the framework to other financial entities by notification. It remains a pending bill and would take effect only after passage and notification.
sound_smarter: This is long overdue. Since most banking processes are now digital, allowing electronic records would make evidence collection much faster and easier.
anchor: India is dragging a 135-year-old banking evidence law

title: Goyal calls for doubling India-Uzbekistan trade in three years
text: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal called for doubling bilateral trade with Uzbekistan within three years, addressing the India-Uzbekistan Business Forum in New Delhi on Monday. He put current trade at approximately USD 1.5 billion and named mining, textiles, pharmaceuticals, food processing, and digital public infrastructure as sectors for co-investment, citing the Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT) which entered into force in May 2025. The forum ran alongside the visit of Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov, in India from August 2 to 5, who called on President Droupadi Murmu at Rashtrapati Bhavan earlier in the day. Saidov also met External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar at Hyderabad House later on Monday.
anchor: Goyal calls for doubling India-Uzbekistan trade in three years

title: A distancing act
text:
The Ministry of External Affairs said it has no involvement in Sheikh Hasina's planned August 5 virtual address from New Delhi, a day before the ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister’s first public appearance since fleeing Dhaka in 2024.

The disavowal: Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the event, organised by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia, is a private affair the government neither endorses nor is involved in. Hasina, sentenced to death in November 2025 over her crackdown on the uprising, will address the event by video.

Dhaka's pushback: Bangladesh had asked New Delhi to clarify its stance, warning that hosting a fugitive's political activity could hurt improving ties. Dhaka's information adviser separately warned Bangladeshi media against publicising the speech, citing a December 2024 order by Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) barring outlets from broadcasting her statements.

Same briefing, different signal: Jaiswal also confirmed Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has been invited to the outreach session of September's BRICS Summit as chair of BIMSTEC (Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation). India had earlier extended an invitation in February, addressed to Rahman in his official capacity as prime minister.

Unfinished business: Dhaka still wants Hasina extradited. India has kept the request "under examination" since Bangladesh's first note verbale in December 2024, citing due judicial and legal process without committing to an outcome (we covered it here). Hasina states she plans to return around December to face trial.
sound_smarter: India can disavow Hasina publicly while courting Rahman’s government with two separate invitations because that compartmentalisation only has to hold until December. Her own plan to return and face trial buys India relief from the immediate dilemma, but the deeper trust deficit stays exactly where it was.
anchor: The Ministry of External Affairs said it has

title: Red tape on a diet
text:
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman introduced the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, on Tuesday to lure foreign capital and boost local manufacturing.

Electronics extension: Foreign suppliers delivering machinery and tooling to Indian factories get their tax holiday extended through 2040-41, a long-term win for tech giants like Apple. The tax holiday was initially valid only until 2031.

Cloud expansion: Global cloud providers using Indian data centres bypass multi-layer approval red tape, while facilities gain flexibility to operate on a leased basis.

Fund manager homecoming: Skilled fund managers can relocate to India without subjecting their entire offshore fund to local corporate taxation.

REIT reset: Tax-free dividend perks for real estate investment trust and infrastructure investment trust investors are restored, protecting yields even as operating firms transition to the new tax regime.
sound_smarter: Structural, long-term regulatory certainty and perks are key to attracting foreign investment, especially those in manufacturing that take years to become profitable. New Delhi is quietly dismantling the bureaucratic headaches that keep capital hesitant to invest in India by solving niche friction points around attractive industries.

title: Supreme Court orders time-bound fixes to curb digital arrest scams
text: The Supreme Court has directed the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to frame a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) on mule accounts within four weeks, as part of fresh nationwide directions to combat digital arrest scams. States and Union Territories must operationalise grievance redressal and money restoration modules under the Ministry of Home Affairs' cyber fraud portal, and set up their State Cyber Crime Coordination Centres within the same window. The Centre's Inter-Departmental Committee has also been asked to examine a shared liability and victim compensation framework.
anchor: Supreme Court orders time-bound fixes to curb digital arrest scams

title: ICAR unveils India's first indigenous African Swine Fever vaccine
text: The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) has developed India's first indigenous vaccine against African Swine Fever. Built by ICAR's National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (ICAR-NIHSAD) in Bhopal, the vaccine uses the widely available MA-104 cell line and is recommended for pigs above eight weeks as a single dose with a booster after 14 days. ASF has spread across India since 2020.
anchor: ICAR unveils India's first indigenous African Swine Fever vaccine

title: Stock options
text:
The government on Wednesday operationalised a framework letting foreign-invested e-commerce companies hold inventory in India for the first time, but only if every unit is bound for export.

The plumbing: Companies must route exports through a registered Exporter-on-Record (EOR), which buys from Indian Sellers-on-Record (SORs) only after an overseas order is confirmed, then exports the goods under its own name. The EOR handles customs paperwork and destination-country compliance, and can also take on testing, certification, packaging, labelling, and returns for sellers who want it.

Who benefits: Amazon and Walmart-owned Flipkart, India's two dominant foreign-invested platforms, are the obvious winners. An Amazon spokesperson linked the move to the company's USD 80 billion cumulative export target for 2030.

The fine print: This follows an earlier amendment to India's foreign direct investment (FDI) policy and applies to exports alone; the domestic ban on foreign-owned inventory-led e-commerce is unchanged. Export inventory must be kept in a separate, digitally tracked repository and cannot be diverted into the Indian market.

Seller protections: EORs must pay Indian sellers on a fixed timeline regardless of whether the overseas buyer has paid, pass through export rebates in proportion to each seller's free-on-board (FOB) value, and give sellers visibility into final sale prices, order status, and shipment tracking. Returned goods must be re-exported, sent back to the seller, or disposed of under the rules, and EORs face annual compliance certification.
sound_smarter: The domestic inventory ban has been the single most sensitive line in India's e-commerce policy for a decade, the rule that stops Amazon and Flipkart from taking direct stock control away from small retailers. Rather than touch that fight, Delhi has handed them the same right pointed strictly outward, trading access to their global fulfilment and compliance infrastructure for an export push that costs it nothing at home.
anchor: The government on Wednesday operationalised a framework letting

title: Breaking the zero-fee habit
text:
New Delhi is moving to end the era of free digital payments. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman tabled amendments to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act in parliament on Tuesday, creating the legal framework to reintroduce a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) – a processing fee merchants pay to banks and payment service providers – on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions.

The shift: UPI has been a merchant-fee-free zone since 2019, turning it into a global juggernaut that processed transactions worth INR 30 trillion (~ USD 314 billion) in July. But it’s a financial black hole for providers like PhonePe and Google Pay. Industry players argue the current model is unsustainable; they need transaction fees to cover infrastructure costs and drive future innovation.

The proposal: Nothing is set in stone, but officials are weighing a 0.3% to 0.5% MDR on transactions above INR 2,000 (~ USD 2.10) for merchants with annual turnover exceeding INR 15 million (~ USD 158 thousand). In contrast, credit card MDR can reach as high as 3%, whereas debit card fees are capped by regulations at a maximum of 0.9%.

Follow the money: Per Jefferies, an investment bank, while transactions over INR 2,000 account for only 4% of volume, they represent 67% of total value. This shift could unlock a revenue pool of up to INR 100 billion (~ USD 1 million) for the payments ecosystem.
sound_smarter: This shift marks the maturation of the UPI model, transitioning it from a state-subsidized growth phase into a self-sustaining commercial ecosystem. However, it will be a long journey. Wary of sparking a consumer and small-business backlash, New Delhi will likely proceed cautiously by targeting low-volume, high-value transactions to insulate the broader market just like its current proposal.
anchor: New Delhi is moving to end the era

title: Reverse gear
text:
India's carmakers said the mandatory fuel was corroding their cars, then backed off. On August 5, the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) withdrew a letter that had told the government contaminated ethanol-blended petrol was corroding vehicle parts, hours after it reached the media and set off a consumer backlash.

The warning: In a July 28 letter to the petroleum ministry, SIAM said its members were tracing a sharp rise in part failures to corrosion from high chloride levels in E20, the petrol blended with 20 per cent ethanol. The failing components were fuel injectors, fuel pumps, and exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) valves. The letter put chloride at up to 500 parts per million (ppm) in fuel drawn from affected vehicles and up to 350 ppm at the pump, against the Centre's precautionary ceiling of 3 ppm for chloride in blending ethanol. SIAM also flagged excess moisture it said could stall a car straight after fuelling, and asked for mandatory chloride limits and tougher checks across the retail network.

The retraction: SIAM did not take back the contamination claim. It said the reported figures needed authentication through wider data collection, called the letter part of routine technical deliberations with oil marketing companies and testing agencies, and pulled the communication pending that work, without saying when it would finish. It also reaffirmed its support for the E20 programme and said existing checks already met the industry's needs. Its members include Maruti Suzuki, Tata Motors, Toyota, and Mercedes-Benz.

The politics: E20 replaced the older E10 blend nationwide in 2025, five years ahead of a 2030 target, as the Centre moved to cut the oil import bill of a country that buys more than 85 per cent of its crude abroad. E20-ready cars reached showrooms only in 2023, so most vehicles on the road were built for weaker blends, and the rollout drew protests, court cases, and demands for a lower-blend option, with owners blaming E20 for corrosion and lost mileage (we covered the backlash here and the rollout here). The Centre has already mounted a defence: at a July 4 press conference, Maruti Suzuki reported no corrosion or wear across more than 15 million older, non-E20-certified cars in its service data, and Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri called the opposition a misinformation campaign. The ministry says only two of more than 2,000 samples showed chloride contamination.
sound_smarter: SIAM pulled its figures for validation without recanting the corrosion claim behind them, so it bought time rather than conceding the point. What it did not take back is the demand for tighter fuel-quality standards, and if the Centre wants to keep pushing its flagship programme, that is where it will have to focus.
anchor: India's carmakers said the mandatory fuel was corroding

title: A not so safe harbour
text:
A parliamentary panel gave Zuckerberg three days to apologise or lose India's legal shield. Government sources say the Meta chief executive conveyed an apology covering child sexual abuse material, deepfake content, and operational errors on the company's platforms.

The demand: The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology met on August 3 and sought an unconditional apology from Zuckerberg within three days over Facebook's brief removal of a video posted by Prime Minister Modi. Failing that, it said, the immunity under safe harbour regulations "may be withdrawn and action taken against him as a publisher". We covered the takedown and the ministry summons here.

The gap: Meta’s apology, as reported, names no video. Chairperson of the Parliamentary Standing Committee, Nishikant Dubey, had called the removal an attack on democracy and said it could not be dismissed as a technical error. Meta has issued no public confirmation, and Zuckerberg has released no statement of his own.

The legal theory: Safe harbour shields platforms from liability for content posted by users. The committee argues that removing the Prime Minister's post was a publisher's act. A Meta delegation led by chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan has since met ministry secretary S. Krishnan, where officials said the company no longer qualifies as an intermediary because it selects who receives content.
sound_smarter: Apologising for the takedown itself would concede the editorial judgment the publisher argument requires, so Meta offered regret for everything else instead. Child safety also gives the Centre a far stronger public case for stripping safe harbour than a removed video of PM Modi ever could.
anchor: A parliamentary panel gave Zuckerberg three days to

title: ONGC eyes Venezuelan operatorship, restores Sakhalin-1 stake
text: State-owned Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) hopes to sign agreements soon to operate two Venezuelan oil projects under the country's new petroleum law. Its overseas arm holds 40 per cent of the San Cristobal field and, alongside other Indian companies, 18 per cent of Carabobo-1. ONGC would take over operatorship from PDVSA, Venezuela's state oil company, after previously limiting activity over sanctions risks. Separately, the company regained its 20 per cent stake in Russia's Sakhalin-1 project last December after four years, lifting quarterly revenue from the asset to roughly INR 10 billion (USD 105 million), from INR 5 billion to 6 billion earlier. ONGC retained the stake by paying into the project's abandonment fund in rubles using dividends frozen in Russia.
anchor: ONGC eyes Venezuelan operatorship, restores Sakhalin-1 stake

title: New captain, same headwinds
text:
Air India's turnaround has a new chief for its hardest stretch yet. On Wednesday, Air India appointed former Ethiopian Airlines chief Tewolde Gebremariam as its chief executive, concluding a months-long search for someone to steer the loss-making carrier.

Crash-tested: Tewolde spent 11 years running Ethiopian Airlines, building Africa's largest carrier and steering it through the COVID-19 pandemic. Ethiopian Airlines survived the pandemic without needing a state bailout, and under Tewolde, revenue more than quadrupled and the fleet nearly tripled.

The in-tray: Air India is still absorbing the June 2025 crash of a Boeing 787 in Ahmedabad, which killed 260 people and drew intense regulatory scrutiny. Air India Group posted a record loss of more than USD 2 billion in fiscal 2025-26, up from about USD 1.13 billion a year earlier, and has not turned a profit since Tata regained control in 2022. Regulators have since reprimanded it over safety lapses, including operating an Airbus A320 on multiple flights without a valid airworthiness review certificate.

The route squeeze: Since April 2025, Pakistan has barred Indian carriers from its airspace, and the war in West Asia has deepened the disruption, forcing Air India onto longer routes, flight cancellations, and cutbacks on some of its most valuable international services. Foreign rivals have used the opening to expand further into the Indian market.

The handover: Tewolde succeeds Campbell Wilson, who resigned in April after four years overseeing the Vistara merger and a fleet overhaul. Tata Sons own about 75 per cent of Air India, with Singapore Airlines holding the rest, and Chairman N. Chandrasekaran has said the turnaround could take up to a decade. Singapore Airlines similarly characterises Air India’s transformation as a “long game.”
sound_smarter: While geopolitical tensions remain the primary drag on Air India's performance, these external factors lie completely outside Tewolde's control. Instead, he is likely to focus on the harder internal work: rebuilding the airline’s reputation following a fatal crash and shifting its corporate culture. Though less headline-grabbing, these overhauls are essential for building a foundation for sustainable growth once routes can be restored.
anchor: Air India's turnaround has a new chief for

title: From muck to money
text:
India wants its cow dung and crop waste to start displacing imported gas. On August 6, the Union Cabinet approved GOBARdhan, a national compressed biogas scheme worth INR 237 billion (USD 2.5 billion), aiming to raise domestic output nearly tenfold over the coming decade.

The scheme: GOBARdhan, whose name plays on the Hindi word for cow dung, is formally the National Unified Scheme for Compressed Biogas and runs from the 2026-27 financial year to 2035-36 under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. Compressed biogas (CBG), made from crop residue, cattle dung, press mud, and municipal waste, is chemically close to natural gas and travels through the same pipelines. India imports close to half its gas, and the Centre wants natural gas to supply 15 per cent of the energy mix by 2030, up from about 6 per cent today.

Assured demand: The core of the scheme is offtake certainty. It guarantees producers a buyer by tying purchases to a notified blending obligation that requires City Gas Distribution companies, which pipe gas to homes and vehicles, to take a rising share of CBG: 3 per cent in 2026-27, 4 per cent the next year, and 5 per cent from 2028-29. It also fixes an administered CBG price of INR 2,110 per million British thermal units (BTUs) for at least ten years.

The support: Producers can claim capital assistance of up to INR 20 million for each tonne of daily capacity, alongside a credit-guarantee scheme for smaller firms, funding for pipelines that connect plants to the grid, and a district-level fund to build feedstock and local supply chains.

Starting small: About 200 CBG plants operate today, built under a patchwork of earlier programmes. The largest, the 2018 SATAT scheme (Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation), had targeted 5,000 plants producing 15 million tonnes a year by 2023-24, and delivered only a fraction of that.
sound_smarter: The catch is cost: compressed biogas is costlier than the gas it displaces, so the gap has to be bridged by government support and cost-sharing, which the release spells out in its own note on affordability. That makes GOBARdhan a subsidy for a costlier domestic fuel, and its ambition will hold only as long as the Centre keeps funding the premium.
anchor: India wants its cow dung and crop waste

title: Parliament passes UPI fee bill without debate, RBI flags timing
text: The Lok Sabha passed the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 on Thursday, which amends the Payment and Settlement Systems Act to permit Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) charges on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions (we covered it here). It cleared the Lok Sabha by voice vote without debate, with Opposition MPs' attention on the alleged Ram Mandir donation embezzlement case, and still awaits the Rajya Sabha. The passage came a day after Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra called the MDR discussion "premature." No notification setting an actual fee has been issued yet.
anchor: Parliament passes UPI fee bill without debate, RBI flags timing

title: FCRA bill deferred again, drawing international scrutiny as protests continue
text: The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, which tightens the rules on NGOs' foreign funding, was again not tabled on Thursday, as Opposition MPs continued protests over the alleged Ram Mandir donation embezzlement case and police action against student protesters at Jantar Mantar. Since our last update, opposition has broadened beyond Parliament: Christian organisations, Amnesty International, and the Kerala government have joined Congress in criticising it. Critics also point to the Financial Action Task Force's (FATF) 2024 review, which urged a narrower, risk-based approach, and earlier United Nations (UN) Special Rapporteur warnings on the FCRA. Several organisations have signalled they would challenge the bill in the Supreme Court on constitutional grounds if it passes.
anchor: FCRA bill deferred again, drawing international scrutiny as protests continue

title: Stacking the deck
text:
India's discounted Russian oil habit is about to get pricier. On Saturday, the US Senate passed a bill authorising tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian oil.

The rerun: India was previously hit with a 25% additional levy over its purchases. Delhi called the move unfair given how many other countries also buy Russian exports, and says its energy purchases are guided by energy security needs. Washington separately waived sanctions on Russian crude during an energy crunch after the Strait of Hormuz's near-closure. That waiver has since expired.

The exposure: India is one of five named targets, alongside China, Slovakia, Hungary, and Azerbaijan; sponsors of the bill have framed a high tariff as necessary specifically to discourage Chinese and Indian purchases.

The softening: The bill started as a blanket 500 per cent tariff on any country doing business with Russia's energy sector. What passed the Senate narrows that to the five largest oil and gas importers, with a separate carve-out shielding countries that account for less than 15 per cent of Russia's total gas exports and are actively cutting that share. The US Trade Representative can set the applied tariff anywhere from zero to 100 per cent on the named countries, which will be reassessed every 180 days.

Not law yet: The bill passed the Senate 86-11 and moves next to the House, which is not expected to take it up before early September due to the summer recess. Passage in identical form is the last hurdle before Trump's assent.

Parallel track: India's chief trade negotiator Rajesh Agrawal and a senior US official both called the US-India bilateral trade agreement "effectively complete" in July (we covered it here), but that claim rests on February's interim framework, which the US Supreme Court partly struck down weeks later. The temporary 10 per cent tariff that the court left in place lapsed on July 24, with no replacement agreed.
sound_smarter: Washington doesn’t need this bill to fully bite to be effective. By granting the US Trade Representative discretion over rates, it creates a permanent, oscillating threat that forces Delhi to constantly justify its energy choices to avoid a spike.
anchor: India's discounted Russian oil habit is about to

title: Security in threes
text:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have put collective defence on paper. Signed in Mecca on Friday, the agreement says an armed attack on one will be treated as an attack on all three. The precise military obligations remain undisclosed.

Long in the making: Negotiations began nearly a year ago. The process predates February’s US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which triggered Iranian attacks across the Gulf and severe disruption to regional energy flows.

From two to three: Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed their own defence pact in September 2025. Pakistan has long trained Saudi forces. Turkey now adds NATO’s second-largest military and a defence industry already supplying Saudi drones.

India watching: New Delhi says it is following the agreement closely. It previously warned that Saudi-Pakistani defence cooperation could affect Indian security.
sound_smarter: India's warnings about Saudi-Pakistan defence cooperation predate the Mecca Agreement. What has changed is Turkey's entry, which now gives Pakistan a formal claim on NATO's second-largest military and extensive Turkish drone capacity. New Delhi must now weigh hard military capability alongside Gulf capital in its own security calculus.
