title: Qatar links its post offices to UPI
text: Customers in Qatar can now send money from Qatar Post outlets directly to UPI enabled bank accounts in India. Senders provide the recipient’s UPI ID and identification details, while recipients must activate foreign inward remittances through their UPI app. The service was developed by Qatar Post, India Post, the Universal Postal Union and NPCI International Payments. India Post is working to open similar corridors with other postal operators.
anchor: Qatar links its post offices to UPI

issue_title: Don’t be (that kind of) an influencer
title: Delayed renewable projects can pay to keep grid access
text: India’s power regulator has allowed clean energy developers that miss project deadlines to retain their transmission access by paying INR 1,000 (USD 10.48) per megawatt each day for land or financing delays, or INR 3,000 (USD 31.43) for delayed commercial operations. Developers can receive up to three additional months for land, six for financing and 12 for commissioning. Missing those deadlines could still cost them their grid access and bank guarantees.
anchor: Delayed renewable projects can pay to keep grid access

title: Reelpolitik
text:
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has replaced the architect of its social media dominance. The party has appointed Deepak Mhaskey, a chemistry professor and former spokesperson, as its new social media convenor, ending Amit Malviya's eleven-year run at the helm of its digital operation.

The new man: Mhaskey comes up from Chhattisgarh, where he ran the party's regional social media. Malviya had led the national operation since 2015, perfectly timed with Reliance Jio's launch a year later that collapsed mobile data prices and brought hundreds of millions of Indians online. Under his leadership, the BJP's WhatsApp and Facebook networks reached a scale its rivals could not match.

The reshuffle: This is Nabin's first overhaul since he took over as BJP president in January, and it runs well beyond the digital team. He has made Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal treasurer and dropped Bangalore South MP Tejasvi Surya as youth-wing chief, in favour of Gujarat's Hemang Joshi. Nabin gave no reason for removing Malviya, framing the reshuffle only as a way to strengthen the organisation and give it fresh momentum.

The backdrop: The reset caps a summer in which youth protests drove education minister Dharmendra Pradhan from office over a leaked medical-entrance exam paper. Since then, Modi has posted selfie-style Instagram reels and told his cabinet to be more active on the platforms young Indians use. Gen Z is on course to be one of the largest voting blocs by the 2029 general election.
sound_smarter: The BJP industrialised political social media in India, and for a decade no rival matched its reach. The Cockroach Janata Party erased that edge in weeks, out-posting the party on the platforms it once dominated and driving a sitting minister from office. Removing the man who built that machine is the BJP conceding that it no longer owns the young voter, and it has until 2029 to earn them back.
anchor: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has replaced the

title: Trading up
text:
Kerala’s Vizhinjam port has begun handling India's own imports and exports. On Tuesday, Chief Minister V D Satheesan flagged off the first export containers, moving the deep-water port beyond the transshipment role that it has played since it opened in December 2024.

What changes: India's exporters can now ship directly to overseas markets from Vizhinjam, which sits on one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes, instead of routing cargo through hubs like Colombo, Singapore, and Dubai. The port's first export container, a trial shipment, has already reached Valencia, Spain.

Mission Samudra: Satheesan paired the launch with Mission Samudra, a port-led industrial plan backed by an INR 4 billion (USD 42 million) catalytic fund. It casts Vizhinjam as a port city anchoring a maritime economic region of eight industrial clusters, three new cities, and Kerala's 600-kilometre coastline, and the government projects it will draw more than ten times the public money in private investment by 2031.

The backstory: Vizhinjam is owned by the Kerala government, built under a public-private partnership at INR 88.67 billion (USD 927 million), and operated by Adani Ports. In July, the world's largest shipping line, MSC, bought a 49 per cent stake in the operating company (we covered it here). Satheesan's Congress-led government took office in May, inheriting the port from the Left administration that built it out.
sound_smarter: Kerala's own cashew and spice shipments are too light to justify a deep-water port. The freight that would fill Vizhinjam's berths sits next door in Tamil Nadu, one of India's industrial powerhouses, and Mission Samudra's road and rail links are the bid to pull that cargo.
anchor: Kerala’s Vizhinjam port has begun handling India's own

title: Defence ministry places 405 more items on its domestic production list
text: The Department of Defence Production notified its sixth Positive Indigenisation List, covering components and materials with an estimated business potential of INR 30.7 billion (USD 321 million). It includes 389 items used by defence public sector companies and 16 used by the Coast Guard, spanning aircraft, armoured vehicles, warships, missiles, and defence electronics. Once developed domestically, the items will be bought from Indian suppliers, including smaller businesses.
anchor: Defence ministry places 405 more items on its domestic production list

title: Murmu signs mining tax limits into law
text: President Droupadi Murmu granted assent to the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2026, which bars states from imposing taxes, cesses, or other levies on mineral rights and mineral bearing land except under conditions set by the Centre. Levies not collected before the law takes effect will become invalid, while payments already received by states will not be refunded. The Act overturns a 2024 Supreme Court ruling that let states tax mineral rights, which we covered here.
anchor: Murmu signs mining tax limits into law

title: Clause for concern
text:
Bangladesh wants a binding water guarantee back in its treaty with India. Bangladesh’s Water Resources Minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee said Dhaka would seek a guarantee clause in the renegotiated Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, and was ready to take the dispute to international forums.

The missing clause: The 1996 Ganges Water Sharing Treaty between India and Bangladesh, which expires in December, dropped the minimum-flow guarantee that its 1977 predecessor carried. The earlier treaty had assured Bangladesh a fixed share regardless of how much water India drew upstream, and Dhaka wants it to be restored.

Upstream pressure: Underlying the demand is India's National River Linking Project, which plans to divert Himalayan waters, including the Ganges, towards southwestern India. The links that would affect Ganges flows remain at the feasibility-study stage, held up for years by protected forests along the route and the absence of water-sharing deals with Nepal and Bhutan.

A harder Dhaka: The demand is the latest in a run of tougher signals to New Delhi. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has already made warmer ties conditional, pressing India to extradite ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina (we covered it here). Anee said past relations had leaned on Indian support for one political party over Bangladesh's interests, a clear reference to New Delhi's long alignment with Hasina's Awami League. Dhaka also joined the 1992 United Nations Water Convention in June 2025, the first South Asian country to do so. India is not a signatory, so the treaty gives Dhaka an international platform to press its case but no legal claim over how India uses shared water.
sound_smarter: India has refused to join global water conventions and insists that shared-river disputes stay bilateral. Its disputes are never handed to an outside tribunal – be it the Ganges water treaty or the status of Kashmir. A minimum-flow guarantee won under the threat of a forum would break that rule, and every downstream neighbour would reach for it.
anchor: Bangladesh wants a binding water guarantee back in

title: Hard surface, harder bargain
text:
India has taken America’s countertop tariffs to the WTO. On August 14, New Delhi requested consultations over a US safeguard on quartz surfaces.

Stonewalling: First-year imports face an additional 25 per cent tariff within quota and 50 per cent above it. The US International Trade Commission found rising imports had seriously injured domestic manufacturers. India is not exempt. The Global Trade Research Initiative, a New Delhi-based trade research group, estimates the US bought 72.5 per cent of India's quartz-surface exports in the 2026 financial year, worth USD 233.3 million.

Fourth time lucky?: India previously sought consultations over US tariffs on steel, aluminium, automobiles and copper. Washington rejected them as national-security measures, not safeguards. Quartz is explicitly a safeguard, giving India cleaner procedural ground.

Deal, no deal: February’s interim trade framework remains unsigned after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s global tariffs. Washington has since added forced-labour tariffs and pursued an overcapacity probe covering India (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Washington is rebuilding its tariff leverage one product at a time, so even a signed interim deal would coexist with a rolling stack of sector-specific duties. India can clear the WTO on quartz and still be fighting the next barrier before the deal is inked.
anchor: India has taken America’s countertop tariffs to the

title: Groundhog Day
text:
SpiceJet has dodged insolvency without winning the case. On Wednesday, the National Company Law Tribunal ordered seven lessor petitions reheard from scratch, leaving management in control.

One deal, seven delays: The tribunal had prepared one judgment covering eight petitions. SpiceJet settled with one lessor at the last minute, forcing a rewrite. A judge retired before it could be delivered, sending the remaining cases to a new bench. Any petition admitted could put the airline under an independent insolvency professional.

The Go First hangover: Go First’s 2023 bankruptcy trapped more than 50 leased aircraft under a court moratorium, earning India a risky-jurisdiction label. New Delhi responded with the 2025 Aircraft Objects Act to speed repossession. SpiceJet’s cases concern unpaid debts, not repossession, but expose a parallel enforcement problem.
sound_smarter: Systemic legal and tribunal instability forces investors to price in procedural friction, elevating capital costs across the entire market.
anchor: SpiceJet has dodged insolvency without winning the case.

issue_title: Sweet dreams are made of imports
title: For the watch
text:
India and Japan are connecting their maritime defences. On Thursday, defence ministers Rajnath Singh and Shinjiro Koizumi signed a framework covering maritime-domain awareness, information sharing, and closer naval operations.

All eyes at sea: The two navies will expand exercises, ship visits, logistics and coordination protecting sea routes. They will also work towards reciprocal access to ports and repair facilities.

From summit to sea: The statement follows July’s summit, where the two countries signed their first defence co-development agreement for the Unified Complex Radio Antenna system and committed to exploring more projects (we covered it here). The ministers now want cooperation in mine countermeasures, unmanned systems, and naval shipbuilding.

More eyes: This week, India leased two MQ-9B Sea Guardian drones to provide persistent surveillance over the Indian Ocean (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: India cannot monitor the Indo-Pacific through hardware alone. Its emerging model combines national surveillance with information from carefully chosen partners, extending visibility without dependence on one ally. Japan is especially valuable because its strategic geography begins where India’s strongest coverage weakens.
anchor: India and Japan are connecting their maritime defences.

issue_title: Sweet dreams are made of imports
title: Sweet dreams are made of imports
text:
India has gone from exporting sugar to importing it within one harvest. On Thursday, New Delhi allowed mills and refiners to import 1 million metric tons of raw sugar duty-free until October 31, replacing the usual 100% tariff. It is India’s first sugar import in nearly a decade.

Forecast failure: Output was initially expected to reach 30.95 million metric tons after ethanol diversion. The harvest is now forecast at 27.9 million, below annual consumption of 28.5 million. India approved 1.59 million metric tons of exports before the shortfall became clear, shipping more than 600,000 before halting trade in May (we covered it here).

Fuel on the fire: Mills diverted around 3 million metric tons of sugar equivalent into ethanol as India locked in petrol containing 20% ethanol. The programme’s costs and contradictions have been a recurring policy debate (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Grain ethanol gives New Delhi room to meet its blending target, but another weak harvest that diverts more sugar into fuel would force a clear choice between pump and pantry.
anchor: India has gone from exporting sugar to importing

issue_title: Sweet dreams are made of imports
title: US envoy signals review of Jammu and Kashmir travel warning
text: US Ambassador Sergio Gor said Washington would reconsider its travel advisory for Jammu and Kashmir after steps by the central government and Chief Minister Omar Abdullah to improve security. Speaking during his first visit to Srinagar, Gor called the Union Territory an “important part of India” and said a revised advisory could encourage more Americans to visit.
anchor: US envoy signals review of Jammu and Kashmir travel warning

title: Cleared for takeoff
text:
India is nudging its exporters to get paid in rupees. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), which administers India's Foreign Trade Policy (FTP), has placed rupee export earnings on the same footing as dollars and euros for trade-policy benefits.

The fix: Exports to any country other than Nepal and Bhutan, if paid for in rupees through approved banking channels, now earn FTP benefits and count towards export obligations, just as foreign-currency exports do. Rupee settlement has been legal since July 2022, when the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) set up Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVAs) for overseas banks to hold rupees, but until now exporters could not be sure if those receipts qualified.

The backdrop: The move lands as US President Donald Trump warns the BRICS nations against building a rival to the dollar and threatens tariffs on those that try. India has rejected a common BRICS currency, with Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal stating that New Delhi does not back one, framing rupee internationalisation as widening the currency's acceptance.
sound_smarter: Permission alone will not create large-scale rupee trade. Foreign buyers need easy access to rupees, and their banks need practical ways to invest, convert, or repatriate the balances. Without reasons to hold on to the Indian rupee, adoption will stay limited.
anchor: India is nudging its exporters to get paid

title: Repair job
text:
India is expanding the yards that build and repair its warships. On August 23, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh broke ground on five expansion projects worth about INR 35 billion (USD 366 million) at Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers (GRSE) and Yantra India Limited (YIL).

Steel and slipways: GRSE's new 32-acre yard at Raichak in West Bengal will build warships up to 200 metres long, letting it bid for next-generation destroyers alongside commercial vessels. YIL's new forging presses at Ishapore, also in West Bengal, will turn out gun barrels and naval-weapon components.

Riding the vacuum: Singh framed a global "capacity paradox," with demand for ships rising as traditional shipbuilding nations lose capacity, opening a gap in design, manufacturing, and maintenance. He called ship repair and overhaul the "low-hanging fruit" and urged India to become a maintenance hub for the Indian Ocean region.

Small in the water: India still builds only a sliver of the world's ships, with China, South Korea, and Japan dominating global tonnage. GRSE has built over 800 vessels to date, most for the Indian Navy.
sound_smarter: India won't out-build China or East Asian shipyards this decade, but it can gain significant ground in ship repair. Repair runs on dry docks and fast turnaround times, infrastructure Delhi can set up cheaply. Plus, geography is on India's side: it sits right across vital Indian Ocean trade lanes, with no established repair hub in the region.
anchor: India is expanding the yards that build and

title: Call it your own
text:
India has moved its phone-ownership push from approval to implementation. On Friday, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology notified detailed rules for the five-year, INR 625 billion (USD 6.5 billion) Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme.

Paper to programme: The Cabinet approved the broad framework alongside Semicon 2.0 last month (we covered it here). The notification now sets the turnover, ownership, design and sourcing requirements companies must meet.

Two tracks: Large manufacturers with INR 100 billion (USD 1 billion) in annual turnover can earn 2.25%–5% on eligible sales. Indian brands need INR 10 billion (USD 104 million) and receive 5%, plus 3% for domestic design and research.

Ownership test: Indian brands must be majority-owned and controlled by citizens, hold their trademarks and intellectual property locally, and maintain domestic design capabilities. Both tracks can earn another 1.5% by using Indian components in at least 25% of their phones.
sound_smarter: India is shifting from “Made in India” to “Owned in India.” Subsidies can narrow a new brand’s cost disadvantage, but cannot manufacture compelling products, distribution or customer loyalty. Success is going to be marked with an Indian phone consumers still choose after the incentives end.
anchor: India has moved its phone-ownership push from approval

title: Refined influence
text:
Indian Oil Corporation (IOCL) will supply all of Mauritius's petrol, diesel, and jet fuel imports for five years, India's first such long-term deal outside South Asia.Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri sealed the deal on 20 August

Sole supplier: Mauritius's State Trading Corporation (STC) remains the importer, but the new Sales and Purchase Agreement, tied to a government-to-government MoU, locks in roughly 750,000 tonnes of annual demand for five years, replacing STC's old competitive tenders. Value and pricing are undisclosed.

Refining muscle: India imports nearly 90% of its crude, then refines it into fuel. Its 23 refineries produced 267 million tonnes last year, more than it consumes, making India a net exporter: exports reached roughly 61.4 million tonnes in FY 2025-26. It already supplies Nepal and Bhutan in full, even through the West Asia crisis.

Beyond the barrel: The same visit saw groundbreaking on a 27,500-tonne bunker-fuel facility at Port Louis, training for Mauritian officials, and a joint biofuels policy launch. It all sits under MAHASAGAR, India's Indian Ocean doctrine, unveiled in Mauritius in March 2025.
sound_smarter: Bundling fuel supply with storage infrastructure and training raises the cost of ever switching suppliers, turning a single contract into a template New Delhi can offer any import-dependent island economy.
anchor: Indian Oil Corporation (IOCL) will supply all of

title: India advances trade and telecom partnerships with Mexico and Brazil
text: India and Mexico finalised the Terms of Reference (ToR) for a preferential trade agreement covering goods, market access, and dispute settlement, with signing expected once dates align. The talks followed Mexican tariffs of up to 50 per cent on more than 1,400 products from non-preferential partners, including India. Separately, Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia signed a telecom and technology Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Brazil, covering artificial intelligence, 5G and 6G, and cybersecurity, at the BRICS Communications Ministers' meeting in Pune.
anchor: India advances trade and telecom partnerships with Mexico and Brazil

title: Relaxed China-adjacent FDI rules draw nearly INR 49 billion
text: India's revised foreign direct investment (FDI) rules have drawn 29 investment proposals worth nearly INR 49 billion (USD 512 million) up to August 20, the Commerce Ministry reported, spanning information technology, artificial intelligence, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, and data centres. The reform, which we covered here, lets investors with non-controlling stakes of up to 10 per cent from land-bordering countries use the automatic route, dropping the prior government approval that was required for such investment. The reported investors are based in third countries such as Mauritius, the United States, Singapore, and the Cayman Islands.
anchor: Relaxed China-adjacent FDI rules draw nearly INR 49 billion

title: Jaishankar visits Russia to co-chair trade commission, meet Lavrov
text: External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar will visit Russia on August 23-24 to co-chair the 27th India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation (IRIGC-TEC), at the invitation of First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov. He will also meet Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov to exchange views on regional and global issues.
anchor: Jaishankar visits Russia to co-chair trade commission, meet Lavrov

title: Doval heads to Beijing for 25th round of border talks
text: National Security Advisor Ajit Doval arrives in Beijing on Monday for the 25th round of Special Representatives (SR) talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, the first such meeting in a year and the main forum for the two countries' unresolved border. The talks, held on Tuesday, come weeks ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's expected visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit on September 12-13. Speaking on Saturday, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said border peace remains a prerequisite for normalised ties, amid reports of renewed Chinese posturing in Arunachal Pradesh.
anchor: Doval heads to Beijing for 25th round of border talks

title: Chhattisgarh clears 45 critical-mineral exploration projects in Bastar belt
text: Chhattisgarh's State Geological Programming Board (SGPB) cleared 45 mineral exploration projects for 2026-27 at its 26th meeting in Raipur on August 19, covering lithium, graphite, rare earth elements, niobium, tantalum, titanium, and iron ore, several of them in the Bastar belt that until this year was the heart of India's Maoist insurgency. When security forces arrested the insurgency's last politburo member in July, we said mining companies would start looking at this land.
anchor: Chhattisgarh clears 45 critical-mineral exploration projects in Bastar belt

title: Bread winner
text:
The world's second-biggest wheat grower is back in the export market. India scrapped a years-long ban on wheat exports on Monday, clearing shipments of wheat, the durum variety, flour, and related products through notifications from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT).

The backdrop: The Centre banned wheat exports in May 2022 and extended the curbs to flour that August. A price spike after Russia's invasion of Ukraine had pulled record volumes of Indian wheat abroad just as a March heatwave cut the domestic harvest.

Bumper harvest: India's last harvest hit an all-time high of 120.6 million tonnes, rebuilding the buffer the 2022 crop had drained. Escalating Russia-Ukraine attacks on commercial vessels and ports in the Black Sea have disrupted grain flows from some of the world's top exporters and pushed Chicago wheat futures to a two-year high. India's shipments could ease pressure in import-dependent countries across Asia, Africa, and West Asia.
sound_smarter: New Delhi earns real diplomatic credit by stepping up now, boosted by a record harvest and surging global prices. But rising heat driven by climate change threatens future surplus yields, creating a very real risk that India could ban wheat exports once again.
anchor: The world's second-biggest wheat grower is back in

title: Runway reset
text:
Chennai's second airport is back to the drawing board. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Joseph Vijay told the Assembly on Monday that the state is scrapping the INR 274 billion (USD 2.86 billion) Parandur project, a site he had opposed on the campaign trail before becoming Chief Minister in May.

Why it collapsed: Parandur drew sustained protests from farmers facing displacement. Nearly half the site was irrigated farmland and about a quarter water bodies. Vijay said the alternative locations would take far less agricultural land.

The gap it leaves: Parandur was designed for 100 million passengers a year, with central clearance secured, land acquisition underway, and a dedicated metro line drawn to reach it. The existing Chennai airport handles 30 million and will now stretch to 55 million through a terminal upgrade and a new build, still short of Parandur's plan. The state has named alternative areas but no final site or timetable.

The other signal: Investor interest has held regardless. Vijay's first conclave since taking office landed 97 agreements worth INR 674.52 billion (USD 7.05 billion), most of it from firms already operating in the state (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Watch for how fast the replacement site lands. Move too slowly and Vijay looks anti-industry to the investors funding his state; move too fast and he betrays the farmers who just won a reprieve. The site he picks, and when, is the signal that he can hold both, because the factories bankroll the welfare that keeps his base loyal, and the base is what keeps him in office to court the factories.
anchor: Chennai's second airport is back to the drawing

title: MoHFW eases medical device rules, recognises EU approvals
text: India has amended its Medical Devices Rules, 2017 to cut compliance costs for manufacturers and speed up market access, in changes the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) notified on Monday. Manufacturers that outsource product sterilisation will no longer need a separate licence, a step the ministry says reduces duplication and paperwork. A second change adds the European Union (EU) to the list of regulatory jurisdictions whose approvals qualify a device for a waiver of local clinical investigation, joining the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and Japan.
anchor: MoHFW eases medical device rules, recognises EU approvals

title: Firepower to the private sector
text:
India is opening its conventional missiles to more manufacturers. On Tuesday, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh approved transfers of Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) technology for every conventional missile to qualified Indian companies.

No names yet: Firms must pass certification. The announcement names no systems, manufacturers, timetable or selection process.

Default setting: After development, production has typically flowed through state-owned Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL). DRDO transferred Astra Mk-I and its associated systems to BDL in 2022.

Long runway: Private participation is already underway. Solar Defence produced guided Pinaka rockets for export to Armenia (we covered it here). In June, Singh warned that production capacity now matters as much as research (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Licensing tech to private players sounds big, but true disruption only happens if New Delhi lets them lead production instead of just supplying parts. If BDL keeps getting first dibs on the big contracts, this just gives state-run plants extra help; it doesn't actually break their monopoly.
anchor: India is opening its conventional missiles to more

title: US sanctions four India-based firms over Iran trade
text: The US State Department sanctioned Portease Partners, Sadashiva Overseas, PP Softtech and Prakrutees Infra Impex, alongside three Indian nationals, for allegedly facilitating Iranian petroleum and petrochemical imports. Washington says three of the firms imported products worth USD 119 million. The measures form part of Operation Economic Outcast, which targeted nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels linked to Iran’s military and energy trade.
anchor: US sanctions four India-based firms over Iran trade

title: Putin promises India fuel and fertiliser supplies
text: Russian President Vladimir Putin assured External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar that Moscow would sustain energy supplies and increase fertiliser shipments amid West Asia disruptions. Jaishankar meanwhile pressed Russia to narrow a bilateral trade deficit that exceeded USD 50 billion in 2025–26, calling for better market access, payment mechanisms and business ties.
anchor: Putin promises India fuel and fertiliser supplies

title: Lines of communication
text:
India and China have added new military guardrails along their disputed border. On Wednesday, the governments announced two additional meeting points for senior commanders and two military hotlines in the eastern and middle sectors, following talks between National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, the two countries' designated Special Representatives on the boundary question, in Beijing.

New guardrails: Both sides will use diplomatic and military channels to contain incidents along the Line of Actual Control. An expert group will pursue an “Early and Substantial Harvest” of boundary delimitation, while another tackles border management. Both were proposed last year and must still agree to their terms of reference. No map, troop reductions or timetable emerged.

From freeze to thaw: Relations froze after the 2020 Galwan Valley clash killed 20 Indian soldiers, before a 2024 patrolling deal reopened diplomatic engagement. We previewed this week's talks on Monday (we covered it here). The wider thaw has since reopened all three Himalayan border trade posts, at Nathu La, Shipki La, and Lipulekh, from early August (we covered it here), alongside the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage. The two sides also agreed to hold their next trans-border rivers meeting in September.
sound_smarter: These hotlines are meant to contain the border conflict, not settle it. By using military guardrails to stop local skirmishes from freezing broader ties, India and China are constructing a workable relationship around an open dispute. The risk for India is that relations normalise before a clear path to managing relations at the border is agreed upon, handing China normalised ties without any territorial concessions.
anchor: India and China have added new military guardrails

title: Thrust fund
text:
Rolls-Royce will offer a full transfer of technology on the engine for India's planned fifth-generation fighter, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), with India keeping the intellectual property and the design staying outside US export controls.

The gap: India builds airframes, missiles, and radar, but decades of effort to build a high-thrust jet engine have fallen short. The current Tejas fighter relies on engines from US’s General Electric (GE), whose deliveries have run late.

The terms: Rolls-Royce would hand over the full technology and let India keep the intellectual property rights (IPR). India is pressing for the hardest piece of all: the single-crystal turbine blade which lets an engine run hotter and therefore push harder. The offer runs through a UK inter-governmental agreement, and falls outside the US International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) that let Washington block the export, sale, or upgrade of any weapon carrying American technology.

The field: The terms follow the statement of intent between Rolls-Royce and Reliance to explore a joint aerospace engine complex in India (we covered it here). Rolls-Royce is up against France's Safran, which has proposed co-development with the Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE), India's state engine lab.
sound_smarter: A complete transfer of technology grants India the autonomy to upgrade, modify, and export the engine independently. This elevates the AMCA into a competitive foreign policy tool, positioning India to market a fighter free from the end-user restrictions that bind American, French, and Chinese platforms.
anchor: Rolls-Royce will offer a full transfer of technology

title: DN Solutions opens first factory outside China in India
text: South Korean machine-tool maker DN Solutions opened a 25-acre plant in Bengaluru after deploying INR 6 billion (USD 63 million) in its first phase, its first overseas manufacturing investment since opening a Chinese factory in 2003. The facility combines manufacturing, research and development, technical support, and after-sales services, and will initially produce vertical machining and horizontal turning centres. Around 80 per cent of components are already sourced locally by parts count, with most of the remainder targeted within five years.
anchor: DN Solutions opens first factory outside China in India

title: HAL and Safran to co-develop engine for India's new helicopter
text: State-run Hindustan Aeronautics (HAL) and France's Safran Helicopter Engines signed to co-develop the "Aravalli" engine for India's under-development 13-tonne Indian Multi-Role Helicopter, through their SAFHAL joint venture. The engine covers design, manufacture, and lifecycle support in the 3,500 to 4,000 shaft-horsepower class, and would power a domestic replacement for the Russian Mi-17 helicopters currently in use.
anchor: HAL and Safran to co-develop engine for India's new helicopter

title: High water
text:
288 Indians are among the hundreds missing after catastrophic flash floods tore through Nepal's border with China on August 26. The deluge, triggered by a glacial collapse on the Chinese side of the border, has killed at least 270 people in Nepal and left more than 1,500 unaccounted for across both countries, many of them pilgrims bound for Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar.

The trigger: A wall of mud and debris crashed down the Bhote Koshi River valley from Tibet's Gyirong county early on Wednesday morning after a glacier gave way. The US Geological Survey (USGS) initially logged the event as a 4.4 magnitude earthquake before revising its assessment to a glacial collapse.

The human toll: The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said 288 Indian nationals remain missing in Nepal, including tourists and workers on hydropower projects. Nepal's Tourism Board listed 517 foreign nationals as out of contact, including 178 from India, 65 from the United States, and 53 from Ukraine.

India's response: Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke to his Nepalese counterpart Balen Shah on August 26 and pledged all possible assistance. The Indian Air Force (IAF) flew in an initial 10 tonnes of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief material aboard a C-130J, followed by a second sortie carrying 37.5 tonnes of supplies, medicines, and food packets on August 27. The MEA established a 24x7 control room in New Delhi, and the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu activated emergency helplines.

The route: The Rasuwagadhi crossing is the cheapest and most popular private route for Indian pilgrims embarking on the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, a sacred pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar, which had only recently resumed after a five-year gap. The MEA organises the Yatra through two official routes, Lipulekh Pass in Uttarakhand and Nathu La Pass in Sikkim, but caps participation at roughly 1,000 pilgrims a year selected through a lottery. Private operators through Nepal face no such cap, and more than 13,500 pilgrims transited through Rasuwagadhi in the last fiscal year alone.
anchor: 288 Indians are among the hundreds missing after

title: Modi to visit Uzbekistan, attend SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan
text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will travel to Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic from August 29 to September 1. He begins with a state visit to Tashkent on August 29-30 for talks with President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on trade, defence, critical minerals, and energy, then flies to Bishkek for the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit on August 31 and September 1.
anchor: Modi to visit Uzbekistan, attend SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan

title: Tashkent takes five
text:
India and Uzbekistan want to turn a USD 1.3 billion trade relationship into a USD 5 billion one. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev elevated ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership on Sunday and reported progress on a long-term uranium supply arrangement.

From double to quadruple: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal had called earlier this month for trade to double within three years. The new 2030 target raises the bar. Trade grew 33.3 per cent in 2025, but reaching USD 5 billion requires roughly 31 per cent annual growth for five years. It is also lopsided: Uzbekistan imported USD 1.15 billion from India but exported only USD 164.6 million in return.

More wiring: The leaders created a foreign ministers’ oversight mechanism, elevated their Intergovernmental Commission and proposed a working group on trade and investment barriers. A completed feasibility study could lead to a Preferential Trade Agreement, though negotiations have not begun. Among 11 signed instruments were deals on mineral resources and financial dialogue, plus an agreement allowing Indian Unified Payments Interface apps to scan Uzbekistan’s UZQR payment codes.

Fuel line: A 2019 contract already covers 1,100 metric tonnes of Uzbek uranium through 2026. The latest talks point to a successor arrangement, but disclosed no quantity, price or timetable.

The missing route: Landlocked Uzbekistan has no direct connection to India. The leaders previously backed Iran’s Chabahar port and the International North South Transport Corridor, but announced no new logistics project on Sunday.
sound_smarter: The package is stronger on uranium than trade. Renewing an established fuel relationship means extending a working supply chain; hitting USD 5 billion means almost quadrupling commerce across unresolved geography. The partnership earns "comprehensive" when its payment links and committees produce a freight route, not before.
anchor: India and Uzbekistan want to turn a USD

title: A sugar-coated warning
text:
India's food regulator has proposed warning labels for packaged food and drinks. In a Supreme Court filing on Friday, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) called for a red hexagon on products high in two or more of saturated fat, sugar, or salt.

What it says: Flagged products would carry 'HIGH FAT', 'HIGH SUGAR', 'HIGH SALT' or 'HIGHLY SWEETENED BEVERAGE'. Rollout is phased and single-ingredient foods are exempt. At present only back-of-pack nutrition information is required.

The climbdown: Earlier in August the regulator had backed off, telling the court that matching international standards was "difficult" and offering only the nutritional table currently in place. That followed a tense March meeting where executives argued warning labels were confusing and ineffective. Public anger built as recordings of the meeting surfaced, causing the FSSAI to reverse course within days.

Why the table fails: The nutritional panel that firms favour lists values per 100 grams, not per portion. A shopper sees the sugar in 100 millilitres of a soft drink, not in the 250 millilitre bottle they are about to finish, so the number rarely tells them what they are actually consuming. A front-of-pack symbol removes the guesswork.

Tale of two recipes: The same firms often sell cleaner versions abroad. Indian Fanta carries about three times the sugar of the British recipe, Indian KitKat a fraction of the cocoa, and Indian Maggi is made with palm oil where British packs use sunflower. At Indian price points, reformulation means either raising prices in a cost-sensitive market or absorbing the hit to profit margins.

The stakes: Coca-Cola, Nestle, and PepsiCo industry groups have long opposed labels as confusing, though many use them abroad, from traffic-light ratings in the UK to Nutri-Score across Europe. By the industry's own estimate, nearly 80 per cent of India's USD 100 billion packaged food and drink market would count as high in fat, sugar, or salt. India has among the highest diabetes burdens in the world, with one study putting it at a quarter of all cases, and around 450 million Indians could be obese or overweight by 2050.
sound_smarter: The fine print still favours the manufacturers. The Supreme Court had floated a one-nutrient trigger; FSSAI set it at two, so a fizzy drink high only in sugar, or a potato chip high only in salt, escapes the warning.
anchor: India's food regulator has proposed warning labels for

title: India chases Latin American minerals in back-to-back trade talks
text: Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal visited Chile and Argentina days apart. In Santiago he met Chilean Vice-Minister Paula Estévez Weinstein to advance a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) India wants concluded this year, upgrading a preferential pact in force since 2007. Days earlier in Buenos Aires he led the fourth India-Argentina Joint Trade Committee, where state-owned miner KABIL reported progress on its Catamarca lithium project, the first by an Indian company in Argentina. Trade with Argentina topped USD 6.5 billion in 2025, up 17 per cent.
anchor: India chases Latin American minerals in back-to-back trade talks

title: India puts every official system on the same clock
text: The government has notified rules making Indian Standard Time (IST) the common reference for legal, administrative, commercial, and official purposes. Organisations have 180 days to adapt their systems. The government is also building domestic time-distribution infrastructure using NavIC, India's satellite navigation system, and other Indian sources, reducing critical systems' reliance on foreign satellites.
anchor: India puts every official system on the same clock

title: Vice-President launches homegrown sovereign AI stack
text: Vice-President C. P. Radhakrishnan launched Gnani Artha, developed by Bengaluru-based GNANI AI. The stack combines Evon 3.3, a large language model, with Plexus, a platform connecting AI tools to institutional workflows.
anchor: Vice-President launches homegrown sovereign AI stack

title: Boom amid gloom
text:
India's economy grew 7.8 per cent last quarter, outpacing every major forecast. The April to June expansion cleared the 7.1 per cent economists had predicted and the Reserve Bank of India's own 7 per cent estimate, though it eased from the previous quarter's 8.6 per cent.

The drivers: Private investment nearly doubled its pace to close to 12 per cent, from 5.8 per cent a year earlier, while personal consumption rose to 7.1 per cent after cuts to income tax and the Goods and Services Tax (GST). Manufacturing grew 9.2 per cent and financial services 12.1 per cent. Gross value added, a cleaner read on activity, rose 8.2 per cent.

Credit surge: Bank lending expanded 18.3 per cent by the end of the quarter, the fastest pace in more than a decade.

The reaction: Modi called the figures "a herculean feat" and declared on X, "Doomsayers were doomed and India bloomed…yet again!"

The overhang: India imports about 85 per cent of its crude, mostly from West Asia, and prices sit near USD 90 a barrel as the war on Iran drags on. The RBI expects inflation to average about 5 per cent this year, and its August minutes show the governor open to raising rates if prices climb. A patchy monsoon, which delivers 70 per cent of annual rainfall, adds a further risk.
sound_smarter: The number's composition is what should catch an investor's eye. Private investment nearly doubling, rather than consumption alone carrying the quarter, points to a capital-spending cycle finally turning, the durable kind of growth that supply-chain diversifiers look for. It also gives the Reserve Bank room to lean against oil-driven inflation, even to raise rates, without fear of stalling the economy.
anchor: India's economy grew 7.8 per cent last quarter,

title: Hague and dry
text:
The Hague has ordered India to honour the water-sharing treaty it suspended with Pakistan. The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) ruled on Monday that the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force, and that India had no justification for suspending it.

The backstory: India suspended the treaty in April 2025, after the Pahalgam attack in which gunmen killed 26 people, most of them tourists, in Jammu and Kashmir. Islamabad denied any role and pressed its case at the court after India began expanding reservoir capacity at two hydroelectric projects. Signed in 1960, the treaty irrigates about 80 per cent of Pakistan's farmland, and had held through three wars.

The ruling: The court stated India must meet its treaty obligations, including on the design and operation of its projects on the Western Rivers: the Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab, which the treaty reserves largely for Pakistan while letting India build run-of-river hydropower. A World Bank-appointed neutral expert will decide by July 2027 whether India's projects on those rivers comply. The court singled out the Ratle Hydro-Electric Plant, an 850-megawatt run-of-river project on the Chenab: until 90 days after the decision, India cannot raise Ratle's dam wall or power intake above set levels.

Delhi's answer: India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) rejected the ruling "categorically," calling the tribunal an "illegally constituted" body that the World Bank set up in breach of the treaty. India says it has never recognised the court, has never appeared before it, and that the panel "has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India's sovereign decisions." New Delhi added that its decision to hold the treaty in abeyance remains in force.
sound_smarter: Delhi's flat rejection of the tribunal matters more than the ruling itself. By refusing to recognise the court at all, India is asserting that upstream water is a sovereign lever no arbitrator can touch. Downstream neighbours, Bangladesh above all, should be watching. The Ganga Waters Treaty expires this year, and India has just shown that an international ruling is a shield it feels free to ignore.

title: Silicon, the sequel
text:
India has notified the full rulebook for its second semiconductor push. On Monday, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued notifications for all six pillars of the Semicon 2.0 scheme: chip design, machines and materials, fabrication plants, assembly and packaging, research, and talent.

The scope: Semicon 1.0, which was launched in 2022, concentrated on landing fabrication plants, and had twelve projects approved. Semicon 2.0 funds the whole value chain and aims to build an ecosystem. The India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) will run it as the nodal agency, appraising applications and overseeing projects that can last up to six years. The scheme stays open for applications for three years.

By the numbers: Vaishnaw said India hit its target of 85,000 semiconductor engineers, a ten-year goal, in four years, and now aims for 100,000 more. He added that the ecosystem should create 50,000 to 60,000 direct jobs, and expects close to 10 per cent of the global semiconductor market to sit in India in the coming years.
sound_smarter: The updated programme marks a real shift down the value chain, into design, materials, and equipment, the choke points where export controls actually bite. By pitching the scheme as national security, Delhi is building for a world where chip access is a critical exposure Delhi cannot leave in external hands.

title: Modi holds four bilaterals on SCO summit sidelines in Bishkek
text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi held four bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek on August 31, 2026. He told Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian that the escalation in West Asia was a concern, and pressed for freedom of navigation and the safety of civilians, commercial shipping, and seafarers. He struck the same note with Russia's President Vladimir Putin, in their first meeting this year, weighing the toll of the West Asia and Black Sea conflicts on maritime trade and Indian seafarers, and welcoming the outcome of the 27th India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on trade and economic matters, held in Moscow on August 24. Modi invited both leaders to the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12 and 13. He also met Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov, thanking him for hosting the summit and reaffirming the India-Kyrgyzstan Strategic Partnership, and held his first talks with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan since Pashinyan's re-appointment in June. The talks covered defence, mining, and pharmaceutical ties.
anchor: Modi holds four bilaterals on SCO summit sidelines in Bishkek

title: Belgian Prime Minister to visit India from September 2 to 4
text: Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever will visit India from September 2 to 4, 2026, his first trip since taking office in February 2025, and will be accompanied by Defence Minister Theo Francken. De Wever will hold talks with Modi on September 3 spanning the full range of bilateral relations, and deliver a keynote at a Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) business event pegged to the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement. He will then travel to Mumbai to meet stakeholders in the diamond, ports, and logistics sectors.
anchor: Belgian Prime Minister to visit India from September 2 to 4

title: India, Brazil target USD 30 billion trade by 2030
text: India and Brazil used the eighth meeting of their Trade Monitoring Mechanism in Brasília to reaffirm a goal of lifting bilateral trade to USD 30 billion by 2030, from USD 15.07 billion in 2025-26. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal co-chaired the talks, which reviewed the terms of reference for widening the India-MERCOSUR Preferential Trade Agreement. Agrawal pushed for greater access for Indian pharmaceuticals, and advanced agricultural market-access requests. Both sides welcomed the Brazilian Trade and Investment Promotion Agency, or ApexBrasil, announcing a new office in New Delhi.
anchor: India, Brazil target USD 30 billion trade by 2030

title: Few and far
text:
The Indian Navy has commissioned INS Nipun, an indigenously built vessel designed to reach and rescue the crews of submarines stranded on the seabed. The ship is the second Diving Support Vessel of the Nistar class, built by Hindustan Shipyard Limited.

The capability: Nipun is designed for deep-sea diving and underwater work, supporting deep saturation dives and carrying remotely operated systems for inspection and repair. Its core role is in submarine rescue: reaching and evacuating the crew of a disabled submarine sitting on the seabed.

Made in India: The Navy casts the ship as a step towards Aatmanirbharta, the government's self-reliance drive, in defence shipbuilding. INS Nipun joins its sister ship INS Nistar, giving the fleet two purpose-built platforms for diving, salvage, and rescue.

The regional pitch: Few Indian Ocean navies currently have the ability to rescue a stranded submarine crew. Naval chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan cast India as the region's "Preferred Submarine Rescue Partner", able to answer distress calls from partner fleets as well as its own.
sound_smarter: A submarine rescue ship is a quiet piece of capital. The capability is rare and takes years to build, but a crippled submarine is a race against the clock. The navy that shows up first makes itself indispensable. By offering rescue services across the Indian Ocean, India turns a military asset into real diplomatic pull, right where it’s competing with China for control of the region.

title: Not so fast
text:
VinFast has frozen plans to build three electric cars in India. The Vietnamese carmaker has told suppliers to stop all work on the VF3, VF6, and VF7 programmes while it reviews costs.

The stop order: In a July memo, VinFast asked suppliers to "hold all activities" on the three programmes and to itemise what they had spent so far on tooling, engineering, and materials. The company frames the pause as temporary. One source said VinFast halted the work after the company failed to hit its cost targets for localisation.

What is still running: VinFast disputes that it is retreating from the market. It says the VF6 and VF7 already on sale are unaffected and will keep rolling off its Indian line, where it assembles them from kits shipped from Vietnam. The suspension applies to plans to develop and manufacture the cars locally.

By the numbers: VinFast opened its first factory outside Vietnam in Tamil Nadu last year, pledging USD 2 billion for a plant that can build 50,000 cars a year and scale to 150,000. It has sold about 10,000 cars in India since launching in September 2025. VinFast had positioned the base to serve South Asia, West Asia, and Africa.
sound_smarter: VinFast’s primary reason to make cars in India was cheap local parts. The cost savings underpinned its USD 2 billion investment: affordable cars for Indian buyers, and for export across other emerging markets. Local production only pays off at high volume, and Vinfast is nowhere close.
anchor: VinFast has frozen plans to build three electric

title: DGFT automates key export certificates
text: The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) has automated the issuance of Free Sale and Commerce Certificates, the documents exporters use to prove a product is sold freely in India. Eligible applications will now clear the DGFT portal without manual scrutiny, cutting processing time, while cases that fail the system's risk checks still route to a regional officer for review.
anchor: DGFT automates key export certificates

title: The A Club
text:
India has regained an A-category sovereign rating after more than 35 years. Japan Credit Rating Agency (JCR) raised India’s foreign and local-currency ratings from BBB+ to A-, with a stable outlook.

Why now: JCR cited strong growth, lower deficits, healthier banks, and robust external buffers. Real gross domestic product (GDP) grew 7.8% in the first quarter of FY26. The Centre's fiscal deficit fell from 4.7% of GDP in FY25 to 4.4% in FY26, while banks' bad-loan ratio fell below 2%. Foreign-exchange reserves remain well above short-term external debt.

The wider scorecard: This is India's fourth sovereign upgrade since May 2025, following Morningstar DBRS, S&P Global Ratings, and Japan's Rating and Investment Information (R&I). However, S&P kept India at BBB last week, while Fitch remains at BBB- (we covered it here), flagging high government debt and weak fiscal metrics.
sound_smarter: Japanese agencies have a long record of scoring India a notch or two above the big three.The ratings that price India's foreign borrowing come from the Big Three: S&P, Moody's, and Fitch. The A- rating gives New Delhi a news headline, but it only turns into cheaper money the day the big three follow upgrade it into the A band.
anchor: India has regained an A-category sovereign rating after

title: Jaishankar heads to Ukraine and Poland
text: External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar will visit both countries from 3–5 September. He will meet Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski to discuss bilateral ties, regional developments and other issues of mutual interest.
anchor: Jaishankar heads to Ukraine and Poland

title: Same pay, smaller job
text:
India’s maternity law now reaches beyond the payslip. On Monday, the Delhi High Court ruled that women returning from maternity leave must receive the same job, or one equivalent in pay, authority, and career prospects.

The quiet demotion: A HashiCorp accounting manager returned to find her duties gone, although her salary and title survived. She later resigned. The court treated the reassignment as discriminatory and awarded INR 1 million (USD 10,600) in compensation.

Rulebook rewrite: In the judgement, Delhi High Court has ordered the Centre to draft rules within six months covering reinstatement, crèches, complaints and retaliation under the Code on Social Security.

The catch: India extended mandated maternity leave to 26 weeks in 2017. Yet, research finds the 2017 expansion of maternity reduced employment and wages among women aged 20–29.
sound_smarter: The ruling closes a loophole that lets employers preserve a mother’s salary while hollowing out her career. It should improve retention, but employer-funded benefits can still encourage discrimination before hiring. Sharing maternity costs across employers and the state would protect mothers without turning potential motherhood into a hiring liability.
anchor: India’s maternity law now reaches beyond the payslip.

title: The fast lane hits a checkpoint
text:
India’s Asian payments shortcut runs through a country it distrusts. New Delhi has stalled a link between the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and Alipay+ over security and data concerns.

The pitch: January’s proposal would let Indians pay Alipay+ merchants abroad through UPI, then let international visitors use Alipay+ in India.

China checkpoint: Officials reportedly fear data misuse, money laundering, and cyberfraud. Ant International has been Singapore-headquartered and operationally independent since 2024, but New Delhi remains unconvinced. The proposal remains in limbo.

Going global: UPI already powers cross-border remittances with Nepal, merchant payments in Greece, and Qatar-to-India transfers. With a much stronger geographic footing, Alipay+ offered one connection into a vast Asian merchant network.
sound_smarter: By offering its services in the region, Alipay+ is essentially asking India to rely on Chinese-linked infrastructure. Ultimately, UPI’s global expansion will be driven as much by geopolitics as by payment technology, forcing New Delhi to accept slower growth wherever it lacks influence.
anchor: India’s Asian payments shortcut runs through a country

title: Tata for now, Kenya
text:
Kenya has told Tata Chemicals to pack up. On Thursday, President William Ruto ordered the company out and said its replacements must build glass and chemical plants in Kajiado.

Imported inheritance: Tata acquired Magadi through its 2005 purchase of Britain’s Brunner Mond, gaining low-cost natural soda ash. The operation dates to 1911 while Tata’s ownership is only decades old.

Why now: Kenya’s mining ministry suspended production and exports on 28 July, alleging gaps in royalties, reporting, local processing, procurement, Kenyan jobs, community commitments, and environmental compliance. Tata says it submitted all requested documents and complied.

Capital mismatch: Tata’s roughly USD 100 million soda ash plant was shelved in 2014 when energy costs made it unviable. New electric and solar facilities later made the export operation cleaner and more efficient.

Loose ends: Operations are halted, but Tata’s lease runs to 2053 and the licensing fight remains in court.
sound_smarter: High energy costs sank the USD 100 million soda ash plant, and changing operators won't solve that. Without fundamental economic reforms in production, Nairobi risks sacrificing a revenue-generating exporter for an idle industrial site that other companies would be hesitant to take over.
anchor: Kenya has told Tata Chemicals to pack up.

title: Crude limits on peacemaking
text:
External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar arrived in Kyiv offering diplomacy, with one boundary firmly drawn. On Thursday, he used the first standalone visit by an Indian foreign minister to Ukraine to defend Russian oil purchases.

The line: Jaishankar argued that oil purchases would not decide the war and asked Kyiv to respect India’s responsibility to fuel 1.4 billion people.

Pressure point: Washington has already penalised Indian imports over Russian oil. Congress is now weighing tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers (we covered it here).

Crude reality: Russia supplied 45% of India’s crude imports in August. During this year’s West Asia disruption, Moscow offered emergency barrels potentially covering 40% of India’s imports, underscoring the relationship’s value (we covered it here).

Kyiv’s answer: Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed India’s role but said peace requires economic pressure alongside persuasion.
sound_smarter: While India provides Kyiv with a diplomatic conduit to Moscow, its refusal to exert pressure keeps it in the role of a messenger rather than an influential peace broker. US pressure may heighten this dynamic, but India’s critical reliance on Russian energy guarantees this position will persist.
anchor: External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar arrived in Kyiv

title: Defence Minister reveals defence diplomacy for the next decade
text: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh unveiled Raksha, Hindi for “protection,” on Thursday, a ten-year roadmap for India’s defence diplomacy. The framework prioritises deeper bilateral and multilateral security partnerships, joint military exercises and training, Indian-made defence exports, and a larger role for India as a security provider and first responder in the Indian Ocean.
anchor: Defence Minister reveals defence diplomacy for the next decade

issue_title: Not so quiet on the eastern front
title: Not so quiet on the eastern front
text:
India and China held their first corps commander-level talks in the eastern sector. On Sunday, Lieutenant General Girish Kalia, who commands the Army's 3 Corps, met his Chinese counterpart at the Wacha-Damai border point in Arunachal Pradesh, the north-eastern Indian state China claims as South Tibet.

What is new: This is the first time the corps commander mechanism has convened in the eastern sector. Following the fatal clash in Galwan Valley in June 2020, meetings had occurred exclusively at the Chushul-Moldo border point in Ladakh, on the western frontier. Two formations hold the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh: the 3 Corps, based at Rangapahar in Nagaland, and the Tezpur-based 4 Corps in Assam.

The thaw backdrop: The talks follow National Security Adviser (NSA) Ajit Doval's visit to Beijing to meet Foreign Minister Wang Yi (we covered it here), after which both governments announced measures to keep the border calm. They also come days before Xi Jinping is due in New Delhi for the BRICS summit on September 12 and 13, his first visit to India since 2019.
sound_smarter: The corps commander talks were the specific channel forged to manage the Ladakh standoff after Galwan. Neither side can afford a flare-up, and External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has made border calm an explicit precondition for a wider relationship. A second front for managing the border is both governments protecting their economic interests without resolving their deeper mistrust.
anchor: India and China held their first corps commander-level

issue_title: Not so quiet on the eastern front
title: Counting votes, counting castes
text:
Centre advanced Census 2027 operations in Uttar Pradesh (UP), Punjab, Goa, and parts of Uttarakhand to December 1, clearing the slate before state elections.

The logistics fix: Teachers and government employees run both election booths and census drives. Moving the door-to-door headcount to December prevents an operational deadlock during peak campaign season.

Pre-poll caste count: Fieldwork finishes on January 4, 2027. This places independent India's first official caste enumeration weeks before voters head to the polls, a sensitive variable in caste-heavy battlegrounds like UP and Punjab. Respondents are asked an open-ended format question on caste and tribe self-declaration (we covered it here).

Tech and timeline: The all-digital census includes 40 questions – 11 more than in 2011– asking for Aadhaar numbers, parental details, and open-ended caste declarations. The rest of India gets counted starting February.

Manipur sidelined: The Centre deferred the census in Manipur indefinitely, citing ongoing violence and unresolved demands to update the National Register of Citizens.
sound_smarter: This could become the most significant census in independent India as the results may be used to shape Parliamentary seats, frozen since 1976 to avoid penalizing southern states for successful population control. The recent attempt to unfreeze it failed (we covered it here). Once published in two to three years, expect a fierce political battle: Southern states will resist population-based reallocation, while BJP-dominant Northern states will push for it.
anchor: Centre advanced Census 2027 operations in Uttar Pradesh

issue_title: Not so quiet on the eastern front
title: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh to visit Sri Lanka
text: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh will make an official three-day visit to Sri Lanka from September 8 to 10, 2026, leading a delegation of senior defence and external affairs officials for talks with the island's leadership and an interaction with the Indian diaspora in Colombo. The visit focuses on maritime and defence cooperation under India's Neighbourhood First policy and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's MAHASAGAR (Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions) vision.
anchor: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh to visit Sri Lanka

issue_title: Not so quiet on the eastern front
title: ISRO launches EOS-05, India’s first geosynchronous-orbit imaging satellite
text: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) launched EOS-05, India's first imaging satellite to operate from geosynchronous orbit, on Friday. EOS-05 can hold near-continuous watch over the same area rather than passing over it every few days, sharpening India's ability to track cyclones, floods, and its own borders in real time.
anchor: ISRO launches EOS-05, India’s first geosynchronous-orbit imaging satellite

issue_title: Not so quiet on the eastern front
title: TCS unit plans 1 GW Hyderabad AI campus
text: HyperVault, a Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) subsidiary, and its partners will invest up to INR 700 billion (USD 7.4 billion) in a 1 gigawatt AI data centre campus in Hyderabad. The site will be built in phases as customers sign on, aimed at AI firms and hyperscalers running dense GPU workloads, and HyperVault expects it to rank among India's largest AI facilities at full buildout. OpenAI signed on as HyperVault's first customer in February, starting at 100 megawatts with an option to scale to 1 GW.
anchor: TCS unit plans 1 GW Hyderabad AI campus

title: Terrain of thought
text:
The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) granted in-principle approval to military procurement worth about INR 1.1 trillion (USD 11.7 billion), with roughly 98% earmarked for Indian manufacturers.

On the list:

- Army: Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) detection vehicles; rough-terrain trucks; self-propelled minelayers; Advanced Light Helicopters; portable bridges and mine-clearing tanks.
- Navy: Arudhra radars, which track aircraft around naval air bases; and a programme to build marine gas turbines, the engines that power warships, in India rather than abroad.
- Air Force: upgrades for fighter jets, transport planes, and helicopters; and a ground-based jammer that scrambles enemy radar.

Additionally, all three services get a switch from paper ID passes to electronic smart cards.
sound_smarter: A quick look at what the Army is buying tells you that almost all of it is aimed at one thing: moving and fighting across rough terrain. That is the exact problem India faces on its borders with China and Pakistan, where the hard part is holding ground.
anchor: The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) granted in-principle approval

title: India backs fairer world maps, with a caveat
text: India joined 163 other countries in backing the UN General Assembly’s “Correct the Map” resolution, which encourages map projections that preserve continents’ relative sizes instead of making northern regions appear disproportionately large. The United States cast the only opposing vote, while six countries abstained. New Delhi supported the principle but stressed that its vote did not endorse the Equal Earth map because different maps serve different purposes.
anchor: India backs fairer world maps, with a caveat

title: Goyal floats a 10-million medical-tourism goal
text: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said India should aim to serve 10 million international patients annually, compared with 3.5 million patients over the past seven years. His five-point pitch calls for certified caregivers, transparent hospital packages, cashless payments, accredited providers and expansion beyond the biggest cities. No deadline, funding or binding government target accompanied the figure.
anchor: Goyal floats a 10-million medical-tourism goal

title: Seven killed in Delhi student-hostel collapse
text: At least seven people died after an ageing five-storey building used as a boys’ paying-guest hostel collapsed near Delhi University’s South Campus on Sunday. Preliminary findings point to water accumulating in the basement while repair work was underway. Police arrested the building’s owner, five municipal officials were suspended, and the Delhi government ordered an inquiry and promised mandatory structural-safety certification for buildings used by the public.
anchor: Seven killed in Delhi student-hostel collapse

title: Free wheeling
text:
On September 7, NITI Aayog, the government's top policy think tank, launched two new platforms to help India sell more electric trucks.

The platforms:

- Zero Emission Truck (ZET) Marketplace: an online marketplace for electric trucks
- Platform for Aggregating Clean Transport (PACT): a system to connect buyers, lenders, and truckmakers

Why it matters: Trucks are only 3 to 4% of India's vehicles, but they cause more than a third of transport-sector pollution. With roughly 70% of India’s freight moving by road, NITI Aayog says electrifying trucking will be critical to India’s net-zero ambitions.

Meanwhile, China: In 2025, only around 800 heavy electric trucks were sold in India, and Chinese brands are in the lead: SANY and Foton (sold here through distributor Energy in Motion) together hold more than half the market. India taxes most imported vehicles heavily to protect local manufacturers, but electric trucks currently attract a low rate of 10%. Tata Motors has asked the government to fix it.

The catch: Though India has relaxed some limits on Chinese investment, electric vehicles and battery technologies are scrutinised closely, making it difficult for Indian firms to form joint ventures with Chinese manufacturers.
sound_smarter: India’s electric mobility push exposes a policy dilemma: the restrictions designed to limit Chinese involvement also restrict access to the technology and partnerships Indian manufacturers need. India’s path to electrification will inevitably pass through China, and it must find a way to build domestic capability without cutting itself off from the industry leader.
