title: Taking credit in London
text:
The UK has recognized India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) as a qualifying carbon pricing mechanism, offering Indian exporters relief under Britain's upcoming border tax regime.

What changed: HM Treasury notified India’s Bureau of Energy Efficiency that CCTS meets qualifying criteria for carbon price relief under the UK’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), set to roll out on January 1, 2027. This means eligible Indian exporters – especially those involving iron and steel, aluminium, and cement – won't face duplicate carbon taxation when Britain's CBAM kicks off if they have paid carbon prices in India’s CCTS, which is expected to begin trading in October 2026.

What’s pending: Both governments are still hashing out the fine print. Ongoing technical talks will determine the exact valuation of Indian credits and the specific evidence required for UK importers to claim deductions.

The last hurdle: The issue of the UK’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism was one of two measures that stalled negotiations of the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, which took effect on July 15 (we covered it here). The other measure being steel import quotas, for which India was ultimately able to negotiate carve-out exemptions.
sound_smarter: Complete relief from CBAM liabilities is unlikely; partial reduction is the far more probable outcome. While there are concerns that exporting nations like India might establish nominal domestic carbon markets with artificially low prices to skirt regulations, a competing incentive exists: setting higher domestic carbon prices enables governments to retain tax revenue locally rather than surrendering it to the EU or UK. However, given the political pushback against raising costs for Indian enterprises, Indian CCTS prices will likely remain low, offering only modest relief against CBAM.
anchor: The UK has recognized India’s Carbon Credit Trading

title: India canvasses manufacturers before China trade talks
text: Ahead of the Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa (BRICS) summit in New Delhi next week (12-13 September), the Commerce Ministry consulted Indian industry groups about Chinese restrictions on critical technology and components. Companies cited barriers affecting rare-earth magnets, battery technology, solar equipment, and specialised power-transmission components. India may raise these barriers with Chinese officials during the summit, and no formal negotiating position has been announced.
anchor: India canvasses manufacturers before China trade talks

title: NIA charges US citizen and six Ukrainians over Myanmar training camps
text: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) has chargesheeted US citizen Matthew Van Dyke and six Ukrainian nationals for allegedly entering India through Mizoram, crossing into Myanmar, and training ethnic armed groups in drone warfare. Arrested in March under the anti-terror law (UAPA), the seven now face only immigration charges, though the NIA says the terror probe stays open. Van Dyke, who runs a US security firm that trained Ukraine's military, was reportedly tracked with intelligence which the NIA suggested Russia may have shared.
anchor: NIA charges US citizen and six Ukrainians over Myanmar training camps

title: India joins US-led 25-nation group shaping 6G standards
text: India has joined the United States and 24 other countries in a global initiative to guide the development of next-generation 6G telecom networks, the US Department of Commerce announced on September 8. The deal was sealed at a meeting between US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Minister of State for Commerce Jitin Prasada on the sidelines of the G20 Innovation Ministerial. The initiative aims to keep future networks aligned on shared security interests and competitiveness, the language countries use for writing standards that lock out Chinese vendors like Huawei.
anchor: India joins US-led 25-nation group shaping 6G standards

title: Modi wants UPI linked with more national payment systems
text: At the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai on Tuesday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) to connect with payment systems in more countries, prioritising major diaspora and trade partners. He cited the existing link with Singapore’s PayNow as a model for faster, cheaper remittances. UPI is live in 11 countries, but Modi named no new partner, agreement, or timetable in his speech.
anchor: Modi wants UPI linked with more national payment systems

title: High toll for low orbit
text:
The government just outbid its own regulator on what to charge for space. The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) is set to charge satellite broadband operators 5% of their adjusted gross revenue (AGR) for spectrum.

The standoff: The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) recommended 4% and held that line twice, arguing a steeper fee would push up costs and slow rural access. The DoT countered that 4% undervalued a scarce public resource and could let operators sit on spectrum cheaply without using it. It has settled on 5%, with a 1% discount for operators serving hard-to-reach areas. Final pricing still needs Cabinet approval.

Who pays: The three contenders for India's skies are Elon Musk's Starlink, Bharti Airtel-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Reliance's Jio-SES venture. All three have already been cleared by India's space regulator to operate their satellites over the country, yet their commercial launches remain held up by the unresolved pricing and pending security checks.

The reversals: The DoT is also set to scrap a planned cap on subscriber numbers in favour of capacity-based limits, and has dropped a proposed subsidy for rural user terminals that can cost up to INR 50,000 (about USD 525).
sound_smarter: Delhi is betting that access to hundreds of millions of unconnected Indians in remote, hard-to-wire places keeps Starlink and OneWeb at the table even at what analysts call the world's highest satcom levy. The demand is real – India crossed 1.09 billion internet users in early 2026, but urban connections are saturated and rural penetration runs at barely half the urban rate.
anchor: The government just outbid its own regulator on

title: The offshore squeeze
text:
India has opened a new front against offshore crypto platforms. On Wednesday, the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND) issued compliance notices to 15 crypto platforms, including Weex, Blofin, WOO X, Pionex and WhiteBIT, and moved to have their apps and websites pulled from public access in India. The move tightens one of the world's harshest crypto tax regimes – a flat 30% on gains, no set-off for losses, and a 1% tax deducted at source on transfers.

The rule: Any platform serving Indian customers must register with the FIU-IND, wherever it is based. Registration brings it under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act: it must verify customers, preserve transaction records, and report suspicious transfers. The 15 are accused only of skipping those steps, with no laundering charge and no fine at this stage.

The playbook: All 15 are centralised exchanges that hold customer funds and run consumer apps, websites, and rupee on-ramps for Indian users. India has run this drill before, notifying nine offshore platforms in December 2023 and another 25 in October 2025; Binance and some others later registered and paid penalties to return.
sound_smarter: Crypto sold itself as money beyond any government's reach, but the 15 platforms named are centralised exchanges, each with a company, an app, and a rupee gateway. Delhi has found the chokepoint where digital coins meet real money, and closing it pulls Indian trading onto platforms the state can see and tax.
anchor: India has opened a new front against offshore

title: India funds upgrades to Sri Lanka’s air defence guns
text: On Wednesday, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh met Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in Colombo, and the two countries signed agreements to upgrade six Indian-supplied L70 guns under an Indian grant and expand cooperation between their cadet corps and defence colleges. They also inaugurated three bridges built by Indian defence forces. Dissanayake said Sri Lankan territory would not be used against India's security interests.
anchor: India funds upgrades to Sri Lanka’s air defence guns

title: India and Japan begin two-week fighter exercise in Jodhpur
text: On Wednesday, the Indian Air Force and Japan Air Self-Defense Force began Veer Guardian 2026 at Air Force Station Jodhpur. Running through September 22, the exercise brings together India’s Tejas, Su-30MKI, and Rafale fighters with Japan’s F-2A aircraft for operational drills, joint mission planning, engineering exchanges, and aerospace-safety training.
anchor: India and Japan begin two-week fighter exercise in Jodhpur

title: Cart blanche
text:
India is tightening the rules around the fake festive-sale discount. On Thursday, the Department of Consumer Affairs amended India's e-commerce rules, adding disclosure and fair-practice duties for online marketplaces. It cited the 1.77 million consumer complaints logged in 2025, nearly a third of them about e-commerce.

What changes: Platforms can no longer manipulate search results to mislead shoppers, and must clearly label sponsored listings. They must also self-audit every year against India's 2023 dark-patterns guidelines and post a compliance certificate. Any advertised price cut must now show the genuine prior price, defined as the lowest the item sold for in the previous 30 days. That targets the inflate-then-slash tactic behind many festive-sale bargains. The new rules come into effect from January 1, 2027.

Already tested: A 2025 advisory had already asked platforms to self-audit for dark patterns, but an independent review by consumer group LocalCircles had found every major platform non-compliant. Hyperlocal delivery app Zepto declared itself clean in November 2025, only for the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) to fine it INR 700,000 (USD 7,400) weeks later for adding a paid membership to carts by default and showing mandatory charges only at checkout.
sound_smarter: Platforms still audit themselves, still issue their own certificate, and still answer only when the CCPA catches a breach after the fact. The amendment writes the 2025 advisory into the rules, giving it firmer legal footing but the enforcement gap stays the same.
anchor: India is tightening the rules around the fake

title: Cane mutiny
text:
Australia says India's sugar farmers get too sweet a deal. On Thursday, Canberra asked India to defend its sugarcane policy at the WTO, claiming support breached limits for seven straight seasons.

The charge: Australia puts support at 90%-95% of crop value, against India's 10% WTO threshold. The gap comes from India's Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP), a government floor price mills must pay cane farmers, set well above open-market rates and counted in full toward the WTO's support tally.

Why Canberra cares: Australia exports four-fifths of its sugar, exposing growers to world prices. India shipped a record 11 million metric tonnes in 2021-22, triple Australia's usual exports. Canberra says Indian surpluses depress global prices.

Delhi's sugar game: The Centre's cane-price floor supports 50 million rural livelihoods. In bumper years like 2026, exports clear stocks and ethanol turns cane into fuel (we covered it here). This season, India halted exports and opened duty-free imports after production fell below demand (we covered these developments here, here and here).

What next: India can challenge the claims at the WTO agriculture committee on 24-25 September.
sound_smarter: India has little reason to worry. Australia’s submission is merely a request for clarification before WTO committees, meant to exert diplomatic and political pressure rather than trigger binding legal rulings. Even if this escalates into a formal dispute, enforcement will stall: India can simply appeal any adverse decision to the WTO’s Appellate Body, which remains non-functional due to a lack of quorum, mirroring what happened with the 2021 panel report that found India exceeded the 10% support threshold.
anchor: Australia says India's sugar farmers get too sweet

title: A border-line truce
text:
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping met on Saturday on the sidelines of the New Delhi BRICS summit, marking Xi’s first visit to India since 2019 and pushing a cautious thaw after their 2020 border clash.

The border bottom line: Modi stressed that border peace remains the precondition for normal ties, urging adherence to existing protocols and noting that "differences should not become disputes." The two countries recently held their first eastern-sector corps commander talks at the Wacha-Damai border point in Arunachal Pradesh (we covered it here).

Trade friction: On paper, both agreed to tackle structural trade imbalances and supply chain access. In practice, New Delhi remains wary of its massive trade deficit with Beijing while trying to position itself as a Western-backed alternative to Chinese manufacturing.

The 'Greater BRICS' pitch: Xi used the summit to advocate for a "Greater BRICS" integrated market, offering a China-led BRICS AI Open-Source Zone and a Special Economic Zone framework to entrench Beijing’s influence across the Global South.

Multi-alignment in action: Modi urged that BRICS solutions be adaptable across non-member developing nations, framing India as the natural bridge between Western partnerships and the Global South.
sound_smarter: While Xi wants better relations to keep India from leaning stronger into Washington's orbit, Modi is happy to take the diplomatic win of a tranquil border to focus on domestic economic scaling. A border calm will be followed by warm rhetoric on growing the economic relationship, but zero movement on India opening the floodgates to Chinese investment.
anchor: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President

title: American sunblock
text:
Washington hits New Delhi with another tariff. The United States Commerce Department on Friday finalised a 123.04% anti-dumping margin and a 126.09% countervailing duty rate on Indian solar cells and panels.

Locked in: The anti-dumping margin is unchanged from the preliminary finding (we covered it here). The countervailing rate rises slightly from 125.87% to offset government subsidies. Friday’s decision makes both rates final at the Commerce Department.

The exposure: The United States bought more than 95% of India’s solar cell and module exports when the preliminary rate landed. Since June, India has required government-backed, net-metered, and open-access solar projects to use domestically manufactured cells, building a protected market at home (we covered it here).

Last gate: The United States International Trade Commission will vote on 14 October on whether Indian imports injured or threatened American manufacturers. A yes vote would clear the way for duty orders in November.
sound_smarter: New Delhi’s solar localisation rules were designed to pull investment into Indian cell manufacturing. With the US tariff likely to soar, domestic projects will struggle to absorb output that factories can no longer sell to their largest customer.

title: BRICS adopts Delhi declaration with softer language on Iran
text: On Saturday, leaders of the expanded BRICS issued the New Delhi Declaration at their India-hosted summit, calling for restraint in West Asia and protection of trade and energy flows. Last year’s Rio declaration explicitly condemned military strikes against Iran, a member of the bloc. This year’s corresponding clauses express concern about attacks on civilian infrastructure and nuclear facilities without naming Iran or the attackers. The text also drops last year’s separate paragraph supporting diplomatic efforts towards a settlement in Ukraine.
anchor: BRICS adopts Delhi declaration with softer language on Iran

title: European Commission sends India trade deal for approval
text: On Friday, the European Commission submitted the free trade agreement with India to the Council of the European Union for authorisation to sign and conclude it. This is the first formal approval step since negotiations ended in January (we covered it here). The Council must approve its signature, followed by consent from the European Parliament, formal conclusion by the Council, and ratification by India before the agreement can enter into force. No date was announced.
anchor: European Commission sends India trade deal for approval

title: Growing pains
text:
Food and energy costs are testing India’s growth momentum. India’s retail inflation rose to 4.82% in August, while wholesale inflation reached 9.92%.

The household bill: The Statistics Ministry reported that retail inflation increased from 4.45% in July. Food inflation climbed to 5.95%, from 5.52%.

Business costs: The Commerce Ministry’s wholesale figures showed fuel-and-power inflation accelerating to 22.93%, from 20.05%. Manufactured goods inflation edged up to 8.37%. Wholesale prices cover a different basket from consumer prices, so these increases do not translate directly into household bills.

Growth provides a cushion: India’s economy expanded 7.8% in April–June, supported by stronger investment and consumption (we covered it here).

Rates in play: The Reserve Bank of India held its policy rate at 5.25% in August. Meeting minutes showed some officials would favour raising it if inflation spread more widely.
sound_smarter: Higher rates could curb spending and contain broader price increases, but would also make borrowing for expansion more expensive. Strong growth gives the central bank room to respond with higher rates, which are likely to come in October and/or December.
anchor: Food and energy costs are testing India’s growth

title: Steel a way in
text:
India would receive annual steel quota access of approximately 1.64 million tonnes under its proposed free trade agreement with the EU.

The breakdown: The published draft allocates roughly 947,000 tonnes under ordinary trading terms and another 695,000 tonnes through the agreement. The breakdown clarifies how much steel access is tied to the deal, which was one of Delhi’s core priorities (we covered it here).

A tighter market: Europe’s new steel regime, introduced in July, reserves half its import quota for free-trade partners. Shipments exceeding applicable quotas face a 50% additional duty.

The carbon bill: Quota access leaves the separate carbon levy in place. The European Union already allows deductions for eligible carbon prices paid abroad. But Delhi’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) has yet to gain recognition from Brussels.

Still pending: Last week, the European Commission submitted the agreement for approval. Its concessions await entry into force (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Europe’s tighter steel rules make preferential access more valuable. The agreement gives Indian producers an advantage over suppliers without a trade pact, but the carbon bill still affects the price European buyers pay. New Delhi will push hard for recognition of its CCTS, just like it has with the UK (we covered it here).

title: India approves electricity exports to flood-hit Nepal
text: On Monday, India’s Ministry of Power approved exports of up to 654 megawatts to Nepal for 18 hours daily, from midnight to 6 pm, between 13 September and 31 December. Floods damaged Nepal’s hydropower infrastructure, reducing domestic generation. The approval covers supplies through two existing cross-border transmission lines. The ministry will review export volumes for January 2027 in December.
anchor: India approves electricity exports to flood-hit Nepal

title: Damming the discord
text:
A wave of long-frozen Himalayan dams is coming unstuck. On Tuesday, the chief ministers of six northern states signed the Kishau Multipurpose Project agreement, ending a deadlock that had stalled the Himalayan dam for decades.

The deal: Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana, and Delhi backed a 232.6-metre concrete gravity dam on the Tons river along the Uttarakhand-Himachal border. With 1,562 million cubic metres of storage and 660 megawatts of installed capacity, the dam will irrigate 97,000 hectares of land.

The lion’s share: Delhi is the biggest beneficiary of the project. A quarter of the flow is reserved for the Yamuna's environmental needs, which Home Minister Amit Shah linked to a clean-Yamuna target of 2029. As a national project, Kishau draws about 90% of its funding from the Centre, with the six states splitting the rest.

The pattern: The Centre counts Kishau as the tenth water dispute settled since 2018. On the upper Yamuna the formula has been consistent. Lakhwar was signed in 2018 and Renukaji in 2019, both national projects funded by the Centre and backed by these same six states as Kishau.
sound_smarter: The 90% formula has now broken three deadlocks, which is also its risk — any state still holding out on a river project can see that waiting for Delhi to declare a national project costs less than compromising with its neighbours. The lever that clears the backlog is the same one that gives states a reason to stall.
anchor: A wave of long-frozen Himalayan dams is coming

title: Mind the gap
text:
India’s goods exports rose 26.1% year on year in August, but its trade deficit narrowed only slightly on the same comparison. The Commerce Ministry reported exports of USD 43.81 billion and imports of USD 70.67 billion, leaving a USD 26.86 billion gap.

Two comparisons: The deficit fell from July’s reported USD 31.98 billion. Compared with August 2025, however, it narrowed by just USD 360 million. Exports increased by USD 9.07 billion, while imports rose by USD 8.71 billion.

Gold’s reversal: Gold imports fell 57.75% compared with a year earlier. That reversed its direction in June, when rising gold, petroleum, and electronics imports helped widen the deficit (we covered it here).

The wider gap: Excluding petroleum and gems and jewellery, August’s exports rose 22.7%, while imports increased 18.9%. Imports started from a larger base, so the deficit in those goods widened to USD 14.54 billion, from USD 13.13 billion a year earlier.
sound_smarter: Lower gold imports can ease the monthly deficit, but closing the broader gap requires export gains to outstrip the additional import bill. August shows how demanding that is. Even a 26% export increase delivered little year-on-year improvement.
anchor: India’s goods exports rose 26.1% year on year

title: Sharing the crown jewels
text:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh unveiled new policies to turn private defense vendors into long-term technology partners at the ‘VIMARSH’ DRDO-Industry meet in New Delhi on Tuesday.

Code drop: The state R&D agency launched a framework to share Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) software source codes with licensed private companies, a major departure from historical secrecy meant to speed up software updates and weapon upgrades.

Lowering the bar: The government is easing access to DRDO testing facilities, offering direct funding, and providing incubation support specifically targeting deep-tech startups and MSMEs.

By the numbers: DRDO handed over nine technology transfer agreements to 13 manufacturing partners. The agency has now completed over 2,300 transfers to more than 1,100 domestic firms to date. This is part of a broader push towards increasing private sector participation in defence manufacturing, with DRDO missile production recently opened to qualified domestic manufacturers (we covered it here).

Standardizing maturity: DRDO rolled out the System for Advance Manufacturing Assessment and Rating (SAMAR) version 2.0 with the Quality Council of India to benchmark the manufacturing capability of domestic defence suppliers before handing over critical tech.
sound_smarter: Integrating private firms directly into software development enables faster patches, continuous upgrades, and rapid iterations for DRDO equipment. By actively involving the private sector, New Delhi accelerates the leap from prototype to combat readiness and creates a compelling incentive for defence vendors to co-invest alongside the state.
anchor: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh unveiled new policies to

title: India-US armies begin 22nd Yudh Abhyas exercise in Uttarakhand
text: The 22nd edition of Yudh Abhyas, the annual India-US army exercise, opened on Tuesday at Auli in Uttarakhand and the Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan, with 600 troops a side. The training covers Integrated Battle Groups in mountainous terrain, drones, autonomous systems, and multi-domain warfare.
anchor: India-US armies begin 22nd Yudh Abhyas exercise in Uttarakhand

title: India sets fees for larger merchant payments through UPI
text: On Tuesday, the Finance Ministry specified a 0.4% merchant discount rate, a payment-processing charge, on eligible UPI merchant transactions above INR 2,000 (USD 20.85), capped at INR 300 (USD 3.13). This follows August’s legislative move to enable merchant fees (we covered it here). Payments above the threshold in sectors such as fuel, railways, and insurance will carry a flat fee of INR 5 (USD 0.05). Mutual fund and securities payments will be charged 0.02%, with the same cap. Transfers between individuals remain free. Merchant payments up to the threshold and those covered by the small-business exemption also remain free. The ministry says 96% of merchant transactions will be unaffected. Banks have been told to ensure merchants do not pass fees to customers, and payment apps cannot add platform or hidden charges. An amount equal to 5% of fee collections will support UPI adoption among small merchants.
anchor: India sets fees for larger merchant payments through UPI

issue_title: To be or not to be tariffed
title: To be or not to be tariffed
text:
The US House passed a bill that would let Trump impose a tariff of up to 100% on India for buying Russian oil, days before Trump hosts Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.

The amendments: An amendment from Congressman Steny Hoyer would have named India and nine other countries, including China, as explicit targets for the tariff. A separate amendment from Congressman Gregory Meeks would have changed the standard for waiving sanctions against Russia's enablers. The House Rules Committee voted down both before either reached the floor. The bill that passed keeps the Senate's version, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which applied only to the top five buyers of Russian oil and gas by volume, a group India tops alongside China. We covered the bill's mechanics and India's exposure here.

Why this week: Xi Jinping visits Washington on September 24 for his second summit with Trump this year, and a fresh, specific tariff gives Trump something to hold over Beijing at the table. Graham, the bill's Republican co-author, died in July days after securing the White House's backing; colleagues renamed the bill in his honour. The House also has little time left before recess ahead of the November 3 midterms.
sound_smarter: The timing is bad for New Delhi regardless of which amendment wins. India's Bilateral Trade Agreement with the US is already stalled, with Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal saying this month that India will not sign until it beats the rates Vietnam and Bangladesh get. Trump now walks into his September 24 summit with Xi holding a new tariff built for Beijing that happens to carry India's name too, a source of pressure he can exert in either negotiation.

title: A little more room
text:
New Zealand’s Parliament passed legislation on Tuesday to implement its trade agreement with India. Once it takes effect, Indian goods meeting the agreement’s origin rules will qualify for zero tariffs across all product categories.

Following through: Signed in April, the deal formed part of the trade-growth plans behind July’s Strategic Partnership (we covered it here). Parliament’s approval brings those tariff concessions closer to implementation.

A small market: India exported USD 566.5 million of goods to New Zealand in 2025–26, about 0.13% of its total goods exports.

Where it helps: Some Indian exports, including clothing and footwear, face duties of up to 10%. Qualifying Chinese goods already enjoy tariff-free access.
sound_smarter: Removing tariffs addresses one disadvantage Indian suppliers face against competitors. But winning more orders still depends on price, quality, and delivery. New Zealand offers a small opening for diversification and reducing dependence on India’s biggest customers requires export growth across several markets.

title: Cabinet raises EPFO wage ceiling to INR 25,000
text: The Union Cabinet on Wednesday raised the wage ceiling for mandatory Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) coverage from INR 15,000 (USD 158) to INR 25,000 (USD 263) a month, the first change since September 2014. The government expects the ceiling to bring more than 5.1 million additional workers into mandatory provident fund, pension and insurance coverage. The extra annual budgetary outgo is estimated at INR 113.39 billion (USD 1.19 billion), up from INR 102.5 billion (USD 1.08 billion) currently, with five-year costs projected at INR 566.96 billion (USD 5.97 billion).
anchor: Cabinet raises EPFO wage ceiling to INR 25,000

title: India summons Pakistan envoy over naval collision
text: India summoned Pakistan's Charge d'Affaires in New Delhi on Wednesday after a Pakistan Navy vessel collided with an Indian Navy ship during a routine surveillance mission in the Arabian Sea on Tuesday, September 15. The Ministry of External Affairs called the Pakistani vessel's conduct "unacceptable and unprofessional," saying it was manoeuvring at high speed when the collision occurred. No major damage was reported.
anchor: India summons Pakistan envoy over naval collision

title: Chip off the old block
text:
India has attracted INR 1 trillion (USD 10.4 billion) in semiconductor commitments, Electronics Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said Thursday. Investment is expected over two to three years, subject to corporate approvals.

The wider ambition: Semicon 2.0 backs chipmaking and its suppliers (we covered it here). India wants more value from electronics manufacturing, where domestic value addition remains 18–20%, according to industry estimates.

Factory neighbours: Tata Electronics, building a chip plant in Dholera, Gujarat, signed memoranda for a 147-hectare supplier park, materials localisation with Fujifilm, and chemicals supply from JSR Corporation. Other announcements included commercial-device delivery and six regional chip-design centres. Applied Materials announced it will invest USD 5 billion in India over the next decade.

People and products: Targets include supporting 200 design start-ups and training 100,000 technicians over five years. Twenty previously supported start-ups have secured venture capital. Vaishnaw projects nearly 100,000 jobs across the ecosystem, a broader measure than August’s direct-jobs forecast.
sound_smarter: India’s first chip foundries give global suppliers an anchor to build local operations. As these suppliers scale, future entrants can source locally rather than importing, lowering entry barriers.

title: In the news
text:
European Union draft excludes India from metal-scrap export permissions: The European Commission has proposed excluding India from permissions to import European Union (EU) metal scrap, including aluminium, under waste-export rules applying from May 21, 2027. Its assessment cites insufficient evidence of pollution controls and enforcement in India’s recycling system. The draft remains open for consultation until 16 October. In June, India had sought an exemption, warning that restrictions could raise manufacturers’ costs and undermine gains from the bilateral trade agreement (we covered it here). The proposal follows Brussels’ abandonment of a separate 15 per cent aluminium-scrap export duty.

Trump signs sanctions law exposing India to additional tariffs: US President Donald Trump signed the Russia and Iran sanctions legislation into law last Friday, following the House passage (we covered it here). The law provides for additional tariffs of up to 100 per cent on qualifying buyers of Russian energy, a list that includes India. The signing does not itself establish a 100 per cent tariff on Indian goods. The President retains authority to waive duties after submitting a national-interest certification and explanation to Congress.
anchor: European Union draft excludes India from metal-scrap export

title: Disconnected committee
text:
The Centre has pulled the plug on its apex telecom decision-making body. The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) has dissolved the Digital Communications Commission (DCC) with immediate effect, eighteen days after the panel cleared terms for satellite broadband operators. We covered the disagreement in pricing between the DoT and the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) here.

One desk, not eight: DCC decisions ran through DoT's own full-time members plus part-time secretaries from NITI Aayog, the Department of Economic Affairs, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). That inter-ministerial panel has now been replaced with the telecom secretary, with the Minister of Communications and the Cabinet weighing in where needed. While budget approvals had already moved to the Finance Ministry, the DoT has now gained full policy control.

A familiar approach: The satellite spectrum the DCC cleared was allocated at a fixed percentage of revenue, instead of being auctioned. That is the same method that priced 2G licences below market in 2008, drew Supreme Court criticism, and became one of the defining corruption charges against the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) before it lost power in 2014.
sound_smarter: One desk now decides how a market of over 1.3 billion users connects. The inter-ministerial panel that reviewed decisions before they were final is gone. What is left – the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG), the courts, and Parliament – only catches problems after the fact.

title: IG Defence flight-tests India's first long-range attack drone
text: Noida-based IG Defence flight-tested KAL, India's first indigenous long-range one-way attack drone, at the Pokhran range on September 20. The vehicle-launched system carries a 1,000 km range, up to eight hours of endurance, and a 50 kg payload, placing it in the same loitering-munition class as the Iranian-made Shahed drones.
anchor: IG Defence flight-tests India's first long-range attack drone

title: India, Vietnam more than double weekly flight capacity
text: India and Vietnam have lifted their bilateral air-seat cap to over 16,000 a week, more than double the existing 8,000. The increase comes as airlines in both countries have used up or are close to exhausting their existing flying rights.
anchor: India, Vietnam more than double weekly flight capacity

title: In the news
text:
TRAI mandates cheaper, shorter voice-and-text mobile plans: On Tuesday, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) mandated more voice-and-text-only prepaid plans at reduced tariffs. Operators must offer an option matching every validity period of 30 days or less in their bundled voice, text, and data plans, alongside a calendar-month renewal option and at least one longer-duration plan. The rules address limited short-term choices for low-income consumers and those who do not need mobile data.

NHAI standardizes design rules for high-speed highways: The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has issued uniform design guidelines for upcoming four- and six-lane access-controlled highways, excluding expressways. Covering new roads and upgrades, the rules link lane configurations to traffic volumes and prescribe advance warnings for exits and entries, ramp-based interchanges, and one-metre boundary walls to prevent unauthorised access and stray cattle entering the roads. They fill a gap in dedicated design standards for this highway category.

title: Berth certificate
text:
The environment ministry has doubled the life of green clearances for ports to twenty years from the earlier ten. The September 21 notification covers ports, harbours, breakwaters, and dredging projects, and allows two further five-year extensions, for a maximum of 30. Environmental clearances (ECs) are required for a project to get started, and remain valid from approval until operations begin.

Shipping's pull: The environment ministry said port projects take years to build and are developed in phases. Its own expert committee had recommended 15 years plus a five-year extension, published as a draft in May. At a June 16 meeting chaired by Shipping Secretary Vijay Kumar, the ministry was asked to tie port clearances to the full project timeline or 30 years, whichever is longer, matching the rules for mining.

The Nicobar question: Congress leader and former environment minister Jairam Ramesh said the change was "clearly being done for the proposed transshipment port in Great Nicobar." The port at Galathea Bay is part of the wider Great Nicobar project, which received its EC in November 2022 and is to be built in three phases over 30 years (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: By extending green clearances to 30 years, the Centre is insulating slow, multi-phase mega-projects like Great Nicobar from future legal battles and political delays that a fresh clearance application would trigger. However, this creates a major ecological trade-off, allowing high-impact activities like dredging to proceed decades later based on outdated environmental baseline data.
anchor: The environment ministry has doubled the life of

title: India’s Russian oil imports fall
text: India's Russian oil imports fell 16.5 per cent in August to about 2.1 million barrels a day, and preliminary data from analytics firm Kpler shows a further drop to 1.9 million in September. Last week, President Donald Trump signed the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, allowing tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil, exposing India to further trade pressure (we covered it here). Russia remains India's largest supplier, but refiners are now lining up alternative cargoes for October and November.
anchor: India’s Russian oil imports fall

title: Canada targets December to finalize trade pact ahead of Modi visit
text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that Canada and India aim to conclude trade negotiations by the G20 summit in Miami on December 14 and 15. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit Canada around the same time. The push follows renewed commercial engagement, including Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal's May visit to Canada (we covered it here).
anchor: Canada targets December to finalize trade pact ahead of Modi visit

title: Roach Test
text:
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) wants India's election chief out. At a press conference in New Delhi on Thursday, founder Abhijeet Dipke gave Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar 48 hours to resign or face nationwide protests, following an Indian Express investigation into internal objections at the Election Commission of India (ECI).

An old fight: Opposition parties have accused the ECI of using its Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls to exclude eligible voters and favour the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. Court challenges have also questioned who can authorise voter deletions (we covered it here).

Trouble inside: The investigation found at least 14 objections over ten months from the other two commissioners, including complaints about steps taken without their knowledge or approval. The ECI said differences were normal in any institution and that all its actions were legal, while Commission sources said its decisions were unanimous.

No easy exit: In July, the CJP ended a month of protests over alleged exam-paper leaks after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned and the government agreed to examination reforms, withdrawal of cases against demonstrators, and compensation for bereaved families (we covered it here). A Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only the way a Supreme Court judge is, by a special majority in both houses of Parliament.
sound_smarter: The CJP won in July because it pressed a government that could meet its demands. This time it is pressing for the exit of an official the government cannot remove on its own. Protests can raise the cost of defending the SIR, but only Kumar can decide to step down. If he stays past Saturday, the CJP has no concession on offer that would let it declare victory.
anchor: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) wants India's election

title: Germany says submarine deal awaits only India's approval
text: Germany's new ambassador to India, Jasper Wieck, said on Wednesday that Berlin has finalised an estimated USD 8 billion deal for six conventional submarines, and the deal now waits on India to complete internal approvals, including clearance from the Cabinet Committee on Security. Under Project 75(I), Germany's ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS) will partner with state-owned Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders to build the submarines in India. "From the German side, we could sign tomorrow," Wieck said, adding that Berlin has eased earlier restrictions on export licences and technology transfers to India.
anchor: Germany says submarine deal awaits only India's approval

title: Government cuts edible oil import duties to curb prices
text: The Centre has cut basic customs duty on crude sunflower oil from 10 per cent to zero, and on crude soybean and palm oil from 10 per cent to 5 per cent, citing a sharp rise in international edible oil prices. Duties on the respective refined edible oils were also reduced. The new rates took effect on Thursday. The previous cut came in May 2025, when India halved crude edible oil duties to 10 per cent.
anchor: Government cuts edible oil import duties to curb prices

title: No rest for coal
text:
India has ordered 112 coal-fired plants serving factories to maximise generation from October 1 through December and sell surplus electricity to the grid. The emergency order covers plants supplying steel mills, aluminium smelters, and other industries.

After dark: Nighttime electricity shortages reached 7.7 gigawatts in September, exceeding this year’s summer shortfalls. Weaker rainfall reduced hydroelectric generation, forcing coal plants to compensate.

Reserves running low: Power-station coal stocks fell 24% between end-August and 26 September, leaving roughly seven days’ supply without replenishment. However, relief is uneven and cooler weather and increased electricity purchases helped Kerala avoid cuts on September 24–25.

A recurring strain: India’s coal-dependent power system has faced repeated pressure this year. In March, disrupted gas supplies prompted preparations to force imported-coal plants to increase generation (we covered it here). September adds weaker hydropower output and depleted coal stocks to the strain.
sound_smarter: While directing captive power offers a high-cost tactical stopgap, lingering El Niño conditions threaten a severe double-jeopardy: suppressing post-monsoon rainfall and depleting reservoirs just as heat-driven evening cooling demand peaks.Relying on industrial backup generation to cover structural hydro shortfalls merely shifts risk from factory floors to broader grid reliability
anchor: India has ordered 112 coal-fired plants serving factories

title: India joins Russia-EU carbon tax dispute as third party
text: India has reserved third-party rights in Russia's World Trade Organization (WTO) case against the European Union's (EU) Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a levy on the carbon emitted in making imported goods, after the WTO agreed on Friday to set up a dispute panel. Third-party status lets New Delhi follow the case and present its views without becoming a principal party. Indian steel and aluminium exporters face carbon costs under CBAM, though the UK recently recognised India's carbon credit scheme under its own version (we covered it here).
anchor: India joins Russia-EU carbon tax dispute as third party

title: Health ministry cracks down on nicotine pouches
text: India's health ministry has ordered state governments to enforce a strict crackdown on the illegal sale of nicotine pouches, citing major health and addiction risks, particularly to children. Despite growing global popularity and availability via online channels, local shops, and duty-free outlets, nicotine pouches remain unapproved and illegal under Indian drug laws. The directive comes as an Indian court quashed the Adani Group's defence that its airport duty-free shops were immune from domestic laws after being caught selling the unapproved products. Moving forward, the country's federal drug advisory panel has recommended a complete ban on approving any new nicotine formulations.
anchor: Health ministry cracks down on nicotine pouches

title: Foundation laid for first port-based e-methanol plant
text: On Saturday, Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel, Ports Minister Sarbananda Sonowal, and Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma laid the foundation stone for India's first port-based e-methanol plant, at Deendayal Port in Kandla, Gujarat. The plant is an INR 23 billion (USD 240 million) venture between Deendayal Port Authority and Assam Petro-Chemicals. It will make 150 tonnes a day of the green shipping fuel from renewable power, water, and biogenic carbon dioxide. Construction runs in two phases and is due to finish by March 2027. The government says the fuel will cost USD 750 a tonne, against a global rate of USD 1,300, and will supply ships on Asia-Europe routes.
anchor: Foundation laid for first port-based e-methanol plant

title: Agnikul gets state funding for fully reusable rocket
text: The Technology Development Board (TDB), part of the Department of Science and Technology, signed an agreement on Friday to fund a fully reusable version of Chennai-based start-up Agnikul's Agnibaan rocket with INR 2 billion (USD 20.9 million). The funding comes from the Research Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund as optionally convertible debentures, a form of debt that can convert into equity. Most reusable rockets recover only the first stage, and Agnikul plans to recover the upper stage as well, using a restartable semi-cryogenic engine.
anchor: Agnikul gets state funding for fully reusable rocket

title: Dirham come true
text:
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) plans to invest another USD 25 billion in India, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday. Goyal was speaking after co-chairing the 14th India-UAE High-Level Joint Task Force on Investments in Mumbai on September 28, alongside Sheikh Hamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, managing director of the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA).

Money on the table: Goyal said the UAE has invested USD 25 billion in India so far, making it the seventh-largest source of foreign direct investment, and that both sides are working towards a future investment target of USD 100 billion. At the meeting, the two sides welcomed three recent deals: Emirates NBD's purchase of a majority stake in RBL Bank for roughly USD 3 billion, International Holding Company's USD 1 billion investment in housing finance company Sammaan Capital, and plans for a USD 11.5 billion integrated aluminium complex in Odisha.

Trade target: Bilateral trade reached USD 101.25 billion in the 2025-26 financial year. Goyal credited the four-year-old Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) with doubling it, stating that the new goal is USD 200 billion by 2032.

Ports and ships: The two sides intend to create working groups focused on six aspects of the shipping industry: vessel ownership, port development, shipbuilding, maintenance and repair, ship dismantling, and container production. Goyal said India must double its port capacity within a decade. Dubai-owned DP World already operates five container terminals in India. Four of them are gateway ports that handle India’s own imports and exports, while the terminal at Kochi also handles transhipment.
sound_smarter: India’s new transhipment hubs are pulling cargo away from Emirati operators. Over the past year, Adani’s Vizhinjam port cut transhipment volumes in half at DP World’s Kochi terminal, while the Indian government blocked foreign firms from bidding on the upcoming Great Nicobar port. In response, Emirati investors are pivoting their capital toward a bigger prize: the gateway ports and shipyards set to handle the USD 200 billion in trade both nations are chasing.
anchor: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) plans to invest

title: Great growth expectations
text:
India’s industrial output grew 8% in August from a year earlier, government figures released on Monday showed, up from July’s revised 7.4%.

Factory floor: Manufacturing expanded 9%, its third consecutive month of growth above 8%. 18 of 23 manufacturing industries grew. Electricity and gas output rose 12.3%, while mining contracted 5.6%.

Uneven speeds: Capital goods, including machinery used by businesses, grew 16.9%. Consumer durables, such as appliances, rose 11.1%, while non-durables, including everyday items such as food and toiletries, increased just 2.1%.

The earlier signal: India’s economy expanded 7.8% in April–June, with investment accelerating and manufacturing growing 9.2% (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: An 8% headline growth rate makes India’s expansion look solid, but the weak spot is everyday consumption. While wealthy households are buying high-end appliances, sluggish growth in daily essentials shows that the broader population isn't feeling the boom.
anchor: India’s industrial output grew 8% in August from

title: Goyal likely to meet USTR Greer in Wisconsin
text: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal is likely to meet US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer at the G20 Trade Ministerial in Wisconsin on September 30 and October 1. This would be their first meeting since President Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law, which lets Trump impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on buyers of Russian oil and gas, a list that includes India. Separately, the USTR is investigating alleged excess capacity in Indian manufacturing under Section 301 of the US Trade Act. On the trade deal, Goyal said on September 24 that the terms were "almost done and dusted", and that India is waiting for Washington to guarantee it lower tariffs than competing economies.
anchor: Goyal likely to meet USTR Greer in Wisconsin

title: IAF exercises with US F-35s for the first time
text: For the first time, US F-35 stealth fighters are training with the Indian Air Force (IAF) at the multinational Exercise Tarang Shakti 2026 in Jodhpur, Rajasthan. The exercise opened on September 26 and runs until October 12. Australia, the United Arab Emirates, France, Germany, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh are also flying in the drills.
anchor: IAF exercises with US F-35s for the first time

title: Tariff-ic prescription
text:
The United States named India among 19 other eligible suppliers of specialty medicines exempt from its pharmaceutical tariffs, as the wider duties take effect for more companies on Tuesday.

What qualifies: The 23 September notice covers selected treatments, including qualifying rare-disease medicines, fertility drugs, cell and gene therapies, and animal-health products, alongside their ingredients. Eligibility extends to trading partners with existing or forthcoming trade and security frameworks with Washington.

The wider squeeze: President Donald Trump’s April order established a default 100% tariff on covered patented medicines and ingredients, with country and company exceptions. Generic medicines, cheaper alternatives to original drugs, remain outside this tariff programme.

The unfinished business: India and the US announced an interim trade framework in February, leaving terms for generic medicines dependent on a US national-security investigation. In July, a senior US official said the wider agreement was largely negotiated but still awaiting signature (we covered it here).
sound_smarter: Offering piecemeal sectoral exemptions serves as Washington’s blueprint for transactional bilateralism: rewarding aligned trading partners with targeted relief to keep them engaged, while ratcheting up terms on comprehensive trade deals to maximize US bargaining power.
anchor: The United States named India among 19 other

title: The empathy gap
text:
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has named trade and terrorism as the two bumps in ties with Washington. Jaishankar was speaking at the Asia Society in New York on Monday, after the UN General Assembly's high-level week.

The trade bump: Jaishankar said expectations of a quick trade deal have run into a more complex reality because of the fundamental differences between the two economies, including India's large base of small producers, farmers, and factories. He said that the two sides now have a broad understanding. The US Supreme Court struck down reciprocal tariffs in February, and Washington is still settling a new legal basis for tariffs. Separately, the US Trade Representative (USTR) is investigating alleged excess capacity in Indian manufacturing under Section 301 of the US Trade Act. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said on September 24 that the terms were "almost done and dusted", and that India is waiting for Washington to guarantee it lower tariffs than competing economies.

The terror bump: Jaishankar said few countries have faced the kind of terrorism India has from a neighbour, which has pursued it as a deliberate policy over decades. He said that when "there isn't enough understanding or appreciation or empathy of that," it creates a problem for the relationship. The remarks come as Washington's ties with Pakistan's military leadership have warmed in recent months.

Meanwhile, Beijing: Jaishankar said ties with China have improved since 2025, and even more since 2024, following President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit. Jaishankar said New Delhi had long told Beijing that a standoff between the two countries only helps outsiders, and he summed up the principle as "don't get locked into a problem which benefits others." Speaking on last week's Trump-Xi summit in Washington, he said the two nations remain competitors, with limits to what they can agree on vis-à-vis the rest of the world.
sound_smarter: Jaishankar did not name the outsiders who gained from an India-China standoff, but a week after Trump hosted Xi, the line pointed at Washington. As New Delhi warms to Beijing, the US can no longer count on a shared rival to keep India close. It will have to take India’s concerns about Pakistan seriously.
anchor: External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has named trade

title: Environment Ministry issues first certificates to aid timber exports
text: Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav on Tuesday handed over the first PRAMAAN certificates under the Indian Forest and Wood Certification Scheme. The scheme was launched in December 2023. The Andhra Pradesh Forest Development Corporation was certified for 33,000 hectares of plantations, and a bamboo farmer from Odisha also received a certificate. Yadav pitched the certificates as a way for exporters to meet the due-diligence and deforestation-free sourcing rules that major markets now impose. Certification depends on third-party audits conducted by bodies accredited under the Quality Council of India.
anchor: Environment Ministry issues first certificates to aid timber exports

title: Ministry of Steel to set up Steel Industry Safety Council
text: The Ministry of Steel will set up a Steel Industry Safety Council, chaired by the steel secretary, to approve industry safety standards and review serious accidents and near misses. Its members will include chief executives of integrated steel producers and officials from the national mine safety, explosives safety, and disaster management agencies. The ministry also announced a new Steel Industry Safety Directorate that will run audits, investigate serious incidents, and issue safety standards suited to Indian conditions.
anchor: Ministry of Steel to set up Steel Industry Safety Council

title: Watt comes next
text:
The Cabinet approved phase three of the Green Energy Corridor Scheme, setting it up with INR 1.9 trillion (USD 20 billion) to upgrade state power grids and integrate renewable energy. New Delhi is backing the plan with INR 540 billion (USD 5.6 billion) in direct central financial support to keep end-user power tariffs low.

A bigger corridor: The Green Energy Corridor builds lines and substations to connect renewable generation to the grid. The initiative aims to move 135 gigawatts of renewable capacity from remote areas to the main grid 2032-2033. That’s a big jump compared to the 20 gigawatts targeted by phase two, approved in 2022.

Saving some sunshine: The initiative includes 50 gigawatt-hours of battery storage to ease congestion and supply electricity outside solar hours. In July, transmission bottlenecks left about 12 gigawatts of India’s solar capacity unable to operate at full output (we covered it here).

Who delivers: State transmission utilities will oversee implementation. New transmission projects will be competitively tendered.

The big picture: The expansion aligns with India’s target of hitting 900 gigawatts of non-fossil capacity by 2035-2036, while boosting domestic battery manufacturing and grid management supply chains.
sound_smarter: Generating green power is easy; getting it to consumers without crashing state grids is where India’s energy transition usually stalls. Direct financial support is crucial to bridge the gap between ambitious central targets and the chronic financial fragility of state-level distribution utilities.
anchor: The Cabinet approved phase three of the Green

title: Ministry of Power finalises CAFE-III norms
text: The Ministry of Power on Wednesday notified the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE)-III norms for passenger cars, keeping the targets and credit buyout proposed in July (we covered the draft here). The rules apply from April 1, 2027, to March 31, 2032, and tighten fleet targets by 16.7 per cent over the period. From April 2027, carmakers must report results under both the Modified Indian Driving Cycle (MIDC), India's standard test for measuring fuel economy, and the stricter UN-developed Worldwide Harmonised Light Vehicles Test Procedure (WLTP). The factor for converting targets between the two tests has yet to be notified.
anchor: Ministry of Power finalises CAFE-III norms

title: Apple Pay launches with Axis Bank
text: Apple Pay has launched in India through Axis Bank. It initially covers Axis credit cards on the Visa and Mastercard networks, and cards on RuPay, India's domestic network, are ineligible. Axis is India's fourth-largest credit card issuer, with 16.3 million of the country's 124 million cards as of August. Apple has also held talks with larger rivals HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank but has yet to agree terms.
anchor: Apple Pay launches with Axis Bank

title: Sea what bids
text:
The Ministry of Mines opened bidding for two offshore mineral blocks in the Andaman Sea on Thursday, with submissions due by 28 December.

What’s on offer: Mineral exploration and mining extraction rights over Sewell Rise-01 and West Sewell Ridge-01, which cover more than 1,632 square kilometres. The ministry says their seabed nodules and crusts contain cobalt, nickel, manganese, copper, and rare earth elements used in batteries, electronics, and advanced manufacturing.

The earlier attempt: Seven blocks near Great Nicobar offered in 2024 failed to attract sufficient qualifying bids. These two are different areas, rather than a re-auction, according to a government official.

What lies beneath: Government surveys have established mineral occurrences in both geological areas. The launch announcement gives no estimate of how much can be recovered or at what cost.

The hard part: Offshore extraction requires massive capital and specialized deep-sea technology. India’s domestic mining giants currently lack deep-sea mining experience, meaning success hinges on foreign partnerships.
sound_smarter: Finding minerals underwater isn't the same as making a profit getting them out. While this new auction tests whether companies are willing to take another gamble after 2024's failed round, the government still hasn't shown these sites are any easier or cheaper to mine. Until financial bids actually roll in, it's impossible to tell if this offer is a real breakthrough or just another false start.
anchor: The Ministry of Mines opened bidding for two

title: Netanyahu and Modi hail Indian captain who foiled Flydubai attack
text: On Wednesday, Flydubai flight FZ1073 was carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv when its co-pilot stabbed the captain, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national. Israeli officials called the incident an attempt to crash the plane. The flight was diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, where the Indian Embassy in Riyadh said Machchhar is in hospital and reportedly stable. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu named him on X late Wednesday, saying Machchhar opened the cockpit door despite his wounds so passengers and crew could overpower the attacker. Modi followed on Thursday morning, calling him a hero whose valour "helped save hundreds of lives.""
anchor: Netanyahu and Modi hail Indian captain who foiled Flydubai attack

title: Modi calls Trump as Russia-oil tariff law looms
text: On Wednesday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with US President Donald Trump by phone, their first call since June. The two reviewed cooperation on trade, defence, energy, and critical technologies. The call came days after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which lets Washington impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries buying Russian oil and gas. Separately, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal arrived in the US for the G20 trade ministers' meeting in Milwaukee, where he is likely to meet US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
anchor: Modi calls Trump as Russia-oil tariff law looms

title: Swiss President Parmelin to make a state visit from October 5–7
text: Swiss President Guy Parmelin will make a state visit to India from October 5 to 7. It will be his first state visit and his second trip to India this year, after February's AI Impact Summit in New Delhi. He is scheduled to hold talks with Prime Minister Modi on October 5. On October 7, he will attend the second India–EFTA Prosperity Summit, which marks a year since the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) between India and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) came into force. The pact commits EFTA states to USD 100 billion in investment in India over 15 years. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) calls Switzerland India's largest trade and investment partner among the four EFTA states.
anchor: Swiss President Parmelin to make a state visit from October 5–7

title: MEA warns Indians against enlisting in Russia's army
text: On Wednesday, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) warned Indians travelling to Russia against joining the Russian armed forces. The ministry said many people were seeking such offers willingly, for the money, expecting that the Indian government would secure their release later. Some had also asked Indian authorities to let them give up their citizenship so they could take a Russian passport and enlist. "It is reiterated that this is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government," the advisory said. It urged Indians to vet any job offer from agents not registered with the ministry.
anchor: MEA warns Indians against enlisting in Russia's army

title: Indian Navy joins ASEAN drills at Subic Bay
text: Indian warships INS Sahyadri and INS Kulish are exercising with maritime forces of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) at Subic Bay, on the Philippines' South China Sea coast, in the second edition of the ASEAN-India Maritime Exercise. The exercise opened on September 28. The harbour phase of expert exchanges comes first, followed by joint manoeuvres at sea. The Ministry of Defence said the drill falls under India's Act East Policy for closer ties with Southeast Asia.
anchor: Indian Navy joins ASEAN drills at Subic Bay
